papers.title: BNCT Triggers Immunogenic Cell Death in B16 Melanoma Without Accompanying T-Cell Infiltration--Implications for Combination Immunotherapy
papers.abstract: Objective: Boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT) is a targeted radiotherapy with highly selective tumor killing; its potential to induce immunogenic cell death (ICD) and modulate the tumor immune microenvironment has attracted attention. However, whether BNCT-induced immune activation can overcome the T-cell exclusion barrier of immunologically "cold" tumors and translate into intratumoral effector T-cell infiltration remains unclear. Methods: A B16 melanoma model was established in C57BL/6 mice. Mice were assigned to CK, N10/N20 (neutron irradiation alone for 10 or 20 min), BPA, and BNCTN10/BNCTN20 groups (BPA 500 mg/kg plus 10 or 20 min irradiation) to evaluate tumor suppression and survival. In a separate cohort (CK, N20, and BNCTN20), the most efficacious regimen (BNCTN20) was compared with CK on days 3 and 7: H&E staining; immunohistochemistry/immunofluorescence for gamma-H2AX, HMGB1, cleaved caspase-3, PD-L1, CD8+, and granzyme B; ELISA for cytokines and chemokines; and ICP-OES for 10B distribution. Results: BNCT significantly suppressed tumor growth. When CK tumors reached the humane endpoint (~2000 mm3), N20 tumor volume was half that of CK (TGI ~ 49.8%), whereas BNCTN20 reached only one tenth (TGI ~ 88.9%, p < 0.001), with prolonged survival (p < 0.001). BNCT induced gamma-H2AX-associated DNA damage, HMGB1 release, and cleaved caspase-3-mediated apoptosis; upregulated PD-L1; induced a Th1-type response (elevated IFN-gamma/TNF-alpha, reduced IL-10); and enhanced CXCL9/10 signaling. However, intratumoral CD8+ T-cell infiltration and granzyme B expression did not increase, indicating that this activation was not translated into a local effector T-cell response. Conclusions: BNCT inhibited tumor growth and prolonged survival while inducing ICD and a systemic Th1 response; nevertheless, systemic activation failed to translate into local CD8+ T-cell infiltration, while PD-L1 was upregulated, a "strong direct killing but blocked immune translation" profile in the B16 cold tumor. PD-L1-associated adaptive immune resistance may limit this conversion, providing rationale for combining BNCT with immune checkpoint blockade.

papers.title: Dated public evidence and known genes for retrospective evaluation of gene prioritization
papers.abstract: Retrospective evaluation of gene prioritization needs evidence that was public before the evaluated genes became known. Public resources are open and reproducible, but are distributed as current releases that also contain evidence produced after the genes became known. This Data Descriptor presents per-gene evidence tables for four areas (oncology, inflammatory bowel disease, metabolism and psoriasis) from public resources. Every feature carries a time axis, the date of its release in a calendar of 183 archived releases of 20 sources, and a leakage axis, a provenance class (A to E) with two risk grades that define five feature sets. Nineteen lists of known genes are dated by the first trial, study, release or classification that supports each gene. They cover targets of a kind of drug, targets of drugs tested in a disease, and genes associated with a disease. The oncology lists also carry the first day the trial registry showed the trial.

papers.title: Hypoxemia is an Independent Risk Factor for Perioperative Thrombosis at High Altitude: A Retrospective Study of 11,084 Patients
papers.abstract: Objective Perioperative thrombosis occurs at a significantly higher rate at high altitudes compared to low altitudes, severely threatening the safety of surgical patients. This study aims to determine the independent risk factors for perioperative thrombosis in high-altitude environments, providing a scientific basis for early clinical screening and targeted intervention. Methods Clinical data from 11,084 surgical patients were retrospectively analyzed. Patients were categorized into thrombosis and non-thrombosis groups based on the occurrence of postoperative thrombosis. Baseline characteristics, operative variables, and laboratory indicators were collected, encompassing 21 potential risk factors including arterial partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2). Univariate analysis and multivariate logistic regression (forward stepwise likelihood ratio method) were performed using SPSS 27.0 to identify independent risk factors for perioperative thrombosis. The predictive performance of the model was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, decision curve analysis (DCA), calibration plots, and nomograms. Results Of the 11,084 patients, 1,631 (14.7%) developed thrombosis. Univariate analysis showed that varicose veins, hemoglobin levels, Preoperative hospital stay, body mass index (BMI), D-dimer, partial pressure of oxygen, and interleukin-6 were significantly associated with thrombosis (P < 0.05). Multivariate logistic regression identified varicose veins,Preoperative hospital stay, elevated BMI, erythrocytosis, elevated D-dimer, hypoxemia, and elevated interleukin-6 as independent risk factors for thrombosis (P < 0.05). The predictive model demonstrated strong discrimination, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.862 (95% CI: 0.848-0.876), a sensitivity of 0.790, and a specificity of 0.773. Among the individual risk factors, hypoxemia exhibited the highest diagnostic performance, yielding an AUC of 0.732 and a sensitivity of 0.763. Conclusion The incidence of perioperative thrombosis at high altitudes is elevated, with hypoxemia serving as an independent predictor beyond traditional risk factors. Clinical management should prioritize correcting pre- and postoperative hypoxic states. Furthermore, implementing individualized prophylaxis that accounts for other risk factors such as multiple surgeries, advanced age, anemia, and coagulation-fibrinolysis system abnormalities is crucial to mitigating thrombotic risk.

papers.title: Language-guided domain adaptation improves protein sequence rep-resentations for antimicrobial resistance analysis
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR), particularly antibiotic resistance in bacterial pathogens, complicates infectious disease management. Because bacterial resistance is often mediated by protein functions, including antibiotic inactivation and efflux, protein sequence analysis provides a molecular basis for digital AMR surveillance and therapeutic intervention. We developed BacLLM, a language guided protein representation framework that integrates annotation-derived functional knowledge into protein language model representations for AMR analysis in WHO priority bacterial pathogens. Through sequence enhancement, semantic enrichment of UniProt annotations, and cross modal contrastive learning, BacLLM transfers LLM encoded annotation priors into the sequence encoder. Compared with baselines, BacLLM provided more informative representations for resistance-gene identification and mechanism prediction, captured resistance associated mutational signals at single-residue resolution, and preserved taxonomic relationships not reflected by phenotype based clinical groupings. Moreover, BacLLM recovered resistance associated functional organization within a TolC-centered protein association network, prioritizing proteins with low sequence identity to TolC but predicted structural similarity to TolC. Extending from AMR characterization to therapeutic prioritization, BacLLM also improved strain-level phage host matching for phage therapy candidate prioritization. Together, these findings establish BacLLM as a protein representation framework supporting AMR surveillance, functional characterization, and therapeutic candidate prioritization.

papers.title: Metformin lowers HMGA1a and RBM3 protein in breast cancer cells, and its effect on ESR1 splicing depends on cell density and exposure time
papers.abstract: The ESR1 gene produces ER46, an N-terminally truncated isoform generated by skipping of exon 1, which is reduced in tamoxifen-resistant breast cancer cells. We have reported that metformin moves the ratio of full-length ER to ER46 in opposite directions in MCF-7 cells and their tamoxifen-resistant subline TAMR1, and that metformin reduces TAMR1 xenograft growth (Harada et al., Am J Pharm Health Res 2022;10(11)). That report leaves two questions open: whether the effect is dosedependent and stable across culture conditions, and what splicing factor might carry it. Here we report the experiments that bear on both. Across a full dose range from 0.25 to 5 mM at high seeding density, metformin produced no consistent change in the full-length share of ESR1 transcript in either line: densitometry of the gel gave 42%, 43%, 42%, 43%, 45% and 48% in MCF-7 cells and 55%, 44%, 52%, 47%, 68% and 43% in TAMR1 cells. The reported shift therefore depends on the seeding density used, and the comparison that produced it is not reproduced at high density. At low density the MCF-7 response persisted to 48 h (52%, 62% and 68% at 0, 2.5 and 5 mM). Metformin lowered HMGA1a protein in MCF-7 cells and showed the same tendency in TAMR1 cells, at both seeding densities, and lowered RBM3 protein in TAMR1 cells at 24 and 48 h. HMGA1a is the factor we previously showed to generate ER46 by trapping U1 snRNP at an upstream pseudo-5' splice site, so a fall in HMGA1a predicts less ER46, the opposite of what was seen in TAMR1 cells at low density. The fall in RBM3, the protein through which metformin alters splicing in myotonic dystrophy, is the more plausible candidate. RT-PCR of the xenograft tumours from the earlier study detected full-length ESR1 transcript in the untreated and tamoxifen-plus-metformin groups but not in the singleagent groups, with amplification failing in several lanes; these panels do not separate the treatments. Taken together, the direction of the metformin effect on ESR1 splicing is conditional on culture density and does not survive a dose-response test at high density, and HMGA1a is unlikely to be the factor that carries it.

papers.title: Harnessing catalytic knowledge to guide enzyme discovery and evolution with AlphaEnzyme
papers.abstract: Retrieving an enzyme for a target reaction provides a starting point for evolution, but predicting how to improve it remains difficult. This requires connecting evolutionary information with the structural and chemical context of catalysis. Here we present AlphaEnzyme, an enzyme foundation model built on a structure-grounded representation of an enzyme paired with its reaction, from which catalytic compatibility, kinetics and mutational response are read out together. On a time-separated benchmark, AlphaEnzyme achieves a top-1 catalyst retrieval success rate of 30.1%, against 17.2% for the strongest baseline. Michaelis constant predictions achieve the highest rank correlations among the compared methods, reaching 0.64 for enzymes sharing at most 40% identity with the kinetic training set. The model also enriches high-fitness TrpB variants at a budget of 16 candidates without target-specific fitness training. In prospective transaminase engineering, several prioritized variants exceed the parent, with the best design yielding a 30.4-fold increase in product signal in a lysate-based assay while retaining (R)-selectivity. Together, AlphaEnzyme provides a common molecular basis for selecting starting enzymes and prioritizing sequence changes for their improvement.

papers.title: Second-site capsule-locus mutations, not Ade efflux disruption, determine phage susceptibility across an Acinetobacter baumannii transposon mutant panel
papers.abstract: Resistance-Nodulation-Division (RND) efflux pumps have been implicated in phage adsorption in several Gram-negative bacteria, suggesting that AdeABC, AdeFGH and AdeIJK, the three characterised RND efflux systems of multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, could play a similar role. We tested this hypothesis using five phages (Equilibrator, Taro, AT01, BB02, and AC03) and a panel of 13 A. baumannii strains, including nine AB5075 transposon mutants affecting AdeABC, AdeFGH, or AdeIJK. Host-range testing, efficiency-of-plating assays, capsule-associated density measurements, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and whole-genome sequencing were performed to assess the relationship between genotype and phage infection. Overall, the data did not support a role for the Ade components as receptors. Phages Equilibrator, Taro and AT01 formed plaques on every strain, and the restricted host ranges of BB02 and AC03 did not correspond to disruption of a particular efflux system. Sequencing instead identified second-site mutations in the KL25 capsule locus in six of the ten AB5075 strains. These included a 1,998-bp deletion affecting wzc, substitutions in mnaA and mnaB, an ISAba13 insertion in a putative glycosyltransferase and a subpopulation-associated frameshift in wzx. AC03 formed plaques on all six strains with capsule-locus changes but on none of the five strains without them. Capsule dependence differed among the other phages: relative to the parental AB5075, infection by these phages, Equilibrator, Taro and BB02, was restricted on the capsule-deficient wzc::T26 strain, whereas AT01 efficiency was only slightly reduced. Insertion-site mapping also distinguished a near-terminal adeK insertion that retained the parental antimicrobial phenotype from an early adeK insertion associated with loss of AdeIJK function. Together, these findings identify capsule-locus variation as the strongest correlation with phage susceptibility in this panel and demonstrate the importance of verifying mutant genomes before assigning phenotypes to their annotated insertions.

papers.title: Live attenuated YFV-17D vaccine induces robust B and T cell immunity in vaccine-draining lymph nodes
papers.abstract: The yellow fever virus-17D (YFV-17D) vaccine is widely regarded as one of the most effective vaccines in existence, with protection linked to robust elicitation of neutralising antibodies1. The features of the germinal centre (GC) reaction driving this durable and potent antibody responses remain unclear. Here we examined immune dynamics in blood and lymph nodes (LNs) after primary YFV-17D immunisation in humans. Using fine needle biopsy (FNB), we identified robust T and B lymphocyte responses within draining LNs, underpinning maturation of antibodies targeting the viral envelope (E). Early antibody responses were largely IgM, with gradual accumulation of E-specific memory B cells and anti-viral IgG in the subsequent months. Monoclonal antibodies derived from GC B cells had specificity for E, with diversification in the LN capable of driving increases in binding and neutralising potency. While circulating vaccine-specific CD4+ T cells peaked two weeks post-vaccination, clonally related GC and IL-10+ T follicular helper populations progressively accumulated in the LN. Comparison of FNB transcriptional datasets following YFV-17D, SARS-CoV-2 mRNA/LNP, and seasonal influenza vaccination identified a conserved GC program involving similar B and T lymphocyte subpopulations. Collectively, we find that while YFV-17D induces robust GC activity, this trait is shared with other vaccine platforms and the notably durable protection against infection may reflect an incapacity of the virus to escape host immunity.

papers.title: Asymmetric detection of relative speed during motion-based figure-ground segregation
papers.abstract: Visual motion can support figure-ground segregation when a local region moves at a different speed from its background, but whether faster- and slower-than-background targets are detected equally well, and how any asymmetry depends on background speed and motion reliability remains incompletely understood. We measured relative-speed detection thresholds in four human observers using an eight-alternative forced-choice localization task. On each trial, one of eight random-dot patches at 10-degree eccentricity moved either faster or slower than a surrounding moving background. Relative-speed detection thresholds were measured with adaptive staircases at five background speeds (2.5-30 deg/s) under 100% and 60% motion coherence. In every observer, slower targets required larger relative-speed differences for detection than faster targets. This increment-decrement asymmetry was strongest at low background speeds and diminished as speed increased. Reducing motion coherence elevated thresholds overall but disproportionately impaired detection of slower targets, amplifying the asymmetry, most strongly at the lowest measurable speeds. Under 100% coherence, increment detection showed approximately Weber-like scaling from 10 to 30 deg/s, whereas under reduced coherence both increment and decrement Weber fractions decreased with increasing background speed. Relative-speed detection therefore depends on the sign of the speed difference, background speed, and motion reliability. The faster-target advantage is consistent with faster-speed weighting reported in cortical area MT and with natural-scene statistics showing that figural regions tend to move faster than their backgrounds, suggesting that relative-speed sensitivity may contribute to motion-based figure-ground segregation. More broadly, such increment-decrement asymmetries can reveal biases in how sensory signals are represented and read out.

papers.title: MAST1 is neuron-specific regulator of mitochondrial trafficking and abundance in human brain tissue
papers.abstract: In human neurons, energy-demanding axonal and dendritic development requires sufficient mitochondrial distribution at distal locations, and the responsible mechanisms remain largely unknown. Here, we characterize rare de novo mutations in microtubule-associated serine/threonine kinase 1 (MAST1) in patients with multiple neurodevelopmental abnormalities, including microcephaly and thin corpus callosum. Experiments using induced pluripotent stem cell-derived telencephalic brain organoids and cortical neurons from patients and unaffected parents, as well as engineered lines demonstrate association of the MAST1 mutations with organoid growth deficits and impaired neurites. Mechanistically, the MAST1 mutations alter its interaction with mitochondria as well as mitochondrial trafficking and abundance, increasing the proportion of hyperactive mitochondria and reactive oxygen species accumulation. Exogenous wild-type MAST1 expression rescues neurite outgrowth in mutant neurons, as does prolonged treatment with creatine or N-acetyl-L-cysteine. This study identifies MAST1 as an important regulator of mitochondrial properties in human neurons and links microcephaly-associated MAST1 mutations to neuronal mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired neurites, and neuronal loss.

papers.title: Sex-specific gene and isoform expression characterizes hippocampal aging in rhesus macaques
papers.abstract: Aging produces widespread transcriptomic alterations that extend beyond changes in gene expression to include changes at the isoform level. Declining splicing fidelity, including increased intron retention and aberrant isoform expression, has been proposed to contribute to cellular dysfunction; however, the extent and biological significance of isoform-specific changes in the aging brain remain poorly understood. Age-related cognitive decline has also been associated with neuroinflammation and the development of a chronic inflammatory state, or ''inflammaging,'' within the brain. Here, we used short- and long-read RNA sequencing to characterize gene- and isoform-level changes associated with hippocampal aging across sex in 24 rhesus macaques. We identified 594 age-associated differential isoform expression events, comprising both shared and sex-specific changes. Inflammatory pathways, including TNF- -- NF-{kappa}B signaling, interferon responses, and complement pathways, were enriched across both sexes. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) further identified sex-specific modules associated with inflammatory, glial, mitochondrial, and hormone-responsive processes. Notably, several age-associated changes were detected at the isoform level despite limited or absent corresponding gene-level differences, highlighting transcript-level regulation as an additional dimension of brain aging that may be overlooked by gene-level analyses. To investigate the relationship between aging and Alzheimer's disease (AD), we independently performed WGCNA on the rhesus macaque cohort and a publicly available human hippocampal AD single-nucleus RNA-sequencing dataset (GSE268609). Cross-species module preservation and gene overlap analyses identified shared genes between age-associated and AD-associated networks, with pathway enrichment implicating glial function, inflammation, and mitochondrial biology. Together, these findings highlight sex-associated differences in hippocampal transcriptomic aging, underscore the importance of isoform-level regulation, and identify shared transcriptional signatures between normal aging and AD-associated pathways.

papers.title: Acute nicotine exposure produces a spatially organized transcriptional response in mouse olfactory cortex
papers.abstract: Nicotine acts on nicotinic receptors throughout the forebrain. Most molecular studies of its effects, however, have focused on reward circuitry and have used bulk tissue, which cannot show which cells respond or how responding cells are arranged relative to one another. We previously found that a single nicotine exposure activates hippocampal astrocytes through the astrocyte-expressed kinase AKT2. Here we asked which cells respond to nicotine in the anterior olfactory cortex, a cholinergic-modulated region that encodes odor associations, and whether their astrocytic surroundings change. Male mice received a single intraperitoneal injection of nicotine or saline, and coronal sections spanning the anterior olfactory nucleus, piriform cortex and adjacent isocortex were sequencing 24 h later using Visium HD. Differential expression on nucleus-based segmentation was concentrated in olfactory excitatory neurons. Pathways centered on calcium-handling, synapse-assembly and extracellular-matrix programs, together with a lasting reduction of the immediate-early gene Egr1. Within the piriform region, the response localized to a continuous population of superficial pyramidal neurons expressing Cartpt and Penk. These neurons upregulated synapse-assembly, receptor-regulation and proteoglycan programs without changes to cell-type proportions. Nicotine also reduced expression of Sparcl1, which encodes astrocyte-secreted synaptogenic protein hevin, within one cell diameter of these neurons. Our study shows that a single nicotine exposure leaves a spatially organized transcriptional program on olfactory circuitry, centered on one neuronal population and the tissue at its border. These results identify candidate cells, genes and tissue locations for testing how nicotine alters sensory cue circuits.

papers.title: Individualized AI-driven Neuromodulation Selectively Enhances and Reorganizes Human Tongue Sensorimotor Networks.
papers.abstract: Precise modulation of brain networks for tongue motor and sensory control (TMSC) is critical for neruorehabilitation. Existing neuromodulation approaches use fixed targets, ignoring individual network architecture. We present an AI-driven, individualized fMRI neuromodulation (iNM) platform adaptively targeting subject-specific TMSC networks in real-time. Using a neurofunctional twin built from each participant's anatomy and function, iNM reinforces targeted activity and suppresses competing states. Unsupervised machine learning and hidden Markov modeling showed iNM increased TMSC-state occupancy from 82% to 97% and suppressed swallow-state interference by 83%. The inferior parietal lobule emerged as a sensorimotor integration hub, with increased magnitude (d' 90.4 right, 84 left) and spatial expansion (134.8% right, 81.8% left). Cortico-subcortical connectivity strengthened 53% to 74% across motor, sensory, and attention networks and persisted into non-iNM blocks. Thus, iNM may offer precision neurorehabilitation for CNS or PNS disorders, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and treatment-induced cranial neuropathy in head-and-neck-cancer survivors, respectively.

papers.title: Hijacking Cellular S-Acylation with Molecular Assemblies Rewires Oncogenic Signaling
papers.abstract: KRAS-mutant cancers are generally treated by suppressing oncogenic signaling. Here, we investigated whether endogenous lipidation machinery could instead be used to spatially perturb that signaling. The thioester-bearing peptide precursor Stb-DPhe-DPhe-SAc (1) potently reduced PANC-1 cell viability and formed a palmitoylated product in treated cells. Synthetic palmitoylated 1 displayed increased assembly propensity, while fluorescent analogue 2 accumulated at the Golgi in a 2-bromopalmitate-sensitive manner. Compound 1 increased plasma-membrane-associated KRAS staining and ERK/AKT phosphorylation and induced pronounced LC3B and p62 remodeling. Inhibition of palmitoylation suppressed Golgi accumulation, attenuated the LC3B response, and rescued cell viability. These findings support a model in which cellular S-acylation drives organelle-localized molecular assembly that perturbs KRAS localization, oncogenic signaling, and associated stress responses. This work identifies endogenous lipidation machinery as a synthetic handle for spatial control of cancer signaling.

papers.title: Protify: A Benchmarking Platform Revealing Task Dependence and Homology Leakage in Protein Language Model Evaluation
papers.abstract: Protein Language Models (pLMs) have become essential tools for computational protein analysis, and the rapid proliferation of architectures, training objectives, and pretraining corpora has produced a diverse and expanding model landscape. Evaluation practices, however, remain fragmented: studies use different datasets, preprocessing pipelines, and reporting conventions, so results rarely transfer between publications. Here we introduce Protify, an open-source platform that standardizes pLM benchmarking across zero-shot, supervised, and transferlearning settings through a unified, low-code interface. Protify currently supports 35 pretrained models and 61 curated datasets and it is easy to add custom versions of each. Leveraging Protify's high throughput pipelines, we benchmarked 23 models on ProteinGym, discovering that DPLM3B is currently the top-performing self-supervised encoder. Another large-scale supervised evaluation across 32 diverse tasks, spanning enzyme classification, gene ontology annotation, protein-protein interaction, subcellular localization, and other functional properties, found that no single pLM dominated: 14 different models took the top score on at least one dataset, and the margins between the best and second-best models fell within run-to-run variability. On enzyme optimal pH prediction, a general-purpose probe pipeline matched or exceeded EpHod, a specialized model selected from 11,550 training runs, after 50 hyperparameter trials (R2 = 0.482 versus 0.425). Under a homology-controlled split of the same data, every pooled-embedding probe collapsed to near-zero R2, and only a transformer probe over full residue embeddings recovered appreciable signal (R2 = 0.248). Model rankings therefore depend as much on evaluation design as on the models themselves. Protify makes those design choices explicit, controlled, and replayable, and is freely available at https://github.com/Gleghorn-Lab/Protify.

papers.title: Temporal Variability in Brain Connectivity for Estimating Two-Year Clinical Severity in Mild Cognitive Impairment
papers.abstract: Resting-state functional MRI measures coordinated activity across brain networks and may reveal early changes relevant to cognitive decline. Conventional static functional connectivity analyses often compute time-series correlations across an entire scan, missing informative fluctuations over shorter timescales. We investigated whether these fluctuations, in fMRI scans collected at baseline, improve estimation of clinical severity two years later in mild cognitive impairment (MCI). In 48 ADNI participants with MCI, we summarized temporal variability using the standard deviation of windowed correlations between 21 pairs of brain networks. Using repeated nested cross-validation, the mean absolute error in predicting follow-up Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) was 1.62 points with clinical covariates alone, 1.66 after adding static connectivity, and 1.51 after adding connectivity variability. With additional motion covariates, the corresponding errors were 1.70, 1.73, and 1.59. Connectivity variability outperformed both conventional models in all three cross-validation repetitions, while randomized signals preserving the complete cross-spectrum did not reproduce the improvement. Perhaps surprisingly though, most of the gain occurred in participants without subsequent clinical worsening, and results were sensitive to the choice of temporal windows. These preliminary findings suggest that compact measures of connectivity variability may capture clinically relevant information beyond conventional measures of static functional connectivity, motivating larger studies to evaluate their value for predicting future cognitive impairment.

papers.title: Dementia Severity Is Associated with Resting-State fMRI Network Responses to Nuisance Regression
papers.abstract: Apparent disease effects in resting-state fMRI may be confounded by the effects of preprocessing, making it essential to understand whether nuisance removal affects patients differently across levels of clinical severity. Yet few studies directly examine whether sensitivity to preprocessing is itself clinically informative. We investigated this in 201 ADNI participants spanning normal cognition, mild cognitive impairment, and dementia. We quantified the coordinated temporal structure of the seven Yeo resting-state networks using a delay-based concentration statistic, comparing estimates after regression of 24 motion parameters and linear trends with estimates obtained after additionally removing five anatomical CompCor components. Adding these components generally reduced the measured temporal concentration, but this reduction was smaller in participants with greater dementia severity (+0.472 percentage points per CDR-SB point). In contrast, the same network measures showed little association with severity before adding CompCor. To determine whether this finding depended on how temporal trends were removed, we repeated the analysis with identical discrete cosine regressors added to both preprocessing designs. The clinical association remained similar (+0.464). Controlled simulations showed that temporal concentration increased with the strength of delayed coupling between networks, even when their individual statistical properties and instantaneous covariance remained unchanged. However, changes in observation amplitude and contamination of nuisance regressors also altered the response to preprocessing without changing the underlying neural signal. These findings suggest that disease-related differences in fMRI may partly reflect differential sensitivity to preprocessing. Systematic sensitivity analyses, including multiverse comparisons across preprocessing strategies, may therefore be essential to distinguish genuine disease effects from preprocessing-dependent associations.

papers.title: The C. elegans Connectome Toolbox: an open, extensible framework for multimodal connectomic data integration and analysis
papers.abstract: The nematode C. elegans is one of the best studied model organisms in biology. Since the initial description of the C. elegans neuronal connectome by White and colleagues, numerous studies have mapped and analyzed the connectome, and released structured datasets of the connectivity, often merging and adding to previous versions. These datasets now serve as foundational resources that underpin studies into the neuronal basis of C. elegans behavior. In spite of their high utility, heterogeneity in the different datasets and their annotation conventions obscures direct comparison where discrepancies between connectomes frequently stem from differences in coverage or nomenclature rather than genuine biological disagreement. Additionally, datasets describing new connectivity modalities - contact-based (the contactome), extrasynaptic (monoaminergic and neuropeptidergic), and functional connectivity - have also recently become available. Thus, there is a need for a unified framework providing standardized access to these diverse datasets while preserving their individual provenance. Here, we present the C. elegans Connectome Toolbox, a comprehensive framework for consolidating, curating and validating historical and newly published multimodal C. elegans connectivity data. Connectome Toolbox includes an accessible online resource (https://openworm.org/ConnectomeToolbox) for interactive data exploration and is accompanied by a Python library for programmatic access. We demonstrate the utility of the toolbox through a series of analyses that illustrate how connectome data can be explored, visualized, and compared across modalities, including integration of the anatomical connectome with a comprehensive neurotransmitter atlas, and comparison with computational models of C. elegans neural circuits.

papers.title: Response to azacitidine and the TIM-3 inhibitor, sabatolimab, in MDS and CMML is associated with distinct immune and antigen-presentation states
papers.abstract: Targeting the immune checkpoint TIM-3 is of interest in myeloid neoplasms, yet the hematopoietic and immune changes associated with anti-TIM-3 therapy remain poorly characterized. We used single-cell RNA sequencing to profile bone marrow (BM) and peripheral blood from patients with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) treated with the hypomethylating agent azacitidine combined with sabatolimab, a monoclonal antibody targeting TIM-3, and integrated Human Cell Atlas reference datasets for comparison. CITE-seq profiling showed that TIM-3 was predominantly expressed on dendritic cells and NK cells, with variable expression across other populations, including CD34 cells and CD8 T cells. At baseline, we identified a population of CD34 myeloid-biased progenitors specific to MDS/CMML samples ("HSPC-like") characterized by inflammatory gene expression programs and features of impaired differentiation. In MDS, elevated baseline HLA class II expression across hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), HSPC-like cells, and multiple myeloid populations was associated with response. Consistent with this finding, trajectory analysis suggested that nonresponders bypassed HLA class II-high states during myeloid differentiation. In MDS, the presence of distinct CD8 T-cell populations and increased interferon-response programs in CD8 T and NK cells at baseline was also associated with response. In both MDS and CMML, treatment among responders was associated with contraction of BM CD8 and CD4 T-cell populations characterized by type I interferon-responsive and inflammatory programs, including IFIT1, IFIT2, and TNF, along with expansion of a distinct GZMH/IFITM1-expressing cytotoxic CD8 T-cell population. Together, these findings identify baseline antigen-presentation and immune-response programs associated with therapeutic response and reveal coordinated remodeling of myeloid and lymphoid compartments during azacitidine/sabatolimab treatment in MDS and CMML.

papers.title: Targeting NF-κB prevents Schwann cell reprogramming and plexiform neurofibroma initiation in mouse model of Nf1
papers.abstract: Plexiform neurofibromas arise in approximately half of all individuals with Neurofibromatosis Type I (NF1). Genetic lesions apart from NF1 pathogenic variants are not present in NF1 mutant Schwann cells, suggesting that tumorigenesis may instead require cellular rewiring. To identify putatively re-wired tumor cells, we used multiplex imaging and flow cytometry to delineate markers that distinguish tumor Schwann cell from non-tumor Schwann cells. We identified tumor Schwann cells as CD44+;CD49f+ cells that show increased transcription of epithelial to mesenchymal plasticity (EMP)- associated genes. CD44+;CD49f+ expression was induced by treating Nf1-/- Schwann cells with stressors or by direct NF-{kappa}B pathway activation via IKK2; treated Schwann cells increased secretion of NF-{kappa}B targets and immune cell chemoattractants CCL2 and CCL3. In established tumors, MEK inhibition plus NF-{kappa}B blockade diminished tumor cell proliferation, tumor Schwann cells, immune cell populations, tumor cytokines and tumor number. Notably, transient single agent NF-{kappa}B pathway blockade was sufficient to significantly delay tumor formation in mice. Thus, Nf1 loss in Schwann cells is followed by NF-{kappa}B activation and cellular reprogramming that drives tumor initiation and targeting NF-{kappa}B activation can reduce NF1-deficient tumor formation.

papers.title: Title: Combinatorial bnAb and T Cell Immunization Enhances Post-Infection Control of SHIVSF162p3 Viremia in Rhesus Macaques
papers.abstract: An ideal HIV-1 vaccine should provide broad protection against most HIV-1 variants, control early dissemination of infected cells after virus acquisition, and avoid the risk that vaccine-induced, HIV-specific CD4+ T cells serve as targets for viral transmission. In this study, we modeled this complex host-virus interaction in rhesus macaques challenged with a single high dose of SHIVSF162p3. Specifically, we evaluated the impact of T cell immunization with a human adenovirus-5-based candidate vaccine encoding an SIV Gag-Tat fusion (AdHu5SIVGag/Tat) alongside a partially protective, limiting dose of the broadly neutralizing antibody (bnAb) PGT121. Immunization with AdHu5SIVGag/Tat elicited Gag-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cell responses in PBMC and mucosal tissue. T cell vaccination did not affect PGT121-mediated protection against SHIVSF162p3 acquisition. However, independently of vaccination, constitutively activated CD4+4{beta}7+Ki-67+ T cells in rectal tissue attenuated PGT121-mediated protection. Crucially, a unique pattern of post-infection control of SHIVSF162p3 viremia emerged in AdHu5SIVGag/Tat-immunized, PGT121-treated animals, characterized by an increased eclipse phase, lower peak viremia, and a late-phase decay in steady-state viremia. These results suggest potential synergy between bnAbs and AdHu5SIVGag/Tat-induced antiviral T cell responses, with significant implications for HIV-1 vaccine development and early interventions following infection.

papers.title: Polymerase and primer biases in eukaryote ultra-long-read metabarcoding
papers.abstract: Ultra-long-read metabarcoding is a recently developed method for biodiversity monitoring that enables both high-accuracy species-level identification and reliable phylogenetic placement of taxa. Ultra-long-read analyses require high-processivity DNA polymerases for amplicons and primer pairs that fully cover the targeted taxonomic groups. So far, there is no published information on the relative suitability of commercial high-processivity polymerase kits and on the relative performance of primer pairs targeting a DNA fragment spanning much of the 18S, ITS and 28S rRNA gene regions in eukaryotes. Using PacBio sequencing, we assessed the performance of five commercial high-processivity DNA polymerases and three ultra-long marker primer pairs relative to a commonly used full-ITS primer pair on producing artefacts and recovering biodiversity in two mock communities and 10 soil samples. Our analyses revealed great differences in both polymerases and primer pairs in data quality and biodiversity. For testing evolutionary hypotheses, we recommend using the Solis or Fusion polymerases and the Euk575F-21Rngs primer pair in ultra-long-read metabarcoding analyses of soil eukaryotes. Compared with a previous study using the same DNA samples, the ultra-long amplicons revealed substantially lower biodiversity than medium-sized, full-ITS amplicons across taxonomic levels, suggesting that medium-sized amplicons may be better suited for routine soil eukaryote biodiversity monitoring than ultra-long amplicons.

papers.title: Provenance-aware handling of identical dengue genome records alters inferred envelope-protein variation in Bangladesh DENV-3
papers.abstract: The reliability of interpreting dengue virus (DENV) envelope (E) protein variations depends on whether identical public sequence records are kept as representatives or eliminated based on provenance reviews. We evaluated three record-handling strategies using a frozen Bangladesh-associated dataset of 426 E sequences: exact-sequence deduplication, a prespecified provenance-sensitive exclusion method, and an independently curated Nextstrain accession list. Within the 2021 DENV3 subset (96 accessions), 18 records dated August 2021 were identical across 10,707 nucleotides to the older Sri Lankan genome AY099336.1. There were 21 variable E positions within the original 96-accession DENV3 cohort. Whole-cohort deduplication (47 retained) and retaining one representative of the 18-record group (79 retained) preserved all 21 positions. Excluding the group (78 retained) resulted in eight variable positions: 13 of 21 (61.9%) were lost due to differences in state at those positions between the excluded group and retained cohort. Nextstrain reference-specific exclusions selected the same 18 records; applying its full saved list produced 77 accessions and the same eight variable positions. E270 and E383, which had pre-2021 antibody-related evidence, did not meet the sequence-variation criteria for follow-up; however, E223 and E224 remained variable. Antibody-position enrichment was not statistically significant. These results indicate that cohort eligibility decisions may impact dengue E-protein variant prioritization despite representative-retaining deduplication. Genome identity does not indicate specimen identity or an antigenic phenotype.

papers.title: Prokaryotic homologs of the major vault protein form engineerable vault nanocapsules
papers.abstract: Vaults are the largest ribonucleoprotein particles in eukaryotic cells, built from 78 copies of the major vault protein (MVP), yet their function remains unknown four decades after their discovery. MVP homologs occur in prokaryotes and bacteriophages, but whether they form vaults is unknown. Here, we show that prokaryotic and bacteriophage MVP homologs assemble into vault particles. We surveyed approximately 15 billion proteins, found MVP homologs in 29 bacterial and 4 archaeal phyla, and used size-exclusion chromatography to rapidly screen and isolate vault particles of eight homologs expressed in Escherichia coli. Cryo-electron microscopy structures of the phage homolog L05 at high resolution reveal a shell of 96 MVP chains enclosing a volume ~25% larger than human vaults, among the largest protein shells of defined size outside virus capsids. Prokaryotic MVPs typically carry seven wall repeats and eukaryotic MVPs nine, and adding wall repeats to L05 yields larger vaults. Prokaryotic vaults expand the known diversity of vault architecture and offer a tractable system for studying vault assembly and a size-tunable scaffold for cargo encapsulation.

papers.title: Dendrite Control Theory: A Unifying Framework Bridging Neuronal Morphology And Dendritic Voltage Behavior
papers.abstract: Control theory and dendritic computation have revolutionized their respective fields, yet they rarely converge. Here, we use control theory as a framework to reveal how dendritic morphology and synaptic input organization constrain structural resilience and energy cost. Treating diverse dendritic trees as connected network nodes, we demonstrate that the degree of structural symmetry dictates easy- versus hard-to-access control states. Notably, control inputs restricted solely to peripheral terminal branches are mathematically sufficient to govern the voltage states of the entire dendrite and soma, granting striking resilience against input loss elsewhere. Conversely, limiting input dimensionality amplifies voltage fluctuations and metabolic costs. These findings expose fundamental biophysical trade-offs between wiring cost, functional flexibility, robustness, and energy efficiency, suggesting interneurons generally exhibit higher resilience while excitatory neurons feature superior controllability. We introduce 'Dendrite Control Theory' as a rigorous engineering framework linking neuronal morphology directly to computation and robustness, offering a new neuroscience research paradigm.

papers.title: HIV-1 Vpu complements HLA-A downregulation by Nef and impairs TCR-mediated recognition of HIV-infected cells through distinct mechanisms
papers.abstract: Many viruses, including HIV-1, target the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class I molecules HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C to evade immune surveillance. HIV-1 Nef selectively downregulates HLA-A and HLA-B, whereas Vpu variants from primary strains reduce cell-surface HLA-C expression. Whether HIV-1 also uses Vpu to target other HLA molecules has remained unclear. Here, we show that Vpu from primary strains reduces HLA-A, including the globally prevalent HLA-A2, on infected cells. Although Nef is the principal modulator of these molecules, Vpu acts independently of Nef and impairs TCR-mediated recognition of infected cells in co-culture systems. However, the reduction in TCR signaling is also dependent on the presence of BST2/tetherin, a restriction factor that retains nascent virions and targets them for degradation. HLA-A2-restricted, HIV-specific CTL responses were lowest when both Nef and Vpu were present. Vpu variants from chronic and transmitted/founder strains, but not from the prototypical recombinant strain NL4.3, were sufficient to reduce cell-surface HLA-A2, although activity varied widely among variants and appears to have arisen independently in different hosts. Coimmunoprecipitation and immunofluorescence analyses showed that Vpu interacts with HLA-A2 and redirects it to a perinuclear compartment which is probably the trans-Golgi network through a mechanism governed by the Vpu N-terminus/transmembrane domain. Overall, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized function of Vpu and show how HIV-1 uses Nef and Vpu to limit HLA-A-mediated viral antigen presentation and promote immune evasion.

papers.title: Infant Sensory Over-Responsivity: Relations to Early Life Adversity, Emerging Behavioral Problems, and Sensory Functional Connectivity
papers.abstract: Background. Sensory over-responsivity (SOR) in mid- to late childhood is associated with early-life adversity (ELA) and psychopathology, yet the developmental origins and timing of these relationships remain unknown. This work leverages a longitudinal pediatric dataset enriched for ELA to characterize predictors and behavioral problems associated with infant/toddler SOR. Methods. Neonatal fMRI and longitudinal behavioral data were obtained from a sample (N=399) recruited during pregnancy and enriched for social disadvantage (SD). Negative binomial regression models were used to identify pre- and neonatal risk factors for and behavioral correlates of SOR at age two (Y2). Mediation analyses tested whether Y2 SOR mediates relationships between ELA and behavioral problems at age three (Y3). Relationships between neonatal functional connectivity (FC) measures and later SOR were also computed. Results. Two forms of prenatal ELA, SD and maternal psychosocial stress (PSS), positively predicted Y2 SOR, which in turn predicted Y2 and Y3 autism and anxiety problems, greater preschool internalizing symptoms, and greater preschool separation anxiety diagnoses. Positive relationships of prenatal PSS with Y3 autism, anxiety, and internalizing problems were partially mediated by Y2 SOR. Greater neonatal FC between the cortical somatomotor hand network and bilateral thalamus was also associated with SOR at one to two years later. Conclusions. The study results demonstrate the importance of infant/toddler SOR as an early predictor of autism and anxiety behaviors in early childhood and a mediating variable that links prenatal ELA with these behavioral outcomes. Results also implicate heightened neonatal signaling in sensory circuits as an early precursor of SOR.

papers.title: SPECHTacle: An Efficient Detection and Visualization of Cell Specific Regulation in Single Cell-Based Experiments Using a Novel Combinatorial Computational Tool
papers.abstract: Herein, we describe SPECHTacle, a novel computational tool affording the ability to efficiently visualize and delineate the specific cellular population(s) impacted by an experimental paradigm utilizing heterogeneous cell-based samples. SPECHTacle can be employed to efficiently determine, in a cell specific manner, the populations preferentially impacted by treatments, drugs, injuries, disease states, and/or development within datasets continuously being generated across nearly countless subfields in molecular biology. SPECHTacle accomplishes this task by harnessing the power of Waddington optimal transport analysis and Shannon entropy in a combinatorial fashion to distinguish cell populations preferentially altered due to nearly any experimental paradigm and generates a visual representation of cellular entropy (i.e. change) across entire datasets. Ultimately, this allows for efficient determination of specific populations preferentially impacted by an experimental paradigm and identifies populations to target for downstream analyses employing quantitative measurements. We propose that SPECHTacle represents an immediately useful computational tool with the potential to be integrated into single cell-based workflows and greatly enhance the efficiency of both manual and machine-based learning workflows.

papers.title: High latitude, high tolerance: Northern juvenile Chinook salmon exhibit substantial thermal plasticity and acute heat tolerance
papers.abstract: In a rapidly warming North, Chinook salmon are facing rising river temperatures, increasing frequencies of heat waves, and greater annual thermal variation. These factors have putatively contributed to substantial declines in Alaska Chinook salmon abundance; understanding the thermal sensitivity and acclimation capacity of Chinook salmon at the northern extents of their range is therefore imperative. To this end, we acclimated juvenile Yukon River Chinook to five ecologically relevant summer temperatures (12.5, 15, 17.5, 20, and 22.5{degrees}C) under two feeding treatments of 100% or 40% satiation. We then assessed whole organism heat tolerance at rest and while swimming, along with the thermal sensitivity of heart rate and cardiac electrical activity. Yukon River Chinook substantially increased whole organism heat tolerance at rest and under exercise with warm acclimation. Cardiac heat tolerance also increased, and fish showed marked thermal compensation of maximum heart rate, resetting it to lower levels with warm acclimation. Feed treatment had a limited effect outside of peak heart rate and the transition temperatures of Q10. Warm acclimation was also associated with a shortening of the PR and QRS intervals and a lengthening of the QT interval. Across all acclimation groups, the PR interval plateaued to an extent far greater than heart rate itself, suggesting that limitations to AV conduction may limit cardiac function at high acute temperatures. Altogether, high latitude juvenile Chinook display remarkable heat tolerance and thermal plasticity, which may be preserved in association with the large seasonal, weather dependent, and spatial thermal variation Yukon River Chinook face during freshwater rearing and along with their extensive seaward and return migrations. The acute heat tolerance of Yukon River Chinook, which is comparable to or outperforming lower latitude Chinook and other salmonids, emphasizes the need for population-specific work for informed conservation efforts.

papers.title: High reproducibility demonstrated in a direct-to-consumer microbiome testing workflow under real-world conditions using fecal reference material
papers.abstract: Recent studies have documented substantial variation in microbiome profiles recovered from identical biological samples across direct-to-consumer (DTC) gut microbiome testing providers and, in some cases, within individual providers. These reports underscore the need for transparent, published assessments of analytical performance from the companies offering these services. To assess analytical reproducibility in our own testing workflow, we processed 10 replicates of a homogenized National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) human fecal reference material (RM 8048) through our full sample processing pipeline, from sample collection to data generation. Replicates were shipped from five U.S. sites over a staggered 35-day window. They were processed amongst over 6,000 customer samples, batched for DNA extraction and sequencing based on their arrival in the lab in nine separate sequencing runs, and analyzed using our standard pipeline. The 10 reference material replicates yielded highly concordant community profiles regardless of shipping time or temperature. Technical variability was minimal (median Bray-Curtis dissimilarity = 0.04) compared with the variation observed in samples from the same Tiny Health customer collected the same day (median Bray-Curtis: 0.08), within one week (0.25), one to two weeks apart (0.28), and between unrelated individuals (0.88). When evaluated using NIST's Coefficient of Disagreement (COD) metric, our workflow yielded a maximum pairwise COD of 0.045, well below NIST's published upper bound of 0.073 for this reference material. All three spike-in control strains were successfully recovered from every sample. These results demonstrate the reproducibility of our DTC microbiome testing workflow under real-world conditions, with robust consistency across sample collection, shipping, laboratory processing, and bioinformatics analysis. They also highlight the value of RM 8048 and similar reference materials for evaluating and transparently reporting analytical performance in DTC microbiome testing.

papers.title: RPI-Zero: Zero-shot RNA-Protein Interaction Prediction
papers.abstract: In vivo protein-RNA interactions are mapped almost exclusively by CLIP-seq, which profiles one protein in one cell type per experiment and needs a specific antibody; only about 10% of the roughly 2,000 human RNA-binding proteins have been assayed, and the Protein Data Bank holds around 5,000 protein-RNA complexes, a quarter of them ribosomes. Sequence-based prediction could extend coverage to unprofiled, newly discovered, or designed molecules, but existing predictors are not built for that case. One family trains a separate model per protein and cannot move beyond proteins with CLIP data; the other scores pairs but targets a single RNA class. Most are evaluated with random splits and randomly paired negatives that leave near-identical sequences on both sides of the split, and many require structure or read only short windows, discarding the context around a binding site. Their accuracy falls sharply when whole molecules are held out. We address this with two contributions. First, a strict benchmark of 2.1 million examples built from 11.6 million peaks of CLIP experiments targeting 209 proteins, taken from four public databases, in which each RNA is a spliced transcript with nucleotide-level labels, and sequence-similarity clusters are assigned whole to training, validation, and test sets, giving separate slices for unseen RNAs, unseen proteins, and unseen pairs. Negatives are matched to positives in length and in the number of other proteins binding the transcript, removing the shortcut by which a model predicts binding from how popular a transcript is without reading the protein. Second, RPI-Zero, a sequence-only model that reads any full-length protein and RNA jointly in up to 4,096 tokens, so the RNA representation is conditioned on the protein, and describes every protein as a mixture of shared motif prototypes, placing unseen proteins in the same terms as training ones. One model covers all proteins and RNA classes, uses no structure, and needs no interaction data for a new molecule. Compared with five state-of-the-art methods, it achieves the highest score in eight different metrics on unseen RNAs, unseen proteins, and unseen pairs. The model and data are available at https://github.com/ciceklab/RPI-Zero and https://zenodo.org/records/23748141, respectively.

papers.title: Elevational filtering reshapes mountain understory communities through diversity decline, functional shifts, and species replacement
papers.abstract: Mountain understory communities are structured along elevational gradients, as environmental constraints filter which species and ecological strategies can persist and where. Yet, how community differentiation, local diversity, functional strategies, and species replacement are shaped by elevational gradients remains poorly resolved. Here, we examine 107 herbaceous species across 27 sites spanning 2,202-3,696 m a.s.l. and three elevational zones. We determine how elevation reorganizes multiple dimensions of community assembly. We hypothesize that increasing elevation differentiates community composition, reduces -diversity, favors persistence-oriented strategies, and drives {beta}-diversity primarily through species turnover, rather than nestedness. We test our hypotheses by integrating taxonomic, functional, and {beta}-diversity patterns across the elevational gradient. A coherent pattern of community reassembly emerges as elevation increases: communities become increasingly distinct with elevational separation and locally less diverse toward higher elevations. Functional composition changes concurrently, with perennial and chamaephytic groups increasing as annual and therophytic groups decline. We find that increasing community differentiation primarily reflects species replacement rather than progressive species loss. Species turnover accounts for 97.95% of total Sorensen {beta}-diversity and increases with elevational separation, whereas nestedness declines. Our findings therefore show that elevation reorganizes herbaceous understory communities through linked changes in diversity, functional strategies, and species identity. Indeed, environmental filtering favors persistence-oriented strategies while progressively replacing species across elevations, linking taxonomic and functional differentiation within a common process of mountain understory community assembly.

papers.title: TRPP Ion Channels Function in the π-Conformation Rather Than the α-Conformation
papers.abstract: PKD2 (TRPP1) is a TRPP ion channel whose dysfunction causes autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Understanding its conformational states and gating mechanism is important for elucidating its function and for structure-based drug discovery. Cryo-EM structures of WT-PKD2 contain a local {pi}-helical turn in the S6 pore-lining helix ({pi}-conformation). In contrast, a fully -helical S6 (-conformation) was observed in the gain-of-function mutant F604P-PKD2 and interpreted as the open state, leading to the proposed {pi}-to- activation mechanism. However, whether the -conformation can support function has never been directly established. Here, using molecular dynamics simulations, we investigate the functional properties of the -and {pi}-conformations of PKD2. The -conformation remains dewetted unless the lower gate is widened beyond the conformational range observed in mammalian TRP channels. By contrast, the {pi}-conformation supports pore hydration and ion conduction following a small opening of the L677 gate, with simulated conductance comparable to experimental measurements. The closely related PKD2L1 (TRPP2) channel shows a similar dependence on conformation, with a hydrated {pi}-conformation and a dewetted -conformation. Together, these findings challenge the assignment of the -conformation as the conductive state and support a model in which the {pi}-conformation represents the functionally relevant state of TRPP channels. This model suggests that activation may involve an -to-{pi} transition rather than the previously proposed {pi}-to- transition, providing a new framework for understanding TRPP channel gating. This work sheds light on the molecular basis of polycystin channel dysfunction and could facilitate the development of PKD2-targeted therapeutic strategies for ADPKD.

papers.title: Earl Grey ParTEA: scalable, consistent transposable element annotation from pangenomes to deep phylogenetic scopes
papers.abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) are major drivers of genomic diversity, yet understanding their mobility and functional impact requires their accurate description in genomes. TE annotation is still typically performed genome-by-genome. TEs are often shared between some members of the same or closely related species. Hence, TE annotation with a library from a single reference misses families absent from that assembly, whereas building independent per-genome libraries fails to consistently surface shared TEs, hindering comparison. Here, we present Earl Grey ParTEA, a fully automated Snakemake pipeline extending the functionality of Earl Grey for comparative TE annotation across genome panels. ParTEA builds a single non-redundant TE library from all input genomes, resolves chimeric consensus sequences, and uses this shared library to annotate every genome, enabling direct comparison of TE family diversity, abundance, shared and private content, and activity landscapes. Optional modules provide TE library saturation analysis, BUSCO-based assembly quality control, and phylogenetic ordering of outputs. We applied ParTEA to sets of genomes spanning evolutionary scales: ten Arabidopsis thaliana accessions, ten Drosophila species, and ten species spanning the fungal kingdom. The Drosophila TE library expanded from 343 to 1,852 curated families including a previously missed rolling circle element with over 6,000 copies in D. miranda. The proportion of TE families shared across all genomes was highest within A. thaliana (97.3%), 37.7% across Drosophila species and only 0.5% across the set of fungi. ParTEA is available through Bioconda and represents a computationally efficient reproducible framework for comparative TE analysis in the era of large-scale genome analyses.

papers.title: Cytomegalovirus Infection in Human Cortical Organoids Induces Unique Developmental and Viral Substates
papers.abstract: Human Cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a ubiquitous {beta}-herpesvirus with exposure resulting in a life-long infection. Severe HCMV disease can occur in conditions of insufficient immunity, and this includes congenital infection. Infection of the developing brain can cause severe birth defects including microcephaly and sensorineural hearing loss. Also, increasing evidence suggests the contribution of HCMV infection in adult CNS diseases. Studying HCMV replication and its impact on CNS is restricted by host tropism and anatomy. In these studies, we define the impact of infection on healthy iPSC-derived cortical organoids using single cell RNA sequencing. We uncovered 16 cell type clusters in uninfected tissues using the Human Neural Organoid Cell Atlas. Following infection by HCMV expressing GFP, several clusters were altered in both GFP-positive and GFP-negative populations, including the likely transition of the Glutamatergic/GABAergic Neuron cluster into a CMV-Infected Cell cluster. Expressions of viral genes varied between cells and cell types, requiring us to introduce a TC (temporal class) indexing score to account for varying stages of infection. This analysis in conjunction with machine learning approaches revealed cells that are likely producing de novo HCMV along with several viral sub-states. Several viral sub-states had significant enrichments of genes involved in epithelial-to-mesenchymal (EMT) transition, including expression of EpCAM. We independently verified HCMV-induction of EpCAM protein expression in cortical organoids and glutamatergic neurons. In summary, our studies reveal unique features of HCMV infection of cortical organoid tissues, including varying viral sub-states and tropisms, and introduced new approaches to analyze these multi-dimensional complex data sets.

papers.title: RNA Polymerase Backtracking Promotes Type III-A CRISPR DNA Targeting
papers.abstract: Type III CRISPR-Cas systems provide transcription-dependent immunity against mobile genetic elements, yet the mechanism underlying their DNA targeting remains unclear. Although the type III effector Cas10-Csm functions as a single-stranded DNase in vitro, type III systems eliminate double-stranded DNA targets in vivo, suggesting that transcription generates critical DNA substrates. Here, we show that conserved RNA polymerase anti-backtracking factors, such as GreA, selectively inhibit DNA-targeting of type III immunity. GreA overexpression abolishes protection against both phages and conjugative plasmids, whereas mutations that disrupt GreA anti-backtracking activity eliminate this effect. In contrast, immunity mediated by the type II CRISPR-Cas system or the auxiliary type III RNase Csm6 remain unaffected, demonstrating that GreA specifically suppresses Cas10-dependent DNA interference. These findings identify RNA polymerase backtracking as a key determinant of Cas10-Csm activity and support a model in which arrested transcription complexes generate substrates for DNA degradation, opening up new anti-CRISPR strategies against type III.

papers.title: Quantitative Spatial Analysis of Matrix Remodelling in Wounds Using Digital Pathology and Fractal Analysis
papers.abstract: Wound healing involves spatially heterogeneous changes in matrix composition and organisation that can be difficult to capture using qualitative histological assessment alone. We developed a reproducible digital pathology workflow to quantify matrix features in cutaneous wound sections, compare them with unwounded skin, and derive an exploratory Histological Wound Index (HWI). Four normal-skin and six wound sections were analysed using QuPath, ImageJ/FracLac and Python. Approximately 500 x 500 micrometer regions of interest (ROI) were assigned to normal skin, wound centre, proximal edge or distant edge. Collagen, mucin and necrotic tissue coverage were quantified using image classifiers and analysed with linear mixed-effects models. Collagen architecture was assessed from collagen-selective binary masks using fractal dimension and lacunarity. Collagen coverage, fractal dimension, mucin coverage, necrosis and lacunarity were z-standardised and integrated into the HWI. Unwounded skin showed high collagen coverage and fractal dimension, with low lacunarity, mucin and necrosis. In contrast, wound-centre tissue showed low collagen coverage and fractal dimension together with higher mucin and necrosis. Distant-edge regions retained comparatively normal-like characteristics, whereas proximal-edge regions showed intermediate values. HWI was highest in normal skin and lowest in the wound centre. A descriptive matched-ROI comparison of two wound sections reproduced this regional ordering when all component measures were derived from identical ROI boundaries. This workflow provides a reproducible framework for quantifying regional ECM features and collagen-mask architecture in wound histology. The HWI is an exploratory histological summary requiring validation in larger longitudinal datasets.

papers.title: Short-read whole-genome sequencing identifies the Tg(Tal1-cre/ERT)42-056Jrg transgene insertion site on mouse chromosome 4
papers.abstract: Tg(Tal1-cre/ERT)42-056Jrg, also known as HSC-Scl-CreERT, is a well-used transgenic allele that enables genetic manipulation in mouse hematopoietic cells. Using short-read whole-genome sequencing, we identified the transgene insertion site on chromosome 4 approximately 6 kb upstream of Echdc2.

papers.title: Higher-order metabolic interactions among oral commensals gate pathobiont expansion through succinate-driven pH modulation
papers.abstract: Despite advances in defining microbiome shifts associated with inflammatory mucosal diseases, the ecological interactions that constrain or facilitate pathobiont expansion remain poorly understood. Using a six-species synthetic oral microbial community and factorial interaction screening, we identified a higher-order interaction governing the growth of the periodontal pathobiont Porphyromonas gingivalis. The core community member Veillonella parvula was the strongest positive determinant of P. gingivalis growth, but this effect was substantially reduced by the health-associated commensal Actinomyces oris. A. oris-mediated antagonism resulted from extracellular acidification and was enhanced under anaerobic conditions. Genetic dissection of A. oris fermentation revealed that lactate dehydrogenase (ldh1) contributes to anaerobic lactate production, but ldh1 deletion only partially relieved P. gingivalis inhibition. Instead, succinate, produced through a succinate dehydrogenase/fumarate reductase pathway (sdh2), emerged as the principal driver of acidification and P. gingivalis suppression. At high cell densities, however, V. parvula consumed both lactate and succinate, reversing acidification and restoring conditions permissive for P. gingivalis growth. To assess the relevance of these interactions in vivo, we analyzed subgingival microbiome from 1,355 adults, including 555 with detectable P. gingivalis. Among these individuals, P. gingivalis abundance was negatively associated with Actinomyces abundance after adjustment for periodontitis severity, whereas this association was attenuated at high V. parvula abundance, consistent with the interaction observed in vitro. Together, these findings identify succinate as a previously unrecognized mediator of interbacterial antagonism and reveal how higher-order metabolic interactions among oral commensals regulate pathobiont expansion through pH modulation, with protective effects shaped by oxygen availability and metabolic cross-feeding.

papers.title: Transportability of mouse gene knockout models to human complex phenotypes
papers.abstract: Mouse gene knockout studies are a valuable resource for understanding human gene function and the mechanisms underlying disease. However, translating insights to humans requires causal similarities between mouse and human phenotypes. A mouse model is transportable if gene perturbations that impact the mouse phenotype also affect (in orthologous genes) the corresponding human phenotype of interest, with consistent directionality. To assess the transportability of mouse models to human complex traits we combined laboratory mouse gene perturbation data from the high-throughput International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium with predicted loss-of-function data from the UK Biobank within the Gene Perturbation Analysis for Transportability (GPAT) framework. Applying GPAT to 30 matched mouse-human phenotype pairs, we found evidence of transportability for 12 mouse phenotypes including biochemical (e.g. total cholesterol), cellular (e.g. lymphocyte counts) and anthropometric (e.g. length/height) phenotypes. In contrast, there was limited evidence for others such as fat mass and body mass index in the context of the murine experimental conditions. We also found some evidence of transportability of mouse glucose measurements to diabetes mellitus in humans. Genome-wide perturbation effects on matched phenotypes were on average positively correlated between mice and humans (meta-analysis GPAT P = 2.3x10-27). However, the degree of correlation was generally modest and heterogeneous across phenotypes with some gene perturbations strongly associated in both species in opposite directions. Our framework illustrates how perturbation data can be used to quantitatively validate experimental models for understanding human disease aetiology and highlights the need for a range of orthogonal model systems, which may include challenges and perturbations to the mouse knockouts, to interrogate the mechanistic basis of human genetic associations.

papers.title: Common attentional mechanisms, but distinct computational dynamics, across Statistical and Reward Learning
papers.abstract: Past experience guides attention through statistical learning (SL) and reward learning (RL). Yet, whether they do so through similar neural and computational mechanisms remains unclear. In a first EEG visual-search experiment, we tested whether RL establishes latent spatial representations, previously demonstrated for SL. Afterwards, we directly compared RL and SL in a double-session experiment. Using multivariate decoding, Experiment 1 showed that high-reward locations could be decoded before target onset following a task-irrelevant, spatially-unspecific visual perturbation. Experiment 2 revealed that SL and RL established comparable neural representations, and similarly facilitated target selection and evidence accumulation (drift-rate). However, combining Rescorla-Wagner and Drift Diffusion Model revealed slower learning-rate for RL than SL. Pupillometry further tracked spatially selective expectation violations during SL, but reflected increased arousal during RL. Together, our results reveal how the brain routes distinct computational algorithms (probability estimation versus value caching) into a unified attentional priority map.

papers.title: A hawkmoth's point of view - Innate symmetry preferences are informed by floral display and foraging function in an insect pollinator
papers.abstract: Floral visual cues are key for flower recognition and feeding in many pollinators. In insects, innate preferences for characteristic floral colour and pattern cues can guide naive foragers during their initial foraging. Symmetry is suggested to be one such foraging cue, since it is a remarkably conserved floral feature, with flowers mainly displaying radial or bilateral morphologies. Insect pollinators like honeybees, bumblebees, and hoverflies have been found to distinguish symmetry from asymmetry spontaneously or through learning. However, whether innate preferences for floral symmetry types, i.e. radial or bilateral, influence naive flower choice, and whether such preferences are linked to functional benefits during foraging remains uncertain.We investigated innate symmetry choice and its associated foraging function in the hummingbird hawkmoth (Macroglossum stellatarum). Besides relying on pattern cues for flower choice, these hawkmoths feed while hovering, making symmetry a valuable visual cue for flight and proboscis control. In choice assays, the hawkmoths' innate preferences for symmetry types depended on the floral display planes, with considerable differences between the horizontal and vertical displays. Tracking the hawkmoths during foraging revealed that in both display planes, the innately preferred patterns increased foraging success by guiding approach and nectary search. While an analysis of flowers visited by hawkmoths in nature did not reveal the same link between symmetry and display plane, a majority of plant species with vertically displayed flowers showed features matching those innately preferred by the hawkmoths. In this study, we provide the first instance of display-dependent innate foraging preferences and highlight how visuomotor strategies in nectivorous insects may have coevolved with flower features.

papers.title: MorphoProt: RNA-Conditioned Integration of Multiscale Histology for Spatial Protein Inference
papers.abstract: Spatially resolved protein abundance reveals cellular states and tissue organization that RNA expression cannot fully capture, yet direct spatial protein profiling remains costly and limited in coverage. Histology images routinely accompany spatial transcriptomics and offer complementary morphological information for protein inference. Here, we introduce MorphoProt, a multimodal framework that jointly predicts spatial protein abundance from RNA expression, multiscale histology and tissue neighborhoods. MorphoProt uses RNA-guided cross-attention over five histological fields of view, so that the morphological context read for each spot is conditioned on its molecular state. The fused representation is refined by gated aggregation of RNA-derived information from physical and transcriptomic neighborhoods before joint protein prediction. On held-out sections of human tonsil, mouse spleen and human liver, MorphoProt achieves mean proteinwise Spearman correlations of 0.652, 0.604 and 0.372, outperforming matched RNA-only and graph-based baselines and the histology-based HIPI and multimodal SPRINT baselines in all three tissues. Combining fields of view, rather than any single one, carries the histology gain: in spleen and liver, the multiscale model outperforms every single-field model, and its learned scale preference separates white-pulp from red-pulp compartments. Predicted proteins preserve protein-defined tissue domains and their marker identity, and recover pathologist-annotated germinal centers as accurately as measured proteins.

papers.title: Pneumocystis phosphoglucomutase links glucose-phosphate metabolism to β-1,3-glucan synthesis and cell-wall integrity
papers.abstract: The fungal cell wall is a dynamic, carbohydrate-rich structure whose composition is closely coordinated with cellular metabolism. Phosphoglucomutase (PGM) interconverts glucose-1-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate, linking carbon metabolism with UDP-glucose-dependent cell-wall biosynthesis. We previously identified functional Pgm2 homologs from Pneumocystis jirovecii and Pneumocystis murina. Here, using a Saccharomyces cerevisiae pgm2{Delta} complementation model, we examined the relationship between Pgm2 activity, {beta}-1,3-glucan, and cell-wall integrity. Pgm2 deficiency reduced {beta}-1,3-glucan content and altered zymolyase sensitivity without major changes in cell-wall thickness. Bulk RNA sequencing revealed that the pgm2{Delta} mutant exhibited coordinated metabolic and cell-wall transcriptional responses, including increased SLT2/MPK1, RLM1, FKS2/GSC2, GFA1, CHS1, CRH1, SED1, and CWP1 expression and decreased FKS1, GAS1, GAS3, and CHS2 expression. Expression of either Pjpgm2 or Pmpgm2 broadly shifted these responses toward wild-type levels. Selected transcriptional changes were further evaluated by qRT-PCR, which supported the major stress and cell-wall responses identified by RNA sequencing. FKS2/GSC2 showed the same directional pattern, although differences were not statistically significant by qRT-PCR. Despite this compensatory response, Pgm2-deficient cells were markedly more susceptible to sublethal caspofungin, whereas either Pneumocystis Pgm2 homolog restored tolerance toward wild-type levels. These findings link Pgm2-dependent glucose-phosphate metabolism with {beta}-1,3-glucan levels and cell-wall function.
