Given the importance of {beta}-1,3-glucan to the Pneumocystis cyst wall and its limited cell-wall biosynthetic pathways, these findings further support Pgm2 as an important component of Pneumocystis cell-wall biology and a potential antifungal target.

papers.title: Failed allogeneic corneal lenticules show fibrosis and identity loss without dominant T cell rejection
papers.abstract: Failed allogeneic corneal stromal lenticules develop progressive opacity, but the state of the implanted tissue is unknown. Here we show that six explants from three patients occupy a fibrotic integration-failure state with scar-matrix production and loss of corneal identity without a dominant T cell rejection program. Scar-matrix, transparency and corneal-identity programs separated every patient from eight unimplanted donor controls, the last defined by independent human single-cell references. Calibrated immune programs and repertoire reconstruction distinguished the explants from canonical adaptive rejection. Exchange reduced interface reflectivity initially, followed by recurrent opacity in two patients and corneal steepening with declining uncorrected acuity in the third. In non-scarring rabbit repair, identity moved toward the uninjured state as backscatter returned toward normal despite increasing similarity to the explant-derived expression signature. Within one culture experiment, marked scar suppression accompanied opposite identity responses. Tacrolimus and rapamycin likewise suppressed canonical rejection while moving identity in opposite directions. Resveratrol combined reduced scar-associated programs and increased identity with improved graft appearance in the source study. These findings establish classic-rejection activity and tissue integration as separable axes and direct treatment of failed lenticules from escalating immunosuppression toward control of stromal remodeling and preservation of corneal identity.

papers.title: HiSpoT: a novel one-tube dual-barcode PCR method for NGS spoligotyping amplicon library preparation in Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex
papers.abstract: Tuberculosis remains one of the leading infectious causes of death globally, making rapid, accurate, and affordable strain typing essential for effective outbreak tracking and epidemiological surveillance. To address the limitations and high costs of current typing methods, we developed a novel one-tube, dual-barcode PCR method for preparing targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) amplicon libraries for spoligotyping of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC), which we termed HiSpoT (High-throughput Spoligotyping by Targeted next generation sequencing). The assay targets 43 conserved spacer oligonucleotides in the CRISPR direct repeat (DR) region and is presented here together with the previously unpublished, difficult-to-design dual-barcode primer set needed to multiplex 96 samples in a single tube. HiSpoT is accurate, fast, high-throughput, and low-cost, eliminating the need for a commercial NGS library preparation kit. Because HiSpoT is PCR-based, the resulting spoligotypes remain directly comparable with the large PCR-based spoligotype databases accumulated over decades, enabling rapid outbreak tracking and biogeographic characterization of the tuberculosis burden of a country, while higher-resolution whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data are obtained. Analysis of 288 clinical MTBC isolates from Israel (2020-2022) demonstrated a broad range of genetic lineages, and comparison of 79 isolates analyzed by both HiSpoT and WGS showed 70% full concordance, with essentially all discrepancies attributable to single-spacer insertion-element disruptions of PCR primer sites. We also present two open-source Google Colab Python tools, Spoligotyping_MTBC_gcl and its condensed HiSpoT_Spoligotyping_v8_ready VIBE variant, freely available on GitHub, which automatically process Illumina paired-end fastq output from HiSpoT or WGS and report binary and octal spoligotypes, spoligo international types (SIT), and MTBC family assignments with accompanying quality-control reports.

papers.title: Nematode species differ in susceptibility and response to the nematode-trapping fungus Arthrobotrys oligospora
papers.abstract: Fungal predators of nematodes are widespread and represent promising candidates for biological control of parasitic nematodes. However, the behavioural and molecular mechanisms underlying nematode-fungus interactions remain poorly understood, especially for nematodes other than Caenorhabditis elegans. We investigated the interactions between the nematode-trapping fungus Arthrobotrys oligospora and three nematode species: (i) free-living C. elegans, (ii) fig-associated C. inopinata, and (iii) the free-living adult life cycle stage of the gastrointestinal parasite Strongyloides ratti. A. oligospora trapped S. ratti more efficiently than either C. elegans or C. inopinata. Behavioural analyses revealed species-specific differences in nematode locomotion. S. ratti moved slower, travelled shorter distances and showed lower displacement than Caenorhabditis spp. To test whether locomotion influences fungal trapping, we examined eight C. elegans mutants with hyper- or hypoactive locomotory phenotypes. Although both groups moved at similar speeds, hyperactive mutants showed greater displacement, which positively correlated with trap formation but did not explain trapping efficiency by A. oligospora. We investigated the fungal response during interaction with the three nematodes. Exposure to S. ratti, but not to Caenorhabditis spp, resulted in reduced sporulation and differential expression of sporulation-associated genes. In nematodes, myosin-related genes responded to A. oligospora in a species-specific manner, including upregulation in C. elegans and downregulation in S. ratti. These transcriptional changes may reflect alterations in muscle structure, including reduction in dense body and mitochondrial size in Caenorhabditis species but not S. ratti during A. oligospora exposure. Together, our findings demonstrate that both fungal and nematode responses are nematode species dependent. These results improve our understanding of nematode-fungus interactions and highlight the importance of nematode species when developing nematode-trapping fungi as a biological control agent.

papers.title: Fluorescence microscopic evidence for intracellular silicon storage pools in diatoms and their partial separation
papers.abstract: Diatoms are unicellular algae that occur ubiquitously in almost every salt- and freshwater habitat on earth. Silicic acid is taken up from the environment and stored in intracellular silicon storage pools (SSPs) to form species specific silica based cell walls (frustules). During biosilica formation in the silicon deposition vesicle (SDV), the silicon is transported from SSPs into the SDV. The present contribution describes the fluorescence microscopic visualization and quantification of silica solely formed from SSPs under silicon starvation. Labeling with the fluorescence marker PDMPO demonstrates continuing cell growth and cell division without silicon uptake from the environment. The SSPs of Cyclotella nana may account for up to 1/3 of total cellular silicon and intracellular concentrations up to ca. 540 mM, significantly beyond the saturation level (2 mM). The chemical state and localization of SSPs within cells are yet unclear. Here, we report a method for subcellular fractionation of C. nana by density gradient centrifugation. Quantification of cytoplasmic silicon yields 3 to 10% of the total cellular silicon corresponding to intracellular concentrations of ca. 50 to 160 mM. Labeling with NMR active 29Si shows that this silicon occurs as condensed silica, i.e., silicic acid is converted into condensed silica after uptake. However, the detected intracellular silicon concentrations are lower than the value of ca. 540 mM predicted by the fluorescence experiments. It is thus concluded that the missing SSP silicon is either present in the form of large aggregates or compartments. Alternatively, they may also be bound to cell wall biosilica.

papers.title: Unlocking Targeted Underwater Delivery of Coral Probiotics
papers.abstract: The rapid global decline of coral reefs has intensified the need for innovative conservation strategies, including microbial therapies to enhance coral health and resilience. A major limitation, however, is the lack of effective delivery systems for administering Beneficial Microorganisms for Corals (BMCs). In this study, we present natural, biodegradable systems for the underwater delivery of probiotic bacteria to corals. Three customized alginate-based delivery formats (beads, hydrogels, and filaments) were developed and loaded with the probiotic Pseudoalteromonas peptidolytica. The materials were loaded with the bacterium at an average concentration of 10^(4) CFU/g of dry polymer and engineered to sink underwater while keeping their structural integrity over time. In vitro assays showed controlled release kinetics, with encapsulated probiotics remaining viable and capable of replication. In vivo experiments compared syringe-based inoculation with the application of alginate beads, hydrogels, and filaments to corals. Microbiome analyses performed before and after inoculation confirmed successful probiotic colonization following deployment of the alginate-based delivery systems. Relative abundance of the probiotic genus Pseudoalteromonas increased markedly in treated corals, reaching 11.5 % after 48 h with alginate beads, 12.7 % after 48 h with hydrogels, and 12.6 % after 24 h with filaments. Furthermore, the degradation mechanisms of the three delivery systems were investigated. As the first biomaterial-based underwater delivery systems specifically engineered for coral probiotics, these alginate-based materials provide a promising foundation for advancing microbial therapies in both controlled aquaria and natural reef environments.

papers.title: Genomic architecture of the major histocompatibility complex genes in the Neotropical Midas cichlid
papers.abstract: The Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) plays a central role in vertebrate adaptive immunity, yet its genomic architecture remains poorly characterized in many evolutionary model systems, including the Neotropical Midas cichlid Amphilophus citrinellus. Here, we integrate chromosome-level functional genome annotation, transposable element (TE) profiling, transcriptomics, phylogenetics, molecular selection analyses, and protein structural modeling to characterize its MHC repertoire. We identified 298 MHC-related loci across 18 chromosomes, including 30 MHC-I genes, 15 MHC-IIA genes, and 20 MHC-IIB genes, together with antigen-processing and regulatory components. MHC-I and MHC-II genes were located on different chromosomes, consistent with the MHC non-linkage pattern characteristic of many teleosts. Gene duplication and phylogenetic patterns support birth-and-death evolution, resulting in a structurally diverse repertoire with broadly conserved protein domains. TE distribution varied across MHC genomic regions, suggesting a potential contribution to genomic diversification. Molecular selection analyses detected positive selection in MHC-I and IIB genes, whereas MHC-IIA showed more limited evidence of positive selection. Expression patterns varied across tissues, with relatively high expression of several MHC genes in the spleen and thymus, while structural models retained characteristic MHC folds. Phylogenetic analyses placed previously characterized MHC sequences with broader multilocus repertoire, suggesting that population level diversity may reflect both allelic polymorphism and variation among paralogous loci. Together, these findings provide a comprehensive chromosome-resolved characterization of the MHC repertoire in a Neotropical cichlid and establish a genomic framework for investigating immune gene diversification during the Midas cichlid radiation.

papers.title: Highly prevalent cargo genes of F plasmids harbored in pathogenic Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Analysis of prevalent orthogroups (OGs) in a collection of F plasmids from extraintestinal Escherichia coli ST131 isolates has led to the identification of two groups of previously uncharacterized cargo genes that may be widely distributed among F plasmids of pathogenic E. coli. Group 1 comprises four OGs whose encoded proteins are predicted to be involved in transport-related functions. The corresponding genes cluster with other genes associated with metabolism and are highly prevalent in extraintestinal ST131 isolates. Group 2 comprises several OGs whose encoded proteins currently have unknown functions. These OGs are present in a large proportion of F plasmids from both intestinal and extraintestinal E. coli isolates. The corresponding genes cluster within an F-plasmid region that also contains genes involved in DNA metabolism, suggesting that the proteins encoded by these newly identified OGs may likewise contribute to F-plasmid DNA biology. Characterizing the functions of these newly identified proteins may improve our understanding of the contribution of F plasmid to E. coli virulence and reveal novel targets for antimicrobial intervention, either by limiting F-plasmid dissemination among multidrug-resistant (MDR) E. coli strains or by directly targeting plasmid-carrying bacteria.

papers.title: Temporal stability for individual differences in both habit learning and expression
papers.abstract: Actions transition from goal-directed to stimulus-driven habits through repetition. Individual differences in the capacity to learn and control habits are central to current models of psychopathology, which assume that overreliance on habitual control drives maladaptive behaviors. However, whether these tendencies reflect stable, trait-like cognitive processes remains unclear. We examined the temporal stability of individual differences in habit learning and expression. Across two preregistered experiments (total N = 313), we assessed stimulus-response habits using the same stimuli after one day or different stimuli after four months. Evidence for stable individual differences in habit commissions was strong and comparable across experiments, with computational modelling further supporting trait-like tendencies for habit learning and expression. Trait-like tendencies were also reflected in action automatization while practicing stimulus-response associations, which was associated with future habitual behavior. Our findings have theoretical implications for our understanding of habit formation and its role in psychopathology.

papers.title: Lipidic α-synuclein fibrils catalyze the formation of pathological mature fibrils
papers.abstract: The aggregation of -synuclein into amyloid fibrils is a hallmark of a collection of neurodegenerative diseases termed synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease (PD). Interactions between -synuclein and lipid membranes modulate -synuclein aggregation and can produce protofibril structures consisting of both protein and lipid, termed lipidic fibrils. These lipidic fibrils can mature into mature fibrils, which resemble ex vivo fibrils extracted from Lewy bodies found in post-mortem brain samples of PD patients. Here, through the combination of experiments and kinetic theory, we study the influence of lipids and lipidic fibrils on the formation of mature fibrils. We find that lipidic fibrils catalyze mature fibril formation via a heterogeneous primary nucleation mechanism, which lowers the activation energy barrier of mature fibril formation relative to lipid-independent primary nucleation. The final stage of the reaction is governed by mature fibril elongation becoming limited by the rate at which protein monomers dissociate from the metastable lipidic fibrils, confirming that fibrils form in order of stability following Ostwald's Rule of Stages. This mechanism is validated using the small molecule inhibitor ambroxol, which selectively suppresses the formation of lipidic fibrils and in this manner shifts the aggregation kinetics to the slow, lipid-independent pathway. Taken together, these findings reveal that lipidic fibrils act as on-pathway intermediates and accelerate the aggregation of mature fibrils, which could provide a quantitative framework to design novel therapeutic strategies to inhibit pathological -synuclein aggregation.

papers.title: Wild wood mouse gut microbiota are influenced by captivity and cross-fostering
papers.abstract: Background Wild and laboratory animals harbour profoundly different gut microbiota, but how microbiomes shift between these states, and the relative roles of captivity, microbial history, and host identity in shaping that shift, remain unclear. Here, we developed a unique wood mouse (Apodemus sylvaticus) system comprising free-living mice (Wild:As), a wild-derived colony maintained in captivity for over a decade (Wild-like:As), and a second colony that we generated from the Wild-like:As mice by caesarean rederivation and cross-fostering to laboratory Mus musculus (Lab-like:As). We compared these three Apodemus cohorts with conventional laboratory Mus musculus (Lab:Mm) to ask how microbial diversity, community composition, and functional potential vary across a spectrum of wild-to-laboratory conditions. Results We found that alpha diversity varied substantially among cohorts but showed no consistent wild-to-laboratory trend: Shannon diversity was higher in Lab:Mm and Lab-like:As than in Wild:As and Wild-like:As mice, whereas phylogenetic diversity was similarly high in both the Wild:As and Lab:Mm groups. Community composition more closely reflected cohort histories. Despite over a decade in captivity, Wild-like:As mice remained most similar to Wild:As conspecifics, whereas Lab-like:As mice shifted strongly away from Wild-like:As and toward, but remained distinct from, Lab:Mm mice. The clearest wild-to-laboratory pattern emerged in microbiome consistency: core ASVs (present in [≥]90% of individuals) increased from 9 in Wild:As to 46 in Wild-like:As, 72 in Lab-like:As, and 138 in Lab:Mm mice. Predicted functional potential revealed a further distinction between taxonomic and functional patterns: Wild:As and Wild-like:As microbiomes did not differ significantly, whereas Lab-like:As shifted toward the Lab:Mm state despite remaining taxonomically distinct. Conclusions Together, these results show that laboratory-associated microbiomes do not emerge through simple loss of wild microbial diversity, but through broader reorganisation of community composition, consistency, and predicted functional potential reflecting microbial history and host context. The persistent Wild-like and Lab-like microbiome states within Apodemus provide a powerful experimental system for future timely work testing how microbiome history influences host physiology, resilience, and responses to environmental challenges.

papers.title: NanoPAMDA enables rapid PAM characterization of metagenome-derived Cas9 effectors
papers.abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 orthologs remain functionally underexplored despite the rapidly growing scale of publicly available metagenomic sequencing data. Here, we applied a multi-stage computational discovery pipeline to two independent sources of metagenomic sequence data, a multi-biome collection of 660,185 metagenome-assembled genomes spanning 17 public catalogs, and raw sequencing reads from human microbiome studies assembled de novo, to identify novel Cas9 orthologs. Candidates were filtered for guide RNA architectural plausibility, sequence novelty, conservation of catalytic residues, and structural integrity, yielding 14 candidates spanning both data sources for experimental characterization. To determine PAM preference at scale, we developed a cost-effective Nanopore long-read-based adaptation of the high-throughput PAM determination assay (NanoPAMDA), enabling rapid, time-resolved, kinetic PAM profiling across many candidates in parallel. One Cas9 effector, E10, showed PAM-specific activity in vitro and was catalytically active in E. coli. Together, these findings demonstrate a scalable, long-read sequencing-based framework for discovering and biochemically characterizing novel Cas9 orthologs from metagenomic data.

papers.title: Age-specific pediatric templates improve EEG source-reconstructed biomarkers in children
papers.abstract: EEG source reconstruction requires an anatomical head model, ideally constructed from individual magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. In developmental studies of children and adolescents, however, MRIs are rarely available. Researchers therefore routinely rely on adult templates, such as the FreeSurfer average (fsaverage), despite substantial anatomical changes throughout development. How much this reliance on adult models biases downstream EEG biomarkers remains unclear. Here, we investigated whether age-specific pediatric templates offer a better alternative to fsaverage for EEG-derived biomarkers in children and adolescents, using individual MRI-based reconstruction as the reference. We analyzed eyes-closed resting-state EEGs from 384 Healthy Brain Network participants aged 5.5 to 17.5 years. For each participant, we tested three anatomical models: their individual MRI, an age-specific pediatric template from a series spanning ages 6-17 at one-year intervals, and the adult fsaverage template. We compared four EEG biomarkers in childhood and adolescence: absolute power, relative power, long-range temporal correlations quantified with detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA), and functional excitation-inhibition (fE/I) ratio. Pediatric templates agreed more closely with individual MRI-based biomarkers in both developmental groups and had fewer parcels with significantly different biomarker values than the adult template, except for absolute power in older adolescents. We conclude that when individual MRI is not available, age-specific pediatric templates match individual MRI-based EEG biomarker values more closely than the adult template across all four biomarkers up to approximately 12 years of age and should be the preferred choice at least up to this age.

papers.title: Bayesian phylogenetic inference accounting for recombination in whole bacterial genomes
papers.abstract: Recombination is a major evolutionary force in bacteria, and ignoring it distorts phylogenies and can invalidate downstream analyses such as dating. We present ClonalFrame2, a new software for Bayesian phylogenetic inference from whole bacterial genomes that accounts for recombination. It replaces both ClonalFrame and ClonalFrameML while using the same evolutionary model, in which both mutation and recombination events occur on the branches of the clonal genealogy. The locations of recombination events are integrated out of the likelihood using a hidden Markov model, so the algorithm targets only the clonal genealogy and three recombination parameters. Ancestral sequences are recomputed whenever the tree changes and are used to propose efficient topology updates. We validated the method by analysing data-free datasets, which recovered the prior, and by comparing the approximated likelihood with the exact one on simulated data. Across 100 simulated datasets of 100 genomes each, the recombination parameters were accurately recovered, and trees inferred while accounting for recombination were many times more accurate than when ignoring it. In Staphylococcus aureus ST239, we showed that accounting for recombination gave a stronger temporal signal and a more robust dated phylogeny. In Neisseria gonorrhoeae, we identified interesting patterns of clustered recombination events happening repeatedly across the branches of the tree.

papers.title: Diversification of budding yeast polarization dynamics after compensatory experimental evolution
papers.abstract: Essential cellular processes evolve under strong selection, yet protein networks underlying conserved functions can vary substantially. To what extent evolution constrains the intracellular dynamics of proteins performing essential functions is currently largely unknown. Here, we characterize budding yeast polarization phenotypes along a previously established evolutionary recovery trajectory, compensating for the loss of near-essential polarity gene BEM1. Through quantitative live cell imaging, we show that loss of BEM1 weakens and destabilizes polarization. Surprisingly, in recovered evolved lineages, protein dynamics change significantly compared to the ancestor: most notably, presence of main regulator Cdc42-GTP is strongly decreased, while polarisome member Spa2 localizes more slowly into mobile foci. Although separate phenotypic characteristics are only weakly constrained, we find evidence of effective protein-independent localization modes, revealing signs of convergence along the evolutionary trajectory. Together, our results show that evolution can restore global cellular function without conserving microscopic organization, instead giving rise to novel molecular phenotypes.

papers.title: Hidden infections: Linking parasite ecology, fish health and stakeholder perceptions in Nile tilapia aquaculture in central Kenya
papers.abstract: Parasite infections in farmed fish may remain unrecognised when fish-health assessment relies mainly on visible signs. We investigated metazoan parasite occurrence, parasite diversity and community composition, associations between gill-parasite burden and histological alterations, and stakeholder recognition of fish-health problems in Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) aquaculture in central Kenya. We examined 157 fish from 20 farms, assessed gill histology in 137 fish, measured water quality once per farm, and collected questionnaire and interview data from 48 stakeholders. Five metazoan parasite groups were recorded, with monopisthocotylans the most prevalent (36.3%). Higher monopisthocotylan burden was associated with a greater cumulative number of gill lesion types (odds ratio 1.86, 95% CI 1.43-2.42, p < 0.001), whereas copepod burden was not. Parasite diversity was higher in the larger operational pond category across all three Hill-number orders (p = 0.006-0.008), and parasite-community composition differed between categories (PERMANOVA, p = 0.034), although these comparisons were exploratory because only four farms were in the larger category and farm category overlapped with county. Single-time-point water-quality measurements showed no clear associations with parasite burden, diversity or community composition after multiple-testing correction. Farmers and fisheries or extension officers recognised signs of poor fish health but rarely identified parasites as a specific cause, and routine diagnostic confirmation was uncommon. The findings reveal a gap between laboratory detection of parasite-associated gill alterations and farm-level recognition and diagnosis.

papers.title: Orsay virus infection is associated with reduced locomotion and alters cue-dependent food choice in Caenorhabditis elegans
papers.abstract: Behavioral responses are an important component of host defense; however, most evidence in Caenorhabditis elegans comes from bacterial pathogens. Here, we tested whether infection with Orsay virus (OrV) alters host dispersal and food choice and whether these responses involve the RNA-processing factor EOL-1. When measuring distance travelled over a certain period of time in control and infected wild-type animals, we observed that OrV infection was associated with lower locomotion. Moreover, when presenting infected and control animals with food choices, we observed that infected animals preferred OrV infected food sources only when the alternative was a pure food source, preferring a non-inoculated food source when both control and viral food sources contained a C. elegans filtrate. Moreover, loss of EOL-1 altered baseline locomotion and attenuated the infection-associated reduction detected in the earlier motility assay, while also modifying the food choice response, suggesting that eol-1 contributes to the motility and behavioral changes induced by OrV infection. Collectively, these results support an overall association between OrV infection and reduced host dispersal, whereas its effect on food choice depends on the sensory context. These findings extend infection-associated behavioral responses to a natural viral pathogen and identify eol-1 as a modulator of their expression.

papers.title: How Fisherian runaway halts: Genomic architecture determines the long-term evolutionary consequences of sexual selection.
papers.abstract: Sexual selection explains the evolution of exaggerated sexual displays, but less obvious is why biased mate preferences--a requirement for sexual selection--evolve. Fisher (1930) proposed that biased mate preferences can spark self-reinforcing evolutionary process (runaway) that drives their own evolution. This occurs because mate choice imposes sexual selection on sexual displays and links them genetically to mate preferences, producing indirect selection on the preferences themselves. While mathematical models have demonstrated the plausibility of the runaway theory, they rely on several idealized assumptions. Consequently, it remains poorly understood how runaway halts once populations deviate from these idealized conditions as a consequence of evolution via runaway, and how the genetic architecture underlying sexual displays influences the resulting evolutionary dynamics. Here, we address these gaps using two complementary approaches. First, we review and synthesize existing theories to classify the mechanisms that halt runaway into four categories, based on which idealized assumptions of Lande's (1981) classic model are violated during evolution via runaway. Second, we conduct individual-based evolutionary simulations varying the genetic architecture of sexual displays from conventional additive to omnigenic inheritance models. Our results show that genetic architecture determines how runaway process halts, thereby governing long-term evolutionary dynamics under sexual selection.

papers.title: Dynamic allocation of MurJ coordinates bacterial growth and division
papers.abstract: Rod-shaped bacteria grow by inserting peptidoglycan into the lateral cell wall during elongation and into the septal cell wall during division. These two modes of growth are driven by distinct peptidoglycan synthesis machineries that consume the shared precursor Lipid II and must be coordinated so that cell enlargement remains matched to division. However, how cells spatially allocate this shared precursor, and whether Lipid II translocation itself contributes to this coordi-nation, remain unclear. Here we show that the spatial distribution of the essential Lipid II flippase MurJ coordinates this balance in Escherichia coli. Increasing nonseptal MurJ abundance shifted cell-wall synthesis toward elongation and reduced septal synthesis. Single-molecule tracking revealed that MurJ diffuses throughout the membrane but is transiently captured at the division site, rather than stably incorporated into the septal synthesis machinery. This recruitment requires active septal cell-wall synthesis, but not ongoing Lipid II synthesis or flipping, indicating that MurJ recruitment is coupled to the active synthesis machinery rather than to substrate availability or transport. Thus, activation of septal synthesis creates transient MurJ capture at the division site, providing a mechanism to preferentially supply Lipid II for septal growth during cytokinesis. These findings reveal a capture-and-release mechanism that dynamically enriches MurJ at active division sites and thereby coordinates elongation and division in bacterial cells.

papers.title: Improving phosphoproteomic kinase activity inference by contextual refinement of Kinase Library relationships
papers.abstract: Kinase activity inference from phosphoproteomic data relies on kinase-specific substrate sets defined by kinase-substrate relationship (KSR) priors. Kinase Library (KL) expands candidate substrate coverage using experimentally derived kinase specificity profiles, but its predictions reflect sequence compatibility rather than established intracellular regulation. We benchmarked KL-expanded KSR priors using 222 perturbation phosphoproteomic samples covering 396 annotated activation or inhibition events across 78 kinases. Broad KL expansion increased the number of scoreable kinases from 108 to 391, but reduced perturbed-kinase discrimination, directional accuracy and ranking performance. Higher error rates occurred among kinases with limited curated substrate support, while broad expansion also increased redundancy among inferred activity profiles. To improve the reliability of motif-derived relationships, we constrained KL-derived KSRs using predicted protein co-localization and protein-association evidence. Protein-association filtering consistently improved inference performance, reduced activity redundancy and provided a more favorable accuracy-coverage balance than co-localization filtering. The selected protein-association-filtered prior retained activity estimates for 308 kinases with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) above 0.75 and extended inference to 200 kinases not scoreable using curated KSRs, which were significantly enriched for dark kinases. These newly scoreable kinases showed structured activity patterns across perturbation contexts and interpretable signaling associations. Our results show that protein-association evidence can refine motif-derived KSR priors while preserving broad kinome coverage, providing a practical framework for more reliable phosphoproteomic kinase activity inference.

papers.title: FeatureMAP enables network-guided interpretation of untargeted metabolomics
papers.abstract: Untargeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) metabolomics generates thousands of features, but incomplete metabolite annotation and reliance on predefined pathways limit their biological interpretation. Here we present FeatureMAP, an LC-MS feature-centric computational framework that integrates multi-evidence metabolite annotation, network-guided refinement, metabolic module discovery, and structured large language model-based functional interpretation. Across ten public datasets, FeatureMAP improved MS1-based metabolite candidate prioritization while reducing annotation redundancy. In semi-synthetic benchmarks, FeatureMAP recovered coordinated metabolic perturbations, achieving 92% recovery of a simulated perturbation, and distinguished concurrent metabolic processes. Controlled benchmarks further evaluated functional interpretation under competing metabolite-level signals. Based on FeatureMAP, we additionally developed PhenoMAP, a phenotype-aware knowledge graph comprising 12,929 dysregulated metabolic modules from 501 human metabolomics studies spanning 326 phenotypes. Module-level comparisons revealed reproducible metabolic similarities across independent studies and biologically supported relationships among phenotypes. Application to Alzheimer's disease cerebrospinal fluid and cellular datasets identified convergent membrane-lipid alterations and implicated galactose-linked glycosphingolipid remodeling. Together, FeatureMAP and PhenoMAP enable network-grounded interpretation of incompletely annotated LC-MS metabolomics data and systematic investigation of metabolic dysregulation across biological conditions.

papers.title: Multi-objective domain adaptation for pan-cancer transfer of pharmacogenomic drug response to patient tumours
papers.abstract: Large-scale pharmacogenomic screens provide rich drug-sensitivity measurements in cancer cell lines, but transferring these measurements to patient tumours remains limited by biological heterogeneity and cross-domain distribution shift. Existing machine learning approaches, including adversarial autoencoder and domain adaptation, address this gap by learning shared latent representations between preclinical models and patient samples. However, alignment without explicit biological constraints can produce unreliable representations when cancer lineage structure and clinically relevant patient heterogeneity are not preserved. Here, we introduce MODAE+, a pan-cancer multi-objective deep learning domain adaptation framework that jointly balances domain alignment, deconfounding, drug-response prediction, survival prediction, and cancer-lineage classification across 9,696 TCGA tumours, 1,293 CCLE cancer cell lines, and CTRP sensitivity profiles for 544 compounds in 738 matched cell lines. This multi-objective design improved cross-domain alignment while preserving cancer-lineage organization and patient heterogeneity. For drugs shared between the pharmacogenomic screen and TCGA treatment records, MODAE+ predicted sensitivity was significantly associated with overall survival among patients who received each drug in 46.3% of evaluated cancer-drug pairs by log-rank testing and 41.5% by multivariable Cox analysis. Biological validation across four curated drug-gene resources identified significant expression differences exceeding 1.5-fold for 34.9-64.4% of drugs in pan-cancer analyses, based on the lowest-p-value annotated gene per drug. Drug-class-specific patterns involved intended molecular targets for targeted therapies and predominantly transport, metabolism, detoxification and resistance-related genes for classical chemotherapies. As an additional validation, we derived pretreatment responder-nonresponder gene-expression signatures from 13 external breast cancer datasets and evaluated their concordance with MODAE+ predictions across 69 signature-drug comparisons in TCGA patients treated with paclitaxel or doxorubicin. Consensus signature scores showed Spearman correlations of 0.791 with predicted paclitaxel sensitivity and 0.724 with predicted doxorubicin sensitivity, averaging 0.758 across the two drugs. Together, these complementary analyses provide supporting evidence for the clinical relevance and biological consistency of MODAE+ predictions, suggesting their potential to identify drug-sensitive tumour subgroups and generate hypotheses about mechanisms of drug resistance.

papers.title: Gut Roseburia hominis-derived 10-hydroxystearic acid alleviates metabolic disorder by restoring hepatic fatty acid metabolism
papers.abstract: Metabolic disorders and health-promoting dietary interventions represent complementary contexts of metabolic impairment and improvement, providing an opportunity to identify gut microbial taxa associated with both disease status and dietary response. Here, we integrated five independent human cohorts spanning metabolic disorders and dietary interventions and identified Roseburia hominis as a gut microbial taxon that consistently decreased in metabolic disorders and increased after dietary interventions. Beyond species abundance, strain-level genetic variation in R. hominis provided additional information for distinguishing metabolic disorder status and stratifying cardiometabolic severity. Integration of phenotype-associated variants with circulating metabolomics prioritized ohyA, encoding an oleate hydratase, as a candidate functional determinant linking R. hominis genetic variation to host metabolic heterogeneity. An ohyA-based genetic burden score was associated with adverse cardiometabolic traits and changed longitudinally during dietary intervention, while circulating metabolites statistically accounted for part of the associations between ohyA variants and host phenotypes. Functional experiments demonstrated that R. hominis OhyA protein converts oleic acid to 10-hydroxystearic acid (10-HSA), whereas an OhyA carrying five prioritized missense substitutions showed markedly impaired enzymatic activity. In high-fat diet-fed mice, 10-HSA attenuated body-weight gain, improved glucose homeostasis and insulin sensitivity, and reduced dyslipidemia and hepatic steatosis. Multi-omics profiling revealed limited remodeling of the gut microbiota but pronounced hepatic transcriptional and metabolic responses, characterized by activation of PPAR-associated lipid-metabolic pathways, altered fatty-acid oxidation and desaturation, and remodeling of hepatic lipid composition. Together, these findings establish a diet-responsive R. hominis-OhyA-10-HSA axis linking microbial variation to host metabolic dysfunction and show that 10-HSA can improve metabolic health in mice.

papers.title: The binding landscape of Ras/effector interactions provides insights on Ras switching and oncogenesis
papers.abstract: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) regulate essential cellular processes, yet the evolutionary principles that shape their specificity, adaptability, and dysregulation in disease remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the evolution of a signaling PPI between the small GTPase Ras and its effector Nore1A, a tumor suppressor involved in Ras-mediated signaling. Ras acts as a molecular switch, engaging effectors in its GTP-bound active state and releasing them after GTP hydrolysis, whereas oncogenic mutations such as G12D lock Ras in the active state, promoting aberrant signaling in cancer. Using yeast surface display, deep mutational scanning, and data normalization, we systematically mapped the Ras/Nore1A binding landscape under different physiological and oncogenic states. We generated and screened $\sim$33,000 Nore1A single and double mutants against RasWT and RasG12D in both GTP- and GDP-bound states. Our data revealed that most Nore1A mutations produce small-to-moderate decrease in Ras affinity, while a small number of substitutions enhance affinity. Unexpectedly, GTP hydrolysis causes minimal remodeling of the interaction landscape. Conversely, the oncogenic RasG12D mutation reshapes the binding landscape, revealing many Nore1A variants with enhanced and selective affinity for mutant Ras. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of Nore1A-Ras variant complexes suggest that the non-optimality of the Nore1A/RasG12D binding landscape arises, in part, from the greater intrinsic flexibility of RasG12D and the pronounced reduction in flexibility induced by affinity-enhancing Nore1A mutations. These findings demonstrate that disease-associated mutations can create new evolutionary trajectories in signaling PPIs by changing interaction dynamics and provide a framework for engineering selective protein-based inhibitors targeting oncogenic Ras variants.

papers.title: TRACE: a framework for traceable biomedical resource construction demonstrated through single-cell glaucoma data
papers.abstract: The growing availability of public omics datasets presents opportunities for biomedical research, yet constructing research question-driven resources from distributed studies remains challenging due to heterogeneous data, incomplete metadata and limited documentation of curation decisions. Here, we present TRACE (Traceable Resource Assembly and Curation Ecosystem), a general framework that links systematic knowledge discovery, data curation and resource delivery while preserving provenance throughout resource construction. We demonstrate TRACE through TRACE-scGlaucoma, a curated single-cell transcriptomics resource for glaucoma and optic nerve biology. Systematic screening identified 57 eligible studies, of which 42 provided accessible datasets comprising approximately 3.3 million cells. The resource provides harmonised metadata, standardised cell-type annotations and reusable expression objects while retaining original study information and curation provenance. We demonstrate its analytical utility through cellular enrichment of glaucoma GWAS-associated genes, comparing candidate drug-repurposing signals across distinct biological contexts and assessment of cell-type annotation reliability. TRACE provides a systematic and traceable approach to transforming fragmented public datasets into reusable biomedical resources, supporting reproducible analyses and future extensions across disease areas and data modalities.

papers.title: A Kernel-Spectral Index for Single-Neuron Input-Output Complexity
papers.abstract: The computational capacity of individual neurons in the brain is a central problem in computational neuroscience and an increasingly relevant link between neuroscience and AI. Recent work fitting artificial neural networks to detailed cortical pyramidal neurons showed that reproducing their millisecond-precision input-output behavior can require temporal convolutional networks with five to eight layers, suggesting that cortical neurons may function as deep computational units inside brain circuits. Yet current quantitative studies of single-neuron complexity are largely surrogate-based; consequently, the obtained results are difficult to interpret, and the process often demands massive computational resources. We introduce the Spectral Complexity Index (SCI), a white-box measure that represents presynaptic histories with an explicit kernel geometry and quantifies how many ordered spectral modes are needed to explain somatic response energy. Across 35 biophysically detailed human and mouse cortical neuron models, SCI yields a statistically significant separation of the two species, strongly agrees with the DNN-based Functional Complexity Index on these cells (Spearman correlation: {rho}=0.797), and remains stable under sampling and kernel perturbations. Additionally, compared to existing methods such as FCI, the computational cost of SCI is reduced to approximately 1/10 or less. SCI turns single-neuron complexity from a black-box surrogate property into an interpretable spectral object, enabling reproducible, fast, and efficient comparisons of neuronal computation across cells and species.

papers.title: Translating chemical reactions into enzyme sequences enables formate dehydrogenase engineering
papers.abstract: Enzyme engineering has broad applications across chemistry and biotechnology but remains costly and susceptible to low success rates. Generative artificial intelligence can substantially expand the sequence space accessible to enzyme engineering; however, directing generation towards enzymes that catalyse a user-defined chemical reaction remains challenging. Inspired by machine translation, we formulate enzyme generation as translation between two molecular languages: chemical reactions and amino acid sequences. Here, we introduce REXzyme, a translation model that generates enzymes conditioned on user-defined reactions. First, we evaluate its designs using multiple in silico metrics and characterize the strengths and limitations of its generalisation capacity. Then, we steer REXzyme towards the generation of enhanced formate dehydrogenases for their reverse natural reaction, i.e., the reduction of carbon dioxide. All 20 generated enzymes were expressed and purified as soluble proteins and exhibited CO2-reduction activity, with the most active design reaching 2.5-fold the specific activity of the reference enzyme. Notably, all substitutions in the designed variants were performed on distal positions outside the catalytic site. Our results show that reaction-to-sequence translation provides a route for efficiently engineering enhanced biocatalysts.

papers.title: Parallel descending neurons differentially encode target and looming information in the hoverfly visual system
papers.abstract: Detecting small, fast-moving objects is crucial for behaviors such as pursuit, territorial defence, and predator avoidance. At long range, however, potential mates, rivals, and predators produce remarkably similar visual signals, potentially making them difficult to distinguish. Nevertheless, many flying insects, including the hoverfly Eristalis tenax, can respond rapidly and appropriately to these ambiguous visual cues, implying specialised neural pathways that extract behaviorally relevant information. Descending neurons link visual processing to motor output, thus transforming visual signals into behavioral actions. In E. tenax, both target selective descending neurons (TSDNs) and looming-sensitive descending neurons respond to small targets, yet their respective contributions to target processing remain unclear. Using electrophysiological recordings, we compared receptive field organization and sensitivity to target size and motion direction across these neuronal populations. Although TSDNs and looming-sensitive descending neurons differed systematically in their target coding, a subset of looming-sensitive descending neurons closely resembled TSDNs, sharing small receptive fields and sharp target tuning despite retaining sensitivity to looming stimuli. These findings reveal previously unrecognized diversity among descending neurons tuned to small targets and suggest that parallel descending pathways encode distinct information from similar visual cues. Such an organization may enable common visual inputs to support both target pursuit and the detection of approaching threats.

papers.title: WheatPanRef: a unified linear pan-reference genome for wheat genomics
papers.abstract: Linear reference genomes provide coordinates for read mapping, variant discovery and multi-omics data integration, yet assembly-specific coordinate systems limit data reuse, particularly in the large, repetitive and polyploid wheat genome. Here, we present WheatPanRef, a scalable linear pan-reference and coordinate framework that integrates wheat sequence diversity within a stable coordinate system. We reconciled independent Chinese Spring assemblies by resolving structural and sequences discrepancies to constructed a 14.50-Gb consensus sequences CS-NP. Using CS-NP as backbone, we incorporated 4.37 Gb of non-redundant non-CS sequences from 37 diverse wheat accessions, generating WheatPanRef (18.87 Gb). WheatPanRef improves read-alignment performance and captures putative wild-relative introgressions and sequences absent or unanchored in conventional references. Bidirectional coordinate-translation system enables accurate projection between WheatPanRef and individual assemblies without remapping, facilitating genomic resource integration and reuse. WheatPanRef provides a common sequence and coordinate foundation for population-scale wheat genomics, with potential utility for genomic resource integration in other complex crops.

papers.title: LCN2+ Astrocytes Mark a Pro-inflammatory Astrocyte State Associated with Secondary Brain Injury After Cerebral Venous Thrombosis
papers.abstract: Cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT) is a cerebrovascular disorder with unique pathophysiological characteristics. Although the mortality rate during the acute phase has declined in recent years, the cellular mechanisms underlying secondary brain injury and long-term neurological dysfunction after CVT remain poorly understood [1,2]. In this study, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing of brain tissues from a murine CVT model to systematically characterize the cellular landscape following CVT and identified a reactive astrocyte state characterized by high expression of Lcn2. This astrocyte subset was markedly enriched after CVT. Notably, despite the absence of significant changes in the overall proportion of astrocytes, this population exhibited enhanced inflammatory/cytokine response signatures, ferroptosis-related stress responses, and vascular-immune microenvironment remodeling programs, suggesting that the major alteration of astrocytes after CVT is driven primarily by state transition rather than cellular expansion. Pseudotime trajectory analysis further demonstrated that Lcn2+ astrocytes were predominantly localized at the late stage of the trajectory and displayed sustained upregulation of multiple inflammation- and stress-associated genes, supporting their characterization as a late-stage reactive astrocyte state under CVT conditions. Cell-cell communication analysis revealed extensive predicted interactions between this subset and myeloid cells, vascular-associated cells, as well as neuronal/synaptic populations, indicating its potential involvement in dynamic remodeling of the lesion microenvironment. Cross-model integration analysis further revealed the presence of Lcn2-high astrocytes in the middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) model; however, their expression breadth and intensity were generally weaker than those observed in CVT, suggesting that this cellular state may represent a common reactive framework following cerebrovascular obstruction, while being particularly pronounced in CVT. Furthermore, genetic deletion of LCN2 alleviated CVT-induced brain tissue injury in vivo, providing functional evidence supporting the detrimental role of the LCN2-associated pathological state. Collectively, our study identifies a distinct Lcn2-high reactive astrocyte state after CVT that is closely associated with inflammatory amplification, ferroptosis-related stress, and microenvironmental remodeling. These findings provide new cellular insights into the mechanisms underlying secondary brain injury after CVT and highlight potential targets for therapeutic intervention.

papers.title: Increased activity without changes in coupling between somata and apical dendrites during visual mismatches
papers.abstract: Leading theories of cortical function posit that sensory processing involves a comparison between top-down predictions and bottom-up sensory data. Tests of these theories have been hampered by experimental challenges related to simultaneously recording top-down and bottom-up signals in response to sensory stimuli that either do or do not match internally-generated predictions. Here, we conduct dual-plane 2-photon calcium imaging near-simultaneously from distal apical dendrites and somata of pyramidal neurons in each of 4 different regions of mouse visual cortex while the mice are presented with visual sequences that can either match or mismatch previously habituated visual stimuli. Specifically, we examine the responses in the distal apical dendrites and cell bodies of pyramidal neurons while mice view either movie clips that reverse unexpectedly or Gabor patch sequences that have orientations that do not match habituated patterns. We find that in response to unexpected reversals in natural movies, both the apical dendrites and somata show increased activity that decreases over repeated exposures, consistent with a prediction error response. However, we do not find any clear evidence for increased activity in response to mismatches in Gabor sequences, beyond possible release from adaptation effects. We additionally use volumetric images to connect dendritic and somatic compartments and examine the coupling between connected dendrites and cell bodies in layer 5 pyramidal neurons. We do not find evidence for changes in coupling in response to mismatch stimuli, either for natural movies or Gabor sequences. Our results are consistent across four regions of visual cortex. We also observe that increased responses to reversals in natural movies are stronger in layer 2/3 than layer 5 pyramidal neurons. Altogether, these data suggest that visual cortex is sensitive to deviations from previously-experienced naturalistic inputs. Our data do not suggest that this mismatch sensitivity extends to artificial stimuli, nor do they support theories of prediction error causing changes in the coupling between apical dendrites and somata.

papers.title: memVar: an integrated resource for interpreting human membrane protein variation in molecular and disease contexts
papers.abstract: Interpreting membrane protein variation requires connecting clinical evidence to the membrane environments and molecular interactions that govern protein functions. Here, we introduce memVar (https://memvar.sunnylab.org), an integrated database of 10,906,688unique single-nucleotide variants from ClinVar, COSMIC, and gnomAD across 7,732 human membrane-associated proteins. memVar reconciles genomic, transcript, and protein coordinates to link variants with membrane topology, bilayer depth, lipid contacts, functional sites, partner-specific interaction interfaces, and variant-effect predictions, alongside disease, tissue-expression and regulatory annotations. Coordinated sequence, structure and variant views retain source provenance and distinguish clinical assertions, experimental observations, and computational predictions. Our analysis reveals that pathogenic/likely pathogenic missense substitutions are enriched in transmembrane segments and predicted protein-protein interaction sites relative to benign/likely benign substitutions, with pooled odds ratios of 2.47 and 6.67, respectively. IntAct-derived interaction loss or decrease was experimentally recorded for 57.9% of pathogenic/likely pathogenic substitutions versus 7.4% of benign/likely benign substitutions. CFTR examples contextualize the established G551D gating defect and prioritize W202R, a variant of uncertain significance, for tests of protein maturation, surface abundance and channel activity. By connecting variant records to specific molecular questions, memVar potentially supports mechanism-oriented investigation and prioritization of functional experiments.

papers.title: TIGRdisco: a tool for the discovery of TIGR arrays and TIGR-associated Tas proteins from nucleotide sequences
papers.abstract: Tandem Interspaced Guide RNA (TIGR)-TIGR-associated protein (Tas) systems mediate DNA targeting through a hypercompact Tas effector, guided by dual spacers within a tigRNA that is processed from TIGR arrays. TIGR-Tas loci are composed of a Tas coding sequence associated with TIGR arrays of short units in either dual-repeat or stem-loop architecture. Unlike CRISPR (Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats) arrays that comprise units of direct repeats interspersed with unique spacers, units within the two distinct TIGR architectures only conform through extremely short box motifs, complicating detection. Here, we present TIGRdisco, an integrated tool capable of discovering both the Tas protein and its associated TIGR arrays directly from unannotated nucleotide sequences. TIGRdisco implements independent engines to detect the two array architectures through a motif-agnostic approach. We benchmarked TIGRdisco against a reference dataset of TIGR-Tas loci, recovering more than 80% of array units within its search window. Furthermore, TIGRdisco recovered arrays for loci within entire clades of Tas where associated arrays were unannotated in the reference. We found that these arrays largely contain non-canonical box motifs or unit lengths. Lastly, as a case study, we utilized TIGRdisco and successfully uncovered TIGR-Tas loci across metagenomic and genomic datasets.

papers.title: Growth-driven mechanical buckling as a mechanism of age-related tortuosity in human cerebral arteries
papers.abstract: Human cerebral arteries become increasingly, sometimes abnormally, winding with age, but the mechanical basis of this change remains incompletely understood. To examine how arterial bends form and what sets their spacing, we modeled a cerebral artery as a slender elastic vessel supported by surrounding tissue. The distance between its ends remains constant, and the vessel can bend only in a plane tangent to the brain surface. As its natural length increases, axial compression builds until the vessel buckles. Bending partly relieves the compression, and the resulting waves grow in amplitude as elongation continues. Arterial bending stiffness and tissue support determine the wavelength, which is much larger than and proportional to vessel diameter, with comparatively weak dependence on other parameters. Numerical simulations captured a pre-buckling phase, rapid amplification of waves, and slow post-buckling growth during continued elongation. We evaluated these predictions using three-dimensional centerlines of cerebral arteries reconstructed from magnetic resonance angiography in healthy adults. Older age was associated with greater arterial length and excess-length ratio. For arterial waves oriented mostly parallel to the brain surface, wavelength increased with vessel diameter. Both this relationship and the observed wavelength-to-diameter ratio were consistent with model predictions. However, wave amplitude was not significantly associated with age. Overall, the modeling and imaging results support growth-driven buckling and post-buckling deformation under spatial constraint as a plausible mechanical explanation for age-related cerebral arterial tortuosity. This framework links vascular aging to growth-driven instability and pattern formation, with potential applications to diseased arteries beyond the brain.

papers.title: ClearGel: a thermoresponsive hydrogel for chronic, near-millimeter two-photon imaging through the intact skull
papers.abstract: The intact skull remains a fundamental barrier to high-resolution two-photon neuroimaging in live mice. Existing skull-clearing methods, however, cannot simultaneously provide deep cortical access, spatial selectivity, reversibility, and biological safety. Here we introduce ClearGel, a thermoresponsive hydrogel that undergoes rapid in situ gelation upon contact with the skull, confining the clearing agents to the targeted region while sustaining their release over time. ClearGel routinely enables two-photon imaging down to approximately 800 m through the intact skull-a depth statistically equivalent to open-skull windows and substantially surpassing all prior approaches. It supports user-defined clearing patterns from focal sites to whole-skull coverage, allows repeated imaging over 14 days through a reversible optical interface, and, critically, enables awake functional imaging of both neuronal Ca2+ activity and the more elusive cAMP dynamics at single-cell resolution. ClearGel requires only simple topical application-no craniotomy or skull thinning-and provides a minimally invasive, chronic-compatible optical window for longitudinal studies of cortical function in behaving mice.

papers.title: Benchmarking Statistical Methods for Differential Composition Analysis in Population-Scale Single-Cell Data
papers.abstract: Population-scale single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data capture cellular composition across cohorts ranging from several dozen to thousands of individuals, enabling the detection of cell-type composition differences between conditions. These differences reveal cellular shifts in disease pathogenesis and suggest potential targets for therapeutic intervention. However, differential composition analysis in scRNA-seq data is challenged by the unique features of cell count data, such as compositionality, prevalence of zeros, overdispersion, and confounding by technical and biological covariates. While this analysis is routinely performed, no study has yet systematically evaluated existing methods. Here, we benchmarked 12 methods for differential composition analysis using three population-scale scRNA-seq datasets with diverse and representative characteristics. Analyses of real data revealed low agreement across methods, while permutations and simulations based on the real data demonstrated excessive false discoveries for most methods. Overall, LOCOM emerged as the top-performing method that controls the false discovery rate while maintaining good statistical power, followed by ANCOM-BC and linear regression with centered-log-ratio transformation. Integrating evidence from real-data analyses and data-informed permutation and simulation experiments, we provide practical guidance tailored to common real-world challenges in differential composition analysis.

papers.title: The Pseudomonas protegens PBL3 secretome exerts antimicrobial activity against Burkholderia glumae by disrupting cell envelope homeostasis and impairing bacterial replication
papers.abstract: The effectiveness of antimicrobials used to manage bacterial infections is increasingly threatened by the emergence of antimicrobial resistance. Many conventional antimicrobials act on a single defined target that pathogens can circumvent through target modification or pathway adaptation. In contrast, antimicrobials that disrupt multiple cellular processes may impose greater fitness costs and reduce the likelihood of resistance development, making their discovery a priority for pharmaceutical and agricultural applications. We previously demonstrated that the environmental bacterium Pseudomonas protegens PBL3 secretes a complex mixture of molecules (secretome) with antimicrobial activity against several plants and human pathogens. However, the mechanism underlying this activity remained unknown. Here, we used the plant pathogen Burkholderia glumae to investigate the mode of action of the P. protegens PBL3 secretome. We showed that the P. protegens PLB3 secretome causes extensive cell envelope damage that results in cell death and interferes with bacterial multiplication. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed broad disruption of processes associated with cell-envelope biogenesis and homeostasis and bacterial replication. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the P. protegens PBL3 secretome acts as a multi-target antimicrobial that could be harnessed in the development of therapeutics to control bacterial infections of agricultural and medical importance.

papers.title: Sex differences in cell type-specific transcriptional programs and GPCR signaling in the human subgenual anterior cingulate cortex
papers.abstract: Psychiatric conditions show marked sex differences in disease onset, symptom presentation, and response to treatments. Understanding how sex differences manifest across molecularly distinct neuronal populations in individuals without psychiatric conditions may help explain sex-dependent variation in neural circuit function and treatment response. Here, we examined molecularly distinct cell types within the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) of non-psychiatric subjects. Using RNA sequencing data previously generated from laser-capture microdissected neurons, we investigated sex differences in gene expression and co-expression networks in excitatory pyramidal neurons (layers 2/3 and 5/6) and somatostatin (SST)-, parvalbumin (PVALB)-, and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)-expressing inhibitory interneurons (N=10 males, 9 females). We identified sex differences in transcriptomic profiles, biological pathways, and co-expression network connectivity. PVALB cells showed stronger overall female transcriptional enrichment, while SST cells exhibited male-enriched transcriptional signatures. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis identified PVALB and SST modules more connected in males and females, respectively, which included hub genes involved in immune, extracellular matrix, and bioenergetic processes. Since G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are viable therapeutic targets, we examined sex differences in GPCR transcripts. Across all GPCR-cell-type combinations, CHRM2 in PVALB cells showed the second strongest sex difference (enriched in females). To test the functional relevance of this difference, we used patch-clamp electrophysiology in mouse prefrontal cortex. M2 receptor activation increased maximal firing rates in PVALB cells from female but not male mice. Collectively, our findings demonstrate cell type-specific sex differences in the sgACC corresponding to functional differences in neuromodulator signaling, with potential implications for treatment response.

papers.title: Temperature alters Culex tarsalis West Nile virus vector competence, tissue bottlenecks, and transcriptional responses
papers.abstract: West Nile virus is an arbovirus transmitted by Culex mosquitoes. Temperature is frequently the strongest abiotic factor impacting transmission in many virus-vector pairings, including WNV and Culex. However, it is unknown how temperature impacts WNV population bottlenecks and transcriptional responses to infection in Culex tarsalis. We found that elevated temperatures led to increased likelihood of transmission of rare virus variants due to increased vector competence and less stringent tissue barriers. Analysis of Cx. tarsalis transcriptional responses confirmed that WNV infection had minimal impacts on transcriptional activity. Temperature, however, induced significant changes to mosquito gene expression, whereas canonical immune gene expression minimally changed in response to infection. Thus, temperature impacts bottlenecks in the Culex-WNV system independent of known antiviral pathways, possibly by altering virus replication dynamics. While temperature had a dramatic impact on bottleneck stringency, this is likely independent of antiviral pathways and instead some other change to mosquito biology. Together, these results shed light on the relationships between temperature, virus evolutionary dynamics and antiviral immunity.

papers.title: Traveling waves in attention networks inherit the rhythms of sensory systems
papers.abstract: Attention emerges from coordinated activity across distributed brain regions, each with their own intrinsic rhythm: alpha (7-12Hz) in visual cortex and theta (3-7Hz) in auditory cortex. When attention is sustained on a visual location, alpha power increases over the corresponding ipsilateral hemisphere, a robust neurophysiological marker of sustained visuospatial attention named alpha lateralization. Hemispheric asymmetry during sustained attention was recently also reported for anterior-to-posterior alpha traveling waves -smooth phase shifts across the cortex. This finding suggests that traveling waves support top-down inter-areal communication within the attention network. Here we asked whether traveling waves indeed reflect top-down attention signals or are merely a byproduct of sustained visuospatial attention. We manipulated attention through different sensory modalities (auditory cueing and visual stimulation), thus engaging different sensory cortices, while maintaining the task as visual discrimination. Using electroencephalography, we tested the hypothesis that if traveling waves reflect attention signals within the network, their frequency should follow the intrinsic rhythm of the engaged sensory system: theta for auditory cueing and alpha for visual stimulation. If instead they are a byproduct of attention allocated to visual information, their frequency should remain in alpha. Our results support the former: auditory cueing led to lateralized theta traveling waves, while visual stimulation produced lateralized alpha traveling waves. Crucially, traveling-wave lateralization in both frequencies correlated with trial-by-trial alpha power lateralization. Together, attention signals appear to propagate as waves at the intrinsic rhythm of the engaged sensory system and locally modulate alpha power lateralization in task-relevant visual regions.

papers.title: Evaluating State-Transition Models in Short Resting-State fMRI with Continuous-Dynamics Controls
papers.abstract: Hidden Markov models (HMMs) are widely used to describe changes in resting-state functional MRI as transitions between a finite set of inferred brain states. However, continuously varying brain activity can produce similar apparent transitions, raising questions about their biological validity. We tested whether discrete and continuous brain dynamics could be distinguished by predicting subsequent fMRI measurements, and if temporal filtering affects this distinction. We compared hidden Markov models (HMMs) with vector autoregressive (VAR) models, which predict signals from preceding measurements without assuming discrete states. Each time point contained signals from the seven Yeo functional networks. Both models used the same preceding observations to predict the next, with accuracy measured by the log probability density assigned to the observed signals. Across 864 simulated conditions, HMMs performed better in 139/144 unfiltered discrete-state cases, whereas VAR performed better in 67/72 continuous cases. Changing only the filter during testing increased the number of continuous cases favoring HMMs from 2/72 with fixed filtering to 68/72, despite unchanged underlying dynamics. We also analyzed resting-state fMRI from 270 ADNI participants (90 cognitively normal, 90 with mild cognitive impairment, and 90 with dementia). VAR outperformed HMM in 160/184 datasets with at least 180 time points and 60/86 shorter recordings. In simulations, HMMs inferred directional state transitions even from smoothly evolving activity without discrete switching. Thus, apparent fMRI state transitions do not necessarily indicate discrete underlying dynamics. Their interpretation requires comparison with continuous models and attention to temporal filtering.

papers.title: Robust T and B cell activation is associated with rapid clearance of infectious SARS-CoV-2
papers.abstract: The immunologic correlates of rapid clearance of SARS-CoV-2 shedding are not well understood, partly due to challenges of collecting samples early after infection and the fact that most studies do not measure infectious virus. Here, we performed mass cytometry profiling of peripheral blood cells collected from people 4-6 days after onset of symptoms from acute SARS-CoV-2 infection who underwent daily nasopharyngeal testing for SARS-CoV-2 culture positivity. We identified broad and coordinated activation of innate and adaptive immune cells in unvaccinated individuals with primary infection. Faster clearance of infectious virus shedding was associated with robust adaptive immune cell activation and proliferation, namely among cytotoxic CD8+, CD4+, and {gamma}{delta} T cells and plasmablasts. In contrast, vaccinated individuals who rapidly cleared breakthrough infection showed minimal cellular immune activation. Our findings identify early immune correlates of rapid clearance of infectious SARS-CoV-2 shedding that may inform future prevention and therapeutic approaches to reduce disease burden and transmission.

papers.title: Mapping the regulatory wiring of endothelial cell differentiation reveals a critical role for Hippo mechanosignaling
papers.abstract: At each step of development, stem cells encounter a branching decision to differentiate into one type of cell or another. This decision is executed through the action of competing gene programs that specify different cellular identities. Consequently, creating a comprehensive map of the gene programs that drive each branching step of human cell differentiation remains a long-sought goal of developmental and stem cell biology. Here, we introduce a framework combining genome-wide CRISPR screens, single-cell readouts, and gene program inference to systematically discover and characterize regulators of cell differentiation. This framework includes a method for CRISPR perturbations paired with single-cell RNA-seq called circular capture Perturb-seq (CC-Perturb-seq), which improves gRNA detection from split-pool combinatorial indexing protocols and enables perturbing many candidate regulators to map their effects on gene programs. We applied this framework to map how human pluripotent stem cells differentiate into arterial endothelial cells (ECs), and identified 174 regulators that promote or inhibit EC differentiation. By tracking gene programs across three stages of differentiation, we resolved when and how regulators divert cells toward alternative fates. This map revealed an unexpected requirement for the Hippo mechanosignaling pathway in EC specification. During lateral mesoderm differentiation, Hippo mechanosignaling was required to activate ETV2, the master transcriptional regulator of endothelial identity. Inhibiting Hippo blocked ETV2 even in the presence of VEGF and diverted progenitors to a mesenchymal fate in vitro. Likewise, Hippo signaling was required for maximal etv2 expression in developing zebrafish embryos. Conversely, pharmacologically activating the Hippo pathway increased the purity of both arterial and venous EC differentiation in vitro. Our framework thus identifies novel regulators of endothelial cell differentiation, improves stem-cell differentiation protocols via manipulation of mechanosignaling, and provides a generalizable platform for mapping the regulatory wiring of human development.

papers.title: ACTIVATION OF THE ARYL HYDROCARBON RECEPTOR REDUCES VISCERAL HYPERSENSITIVITY IN A MOUSE MODEL OF COLITIS IN REMISSION
papers.abstract: The aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) is expressed on gut-projecting transient receptor potential vanilloid-1 (TRPV1)+ nociceptors, but whether it has a role in regulating abdominal pain remains to be determined. Approximately 50% of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients experience chronic abdominal pain, even when their inflammatory disease is in remission. Previous work has shown that tryptophan metabolism to indole derivatives is reduced in IBD patients. Since microbial tryptophan metabolites (indole derivatives) serve as ligands for AhR, we hypothesized that reduced AhR activation contributes to enhanced pain sensitivity. We used a post-colitis mouse model of visceral hypersensitivity to examine the role of AhR as a mediator of nociception. AhR activation using both natural and synthetic agonists reduced visceral hypersensitivity in both male and female post-colitis mice. Conversely, pharmacological inhibition of AhR blocked the antinociceptive effects of indoles. Mechanistically, AhR activation by indole-3-pyruvic acid (IPyA) increased the transcription of the inward rectifying potassium channel Kir2.2, in TRPV1+ neurons and markedly reduced neuronal activation within the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Metagenomic analysis revealed sex differences in indole-producing bacteria, with control males exhibiting enriched abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and Alistipes compared to post-colitis males and female controls. These findings demonstrate that oral IPyA supplementation in post-colitis mice attenuates visceral hypersensitivity in part through activation of nociceptor AhR, providing insights that support the therapeutic targeting of AhR to treat abdominal pain in IBD patients in remission.

papers.title: Social vision expands into auditory cortices of people born deaf: evidence from naturalistic film and encoding models
papers.abstract: Comparing deaf and hearing adults provides insight into the contribution of experience to function of auditory cortical networks. We used naturalistic fMRI and voxel-wise encoding to measure information processing in auditory networks of deaf (n=24) and hearing (n=22) adults who watched a 35-minute silent animated film. Unlike simpler stimuli, naturalistic films are rich in a broad range of perceptual, affective, and social features, including motion, dynamic social interactions, and Theory of Mind. Machine vision algorithms and human coding were used to densely annotate visual and social film features. In both groups we observed a right-lateralized processing hierarchy with encoding of low-level visual features in early visual areas, social visual features along the superior temporal sulcus (STS) and Theory of Mind in temporoparietal junction. In deaf participants, auditory cortices showed enhanced encoding of a broad range of visual information, from low level motion to Theory of Mind. In higher order auditory networks, social interactions emerging as the strongest predictor of neural activity in deaf people and showed the strongest enhancement in deafness. Auditory networks of deaf adults showed systematic anatomical organization within and across hemispheres.
