Treatment with nab-sirolimus significantly suppressed tumour growth and reduced phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6, consistent with suppression of downstream mTORC1 signalling. In this study, the optimized CDX model retains key EHE features and provides an extended observation window with sustained growth of untreated controls, supporting longitudinal assessment of antitumour activity and pharmacodynamic responses. This platform provides a practical framework for evaluating and comparing candidate therapies for EHE.

papers.title: Direct NMR evidence for transient binding of the vesicular SNARE protein synaptobrevin-2/VAMP2 to the α-synuclein C-terminus
papers.abstract: The protein -synuclein (-syn) plays a central role in several neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson's disease; however, its physiological function remains enigmatic. We provide direct evidence by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, microscale thermophoresis (MST), and biolayer interferometry (BLI) measurements that the -synuclein C-terminus binds to the vesicular SNARE (soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor) protein synaptobrevin-2 (syb-2), also known as VAMP2 (vesicle-associated membrane protein). The observed dissociation constant (Kd) in the 10 - 50 micromolar range falls within the estimated concentration range of -synuclein in neurons, while local concentrations may be substantially higher. NMR chemical shift perturbation (CSP) and paramagnetic relaxation enhancement (PRE) experiments mapped the binding site with residue-specific resolution to the -synuclein C-terminus (V118 - E137) and to the synaptobrevin-2 SNARE motif/linker domain interface (region A82 - K87), and also affected the synaptobrevin-2 N-terminus (M1 - S2). NMR CSPs and PREs indicate a transient interaction in the fast exchange (s-ms) regime. These transient weak binding interactions are characteristic of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and allow both proteins to engage in multiple binding interactions, thereby enabling -synuclein to play a regulatory role upstream of or during neuronal exocytosis. While the exact physiological role of -synuclein remains debated, the involvement of its pathological form in several neurodegenerative diseases (dubbed synucleinopathies) is well established. Our data suggest a direct link between proteins involved in neurodegeneration and neuronal exocytosis.

papers.title: The FDA-approved CDK4/6 inhibitor Abemaciclib is a potent agonist of the β-arrestin-biased atypical chemokine receptor ACKR3
papers.abstract: Atypical chemokine receptor 3 (ACKR3/CXCR7) is an intrinsically {beta}-arrestin-biased family-A GPCR that controls chemokine availability by scavenging CXCL12 and CXCL11, and consequently plays a key role in cancer, chronic inflammation, autoimmunity, cardiovascular disease, and CNS repair. Despite its pathophysiological significance, the chemical space available to interrogate and therapeutically modulate this receptor remains limited. Here, by using a drug-repurposing strategy to screen 2,342 FDA-approved compounds in a NanoBRET-based fluorescent chemokine-binding competition assay, we identified the clinically used CDK4/6 inhibitor abemaciclib (Verzenios(R)) as a nanomolar ACKR3 ligand. Abemaciclib inhibited CXCL12 binding to ACKR3 with comparable affinity to the ACKR3-reference agonist VUF15485, whereas the related clinically used CDK4/6 inhibitors palbociclib, ribociclib, dalpiciclib and trilaciclib were inactive on this receptor. Binding and functional profiling across classical and atypical chemokine receptors revealed selectivity for ACKR3, including lack of detectable activity at the CXCL12 receptors CXCR4 and ACKR5. Abemaciclib acted as a potent ACKR3 agonist, recruiting both {beta}-arrestin-1 and 2 and promoting rapid receptor internalization with potencies and efficacies, like the reference ACKR3 agonist VUF15485. Major CYP3A4-derived abemaciclib metabolites retained ACKR3 binding and agonist activity, albeit with reduced potency. Methionine 13C-HSQC NMR confirmed direct receptor engagement and revealed a small-molecule-like ACKR3 conformational signature distinct from the CXCL12-bound state. Cryo-EM of the abemaciclib-ACKR3-CID24 complex at 3.2 [A] uncovered a unique, inverted U-shaped ligand binding pose in the orthosteric pocket and activation-associated rearrangements of TM6, TM7 and helix 8. Functionally, abemaciclib blocked ACKR3-mediated uptake of CXCL11 and CXCL12 in vitro. Moreover, oral administration of abemaciclib in mice resulted in a time-dependent increase in plasma CXCL12 levels, indicative of in vivo ACKR3 target engagement. These findings establish this FDA-approved kinase inhibitor as a potent ACKR3 modulator and reveal an unexpected pharmacological link of this CDK4/6 inhibitor to atypical chemokine receptor biology.

papers.title: Gut Stem Cell Secretome Therapy Promotes Durable Neuroprotection and Functional Recovery After Stroke
papers.abstract: Background: Stroke causes rapid neuronal death and gut barrier disruption in the acute phase, with persistent cognitive-affective impairment in the chronic phase. We previously showed that transplants of intestinal epithelial stem cells ameliorated the acute and chronic impairment of stroke. The current study tested the efficacy of a cell free strategy, specifically, the secretome of intestinal epithelial stem cells. Methods: Middle aged male and female rats underwent middle cerebral artery occlusion or sham surgery and received intestinal epithelial stem cell secretome from healthy sex-matched adult or control media. Behavioral assays (social interaction, novel object recognition and Barnes maze), gut histology, markers of gut permeability, serum cytokines were performed at acute and chronic time points. Group differences were assessed by two-way ANOVA. Results: In the acute phase, vehicle-treated stroke animals displayed histopathological changes in the gut including villus blunting, loss of goblet cells, increased markers of gut permeability and elevated systemic inflammation. In the chronic phase, stroke resulted in cognitive/affective changes including social withdrawal, recognition memory and spatial memory deficits. In middle-aged males, three doses of IESC secretome treatment 4h/24h/48h after stroke restored mucosal architecture, goblet cells and dampened inflammatory cytokines in the acute phase. Cognitive and social outcomes, tested 4+ weeks after stroke, were significantly improved compared to vehicle-treated stroke animals. However, in middle-aged females treated with the same regimen of intestinal epithelial stem cell secretome, gut architecture was not restored and inflammatory cytokines remained elevated. Long term cognitive impairment was only partially improved in this group. Proteomic analysis of the secretome revealed a largely shared core of proteins between males and females with sex differences in pathway level regulation. Subsequently, another cohort of middle-aged females was administered four doses of secretome 4h/12h/24h/36h after stroke. This regimen restored gut architecture and dampened inflammatory cytokines in the acute phase, and improved long term cognitive outcomes. Conclusions: Collectively, these studies underscore the therapeutic potential of IESC secretome and the importance of tailoring post stroke therapy by demographics such as biological sex. These data further support the hypothesis that gut repair is tightly associated with long-term improvement in stroke outcomes.

papers.title: Glioblastoma model mouse rescue from mortality by brain-targeted catalytically-enhanced angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 mutant-antibody fusion protein
papers.abstract: We have discovered that an engineered angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2)-brain-targeted antibody fusion protein, referred to as ACE2dm-s1, improves survival of CT-2A xenograft glioblastoma (GBM) model mice when administered in combination with a small molecule STING agonist cancer therapeutic. Particularly striking about these survival results is that prior efforts that used losartan, a small molecule angiotensin receptor antagonist that acts on the same Renin-Angiotensin System (RAS) axis that is affected by the action of ACE2dm-s1, showed that this small molecule provided no survival benefit when used as an element of combination therapy in the same CT-2A GBM model used in our experiments. The improved CT-2A mouse survival, which was not observed for ACE2dm-s1 or STING agonist monotherapy, combines with our flow cytometry study results that revealed an ACE2dm-s1-mediated shift of brain immune cell populations toward an anti-tumoral composition to establish ACE2dm-s1's utility as a tumor microenvironment (TME) modulator that could serve as an adjuvant in increasing the efficacy of wide range of cancer treatment modalities including chemotherapeutic agents, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and CAR-T cells.

papers.title: ALIGN: A modular framework for quantitative analysis of longitudinal development in Caenorhabditis elegans
papers.abstract: Longitudinal live imaging is a powerful tool for studying growth, development and behaviour. However, reproducible and scalable analysis of the large resulting datasets remains a major bottleneck. Here, we present ALIGN (Automated Longitudinal Image-based Growth aNalyzer), a modular framework that integrates deep learning-based segmentation, automated quality control, computational straightening, feature extraction and interactive annotation within a single configurable pipeline that can be operated end-to-end by users without coding expertise. Applying ALIGN to longitudinal development of C. elegans, we demonstrate accurate segmentation across heterogeneous imaging conditions, detection of larval stage transitions from growth trajectories, and data-driven quality control, ensuring high measurement precision. Computational straightening and alignment enable consistent analysis of motile animals, removing motion artefacts from three-dimensional optical sectioning. Applying ALIGN to measure pharyngeal pumping and growth rates in wild-type and eat-2 mutants uncovered a non-proportional relationship between feeding and growth. ALIGN thus provides generalizable tools and resources for longitudinal, single-animal analysis of development.

papers.title: The mechanism of cysteine sensing by LRRC58
papers.abstract: Cysteine is essential for life but toxic in excess. Cells and tissues are exposed to elevated cysteine from endogenous sources and the environment yet maintain low intracellular concentrations to sustain life. Here we identify a mechanism for sensing cysteine to control its abundance and prevent toxicity and premature death. Using cryo-electron microscopy we determine structures of the CRL5L^RRC58 E3 ligase alone and in complex with the cysteine-catabolizing enzyme CDO1. We show that CDO1 interacts with LRRC58 in the vicinity of a zinc-coordinating cysteine motif, within which Cys296 becomes covalently modified upon cysteine exposure. Covalent modification of Cys296 and zinc ejection from this motif drive large structural rearrangements of LRRC58 relayed through Cys319, which destabilize CDO1 binding and position LRRC58 Lys111 for autoubiquitylation. This reorientation of LRRC58 permits CDO1 accumulation, thereby lowering intracellular cysteine. Mutation of Cys319 abrogates inhibitory rearrangement of LRRC58 upon cysteine modification. This renders the ligase constitutively active and prevents CDO1 stabilization, thereby driving systemic cysteine accumulation and premature death in animals. These findings establish the molecular basis of homeostatic cysteine sensing by LRRC58 and demonstrate its essential role in maintaining cysteine concentrations compatible with healthy life.

papers.title: Stochastic gene expression drives state switching and phenotypic heterogeneity in RNA repair
papers.abstract: Bacterial populations often exhibit variability in cellular responses to antibiotics which can affect treatment success and survival outcomes. This heterogeneity suggests that genetically identical cells can occupy different states of susceptibility within the same population. Better understanding of these dynamic responses is essential for determining how cells respond to stress and survive antibiotic-induced damage. In this work, we investigate heterogeneity in antibiotic responses driven by the Rtc RNA repair system in E. coli. We develop a stochastic model of Rtc-mediated RNA repair to identify the drivers of heterogeneity at the single-cell level. We observe bimodality in cellular translational capacity and a transient memory in predicted responses to RNA damage, demonstrating how intrinsic stochasticity in Rtc-regulation can lead to phenotypic heterogeneity. Classifying single-cell trajectories, we predict drivers of state switching between the resistant and susceptible states, finding that stochastic expression of the rtc regulator determines entry into a resistant cell state, while dilution drives the system back into a susceptible state. These results indicate that heterogeneity in RNA repair emerges from stochastic switching between states, offering a route to understanding how individual cells survive in the presence of translation-targeting antibiotics.

papers.title: STRUCTURAL PLASTICITY ALLOWS DOUBLECORTIN AND DRUG-STABILIZED MICROTUBULES TO ACCOMMODATE EACH OTHER
papers.abstract: Microtubule architecture and dynamics are modulated by small molecules, but how these compounds alter lattice properties and interactions with cellular regulators remains incompletely understood. We used the neuronal microtubule-associated protein doublecortin (DCX), previously reported to preferentially recognize 13-protofilament microtubules, to probe lattices stabilized by different taxanes, including the fluorescent taxane Fchitax-3. We show that DCX binds 15-protofilament Fchitax-3-stabilized microtubules, demonstrating that DCX is not a specific marker of 13-protofilament architecture. Cryo-electron microscopy revealed that the fluorescent moiety of Fchitax-3 inserts into inter-protofilament lateral contacts, explaining its effects on microtubule architecture and dynamics. DCX binds Fchitax-3 microtubules through its N-terminal DC domain, which accommodates the narrower inter-protofilament binding site in the 15-protofilament lattice. Remarkably, although Fchitax-3 induces the longitudinal lattice expansion characteristic of taxanes, DCX remodels its binding site towards its preferred compacted configuration. Thus, taxanes can modify microtubule structure in distinct ways while preserving lattice plasticity and the capacity to undergo conformational remodelling by microtubule-associated proteins. This contrasts with the comparatively rigid lattice of GMPCPP-stabilized microtubules. Consequently, interpretations of microtubule lattice states based on comparisons between taxane- and GMPCPP-stabilized microtubules may conflate structural differences with different degrees of lattice plasticity. Our findings establish the microtubule lattice as a malleable structural substrate whose drug-induced conformations can be further remodelled by cellular binding partners.

papers.title: RAPTORGraph: graph-based pathway modeling for causal discovery in single-cell perturbations
papers.abstract: Experiments involving the perturbation of individual cells are central to understanding cellular mechanisms and can accelerate drug discovery. Causal representation learning allows us to uncover the latent factors that regulate biological systems and predict the impact of novel perturbations. Unfortunately, existing methods fail to address intervention spillover in a closed-world setting where intervention targets are known a priori, such as in Perturb-seq experiments, due to their reliance on dense encoders. Furthermore, incorporating curated biological pathways into the model imposes a confirmatory bias, forcing it to explain the data through preexisting pathways and reducing the set of hypotheses the model can explore, while discarding novel signals that lie outside the annotated pathways. In this work, we introduce RAPTORGraph, a {beta}-variational autoencoder with a GraphPathway encoder that explicitly models complex gene-to-gene interactions within learned pathways. Moreover, our model's preconditioning isolates the influence of perturbed genes, yielding clean, single-node latent interventions required for identifiable causal discovery and eliminating spillover. Finally, we train the model on data preprocessed with optimal-transport alignment, which guarantees a well-defined mapping between control and perturbed samples and further stabilizes the learned latent representations. We demonstrate that RAPTORGraph improves state-of-the-art performance on downstream analyses of unseen perturbations, such as non-additive interactions, while performing competitively on objective metrics, such as mean squared error and maximum mean discrepancy. The source code is available at https://github.com/sXperfect/RAPTORGraph.

papers.title: Autonomous generalizability auditing of scientific foundation models
papers.abstract: Determining where scientific foundation models generalize beyond their development data is essential for reliable use, but aggregate benchmarks obscure performance limits and rigorous audits are difficult to conduct routinely. Here, we introduce AutoSPECTRA, a coding-agent protocol for systematic generalizability auditing. To inform its design, we reviewed 38 studies across five biological domains and evaluated coding agents, which generated hypotheses and empirical analyses but applied inconsistent standards for judging evidence. We then structured AutoSPECTRA around measurable generalization axes, prespecified analyses, controlled comparisons and independent confirmation. Across four biological foundation models, audits linked performance to protein sequence composition and relatedness to pretraining data (ESMFold2), representation of perturbations in training (STATE), effective spatial resolution (CONCH), and residue-level genomic, evolutionary and structural context (AlphaMissense). Agents also evaluated alternative explanations and rejected unsupported hypotheses. AutoSPECTRA provides a systematic approach to discovering and testing the limits of scientific foundation models.

papers.title: A workflow to gather, clean, and standardize species occurrence records at scale for conservation applications
papers.abstract: Biodiversity declines and pressing threats to wildlife necessitate data-driven approaches for conservation and management planning. Natural resource agencies, conservation practitioners, and researchers increasingly leverage digital species occurrence records. However, we still lack user-friendly and flexible tools to aggregate, clean, and standardize such data. These tools are particularly needed for speciose groups like invertebrates and plants whose natural histories are poorly or unevenly known. To provide such a tool and overcome limitations of existing options, we developed a workflow in R that encompasses the entire process of aggregating, cleaning, and standardizing occurrence records within one free software platform. It additionally can return information useful for assessing species' conservation status. Key features include user friendliness, flexibility in data sources and filtering, handling large volumes of data or multiple species, and high transparency. We demonstrate workflow functionality focusing on Texas native bees. We combined bee data from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) and several smaller datasets, then cleaned and standardized the combined dataset including removing duplicates. Processing 145,870 bee records took about an hour on a standard-configuration government computer. We used the resulting records in three case studies that demonstrated various uses conservation practitioners commonly implement. Case study 1 compiled a species list for Denton County, the second described phenology of bumble bees (Bombus genus) in the Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex, and the third assessed conservation status of Bombus pensylvanicus. Our workflow greatly facilitates addressing a range of questions at various spatial and temporal scales from one vetted dataset that are tailored to the needs of a specific research objective, management question, municipality, or audience.

papers.title: A Distinct Mode of Chromosome-End Genome Instability Revealed by Circulome Characterization and Analyses
papers.abstract: Genome instability is a central hallmark of cancer and it is characterized largely from sequence: mutation, copy-number change and rearrangement scored against a linear reference. The genome has additional degrees of freedom, such as the physical form (topology) of the DNA itself. A specific mode of localized genome dynamics changes both dimensions (sequence and topology) at once: defined chromosomal regions are also represented as extrachromosomal circular DNA (eccDNA). The biogenesis of eccDNA is a feature of many cancers, supplying the tumor with genetic elements that can participate in phenotypic selection, and supplying the observer with a window into the genomic instability landscape. Genome-wide maps of where these circles arise have not been available at scale or at high resolution. Building such maps requires physical selection of circular species, because most sequenced reads from unselected DNA derive from unrearranged sequence, conflating the signal from dynamic rearrangements with that from bulk chromosomal DNA. Here we combine biophysical and biochemical isolation of circular DNA with next-generation sequencing, applying it to a panel of cancer cell lines and to patient tumors, with non-cancerous cells and adjacent normal tissues as controls. The resulting genome-wide maps of the circular-element repertoire, the Circulome, reveal a consistent and previously unreported enrichment of these elements at particular chromosome ends. The circles map to regions extending well past the telomeres, reaching varying distances up to tens of megabases inward. This activity is accompanied by corroborating rearrangements within the linear genome, consistent with regions of chromosomal instability. Together these features define a spatially localized mode of instability in cancer, which we term Erosion at Distal Genomic Ends (EDGE). We formulate a classification problem to discriminate bladder tumor from matched normal tissue, finding that the EDGE signal outperforms the mean of all interior chromosomal regions, for each chromosome. These findings define a distinct spatial signature of cancer chromosome instability detectable through Circulome analysis, and connect early models of region-specific instability to the human cancer genome.

papers.title: Neural RNA splicing models rely on reading frame information unavailable to the splicing machinery
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks can accurately predict RNA splice sites from genomic sequence, but whether they do so by simulating the natural splicing process is unclear. We evaluate this question by examining mutations that should not have a strong effect on splicing, but are correlated with it in the human genome. We focus specifically on mutations that affect frame alignment because this is known to be relevant to machinery that operates spatially and temporally separately from the splicing machinery. We find that predictions made by commonly-used neural tools are impacted far more by deletions or mutations that alter translational reading frame, producing in-frame stop codons, than by those that preserve reading frame. This dependence on reading frame causes these models to systematically miss many poison exons, a clinically relevant category of exons where reading frame is disrupted. This dependence is much weaker in "grey-box" models that build in splicing-specific structure. Our results imply that widely-used black-box models of splicing rely on information that is not accessible to the RNA splicing machinery. Code is available at https://github.com/kavigupta/frame-alignment-checks.

papers.title: Sex-specific bone marrow populations regulate skeletal phenotype and identify CD74-marked osteoclast precursor subsets
papers.abstract: While there are clear differences in bone accrual and maintenance between men and women due to hormonal regulation, the potential cell-intrinsic factors governing this difference are poorly understood. To investigate this, we performed bone marrow transplantation assays using male or female bone marrow transplantation into male hosts. Micro-CT analyses of lethally irradiated 8-week-old male mice transplanted with female bone marrow exhibited increased vertebral body trabecular and cortical bone mass. To identify cell types mediating these effects, we performed comparative single cell sequencing analyses and identified several CD11B+CD74+ myeloid cell clusters. Male donor BM chimeric mice had a higher proportion of Cd74-expressing clusters compared to female donor BM chimeric mice. We confirmed that males have greater numbers of bone marrow-resident CD11B+CD74+ cells under physiological conditions. Elevated expression of X-linked genes Tlr7 and Kdm6a marked a population of CD11B+CD74+ cells. Lastly, we show that female CD11B+CD74+ cells exhibit diminished osteoclastogenesis. These findings demonstrate that male and female bone marrow-resident cells have cell-intrinsic differences that regulate bone mass and that CD74 marks a subset of osteoclast precursor-enriched myeloid populations.

papers.title: Rhizobia transform legume nodules via native T-DNA transfer systems
papers.abstract: Agrobacteria can deliver transfer DNA (T-DNA) into plant cells, causing tumorous growth. This process, agrobacteria-mediated transformation (AMT), underlies plant genetic engineering and has been regarded as an evolutionary innovation specific to these pathogens. By screening 63,759 alphaproteobacterial genomes for T-DNA border sequences, we identify mini-T-DNAs in diverse rhizobial genera. Each typically encodes a single cargo, a RolB/RolC family protein or a distant rhizobial homologue. We show that native rhizobia-mediated transformation (RMT) systems deliver these mini-T-DNAs into the root nodules of common bean, pea, and chickpea, where the cargo genes are expressed, with no signal in adjacent root tissue. RMT systems share VirG-dependent activation of the core virulence regulon but respond to distinct upstream signals. Our genome screen identifies many additional candidate T-DNA transfer systems, and phylogenetic analysis places their genes into two of the many type IV secretion system (T4SS) clades. RMT systems occur in both clades, together with other systems unrelated to T-DNA transfer, and typically have an ancestral-like T4SS configuration. In contrast, AMT systems occupy a single subclade, consistent with later acquisition of their T4SS module. AMT and RMT thus represent two specialized outcomes of an older, more widespread capability for bacteria-to-plant DNA transfer.

papers.title: A mitochondrial orphan protein contributes to sperm development in bivalves
papers.abstract: Lineage-specific genes, or orphan genes, are increasingly recognized as important drivers of evolutionary innovation, yet their functional characterization remains largely restricted to nuclear genomes of model organisms. Whether lineage-specific genes encoded by mitochondrial DNA contribute to phenotypic diversification remains virtually unexplored. Here we investigate MORF, a rapidly evolving ORFan protein encoded by the paternally transmitted mitochondrial genome of bivalves with doubly uniparental inheritance (DUI). Combining immunolocalization, functional neutralization, protein interaction assays and proteomics in the distantly related bivalves Mytilus edulis and Venustaconcha ellipsiformis, we characterize MORF localization, function and molecular associations during male germ cell development. MORF localizes to developing sperm cells and mature sperm mitochondria in both species and is additionally detected in the acrosome of M. edulis. In cultured M. edulis germ cells, antibody-mediated neutralization of MORF increases the frequency of spermatids displaying four rather than the canonical five mitochondria, providing functional evidence that MORF contributes to mitochondrial organization during spermatogenesis. Comparative proteomic analyses identify MORF-associated proteins involved in cytoskeletal organization, protein homeostasis and extracellular matrix organization. The association between MORF and laminin is independently supported by western blotting in both species. Despite extensive sequence divergence, the two MORF proteins display overlapping functional and molecular features. Together, these findings uncover a functional role for a rapidly evolving mitochondrial orphan protein and point to mitochondrial orphan genes as a potentially overlooked source of evolutionary novelty.

papers.title: Where single-cell foundation models help: a benchmark of annotation, perturbation and regulatory inference against simple baselines
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models (FMs) are proposed as general tools for cell-type annotation, in silico perturbation and gene-regulatory-network (GRN) inference. To identify where they add value, we benchmarked five FMs (scGPT, Geneformer V1 and V2, Nicheformer, scFoundation), CellOracle, supervised perturbation models including STATE, and task-matched simple baselines on the same data, from K562 Perturb-seq screens and primary cells to healthy-donor and isogenic leukodystrophy brain organoids, a public organoid CRISPR screen and lung cancer biopsies. FMs were most useful when labels had to be transferred across species: from human to mouse lung, Nicheformer reached 0.98 accuracy and Geneformer V2 and scFoundation about 0.90, against 0.68 for the best baseline. Zero-shot in silico perturbations captured the direction of real responses in K562, with up to 75% of perturbations shifted in the expected direction (scFoundation, p < 1e-8), and Geneformer V2 networks recovered patient-level tumour differential expression better than co-expression (fold enrichment 2.9 versus 2.0). Within a species, FM embeddings annotated cells as accurately as principal components. In organoids, predicted knockout effects were largely explained by where the target is expressed, and an expression-matched control test isolated the gene-specific part, 12 to 35% of the effects. Isogenic Canavan and Krabbe organoids and 4H patient organoids, with one library per line and time point, did not yet separate methods from differences between clones and donors, which defines the replication needed for future validation. Fine-tuning changed classification accuracy but not knockout rankings. We release the benchmark, baselines, pipeline checks and the isogenic reference task as the fmaudit package, so that new models can be evaluated on the tasks where FMs already help.

papers.title: Multi-faceted role of dopamine afferents to the ventral pallidum in reward processing
papers.abstract: The ventral pallidum (VP) is necessary for reward processing and a key node in dopamine (DA) pathways. Yet the direct DA inputs have not been studied during reward learning. Here, we elucidate the role of VP DA in reward processing using circuit tracing, fibre photometry, and behavioural pharmacology in male rats. We show that VP receives both non-DA and DA inputs from the midbrain. During an instrumental reward conditioning paradigm, we characterized VP DA activity using a DA sensor (GRAB_DA1h) across learning, extinction, re-acquisition, and motivational test. Followed by pharmacological manipulation using the DA-antagonist (fluphenazine) in VP to demonstrate a causal role in reward learning and motivation. Together our findings advance the functional contributions of non-canonical mesolimbic DA pathways.

papers.title: Active manipulation of surface orientation under directional illumination improves color discrimination
papers.abstract: Two surfaces that appear different colors under one illumination might appear the same color under another illumination. This phenomenon is known as illuminant metamerism and is thought to limit surface color discrimination. However, real-world lighting environments are not directionally uniform. In theory, surfaces that appear the same color at one tilt might not appear the same color at another tilt where they sample a different illumination spectrum. We tested whether human observers could use this directional variation to improve surface color discrimination. Our results confirm that human color discrimination is improved when observers are able to tilt surfaces to sample directional lighting. Observer sampling motions were spatiotemporally structured and appeared to be directed towards the general lighting geometry rather than systematically maximizing color discriminating information for specific surface pairs.

papers.title: Actin pool controls the scaling of dynamic actin networks
papers.abstract: Scaling is a fundamental property of living systems, allowing cells to match the size of their internal components to their volume. The size and shape of cells depend largely on the actin cytoskeleton, whose dynamic self-assembling structures are central to this adaptation. Yet how they self-assemble in a volume-dependent manner remains unresolved. To address this question, we used a biomimetic system consisting of beads propelled by actin polymerization in microwells of different volumes, which allowed us to work with a limited and defined number of components. This approach enabled the first reconstitution, from purified proteins, of dynamic cytoskeletal structures that adapt to the volume of their environment. The scalability of these structures depends on how strongly they deplete monomers from a shared pool, and tuning the disassembly rate is sufficient to shift their scaling regime. Scaling principles also hold for multiple competing structures, with greater competition imposing stronger constraints on the monomer pool. Together, these results establish a mechanistic framework in which a structure's capacity to adapt is set by how much it draws down shared resources as it grows, a principle that may extend to other intracellular structures that scale with the cells that build them.

papers.title: A subtype-specific gene regulatory program controls differential circuit integration of deep CA3 pyramidal neurons
papers.abstract: How closely related neuronal subtypes integrate into different circuits remains poorly understood. Deep and superficial hippocampal CA3 pyramidal neurons (PNs) differ in intrinsic firing and mossy fiber (MF) input at specialized postsynaptic structures termed thorny excrescences (TEs). Combining developmental single-nucleus multiomics with genetic targeting, morphological analysis and electrophysiology, we identify the transcription factor ST18 as a regulator of deep CA3 subtype identity. ST18 marks sparsely thorny and burst-firing neurons, and gene regulatory analyses predict that it represses a superficial-associated program involved in dendritic spine development, synaptic organization, and electrophysiological properties. Postnatal ST18 loss shifts the transcriptional and chromatin landscape of deep CA3 PNs toward a superficial-like state. These molecular changes are accompanied by increased TE elaboration approaching superficial levels, enhanced excitatory synaptic activity, and reduced burst-firing. Together, these findings identify ST18-dependent restriction of an alternative subtype program as a mechanism linking molecular identity to distinct input connectivity patterns and intrinsic firing properties during postnatal circuit maturation.

papers.title: Structural basis of nucleosome recognition by the human NuA4/TIP60 acetyltransferase complex
papers.abstract: The human Tat-interactive protein, 60 kilodalton (Tip60) histone acetyltransferase (HAT) complex (NuA4/TIP60 complex, from now on TIP60-C) is a central regulator of chromatin accessibility, coupling histone acetylation with transcriptional activation and genome stability. But how the catalytic HAT module engages its nucleosome substrate has remained unknown. Here we present the structure of the human TIP60-C HAT module bound to the nucleosome, revealing a defined binding architecture in which TIP60, EPC1, ING3, and MEAF6 cooperatively position the catalytic center on the nucleosome surface, with the HAT module anchored on the histone acidic patch and engaging the linker DNA. The structure uncovers an intramolecular interaction involving the N-terminal Tudor domain of the TIP60 acetyltransferase subunit that suggests a potential mechanism for autoregulation of HAT activity. Together, our findings define the core principles by which the human TIP60-C HAT module recognizes chromatin, establishing a structural foundation for understanding how TIP60-C modifies chromatin in metazoans.

papers.title: NORMA 3.0: aesthetic and group-aware visualization and analysis of annotated biological networks
papers.abstract: Summary: Interpreting a biological network often rests on the relationship between its connectivity and the functional groups annotated on it, such as pathways, complexes, or enriched terms. For example, whether a group forms a cohesive module, how groups overlap, and which proteins connect them. These relationships are often hard to assess visually when groups are numerous or overlap, and most tools represent membership only by node color. NORMA 3.0 is a complete client-side rewrite of its predecessors, delineating and laying out groups with convex hulls, bubble sets, or fog clouds. Multi-group nodes are rendered as pies and directed, and parallel edges retain their evidence channels. Eighteen 2D and nine 3D layouts are scored by silhouette width, outline intrusion and overlap, and benchmarked for group separation and run time. The implementation also includes edge bundling, network importers for six databases, 21 topological measures, group-level and enrichment statistics, comparison of up to ten networks, export of high-resolution images, and an Application Programming Interface. Availability and implementation: NORMA 3.0 is freely available at https://normaviz.org. The source code is available at https://github.com/PavlopoulosLab/NORMA.

papers.title: Non-homologous end-joining is implicated in rapid and efficient caspofungin adaptation in Nakaseomyces glabratus
papers.abstract: Antifungal resistance in Nakaseomyces glabratus is a major clinical challenge, yet the cellular processes that shape its evolution remain poorly understood. Here, we used experimental evolution to investigate the role of the error-prone double-strand break repair pathway, non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), in adaptation to fluconazole and caspofungin. Wild-type and NHEJ-deficient (lig4{Delta}) populations were evolved under antifungal selection for 25 days. Fluconazole resistance emerged rapidly in both genetic backgrounds and was associated with recurrent PDR1 mutations and aneuploidies. In contrast, caspofungin adaptation was delayed and less efficient in lig4{Delta} populations, with several lineages failing to survive. All wild-type caspofungin-evolved isolates carried canonical FKS2 hotspot mutations, whereas lig4{Delta} isolates predominantly acquired resistance through alternative genetic pathways. Caspofungin adaptation also frequently conferred cross-resistance to fluconazole and was accompanied by changes in the abundance of ergosterol-associated proteins. Together, these findings implicate NHEJ in promoting efficient evolution of FKS-mediated echinocandin resistance and demonstrate that DNA repair capacity can shape antifungal resistance trajectories in N. glabratus.

papers.title: Metabolic engineering of Saccharomyces cerevisiae for improved polyphosphate production
papers.abstract: Finite high-grade phosphate rock reserves and rising legislative demand for phosphorus recycling create a need for processes converting phosphorus-containing residual streams into valuable products. Microbial synthesis of inorganic polyphosphate (polyP) could complement its energy-intensive chemical manufacturing while enabling phosphorus recovery in a value-added product with applications ranging from food processing to flame retardants and fertilizer. After orthophosphate (Pi) starvation and refeeding, Saccharomyces cerevisiae naturally accumulates polyP as a cellular Pi reserve, but the current multistage process complicates industrial implementation. Here, we identified metabolic interventions that uncouple polyP accumulation from Pi starvation by systematic evaluation of 57 engineered S. cerevisiae CEN.PK113-7D strains. Constitutive activation of the PHO regulon produced the strongest increase in polyP, whereas disruption of inositol pyrophosphate synthesis, Pi import, or the vacuolar transporter chaperone complex impaired accumulation. This pattern indicates that efficient polyP accumulation depends on coordinated activation of Pi acquisition and vacuolar polymerization. Notably, deletion of PHO80 converted a transient starvation response into a constitutive production phenotype, enabling high polyP accumulation during growth. Optimization of the growth medium increased the polyP content further, and efficient use of the supplied Pi was demonstrated, while electron microscopy paired with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy supported increased vacuolar storage. During aerobic exponential fed-batch cultivation, pho80{Delta} simultaneously formed biomass and polyP, reaching a polyP content of 22.1% of cell dry weight and a titer of 8.2 g/L, both expressed as KPO3 equivalents. These findings establish S. cerevisiae pho80{Delta} as a promising platform for biological polyP production and phosphorus recovery.

papers.title: An Innate Neuroprotective Reflex Activates NRF2 via Phosphorylation of p62 at Ser351 to Mitigate Traumatic Brain Injury
papers.abstract: Rationale: The oxidative crisis in traumatic brain injury (TBI) has remained therapeutically intractable to direct antioxidant therapies. Activating nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) offers a promising strategy, but its translation is hindered by a key question: whether TBI's depleted antioxidant reserves can accommodate canonical electrophilic activation. The diving reflex (DR) is a potential non-electrophilic alternative, but its efficacy in TBI is unknown and its natural induction is clinically impractical. This study tests whether artificial DR, induced by trigeminal nerve stimulation (TNS), can safely engage this non-electrophilic NRF2 pathway and exert a protective role in the acutely injured brain. Methods: In a rat model of severe TBI, we compared TNS-induced DR, natural DR, and exogenous calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) against the electrophilic NRF2 activator dimethyl fumarate (DMF). To define the mechanism of action, we quantified p62 phosphorylation at Ser351 (NRF2-activating) versus Ser403 (autophagy-related), alongside redox homeostasis, lesion volume, and multi-domain functional outcomes. Results: TNS-induced DR fully recapitulated the neuroprotection of natural DR, an effect mimicked by exogenous CGRP, and prevented by CGRP inhibition, confirming a shared, neuropeptide-driven mechanism. This non-electrophilic pathway operated by selectively phosphorylating p62 at Ser351, which preserved glutathione reserves, halted lipid peroxidation, and reduced chronic lesion volume. In contrast, while DMF activated NRF2, its electrophilic mechanism was associated with a further reduction in the brain's already compromised glutathione pools and increased lipid peroxidation. This mechanistic difference was functionally significant, as only the non-electrophilic approaches delivered multi-domain recovery. Conclusion: The TNS-evoked artificial DR is a mechanistically tailored strategy for activating NRF2 in acute TBI. By engaging the endogenous CGRP-p62-KEAP1 pathway, it circumvents the fundamental limitations of both passively consumed direct antioxidants and redox-costly electrophilic activators. Our findings establish a clear translational roadmap for harnessing an innate reflex as a clinically deployable therapy for hyper-oxidative states.

papers.title: Multiparametric Extracellular Vesicle Profiling Identifies a Distinct Circulating Signature of Bicuspid Aortic Valve Disease
papers.abstract: Background: Calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD) resulting in life-threatening aortic stenosis, heart failure and death, develops earlier and progresses more rapidly in patients with bicuspid aortic valves (BAV) than tricuspid aortic valves (TAV), yet the circulating molecular drivers remain poorly understood. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) capture disease-relevant cellular activation and offer a powerful window into a BAV-specific pathophysiology. Methods: Circulating large extracellular vesicle (LEV) abundance and morphology were characterized by complementary single-vesicle nano-flow cytometry and super-resolution microscopy. Proteomic profiling further delineated LEV molecular cargoes and associated biological pathways between patients with BAV and TAV. Results: We demonstrate that patients with BAVs exhibited fundamentally altered circulating LEV profiles compared to TAVs. Super-resolution imaging revealed BAV-specific organization of platelet- and leukocyte-associated adhesion molecules into discrete EV membrane microdomains. Proteomic profiling identified distinct LEV cargoes between BAV and TAV, including a BAV-specific, previously unrecognized neutrophil-associated signature enriched for proteins involved in neutrophil degranulation and innate immunity. Consistent with this phenotype, BAV displayed alterations in platelet- and neutrophil-associated LEV populations, suggesting enhanced (thrombo-)inflammatory activity. Lastly, distinct associations between LEV populations and clinical parameters in BAV and TAV suggest that LEV profiles reflect morphology-specific aspects of disease severity. Conclusions: Comprehensive single-vesicle analysis and bulk proteomic profiling identified a distinct circulating LEV signature in BAV-associated CAVD, characterized by endothelial activation and reciprocal platelet-neutrophil interactions. These findings reveal previously unrecognized differences in circulating LEVs between BAV and TAV and highlight their potential as biomarkers of valve morphology-specific pathophysiology.

papers.title: A large, distinct family of RNase H fold nucleases associated with numerous defense systems in prokaryotes
papers.abstract: During the last decade, systematic efforts aimed at the characterization of prokaryotic immunity resulted in the discovery of several hundred distinct defense systems in bacteria and archaea. This suggests that the common defense systems were already known and only rare ones remained to be identified. Here we present a genomic census and analysis of a vast family of bacterial and archaeal proteins (known as Domain of Unknown Function, DUF3800) that contain a distinct variant of the RNase H fold and are encoded in a striking 15% of the available complete prokaryotic genomes. Most of these proteins are encoded in defense islands, often in a close association with known defense systems, hence the designation WARD (Weaponized Antiphage RNase- dependent Defense). The WARDs display a broad variety of protein domain architectures and genomic contexts, including a strong link to restriction-modification, CRISPR-Cas, retrons, and non-coding RNAs, suggestive of a substantial diversity in defense mechanisms. We experimentally tested 10 WARDs, mostly, encoded by standalone genes, and found that 9 of these conferred robust protection against diverse phages in Escherichia coli. Therefore, WARDs appear to represent the third most abundant defense system type in prokaryotes.

papers.title: Relaxation kinetics controls cell transport in crowded active monolayers
papers.abstract: Soft cancer cells embedded in stiffer epithelial layers migrate in bursts, which prior simulations have attributed to their deformability. In a dense layer, however, interfacial tension sets two things at once: the energy cost of a deformation and the rate at which it relaxes. Here we disentangle the two in an active phase-field model of a near-confluent monolayer in which relaxation rate and free energy can be varied independently. Crowding slows cells not by pushing them back bodily but through the relaxation of their own deformations against neighbours, which cancels most of their propulsion. Slowing this relaxation in a minority of cells, at unchanged energetics and propulsion, more than doubles their transport and speeds up the untouched majority by half. Conversely, the advantage of soft cells vanishes, and at high soft-cell fractions reverses, once their relaxation is made as fast as that of normal cells. Independent of composition, mixtures transport like a uniform layer with the geometric-mean interfacial tension. Passive relaxation kinetics thus emerges as an independent lever on transport, suggesting that the fluidity of heterogeneous tissues may depend on how quickly cells recover their shape, not only on how stiff they are.

papers.title: Squalene as a Candidate Signalling Molecule: Computational Evidence for a Predicted KEAP1 Interaction and Implications for Stress-Induced Altruistic Stem-Cell Niche Protection
papers.abstract: Stem and progenitor cells exposed to cytotoxic stress must preserve both their own viability and the functional integrity of their surrounding niche. Previous investigations from our laboratory have described stress-adapted altruistic stem-cell phenotypes and demonstrated the cytoprotective potential of squalene in normal haematopoietic and mesenchymal progenitor cells through preservation of glutathione homeostasis. More recent studies have associated hypoxia-driven changes in squalene metabolism with intracellular squalene accumulation and protection against lipid peroxidation, while independent experimental evidence has implicated NRF2 in squalene-mediated cytoprotection. However, the molecular basis through which squalene may engage the NRF2 regulatory pathway remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the structural feasibility of a potential interaction between squalene and the KEAP1 Kelch domain using molecular docking across three human KEAP1 crystal structures (PDB IDs: 6TYM, 6SP4 and 5CGJ). The docking protocol was evaluated through native-ligand redocking, yielding RMSD values of 0.826, 0.277 and 0.303 A, respectively. Squalene was consistently accommodated within the canonical hydrophobic cavity, with predicted docking scores of 7.905, 7.513 and 6.756 kcal/mol. The predicted interaction environment was predominantly hydrophobic and involved residues including Arg415, Arg380 and Asn414, without conventional hydrogen-bond formation. These findings support the structural feasibility of squalene accommodation within the KEAP1 Kelch domain and provide a testable hypothesis connecting stress-responsive squalene metabolism with potential KEAP1 NRF2 regulation. However, docking alone does not establish direct binding, physiological accessibility, KEAP1 inhibition or functional NRF2 activation. Further biophysical, molecular-dynamics and cellular investigations are required to establish the biological significance of the predicted interaction.

papers.title: Late radiation-induced brain injury is associated with functional cerebrovascular impairment without structural vessel loss in mice
papers.abstract: Background: Radiation-induced brain injury (RIBI) is a major and often irreversible complication of cranial radiotherapy, affecting up to 90% of long-term survivors. Although cerebrovascular damage is a leading mechanistic hypothesis, whether chronic resting hypoperfusion occurs independently of structural vessel loss remains unknown. The aim of this study was to comprehensively characterize cerebrovascular, structural, and behavioral outcomes in a murine model of late RIBI to determine the primary drivers of vascular dysfunction. Methods: Adult C57BL/6 mice underwent 12 Gy whole-brain irradiation and were assessed one year later using laser speckle contrast imaging (LSCI), 7T MRI, immunohistochemistry, and behavioral testing. Results: Irradiated mice exhibited reduced pial flow velocity and flow area by LSCI, indicative of upstream cerebrovascular dysfunction, while bulk cortical tissue perfusion was preserved. This pial hypoperfusion was accompanied by cerebral atrophy, decreased T2* relaxation time and tissue iron deposition consistent with chronic microhemorrhage across multiple brain regions by MRI, blood-brain barrier disruption reflected by reduced ZO-1 and VE-cadherin expression, and increased anxiety-like behavior. Strikingly, capillary density, pericyte coverage, astrocyte endfeet, and NeuN-positive neuronal nuclei were all preserved. Conclusion: These findings demonstrate that functional vascular impairment - not structural vessel or neuronal loss - drives hypoperfusion and blood-brain barrier disruption in late RIBI. This dissociation between vascular dysfunction and rarefaction reframes the pathophysiology of RIBI and identifies endothelial dysfunction as a tractable therapeutic target for intervention.

papers.title: Steering Before Selection: Energy-Limited Developmental Control as a Phenotypic Capacitor, a Pre-Specified Simulation Study
papers.abstract: Living systems meet environmental change at several speeds: fast physiological control during development, slower learned memory, and genetic change through selection. We asked whether developmental control, which we interpret as bioelectric and which carries a continuous energy cost, steers evolution, and we report what survived twenty-two versions of individual-based simulation, pre-specified from version 11 onwards. After a permanent environmental change, sensing absorbed the change within about 25 generations and genes took over through selection alone 340 to 450 generations later in every seed, a result replicated in a fresh pre-specified test on 20 new seeds. Control did not guide genetic change; it concealed genetic variation from selection. Control hid three to six times more harmful load than no control, and an energy shortfall released it; brief release outperformed prolonged release, and release helped only when control re-locked around the new form. The net value of release depended mainly on whether the concealed harmful load was kept in check: without reversal of harmful mutations it was a cost at 500 individuals (mean fitness 0.103 against 0.122 without control), whereas with reversal it was a benefit at every population size from 250 to 4,000 (0.632 against 0.489 at 2,000). A test that separated the factors showed that population size alone did not reverse the result and that the cost lay in the concealment itself, with release recovering part of it. We conclude that energy-funded developmental control buys time while selection rewrites the genes, conceals rather than directs variation, and acts as an energy-switched phenotypic capacitor whose value depends mainly on whether the harmful load it conceals is kept in check. The models are abstract and contain no voltages or channels, so the bioelectric reading is an interpretation and all results are model results. We set out predictions for testing these claims in developing embryos.

papers.title: Systematic comparison of genetically encoded F-actin probes for visualizing actomyosin dynamics in vivo using C. elegans
papers.abstract: Genetically encoded F-actin probes enable visualization of actin organization and dynamics in living cells, but their performance and effects on cellular function can vary by probe, fluorescent protein, and biological context. Here, we systematically compared three F-actin probes - F-tractin, LifeAct, and Utrophin - fused to mScarlet-I, mNeonGreen, or mStayGold in vivo, using Caenorhabditis elegans. We used single-copy transgenic strains and evaluated fluorescence intensity, photostability, developmental and reproductive outcomes, cytokinetic ring closure, and probe localization across diverse cellular contexts. mStayGold provided the greatest brightness and photostability, making it well suited for long-term time-lapse imaging, whereas mNeonGreen offers an alternative for applications requiring photobleaching. Most of the strains exhibited minimal detectable effects on development and cellular function and outperformed previously generated strains tested. Probe performance varied across tissues and developmental stages. F-tractin generally exhibited lower fluorescence intensity than LifeAct and Utrophin, particularly in embryos. Although the probes largely exhibited subcellular localization patterns consistent with phalloidin staining, differences in their labeling of specific F-actin structures were observed. Together, these results establish a practical framework for selecting genetically encoded F-actin probes for C. elegans, they suggest best candidates for other in vivo systems, and they highlight the importance of considering both fluorescent protein and actin-binding probe when designing live-cell imaging experiments.

papers.title: MicrobeRT: A Framework and Suite of Fine-tuned Language Models for Genomic Sequences
papers.abstract: Accurate and reproducible metagenomic analysis is essential for effective infectious disease surveillance. Targeted diagnostics such as culturing, antigen assays, and multiplex PCR panels identify only predefined organisms and can fail to identify atypical or novel infections. Shotgun metagenomics offers hypothesis-free detection, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity, dependence on mutable reference databases, and high computational cost. To combat these challenges, we introduce MicrobeRT, an integrated suite of genomic language models fine-tuned to classify metagenomic sequencing reads across three tasks: (i) species level taxonomic identification, (ii) antibiotic resistance gene detection, and (iii) pathogenicity assessment. The framework builds on three pre-trained genomic language models - Nucleotide Transformer (Dalla-Torre et al 2025), DNABERT (Ji et al 2021, Zhou et al 2024), and HyenaDNA (Nguyen et al 2024) - leveraging their large-scale genomic pre-training, adaptability to downstream tasks, and, in the case of HyenaDNA, ability to capture long-range sequence dependencies. The models are fine-tuned on large, curated datasets spanning microbial, viral, fungal, and human genomes, including more than 500,000 genomes and 250,000 antibiotic resistance gene sequences. To evaluate the performance of our fine-tuned genomic language models across classification tasks, we developed a benchmarking framework that compares MicrobeRT against state-of-the-art (SOTA) bioinformatics tools. Across both simulated and empirical datasets, the models achieve strong performance while reducing computational overhead. MicrobeRT is released as open-source software, enabling further fine-tuning and reproducible integration of alternative models and classifiers. We also demonstrate seamless, drop-in integration by incorporating our fine-tuned taxonomic classification models as an optional add-on within the open-source TaxTriage pipeline (Merritt et al 2026). MicrobeRT demonstrates the feasibility of three clinically relevant multi-label analyses, offering a practical path to scalable, reproducible metagenomic diagnostics and enabling broader deployment of AI/ML-enhanced infectious disease testing.

papers.title: Bicarbonate-free pH neutralization resensitizes ovarian cancer to chemotherapy and is tracked by 3T CEST MRI
papers.abstract: Ovarian tumors that initially respond to platinum-taxane chemotherapy often relapse as chemoresistant disease. The acidic tumor microenvironment is a well-known but under-exploited driver of this resistance, and neutralization strategies such as oral bicarbonate have not translated. Here we show that inhibiting specific tumor pH regulators at noncytotoxic doses relieves acidosis and restores frontline chemotherapy, monitored noninvasively at clinical 3T. In OVCAR3 and SKOV-3 ovarian cancer cells, MCT1 and MCT4 were overexpressed under acidosis, and the MCT4 inhibitor acriflavine reduced extracellular acidification at concentrations well below its cytotoxic IC50, without bicarbonate buffering. Acidosis blunted the efficacy of both paclitaxel and carboplatin, raising their IC50 values, which acriflavine reversed. In SKOV-3 tumors, acidoCEST MRI with iopromide noninvasively measured baseline tumor acidosis and its normalization following acriflavine treatment. These results establish tumor acidosis as an imageable, druggable determinant of chemoresistance and a bicarbonate-free therapeutic target.

papers.title: Deep Recovery of Effective Migration Surfaces
papers.abstract: The isolation-by-distance (IBD) principle describes the tendency for genetic relatedness to decline with geographic distance. Although the existence IBD has long been documented in natural populations, recent analyses of spatially referenced genotype data have shown that the strength of this relationship can vary across a landscape due to geographic barriers, habitat compatibility, or other factors. Effective migration surfaces (EMS) have emerged as a popular exploratory tool for visualizing spatial patterns in IBD. However, fitting likelihood-based EMS models is often computationally demanding, requiring repeated large-scale matrix calculations. Here, we introduce Deep Recovery of Effective Migration Surfaces (dreems), a graph neural network for amortized inference of effective migration surfaces. dreems maps genetic covariance and sampling locations directly to an effective migration surface, while simultaneously providing predictive uncertainty estimates. Once trained, the network accommodates different graph sizes and sampling designs without needing to re-train. Across independent coalescent simulations that were not seen during training, dreems has roughly 10-30% lower estimation error compared to a state-of-the-art likelihood-based method, with the largest gains observed under sparse sampling designs that are commonly encountered in practice. Reanalysis of several published datasets recovers spatial patterns that are broadly consistent with earlier likelihood-based estimates, while reducing computation time by orders of magnitude.

papers.title: Missing by design: why genomic metadata must be captured at submission, not recovered from the literature
papers.abstract: Plant and metazoan genome assemblies are being deposited in the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC) archives at an accelerating rate, but the biological context needed to interpret them, such as ploidy, cultivar, and subgenome structure, is often missing from the record: these attributes are optional in most submission checklists and, when supplied, are entered as free text. We describe the gap in three layers. Ploidy varies within a species and cannot be inferred from taxonomy; chromosome-naming conventions differ between assemblies of the same crop; and that inconsistency is concentrated in species named by subgenome and is not associated with the size of the research community, which points to the lack of a shared convention. As a case study, we built a pipeline that recovers these attributes from the publications linked to an assembly. On a benchmark of 82 assemblies, its current version reported one wrong ploidy, and across 1,059 plant assemblies an earlier, less strict version found the ploidy in a publication for about half; for nearly a third, it found a publication but no statement of ploidy in it. Recovery from the literature can annotate assemblies already deposited but cannot stop new ones from arriving incomplete. We therefore propose that ploidy, cultivar, and subgenome structure be captured at submission as mandatory, controlled-vocabulary attributes, building on existing INSDC and Genomic Standards Consortium checklists.

papers.title: bL9 prevents recoding in collided ribosomes
papers.abstract: When a ribosome stalls and an upstream ribosome collides with it, the resulting interface recruits factors that initiate ribosome rescue pathways. Recent cryo-EM structures of collided ribosomes from bacteria reveal that bL9 from the leading ribosome reaches back to contact the 30S subunit of the trailing ribosome. The role of bL9 in translation is poorly understood; while bL9 mutants show high levels of recoding (i.e. frameshifting and hopping), the mechanism has remained unclear. Here we show that bL9 functions in the context of ribosome collisions: loss of bL9 destabilizes the interaction between collided ribosomes and sensitizes cells to antibiotics that induce collisions such as erythromycin and fusidic acid. Moreover, luciferase reporters reveal that frameshifting and hopping levels increase in strains lacking bL9 (or with point mutants in bL9 at the collision interface) but only in the context of ribosome collisions. These findings demonstrate that in wild-type bacterial ribosomes, bL9 prevents frameshifting, hopping, and other deleterious recoding events following collisions.

papers.title: Early Progression Cells mark a stem-like state associated with pancreatic cancer initiation and progression
papers.abstract: Pancreatic cancer is deemed to progress from microscopic pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanINs). However, low grade PanINs are frequently detected in the general population without presentation or increased risk of developing cancer, suggesting that many PanINs never progress to tumours. What precisely characterises PanINs that develop into tumours is insufficiently understood. Using a mouse model where pancreatitis-induced tissue injury promotes pancreatic cancer from rare KrasG12D cells, we identify Early Progression Cells (EPCs) as a new entity, a novel population of cancer stem-like cells. Transcriptomic analyses illustrate EPCs as stress-adapted, inflammation responsive stem cells that also upregulate gene programmes indicative of microenvironment remodelling. Using identified EPC protein markers, we show that EPCs are prevalent in early metaplastic stages and in PanIN progression from low grade to high grade but are rarer in tumours. PanIN- and tumour-derived sphere and organoid assays demonstrate that EPCs possess all characteristics of stem cells in vitro and are dependent on Nupr1 stress response pathways for survival and growth. We identify APP-CD74 as a novel cell-cell interaction pathway between EPCs and neighbouring epithelial cells in PanINs and tumours. Inhibition of CD74 activity in vitro induces high-grade PanIN organoid death, suggesting EPCs are critical for high-grade PanINs. Using spatial transcriptomics of human samples, we detect gene signatures of EPCs in distinct regions of human PanIN and PDAC tissues, including APP-CD74 interactions, providing compelling evidence that EPCs are relevant to human disease. Further understanding of EPC biology will likely uncover new knowledge on why rare PanINs progress towards tumours.

papers.title: Enhancers Silence Coupled-coding RNAs in Animals
papers.abstract: The exact working mechanism and biogenesis of regulatory non-coding RNAs (rncRNAs), including enhancer RNAs (eRNAs), microRNAs (miRNAs), piRNAs, small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), transposons, and other non-coding RNAs, remain enigmatic. Conversely, the unique transcriptional regulation mechanism that differentiates animals from simple unicellular organisms remains elusive in life sciences. We find that regulatory non-coding genes are independent transcription units marked with arginine methylation of nucleosomes within their gene bodies, which is regulated by JMJD5. Enhancer RNAs are similar to those of other regulatory RNAs in targeting the 3-prime UTRs of coupled coding RNAs. All regulatory RNA genes share transcription factors with their target coding genes, both of which are regulated by promoter-proximal RNA Polymerase II pausing and may control the development of animals. Temporal and spatial coding genes and regulatory non-coding genes are intrinsically coupled in animals.

papers.title: An integrated workflow for dual-guide CRISPR-Cas9 targeting and amplicon-based genotyping of Pla2g6 in primary mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages
papers.abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 editing in primary bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMD-M{phi}s) requires coordinated assessment of cellular morphology, target modification, and sequence-level editing outcomes. We describe a workflow for dual-guide targeting of murine Pla2g6 that integrates guide design, ribonucleoprotein nucleofection, PCR-heteroduplex mobility analysis (PCR-HMA), and targeted amplicon sequencing. At 24 h after nucleofection, cells receiving ribonucleoproteins assembled with chemically synthesized single-guide RNAs preserved the elongated, adherent morphology, whereas cultures receiving in vitro-transcribed guides contained predominantly poorly adhered, rounded cells and appeared less densely populated; both guide preparations generated indels and deletions, so the difference observed was in cell appearance rather than in target modification. PCR-HMA provided a simple, qualitative screen for sequence heterogeneity and for a putative deletion product, which was subsequently characterized by sequencing. In two independent BMDM samples, one each from C57BL/6 and NOD mice, breakpoint-based analysis identified editing-associated indels in 54.7% and 44.5% of analyzed reads, compared with 0.28% and 0.07% in matched Cas9-only controls. Deletions spanning both target sites represented 33.1% and 26.2% of analyzed reads; none were detected among 4,383 analyzed control reads. The modal spanning deletion was 137 bp, the size predicted from precise joining of the two blunt Cas9 ends. Sequence interpretation depended on verified guide coordinates, deletion-aware analysis settings, and matched controls: scored permissively, the same control reads returned 22-23% apparent editing. Modest-depth Nanopore sequencing recovered the major editing classes, although low-frequency variants and small indels required additional caution. This workflow supports a simple and streamlined screening and sequence-based genotyping of edited BMDM populations, allowing the discernment of the comprehensive mutation spectrum arising from CRISPR-Cas9 gene targeting.

papers.title: Marker-specific pixel attribution for single-cell protein quantification with PixAQ
papers.abstract: Imaging mass cytometry (IMC) typically quantifies all markers within the same cell mask, although their signals have distinct spatial distributions. This quantification method may omit relevant signals or include signals from neighboring cells. We present PixAQ, which improves single-cell protein quantification in IMC through marker-specific probabilistic pixel attribution. PixAQ combines spatial proximity with anchor-group intensity models to assign pixel-marker observations among neighboring cells and an explicit residual component. Original intensities are averaged over marker-specific supports. Across three cohorts (680 regions), comparisons in 366 patients showed improved agreement with predefined population-marker relationships, with cohort-median patient-paired gains of 1.99 to 4.83 percentage points in expected-marker share over shared-mask quantification. Ablation analyses showed that both spatial and intensity evidence contributed to these gains. Conventional and high-resolution IMC images linked supports to visible local and intracellular signal structures. PixAQ improves single-cell protein quantification by determining which local signals contribute to each marker measurement without changing cell segmentation.

papers.title: Seeing danger? Visual constraints and collision risk in the Bearded Vulture Gypaetus barbatus
papers.abstract: The Bearded Vulture, Gypaetus barbatus is highly vulnerable to collisions with human-made aerial infrastructures. Yet, its visual sensory system remains poorly understood, limiting the development of species-specific collision mitigation measures. To address this gap, we characterized its visual ecology across four complementary dimensions: visual fields, spatial resolution, contrast sensitivity and spectral sensitivity of cone visual rhodopsins. Bearded vultures have no blind area in the direction of travel during foraging flight, indicating that frontal visual-field limitations are unlikely to contribute to their risk of collisions. Their axial length predicts high spatial visual resolution, suggesting that insufficient spatial resolution is unlikely to be a primary cause of collisions. By contrast, Bearded Vultures display very low peak contrast sensitivity compared to other birds, which may limit their ability to detect objects when contrast with the background, or within the objects themselves, is low. Functional characterization of the four cone visual pigments indicated sensitivity spanning approximately 350-640 nm, with a potential chromatic-discrimination range from 400 to 602 nm. Together, these results identify that contrast sensitivity, rather than visual-field configuration or spatial resolution, is a key perceptual constraint to consider in collision mitigation of the Bearded Vulture. Visual markers should therefore maximize both internal contrast and brightness contrast against the surrounding environment. More broadly, our multidisciplinary approach highlights how birds differ substantially in how they perceive anthropogenic structures and illustrates the importance of incorporating species-specific sensory ecology into conservation efforts, especially in the design of collision-mitigation strategies.

papers.title: Optimiser Repairs for Living-Cell Self-Driving Laboratories: Performance and Redundancy under Experimental Constraints
papers.abstract: Living-cell self-driving laboratories must optimise experiments despite delayed readouts, changing responses and limited sample availability. In simulations, we evaluate when optimiser repairs improve closed-loop performance and when platform constraints make them redundant, separating consumption of a sample from permanent loss of the ability to repeat its condition. We prove that exclusions and confirmation requests produce exactly the baseline trajectory when they act only on conditions already forbidden by the platform, share the same posterior and selection procedure, and release infeasible requested slots. This result covers the evaluated pending-exclusion, previous-batch and confirmation rules under permanent condition retirement; it does not cover arbitrary selection interventions. We then conduct 33,900 simulated policy runs with 200-300 paired campaign seeds per setting. A public PBMC reference supports characterisation of the target-label readout, while condition-response landscapes remain synthetic. Across 27 landscape, assay-size and kernel settings, previous-batch exclusion changes final normalised performance by -0.004 to +0.283, with positive differences surviving Holm adjustment in 13 settings. Effects are small on the rugged landscape. Permanent retirement can be harmful under noisy rugged responses. All three subsumed interventions reproduce every saved baseline event on 200 of 200 paired seeds. These results establish the importance of explicit availability constraints and evaluation across experimental regimes when assessing optimiser repairs.

papers.title: Sourmash accurately profiles strains from long-read metagenomes preserving gene content
papers.abstract: Background. Metagenomic strain-level profiling remains challenging because closely related bacterial strains often share more than 99% average nucleotide identity (ANI). However, they can differ substantially in gene content and functional potential. Sourmash uses k-mer sketches with FracMinHash to compare sequencing reads against reference databases, which makes it an interesting approach for strain-level profiling. Because it compares sketches rather than full alignments, it enables fast searches against large reference databases. However, its ability to recover biologically relevant strains and preserve community gene content has not been specifically assessed. Here, we evaluated the performance of sourmash for strain-level identification abundance, functional gene content recovery, and abundance estimations using five mock communities of increasing complexity with known composition. Results. We first assessed whether nucleotide similarity reflects functional similarity between strains. Gene content similarity was generally consistent with ANI but revealed important divergences between closely related strains. For example, Escherichia coli strains sharing more than 98% ANI showed gene content similarities ranging from 20% to 57%, highlighting that nucleotide similarity alone is insufficient to assess functional proximity and consequently the accuracy of strain identification. Above sufficient genome coverage, sourmash identified strains either exactly or with closely related strains sharing highly conserved gene content. These closely related strains provided a biologically relevant representation of the expected functional potential of the mock communities. Gene content recovery was highly accurate, with F1 scores ranging from 0.942 to 0.998 across the five mock communities. Genome abundances estimated against sourmash-identified genomes closely matched the expected community composition: Pearson correlation coefficients ranged from 0.823 to 1 at strain level and from 0.978 to 1 at species level. Conclusions. Our results show that sourmash provides a biologically relevant approach for strain-level characterisation in microbial ecosystems. Even when the exact strain could not be identified, closely related strains retained most of the expected gene content and abundance estimations were accurate, supporting the use of sourmash for downstream functional profiling or metabolic network reconstruction.

papers.title: Chronic Sleep Disruption Activates the Transcriptional Unfolded Protein Response and Induces Compartment-Specific Proteomic Changes in Mice
papers.abstract: Sleep disruption (SD) is associated with adverse brain health and increased risk of dementia, including Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the pathological mechanisms underlying this association are not fully understood. Preclinical studies have shown that acute SD impairs cognition by altering vulnerable synapses (molecular composition, ultrastructure, and function). However, the cumulative effects of chronic SD on the adult brain and its vulnerable synapses, that might contribute to AD risk, remain poorly defined. Here, we investigated the impact of chronic SD on brain transcriptomic signatures and subcellular compartment-specific proteomic profiles to identify genes, proteins, and signaling pathways that might confer AD risk. Chronic SD induced a modest transcriptional stress response globally, whereas alterations were more pronounced in the synaptosomal (synapse-enriched P2 fractions) and whole-brain proteomes.
