Remarkably, chronic SD elicited unique proteomic alterations at the synaptic compartment were distinct from whole-brain effects, including increased proteins involved in synaptic vesicle endocytosis, regulation of dendritic spine morphogenesis, and regulation of long-term synaptic depression, compared to increased proteins involved in immune/inflammatory, glial responses and neuronal function at the whole-brain level. Consistent with the chronic SD-induced molecular signatures, we observed subtle ultrastructural changes in vulnerable CA1 hippocampal synapses, including reduced pre-synapse size and decreased synaptic vesicle density, which suggest that chronic SD modifies synaptic transmission and plasticity. Together, our findings indicate that chronic SD differentially impacts the brain and the synaptic proteome, nominating candidate therapeutic targets and signaling pathways for future mechanistic studies of chronic SD and how SD contributes to increased AD risk.

papers.title: Phenotypic plasticity segregates antagonistic species but undermines their coexistence
papers.abstract: Environmental change often induces novel phenotypes in multiple cohabiting species, yet how such common-cue-induced plasticity shapes their coexistence is largely unknown. Testing this link requires disentangling inducing-environment effects from induced-phenotype effects, which remains elusive. We address this gap using two mutually antagonistic bacterial species, Staphylococcus aureus (Sa) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa). In habitual salinity, where both bacteria show unicellularity, Pa severely diminished Sa. In contrast, high salinity induced macroscopic cell clustering that spatially segregated Sa and Pa (Sa: bottom-dwelling vertical filament; Pa: top-dwelling horizontal mat), and led to >10-fold higher coexistence than habitual salinity. Counterintuitively, physically inhibiting cell clustering (abolishing segregation) in high salinity led to a further >100-fold higher coexistence (Sa:Pa::~1:1). This was because salinity-induced clustering was adaptive for Pa, but not for Sa: such adaptive plasticity enabled killer Pa to proliferate by monopolizing oxygen, which diminished Sa in a correlated manner, thereby weakening coexistence (mechanistically explained by diffusion-based killing). Hence, although the inducing environment promoted overall coexistence, the induced phenotype undermined it. Community-wide genomics revealed that the high level of coexistence achieved by abolishing segregation in high salinity allowed rapid coculture-specific evolution. Taken together, we uncover how plasticity can appear to promote antagonistic coexistence despite causally undermining it.

papers.title: SedaDNA metabarcoding reveals hidden histories of within-species sequence variation
papers.abstract: Most genetic data come from contemporary populations, leaving historical changes in within-species variation poorly documented. Sedimentary ancient DNA (sedaDNA) offers an opportunity to recover historical sequence variation, but its potential to reconstruct temporal changes in within-species composition remains underexplored. Here, we analysed dated sediment cores from eight Atlantic and Mediterranean coastal wetlands using COI and 18S metabarcoding, treating amplicon sequence variants as putative haplotypes. Across native, non-indigenous and cryptogenic taxa, accumulated haplotype diversity and geographic sharing varied markedly among species and markers, without consistently distinguishing species status. Temporal reconstructions revealed that accumulated haplotype networks combined distinct sets of variants detected across historical periods. Broader analyses of 18S data further showed substantial variation in haplotype composition among periods, sites and taxa. By resolving the temporal and spatial distributions of within-species sequence variants, our findings demonstrate how sedimentary DNA archives can uncover historical dimensions of biodiversity obscured by time-aggregated analyses, establishing a foundation for historical metaphylogeography.

papers.title: Ecology of gene drives: Organism fitness under larval competition determines gene drive performance
papers.abstract: Gene drives are a promising technology to control disease vectors, such as mosquitoes. However, as these interventions aim to modify and/or control the population of disease vectors, a full understanding of how gene drives interact with the ecology of the target species is essential. In this study, we explore how larval competition determines gene drive performance. We first extend an agent-based model of the larval behaviour of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes to obtain detailed predictions for gene drive designs under realistic larval competition. Using Bayesian optimisation techniques, we explore the performance of different gene drive designs and find the Pareto frontier of optimal underdominant drives with different release thresholds. To understand what determines the structure of the Pareto frontier, we conduct both local and global sensitivity analyses to assess the role different parameters play in determining gene drive performance. We find that ecological parameters, which determine the behaviour of the organism, dominate over genetic parameters for much of the parameter space, although genetic parameters play an important role at the frontier. Finally, we develop stochastic and deterministic surrogate models to enable efficient comparison and simulation without imposing the computational costs of agent-based approaches.

papers.title: All-Atom Structure Tokenizer: AtomLM-9b for Biomolecular Structure Prediction
papers.abstract: We develop an All-atom Structure Tokenizer that compresses biomolecular geometry into discrete structural tokens and achieves high-accuracy all-atom reconstruction. A hierarchical geometric encoder and finite scalar quantization map chemical units to a shared vocabulary of 8,192 tokens, while a joint coordinate de-tokenizer reconstructs backbone, side-chain, nucleic-acid, and ligand heavy atoms. The tokenizer achieves all-atom lDDT scores of 0.832 and 0.835 on CASP14 and CASP15, respectively. Building on this tokenizer, we train AtomLM-9b, an autoregressive language model based on Qwen3.5-9B that predicts structural tokens from molecular identities and connectivity and decodes them into complete atomic structures. We demonstrate, for the first time, protein structure prediction performance comparable to AlphaFold 3 with an all-atom-tokenizer-based structural language model: on the FoldBench protein-protein task, AtomLM-9b achieves a success rate of 75.01%, compared with the published AlphaFold 3 result of 72.93%. These results establish discrete all-atom tokenization as an effective interface between high-fidelity atomic reconstruction and language-model-based structure prediction.

papers.title: Tn-Seq-based identification of genes that play a role in antimicrobial tolerance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa aggregates
papers.abstract: Microbial biofilms, whether surface-associated or in the form of aggregated microbes, cause a variety of persistent infections due to their inherent tolerance to antibiotic treatment. Current knowledge of the mechanistic basis of biofilm-associated antibiotic tolerance is fragmented, and the relative importance of previously identified factors remains unknown. We developed a Tn-Seq-based workflow that enables simultaneous assessment of the relative antibiotic tolerance of thousands of individual clonal bacterial aggregates, each established by a single transposon mutant. Using this genome-wide Tn-Seq analysis approach, we identified several factors and pathways that play a role in antimicrobial tolerance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa aggregates. The majority of these factors are important for aggregate-associated tolerance to specific antibiotics, whereas some factors play a role in aggregate-associated tolerance regardless of the class of antibiotic. This methodology provides a framework that can be adapted to investigate aggregate-associated tolerance for other bacterial species and in response to different antimicrobial agents and stressors.

papers.title: SeCAT (Sequence Consensus Amplicon Trimming): a simulation-informed Nextflow pipeline for cross-study harmonisation of 16S rRNA metabarcoding datasets
papers.abstract: Global syntheses of 16S rRNA metabarcoding data rely on combining datasets, yet amplicon sequence variants generated with different primer pairs can rarely be compared directly. Existing approaches correct batch effects statistically or aggregate taxonomically; none first establishes whether the sequences are positionally comparable. We present SeCAT (Sequence Consensus Amplicon Trimming), a Nextflow pipeline that maps every studys variants onto a 16S rRNA full-length reference alignment, determines the largest window shared across studies, and tests by simulation whether trimming to that window degrades community structure before any data are merged. Applied to thirteen marine studies sequenced with three primer sets, twelve converged on a consensus window with a median trimmed read length of 249 bp (9,582 alignment columns). Degradation tests across twelve studies and six taxonomic ranks (72 study-rank combinations) returned 31 passes, 38 cautions and three confirmed failures. Eleven studies (682 samples after filtering) were harmonised (trimmed to the window and merged), collapsing 20,891 primer-specific variants into 12,667 MetaASVs, trimmed sequences deduplicated across studies. Harmonisation preserved community structure at family level (Mantel r = 1.00; Procrustes m{superscript 2} < 0.001) without adding between-study variance (|{Delta}R{superscript 2}| < 0.001). Alpha diversity, including observed richness, was recovered across all levels (intraclass correlations 0.93-1.00), whereas sequence-level congruence was moderate (Procrustes m{superscript 2} = 0.52), as expected where between-study similarity at sequence level exists only after harmonisation. The harmonised output supports synthesis from aggregated ranks down to exact sequences. By establishing positional comparability before merging, SeCAT opens the archive of primer-fragmented 16S rRNA surveys to sequence-level synthesis.

papers.title: Single-cell transcriptomics of enriched rare neural lineages of Tribolium castaneum
papers.abstract: Background Single-cell transcriptomic atlases have transformed our understanding of cell diversity. However, studies designed to profile entire tissues or organisms often omit or underrepresent rare cell populations. Enriching selected populations before sequencing offers a powerful approach to overcoming this limitation, but its application in insects has largely focused on Drosophila, limiting opportunities for comparative studies. Here, we establish complementary workflows for targeted transcriptomic profiling of rare neural populations in the red flour beetle, Tribolium castaneum. Results We developed two workflows combining population enrichment with single-cell or single-nucleus RNA sequencing. First, we generated cell suspensions from a transgenic reporter line labelling embryonic neuroblasts, enriched fluorescently labelled cells by fluorescence-activated cell sorting, and performed single-cell RNA sequencing. Second, we immunolabelled first-instar larval brains with an antibody against the nuclear transcription factor Rx, isolated and sorted labelled nuclei, and performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing. Both workflows yielded material suitable for transcriptomic profiling, demonstrating complementary reporter-based and antibody-based strategies for accessing selected neural populations at different developmental stages. Conclusions These workflows establish a methodological framework for targeted single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomic studies of rare or specific neural populations in Tribolium. They provide practical starting points for adaptation to other insect systems, expanding opportunities for comparative investigations of neural development and cell-type evolution.

papers.title: Loneliness as a modulator of intersubject neural alignment across social and nonsocial contexts
papers.abstract: Loneliness is associated with cognitive biases that diverge from normative patterns of understanding and may be reflected in altered neural responses to the world. Here, we examined how loneliness modulates neural synchrony across individuals during the processing of social and nonsocial information. Using high-resolution movie-watching fMRI data (n = 178) from the Human Connectome Project, we applied intersubject correlation analyses to identify context-dependent neural signature of loneliness. Lonely individuals primarily showed more idiosyncratic responses in regions within the default mode network, visual association cortex, and amygdala during social contexts, and in reward-related circuitry during nonsocial contexts. This suggests less stereotyped processing of social information and reward in lonely individuals. In contrast, lonely individuals exhibited greater neural synchrony in the nucleus accumbens during social contexts and in somatomotor regions during nonsocial contexts. This potentially reflects shared experiences of social craving and engagement with a socially irrelevant physical environment. These effects were robust against demographic similarities, kinship, depression, and objective levels of social connection. Together, these findings identify loneliness as a modulator of intersubject neural alignment, which may contribute to shaping how individuals process and interpret different aspects of the world.

papers.title: Physiological caffeine concentrations do not affect enteric neural crest cell migration in a mouse model
papers.abstract: The defect in enteric neural crest cell (ENCCs) migration that causes Hirschsprung disease (HD) in newborns is linked to genetic and likely also environmental factors. Among these, maternal coffee consumption has been associated with increased HD risk, yet the role of caffeine on ENCC migration has remained unexplored. Here, we show that although mouse ENCCs express caffeine-sensitive ADORA2A receptors, physiological doses of caffeine do not perturb endogenous ENCC calcium activity. We find that caffeine can modulate ENCC outgrowth in a 2D culture model but that it does not affect migration in a 3D collagen gel and in the ex-vivo embryonic gut. We conclude that physiological doses of caffeine do not hamper ENCC migration in the ex-vivo embryonic mouse intestine, thereby discarding a potential direct environmental mechanism of caffeine in HD.

papers.title: A topoietic model of collective morphogenesis and compartmentalization
papers.abstract: Xenopus laevis embryos survive teratogenic stress at significantly higher rates in larger groups, a phenomenon termed cross-embryo morphogenetic assistance (CEMA) (Tung, Sperry et al. 2024). We introduce topoiesis, a proposed mechanism by which a constitutively secreted stress signal (extracellular ATP or adenosine) diffuses and decays across the group, accumulating more in larger groups where interior volume outpaces absorbing surface. We find that this rising field carries more embryos to survival and demarcates the collective more sharply from its surroundings as collective screening strength grows with size. At intermediate sizes the outcome is spatially organized (a rescued interior enclosed by a failing periphery) and reconstitutes after shuffling. In larger groups the field restructures: its peak concentration keeps rising while its interior gradient flattens into a near-uniform bulk bounded by a sharp rim, sharpening demarcation while blurring distinctions among interior members. This pre-pattern stabilizes well before individual fate commitment, opening a window in which collective geometry can act on survival outcome. A biophysically calibrated minimal model capturing these principles recapitulates CEMA rescue rates across all six observed group sizes (N=1-306; 0%-92%) and the size-dependent craniofacial defect rate among survivors. It predicts that sealing a group's boundary against loss, rather than changing its size or biochemical regulation, moves mean rescue from 0% to 100% and reorganizes the rescue structure, tracking the predicted field geometry. These results reveal a hidden simplicity behind apparent complexity: diffusion and geometry alone may suffice to make a collective both spatially organized and controllable through macroscale intervention rather than microscale engineering of its members.

papers.title: Phage-Inducible Chromosomal Jumbo Islands (PICJIs) spreading antimicrobial resistance, host-adaptation factors and defense systems, a novel satellite family of nucleus-forming Chimalliviridae
papers.abstract: Phage satellites are mobile genetic elements that depend on helper bacteriophages to promote their own dissemination. Here, we identified a novel family of large satellites, named Phage-Inducible Chromosomal Jumbo Islands (PICJIs), that are widespread in Escherichia coli and Salmonella enterica among diverse hosts, worldwide. These largest satellites to date (71.6 {+/-} 15.8 kbp) are specifically transduced by the persistent jumbo bacteriophage Goslarvirus of the nucleus-forming Chimalliviridae family. Furthermore, PICJIs carried numerous accessory genes associated with clinically relevant antimicrobial resistances, host-adaptation, and several anti-phage defense systems.

papers.title: Facilitating the identification of cryo-EM hit matter in drug discovery with Astex-Faro
papers.abstract: Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is emerging as a tool for large-scale ligand screening and fragment-based drug discovery, generating extensive collections of reconstructions. At the same time, the systematic inspection of local density variations remains challenging, particularly when identifying weak or partially occupied features. Here, we present Astex-Faro, a statistical framework that defines an expected specimen state from a reference ensemble and identifies significant structural deviations in a target map through comparison against this reference. Furthermore, the method allows the enhancement of weak or poorly resolved features, enabling the recovery of signals that would otherwise be difficult to interpret. Fourier Shell Coherence (FSCoh) is introduced as a metric that quantifies consistency across reconstruction ensembles. We show that Astex-Faro reliably detects subtle structural features and improves their interpretability across datasets spanning a broad range of experimental challenges, from highly homogeneous specimens to membrane proteins, low-occupancy ligands and fragment-screening experiments. Together, these developments provide a practical framework for cryo-EM screening, increasing confidence in hit identification and reducing the risk of missed binding events.

papers.title: Rapid Electro-optic Two-photon Bessel Light Sheet Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging for Tissue Volume Interrogation
papers.abstract: We report a two-photon light sheet electro-optic fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (TPLS-EO-FLIM) technique based on an electro-optic (EO) modulation detection module. Scanning two-photon Bessel light sheet excitation was used to achieve in-depth volumetric imaging. The low cross-section of multiphoton excitation requires high detection efficiency, and electro-optic detection enables fast wide-field FLIM with a scientific complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (sCMOS) detector. Phototoxicity is minimized by utilizing signal from the entire illuminated sample area in a wide field camera exposure, and time-resolved volume acquisitions are feasible in minutes, with cross-sectional field of view and light sheet length over 300 microns. The method has sub-nanosecond lifetime resolution and is capable of accurate FLIM images in 10 ms exposures with as low as a few hundred photons per pixel. The technique was demonstrated through volumetric FLIM of a green fluorescent protein (GFP) labeled zebrafish embryo heart, of multi-fluorescent protein (multi-FP) labeled plant root structures and of dynamic cardiac cycles in live zebrafish embryos. For the latter, we recorded the cardiac cycle dynamics of a zebrafish embryo at 50 frames per second and measured biomechanical parameters such as heart rate, ventricle/atrium areas, atrioventricular valve dynamics, and fractional area change. Taken together, these studies show the capability of the system for rapid, high resolution, and functional imaging in diverse biological contexts.

papers.title: A single day of natural daylight exposure and physical activity does not conclusively change circadian phase: A Bayesian crossover experiment
papers.abstract: Among the environmental signals that shape human physiology, the daily light-dark cycle is the primary zeitgeber of the human circadian system. Physical activity may provide an additional non-photic time cue and frequently co-occurs with daylight in everyday life. However, their independent and combined effects on circadian phase have rarely been disentangled under naturalistic daylight conditions. In a counterbalanced mixed-design experiment, 41 healthy adults (24 women; mean age = 23.7 years, SD = 4.3) participated in up to three 40-h visits on fixed individual sleep-wake schedules. Each visit comprised an 8-h exposure beginning 1.5 h after wake to natural daylight, daylight attenuated by amber-tinted glasses, or indoor electric light (within subjects; mean photopic illuminances: 1196, 460, and 75 lx), with otherwise dim-light conditions. Participants hiked for approximately 4 h or remained sedentary (between subjects; activity indexed by median heart rate reserve [HRR]; group means: 32.7% and 2.7%). Bayesian hierarchical models used individual photopic illuminance (ActTrust 2) and median HRR to predict change in dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO; primary outcome) and exploratory outcomes (daytime and evening sleepiness, mood, and wellbeing, daytime perceived exertion, and evening psychomotor vigilance). Per standard-deviation increase in log-transformed illuminance and median HRR, estimated DLMO changes were -4.22 min (95% HDI [-10.93, 2.22]; BF = 0.70) and -6.48 min (95% HDI [-13.79, 1.27], BF = 1.56), respectively. Evidence remained inconclusive for both predictors and their interaction. Exploratory findings were largely inconclusive, practically negligible, or favoured the absence of effects. The circadian effects of a single day of natural daylight exposure, with or without physical activity, therefore remain unclear. Resolving this question may require larger samples and brighter, repeated, or habitual exposure timed to phases of greater circadian light sensitivity.

papers.title: Nutrient-responsive midgut turnover is spatially controlled by serotonin signaling
papers.abstract: Barrier epithelia undergo rapid turnover, yet how spatial tissue heterogeneity and environmental cues shape turnover rates remains poorly understood. Here, we show that serotonin signaling spatially regulates homeostatic turnover of the Drosophila midgut epithelium in a nutrient-responsive manner. Organ-wide analysis revealed regions of constitutively high and low turnover, as well as areas whose renewal depends on nutrient intake. In rapidly renewing posterior regions, serotonin accumulates in enterocytes undergoing programmed cell death (erebosis) in response to nutrient availability. Serotonin signals through the conserved 5HT7 receptor to promote enteroblast (EB) maturation and migration-associated morphological changes. 5HT7 signaling is both necessary and sufficient for renewal in high-turnover regions, and its sustained disruption leads to epithelial multilayering. Mechanistically, 5HT7 signaling regulates genes involved in metabolic pathways, such as the serine biosynthesis pathway, and in the actin cytoskeleton, which drive EB maturation and morphological change, respectively. Together, our findings establish a signaling mechanism that links nutritional cues to the spatial regulation of barrier epithelium turnover.

papers.title: Arginine activates a conserved sphingolipid defense axis against infection
papers.abstract: Metabolism is generally viewed as supporting immune responses rather than acting as a direct mediator of host defense. Here, we show that arginine directly activates the sphingolipid metabolic pathway in Plutella xylostella, promoting ceramide accumulation and consequently exerting antibacterial effects. Furthermore, we find that arginine synthesized by the host gut bacteria can activate this pathway, revealing an independent metabolic defense mechanism driven by gut bacterial arginine, which operates independently of classical immune cascades. Cross species validation shows that the ceramide biosynthesis pathway is highly conserved across eukaryotes, and its antipathogen effects display potential universality across insect species. This study opens new directions in gut innate immunity research, provides novel targets for the development of antimicrobial agents against insect pests, offers important reference value for eukaryotic pathology studies, and provides new insights into the development of novel therapeutic strategies against drug resistant bacterial infections.

papers.title: PIM6 Induces Tolerance and Confers Protection against Mycobacterium tuberculosis in Primary Macrophages
papers.abstract: Glycolipids are major components of the mycobacterial cell envelope and play critical roles in host-pathogen interactions. Here we investigate the capacity of the mycobacterial glycolipid phosphatidyl-myo-inositol hexamannosides (PIM6) to modulate innate responsiveness in naive primary human monocytes and monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs). Monocytes and MDMs prestimulated with PIM6, followed by 5 days of rest, secreted attenuated levels of tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-), interleukin 6 (IL-6), and interleukin 10 (IL-10) following LPS challenge. PIM6 pretreatment significantly altered pattern recognition receptor expression through the experimental time course and programmed a tolerized phenotype in myeloid cells independent of TLR2 activity. In an infection challenge with H37Rv Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb), MDMs pretreated with PIM6 secreted decreased levels of TNF- and IL-10 and exhibited early increased bacterial control. Together, these data reveal PIM6 as a complex immunomodulator that tolerizes myeloid cells to subsequent stimuli and exerts direct effects on the control of M.tb infection.

papers.title: The ontogeny of hippocampal spatial memory is supported by postnatal Cajal-Retzius cells
papers.abstract: The functional capabilities of the adult hippocampus depend on specialized circuits that are established during development. Cajal-Retzius (CR) cells persist in the hippocampus long after their disappearance from the neocortex and contribute to the postnatal maturation of hippocampal circuits, but how this developmental role shapes adult hippocampal function remains unknown. Here, we selectively ablated CR cells from the postnatal hippocampus and examined the consequences for spatial learning, navigation, and CA1 spatial representations. CR-cell ablated animals learned reward locations and adapted to changing task conditions, but learned more slowly and made more errors. Reinforcement-learning models suggest that these behavioral differences reflect less stable internal representations guiding behavior. Consistent with this, CA1 spatial representations remained present but were more unstable and showed reduced differentiation of reward locations, particularly when task conditions changed. Our findings identify postnatal CR cells as key developmental contributors to the stability of hippocampal spatial representations and the adaptive behavior they support.

papers.title: Uncovering cross-signal interactions in single-cell and spatial omics
papers.abstract: Individual cells simultaneously encode multiple biological signals in their gene expression profiles, including spatial position, circadian phase, and disease state. These signals can be entangled in complex ways, including circadian patterns that vary along disease progression and cell cycle dynamics that shift along developmental trajectories. While methods to disentangle such signals have been recently developed, characterizing the interaction itself between multicellular signals along with its effects on tissue function, localizing cellular subpopulations which exhibit signal interactions, and identifying potential candidate genes which drive such interactions, all remain major challenges. We present CRISP which characterizes signal interactions in single-cell gene expression data based on the correspondence between the multiple, probabilistic signal-specific projections of the data. Across simulations with tunable couplings and four single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets, CRISP recovers diverse biological signal interactions and localizes them to informative cellular subpopulations and groups of associated genes; CRISP distinguishes healthy from fibrotic liver samples and localizes the loss of zonation-position coupling to individual fibrotic hepatocytes, resolves the asymmetric coupling of TGF-{beta} response, EMT, and cell-cycle phase to specific cell subpopulations, and flags transcriptionally delayed hepatocytes in Plasmodium liver infection. Beyond quantifying and localizing signal interactions, CRISP can refine existing labels, uncover continuous cellular transitions and reveal condition-associated genes.

papers.title: Segmented regression to streamline semi-mechanistic pharmacodynamic modelling of antibiotic effects
papers.abstract: Purpose Semi-mechanistic pharmacodynamic (PD) models quantify bacterial dynamics from time-kill (TK) assays, often showing multi-phasic kill and regrowth dynamics. Regrowth is typically captured with two subpopulations with distinct concentration-effect relationships. Since only total bacterial counts are observed, subpopulation dynamics must be inferred, causing identifiability issues, sensitivity to initial estimates, and model-testing burden. We aimed to establish an efficient and robust approach for developing semi-mechanistic PD models, demonstrated with 24-hour TK data for colistin against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Methods A three-step workflow was developed: (1) log-transformed TK data were segmented into kill and regrowth phases, with linear regression estimating phase-specific slopes per concentration and replicate; (2) empirical slopes were pooled to derive concentration-effect relationships; (3) selected relationships and parameter estimates were incorporated into a semi-mechanistic PD model. Results Segmented regression captured kill and regrowth slopes at all concentrations. Slope saturation with increasing colistin and consistently weaker drug effect during regrowth indicated a less susceptible subpopulation, motivating a two-subpopulation model. The semi-mechanistic model adequately described bacterial dynamics at all concentrations, with parameters comparable to Step 2. Conclusion This three-step workflow enables efficient and robust identification of concentration-effect relationships, reducing model testing and computational burden for streamlined semi-mechanistic antibiotic PD model development.

papers.title: Oocyte-stored Mif promotes preimplantation development as an embryonic extracellular signal
papers.abstract: Mammalian preimplantation embryos develop more efficiently in groups than in isolation, suggesting that embryos secrete embryotrophic factors that promote development. However, the endogenous embryotrophic signals responsible for this long-recognized phenomenon remain incompletely defined. Using an unbiased proteomic screen for stable maternal proteins that may function as embryonic extracellular signals, we identified the cytokine macrophage migration inhibitory factor (Mif) as an abundant oocyte-stored protein that persists for several days after fertilization in mice. Quantitative measurements of spent culture medium reveal that developing embryos release Mif, with a substantial fraction derived from the maternal deposit. Extracellular Mif levels peak 3-4 days post fertilization, the same period when Mif knockout preimplantation embryos produce its strongest phenotype. Embryos lacking maternal, but not zygotic, Mif display defective blastocyst growth even in group culture. Individually cultured embryos exhibit similar blastocyst growth defects that can be rescued by supplementing recombinant Mif at physiologically relevant concentrations. Mif activates the PI3K-Akt-mTORC1 pathway through the cell-surface receptor Cd74 to promote blastocyst growth and cell proliferation. Together, these findings identify Mif as a potential endogenous contributor to the density-dependent embryotrophic effects and reveal that maternally stored proteins may function long after fertilization as extracellular signaling molecules to support preimplantation development in mammals.

papers.title: KDRD: assessing discovery replicability based on summary association statistics from a single study
papers.abstract: Replicability is essential for reliable discoveries in large-scale association studies. However, conventional replicability assessments typically require independent datasets or repeated data splitting, which may be constrained by data availability, computational burden and reduced sample sizes. Here, we developed Kernel Density-based Replicability of Discovery (KDRD), a statistical framework for estimating the expected replicability of statistically significant associations using summary statistics from a single study. Combining Gaussian kernel representations of observed association statistics with a theoretical null component, KDRD estimates replicability between independent studies under comparable conditions and enables sample size calculations beyond those currently available. In random subsampling simulations involving proteomics-based association analyses of 45 brain-related traits in the UK Biobank, KDRD showed a close agreement with the Dice Similarity Coefficients (DSCs). When KDRD was applied to the full available data,33 of the 45 traits showed at least moderate replicability, including 19 with high replicability. In matched-sample comparisons, proteomic associations showed higher KDRD estimates than pQTL associations across all 45 traits, whereas metabolomic associations showed higher estimates than proteomic associations for 33 traits. Higher protein missingness, proportions below the limit of detection, proportions of low-abundance proteins and assay variability were associated with lower KDRD estimates. KDRD-based sample size calculations suggested that approximately 200,000 and 500,000 participants would be needed for all 45 traits to achieve moderate and high replicability, respectively. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that KDRD provides a practical framework for quantitative replicability assessment and sample size calculations.

papers.title: Rho: A Purpose-Driven Workspace for Human-AI Collaborative Analysis
papers.abstract: Agent-assisted bioinformatics has moved the bottleneck from computing a result to judging it: whether a comparison answers the intended question, on which unit of replication, at which version of the input, and what would change the conclusion. These judgments need materials that are usually scattered across conversations, notebooks, figures, run logs and notes, while the agent's context is a transcript rather than the structure the researcher is actually reading. We present Rho, a human--AI collaborative analysis environment that organizes materials by the current scientific purpose: it selects or obtains the materials a judgment needs, declares the relations they serve, composes operable views, and makes this organization a shared state that is at once the researcher's reading interface and the agent's continuation context. We present the design in three parts: a method object---the operations that form a round-trip, the kinds of state that must stay distinct, and the protocol invariants that make each distinction checkable; a three-layer architecture that separates capability providers from the application that composes them; and five illustrative analyses on public data. In a bulk RNA-seq case the recomputed counts differed from the published counts and the interface kept the computation, the choices and the discrepancy available for inspection; a single-nucleus case makes sample-level replication visible behind a cell-level comparison. Under one configuration these analyses show how the design behaves in practice; we present the work as a design contribution rather than an evaluation, and usability, comparative benefit and the scientific validity of individual analyses remain to be evaluated.

papers.title: XRN1 couples RNA granule remodelling to global mRNA decay triggered by the activity of a viral endoribonuclease
papers.abstract: Cytoplasmic mRNA turnover is a fundamental determinant of gene expression, yet the spatial organisation of RNA decay remains unresolved. Although decay factors are enriched in processing (P)-bodies, whether these condensates actively mediate mRNA degradation or serve primarily as storage compartments remains controversial. Here, we exploit the alphaherpesvirus endoribonuclease, virion host shutoff (vhs), to synchronously trigger rapid, global cytoplasmic mRNA accompanied by nuclear relocalisation of the poly(A)-binding protein PABPC1. Expression of vhs caused the dispersal of P-bodies, but when the 5' to 3' exonuclease XRN1 was depleted, PABPC1 remained in the cytoplasm, and P-bodies stayed intact, associating with previously undetected G3BP1-dependent RNA granules. Similarly, catalytically inactive vhs failed to disperse P-bodies but instead induced RNA granules that also contained vhs itself and recruited decay factors in an XRN1-dependent manner. Translational shutoff by this endoribonuclease did not require RNA cleavage, G3BP1 condensation or XRN1 activity supporting a sequential model in which translational arrest precedes endonucleolytic cleavage, promoting transient RNA granules that engage P-bodies and XRN1-dependent machinery for rapid mRNA degradation within the granules, thereby precluding the biogenesis of deleterious RNA condensates.

papers.title: Single-cell geometry of drug responses across malignant glioma states
papers.abstract: Malignant gliomas exhibit substantial transcriptional heterogeneity: AC-, OPC-, NPC- and MES-like states can coexist within the same tumor, and a drug affecting one state may leave others relatively unaffected. Whether these states respond in a shared direction, or diverge, is rarely tested directly, since drug response is usually summarized by one score that collapses this heterogeneity. A public single-cell RNA-sequencing resource of drug-treated glioma slice cultures (391,444 cells) is reanalyzed here to test this directly. After restricting to 252,106 transformed glioma cells, 43 treatment-vehicle comparisons from 19 TissueID-defined units are evaluated for response-direction coherence (C, similarity of state-conditioned treatment vectors) and change in state separation (K, state-centroid contraction or expansion). C proves to be the reproducible signal: it survives high-confidence state filtering (r=0.931), an independently selected 500-gene space (r=0.634), the published Neftel modules (r=0.783) and non-overlapping gene cross-fitting (r=0.809), and exceeds two null models in 41 of 43 comparisons, a result that also holds across the 19 biological units themselves (19 of 19 positive; P=3.8e-6). Within-drug coherence exceeds between-drug coherence in all 52 drug pairs and all 11 multi-drug units (P=0.000488): response direction is drug-specific, not generic. K tells a different story: stable only when the feature space is fixed, it loses concordance whenever that space shifts, with only about half of comparisons separating from the null. Malignant glioma states largely agree on the direction of drug response even when they disagree on its magnitude.

papers.title: Plant-plant communication in tomato: mechanisms underpinning information transfer between plants
papers.abstract: As evidences about plant-plant communication are mounting, we lack a mechanistic understanding of intricate events occurring inside and among pairs of plants. This is needed to untangle proximal causes explaining how volatiles emitted by herbivore-attacked plants can enhance plant defence in intact neighbouring plant. A comprehensive knowledge of these interactions may favour their integration in trait-based agroecological frameworks. Based on an original experiment set-up, we connected infested sender plants and intact receiver plants during 3 days. We monitored metabolomic reprogramming of sender plant and progressive adjustments in their volatile emissions. Plant-plant communication was tested according to metabolomic priming of receiver plant. Information transfer was tracked with kinetics of volatile profiles and chemodiversity metrics grounded in information theory. Our results show that sender plants infested with Phtorimae absoluta undergo deep reconfiguration of immune systems and balance their emissions of mono- and sesquiterpenoids over 3 days. These changes in airborne cues result in similar reprograming of immune system in receiver plants. Additionally, we observed herbivory-driven relationships between chemodiversity of volatile profiles produced by sender and receiver plants. Both metabolome and volatilome suggest that plant-plant communication operates as mirror effects with receiver plants matching up their defences on that of sender plants. From an adaptative standpoint, this supports the idea that information conveyed among plants is explicit enough to warn receiver plant against appropriate stress. More generally, this study points that information transfer could rely not only on composition but also on chemodiversity of volatile cues. We discuss implications related to cue detection at the molecular scale and cue propagation at the plant cover scale. Bridging composition and chemodiversity of volatile cues opens interesting avenues to study the efficiency of communication system in noisy environments.

papers.title: COSMOS: integrated vector-pathogen metagenomics for mosquito-borne disease
papers.abstract: By 2050, almost half of the global population will be at risk of mosquito-borne disease. Effective response requires monitoring both pathogen transmission and vector abundance, yet these are typically assessed using separate assays with limited taxonomic breadth. Here we present COSMOS (COmprehensive Sequencing for MOSquito-borne disease), a targeted metagenomics workflow designed to reconstruct pathogen genomes and mosquito community composition directly from mixed field-collected samples. Over three annual rounds of a major Australian surveillance program, we evaluated >120,000 mosquitoes in 219 traps, with 98.7% agreement with surveillance data across seven monitored arboviruses, and additional detections of Sindbis virus and the state's first detection of encephalitic Little Sussex virus. Of 137 viral detections, 101 yielded near-complete genomes (>90% coverage) at median 95x depth. Using an accompanying computational workflow, COSMOS quantified mosquito composition, matching entomological estimates of reported vector species (CCC 0.78-0.89). Joint analysis of virus and vector composition identified structured mosquito communities associated with spatial and temporal environmental variation, allowing the ecological context of arbovirus detections to be characterised. Detections during the Murray Valley encephalitis virus outbreak in 2023 were concentrated within a narrowly defined mosquito-community space corresponding to rural communities dominated by the inland S-AUS sub-lineage of Culex annulirostris. Integrated vector-pathogen metagenomics provides ecological and evolutionary context for arbovirus activity within a single scalable workflow for surveillance and outbreak response.

papers.title: Structural basis of ribosomal RNA repair by RtcB2
papers.abstract: Ribotoxins disable ribosomes by cleaving ribosomal RNA, but how repair enzymes recognize and restore these damaged machines remains unclear. Here, we report three cryo-electron microscopy structures of the RNA ligase RtcB2 bound to damaged Escherichia coli 30S subunits. An extended interface stabilizes the ribosomal head and decoding-center scaffold while positioning the cleaved 3'-phosphate end within the catalytic pocket. Two structures contain enzyme-linked guanosine monophosphate, whereas the third captures its transfer to the RNA. RNA activation accompanies RtcB2 reorientation and entry of the 5'-hydroxyl-containing segment into an adjacent cleft. Comparisons with assembled ribosomes reveal structural barriers to substrate access. These structures connect recognition of a damaged ribosome to chemical activation of its RNA for repair.

papers.title: Brain Decoding from a Deep Neural Network of Visual Memory Reveals the Maturation Trajectory of Memory Systems across Ages 3-7
papers.abstract: Memories from the first four years of life are largely inaccessible by adulthood, yet these early experiences profoundly shape cognition throughout development. Understanding this phenomenon of infantile amnesia is critical for revealing the mechanisms of early memory development. Here, we developed a new content-based behavioral measure of memory that quantifies how closely children's memory patterns resemble those of adults, which we term the memory maturation score. Using a movie-watching fMRI dataset spanning age 3 to adulthood, we trained a cross-validated model on adults' movie-evoked brain activity to predict adult's propensity to remember each movie snippet, estimated by ResMem, a deep neural network trained to predict visual memorability. We then applied the model to each child's brain activity while viewing the same movie to assess their memory maturation (i.e., cross-decodability from adult patterns). Children exhibited adult-like neural patterns of memory around age 4, extending prior behavioral findings. Structural analyses showed that the volume of the left posterior hippocampus, but not age or total brain volume, significantly predicted children's memory maturation. Memory maturation around age 4 thus likely reflects age-related neural development of hippocampal memory systems, rather than an age increase itself. Functional searchlight analyses revealed a trajectory of memory maturation: the inferior temporal gyrus reflected mature memory-related processing from age 3 onward, the left posterior hippocampus by age 5, and higher-order regions involved in social-affective processing and multimodal integration by age 7. Together, these findings suggest that hippocampal maturation between ages 3 and 5 drives the maturation of memory patterns.

papers.title: Functional analysis of small-molecule and protein binding domains using monomeric streptavidin-based two-component biosensors
papers.abstract: Protein biosensors are important analytical and diagnostic tools that convert molecular recognition into measurable activity. Most common two-component biosensors require two non-competing recognition domains, yet binding affinity and specificity alone do not reliably predict their compatibility with the rest of the biosensor. We report a modular platform that exploits monomeric streptavidin (mSA2) as a surrogate recognition domain, enabling rapid functional evaluation of candidate binders in the context of biosensor scaffold without requiring a second ligand-specific binding protein. We established a chromatography-free protocol for recovering functional mSA2-based biosensor components from Escherichia coli. Using biotinylated small molecules methotrexate and vitamin D3, as well as heart failure protein biomarkers galectin-3 and S100A7 we demonstrate ligand-dependent reporter biosensor activation. The developed platform provides a scalable approach for rapid binder evaluation and biosensor prototyping, streamlining biosensor development using binding domains generated by directed evolution or computational protein design.

papers.title: Neural Crest-Derived Endocardial Cells Required for Heart Valve Development
papers.abstract: Abnormalities in cardiac valves, which maintain unidirectional blood flow through the heart, affect 2-3% of people worldwide and are the most common form of structural heart disease (1).Yet the cell types that make up the valve, and how they communicate to direct development and homeostasis, remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a rare, essential population of highly secretory valve endocardial cells in mouse and human that derive from migrating neural crest cells. Ablation of these cells in mice caused perinatal lethality with thickened leaflets, stenosis, and regurgitation, mirroring human valve disease. This subset of endocardial cells uniquely expresses the secreted signaling protein parathyroid hormone-like hormone (Pthlh). Global disruption of Pthlh caused valve stenosis and lethality and neural crest-specific deletion produced similar valve disease, with impaired maturation of valvular interstitial cells and disrupted bone morphogenetic protein signaling. These findings identify a previously unrecognized cell type and signaling pathway essential for valve morphogenesis, with implications for the pathogenesis and treatment of human valve defects.

papers.title: Comparative molecular analysis of histopathologic subtypes reveals shared epithelial remodeling yet distinct fibroblast programs in scleroderma lung disease
papers.abstract: Rationale: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) drives mortality in systemic sclerosis (SSc), with a subset developing progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) resembling idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). Despite recognition of two distinct histopathologic patterns, the cellular basis of nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) and usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) remains poorly understood. Objectives: To define shared and distinct cellular and molecular features of SSc-NSIP and SSc-UIP compared to IPF. Methods: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics were performed on explanted lungs from patients with SSc-NSIP (n=6), SSc-UIP (n=6), or IPF (n=6), and control donors (n=12) with immunohistochemistry and western blot validation. Main Results: Across 120,254 nuclei from 35 cell types, there was striking similarity across fibrotic subgroups in epithelial, endothelial, and immune compartments, including alveolar type 1 cell loss, pathologic alveolar type 2 (AT2) gene expression, and expansion of COL15A1 endothelial cells and profibrotic macrophages. Diseased AT2s showed activation of the p53/DNA damage pathway. Aberrant basaloid (AB) cells were present in both SSc-ILD subtypes and transcriptionally similar to IPF ABs. They consistently neighbored profibrotic CTHRC1 fibroblasts, even in SSc-NSIP, despite lacking fibroblast foci. Fibroblast heterogeneity differentiated the histopathologic subtypes. Inflammatory fibroblasts were enriched in SSc-NSIP and CTHRC1 fibroblasts in UIP. AB-to-pathologic fibroblast crosstalk was defined by profibrotic signaling, with amplified TGF-{beta} signaling in UIP. Conclusions: Convergent epithelial remodeling is a hallmark of PPF in SSc-ILD and IPF. Fibroblast heterogeneity characterized by altered TGF-beta signaling distinguishes SSc-NSIP from SSc-UIP and IPF. Accelerated aging, DNA damage, and p53-dependent senescence pathways may represent shared drivers of PPF.

papers.title: Leveraging short and long-read sequencing to comprehensively characterize alternatively polyadenylated and alternatively spliced transcripts
papers.abstract: Pre-mRNA processing through alternative splicing and alternative polyadenylation generates diverse transcripts from the same gene. Alternative splicing involves use of different exons and specific 3'Untranslated regions (3'UTRs). When limited to the same terminal exon, 3'end formation through alternative polyadenylation gives rise to transcripts containing 3'UTRs of different sizes which affect their subcellular localization, stability, and translatability. The full repertoire of transcripts arising from alternative pre-mRNA processing under different biological and disease states remains unknown. Using the blood cancer, mantle cell lymphoma's (MCL) as our experimental model we found that two genes, SOX11 and ATM, that contribute to the disease pathology, express transcripts that have short 3'UTRs. Apart from select transcripts, our analysis of short-read sequencing data did not uncover widespread global shortening of 3'UTRs in MCL. However, we discovered that both the canonical and non-canonical polyadenylation signals (PASs), were used for 3'end formation. We experimentally verified the PASs used by specific transcripts. Combining short-read and long-read sequencing data enabled us to characterize, classify and identify alternatively splicing in MCL. We identified splice variants for several genes including PTEN, EZH2 and validated the expression of GLS1 at the protein level and by using GLS1 inhibitors. Collectively, our approach provide insights into how to identify alternatively spliced and alternatively polyadenylated transcripts.

papers.title: The chromatin-associated PWO proteins interface with circadian and epigenetic signaling to regulate flowering time in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: Flowering time is a major determinant of reproductive success in plants and is regulated by several interconnected pathways which converge on few key flowering time-related genes. In the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana (Arabidopsis), both the circadian clock and chromatin-associated proteins integrate environmental cues to coordinate flowering (Staiger et al. 2013; Nohales and Kay, 2016; Du et al. 2019; Haider and Farrona, 2024). However, how the circadian-epigenetic signaling crosstalk regulates this crucial developmental transition has still been underexplored. PWWP-DOMAIN INTERACTORS OF POLYCOMBS 1 and 2 (PWO1 and PWO2) are chromatin-associated proteins that have been linked to the regulation of histone 2A (H2A) mono-ubiquitination (ub) (H2Aub) levels (Zheng et al. 2023). PWO1 and PWO2 also affect flowering time (Hohenstatt et al. 2018; Khan et al. 2026), but the underlying molecular mechanisms, their effects on clock genes, as well as their distinct contributions to flowering-time regulation remain mostly unknown.

papers.title: Evolutionary and acclimatory shifts in ion transporter gene expression across salinity transitions in the copepod Eurytemora carolleeae
papers.abstract: Many aquatic invaders are crossing biogeographic boundaries from saline to freshwater habitats. This transition often requires acclimation or evolution of physiological mechanisms to maintain internal ionic homeostasis. Populations of the copepod Eurytemora affinis complex have repeatedly invaded freshwater environments from saline habitats over the past century, providing an ideal model for investigating rapid adaptation to salinity change. Prior studies have found that ion transport-related genes form the largest functional categories of genes under selection and show evolutionary shifts in gene expression across saline to freshwater transitions in the E. affinis complex. In this study, focusing on the top targets of selection, we investigated evolutionary and acclimatory shifts in gene expression for 19 ion transport-related genes for populations of E. carolleeae (Atlantic clade of the E. affinis complex). Using a quantitative real-time PCR approach, we compared gene expression between ancestral saline and derived freshwater populations through a common garden reaction norm experiment and a laboratory natural selection experiment. We found that different ion transport-related gene paralogs within expanded gene families showed divergent patterns of expression in response to salinity change, consistent with specialization. For instance, Na+/K+-ATPase subunit paralog 1 (NKA--1) and Na+,K+,2Cl- cotransporter paralog 3 (NKCC-3) exhibited the evolution of increased expression in the freshwater population across all conditions, relative to the saline population. In contrast, Na+/H+ antiporter paralog 7 (NHA-7) and NHA-5 showed evolution of elevated expression in the saline population under low salinity relative to the freshwater population. Several genes also showed evolutionary differences in plasticity between saline and freshwater populations, such that saline populations retained phenotypic plasticity, whereas freshwater populations were comparatively canalized. In the laboratory natural selection experiment imposing salinity decline, evolutionary responses of the paralogs NKCC-3, NHA-5, and NHA-7 in the saline selection line largely recapitulated the evolutionary shifts observed in the natural populations. On the other hand, expression patterns of the ion transporters in the freshwater selection line showed little response during salinity increase, suggesting canalization. Together, these results reveal evolutionary and acclimatory divergence in gene expression among paralogs, suggesting the evolution of functional divergence among them.

papers.title: Disentangling visual and motor contributions to continuous psychophysics
papers.abstract: Continuous psychophysics measures visual function by asking observers to track a randomly moving target. Because continuous responses provide more information than traditional discrete judgements, a few minutes of tracking can estimate visual sensitivity, making the approach attractive for testing children and patients. Tracking performance is often summarized by cross-correlating the target and cursor velocities: the resulting cross-correlogram peak, lag and width index how strongly, quickly and sharply the observer responds to the target. Tracking, however, requires both seeing the target and moving the cursor towards it, so poor tracking may reflect impaired vision, impaired motor control, or both. Here, we test whether visual and motor contributions to tracking performance can be told apart. Participants tracked a target with a computer mouse while wearing glasses that simulate two levels of visual impairment, using either their dominant or their non-dominant hand. We find that both manipulations alter the cross-correlogram metrics, lowering the peak correlation and delaying and broadening the response, but in different proportions. Visual impairment mainly delays and broadens the response, and does so in proportion to each participant's loss of visual acuity. The non-dominant hand mainly lowers the peak correlation. Two signatures of motor control explain this difference: with the non-dominant hand, participants pause more often and for longer, and move more noisily between pauses, whereas visual impairment alters neither. Together, response lag, time paused and movement noise reveal whether a change in tracking is visual or motor in almost every participant. Our findings demonstrate that, given a baseline measurement, the same tracking data that measure vision can also reveal whether a change in performance reflects a change in what an individual sees or in how they move.

papers.title: TensorPLS: an R package for exploring molecular and temporal patterns in longitudinal omics data using PLS-DA
papers.abstract: Longitudinal omics datasets combine high-dimensional repeated measurements with missing observations, complicating supervised modelling and temporal interpretation. We present TensorPLS, an R package integrating missing-data handling, matrix-based partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), structured variable importance, subject-level nested cross-validation and downstream functional enrichment. Data are represented as subjects x features x time tensors. Missing values are handled by Tucker3 reconstruction or feature-time mean imputation, after which tensors are unfolded along the subject mode for PLS-DA. Cumulative variable importance in projection (VIP) scores are mapped to feature-time coordinates and summarised across time and cumulative PLS models. During nested cross-validation, imputation, component tuning, VIP-based feature selection and refitting are performed within training partitions. Full-cohort models are fitted separately for descriptive interpretation. We evaluated TensorPLS on two public longitudinal transcriptomic datasets using five-by-five nested cross-validation. In GSE68310 (109 subjects), Tucker3 reconstruction yielded Q2Y = 0.670, AUROC 0.971 and balanced accuracy 0.931. In GSE182616 (66 subjects), feature-time mean imputation yielded Q2Y = 0.294, AUROC 0.827 and balanced accuracy 0.756. Predictive metrics were calculated from pooled outer held-out predictions. TensorPLS supports predictive assessment, functional enrichment of selected genes and temporal interpretation of model-assigned feature importance.

papers.title: Disulfide Crosslink Density is a Key Determinant in the Formation, Dynamics, and Maturation of Cysteine-rich Designer Biomolecular Condensates.
papers.abstract: Biomolecular condensates form through weak, multivalent, non-covalent interactions, but the role of covalent crosslinks in shaping their assembly and material properties remains poorly understood. We previously showed that disulfide bonds between cysteines in designer phase-separating peptides (PSPs) act as redox-reversible crosslinks that lower the saturation concentration (Csat) and help maintain condensate fluidity. Here, we ask which sequence features govern this behavior. We built two peptide libraries: one varying the inter-cysteine spacer length (2-10 residues) and one varying cysteine density (0-33%). Inter-cysteine spacers tuned condensate properties only modestly. Longer inter-cysteine lengths raised Csat from 300 to 900 M, showed greater fluidity (as assessed by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) recovery rate, and resisted loss of fluidity during maturation; all inter-cysteine length variants dissolved and reformed reversibly over three redox cycles. Cysteine density, in contrast, was the dominant control parameter. Increasing cysteine density lowered Csat about 60-fold (1.5 mM to 25 M) and reduced the fluidity by an order of magnitude. Its effect on fluidity was non-monotonic: condensates with up to ~14% cysteine density stayed liquid-like for 10 days, whereas those with 21-33% cysteine density in the peptide showed slower coalescence. Condensates with the highest densities also resisted dissolution under reducing conditions and showed sharply reduced uptake of a protein cargo (eGFP; ~60% to ~9%) and a small molecule (TMR, ~70% to ~45%), consistent with smaller mesh size. Together, these results identify disulfide crosslink density as a key lever for programming condensate assembly, viscoelasticity, redox responsiveness, and porosity. The results offer key design principles both for understanding cysteine-rich disordered proteins in biomolecular condensates and for engineering redox-responsive biomaterials.

papers.title: Conserved synaptic modifications by humanized tau through diverse isoform- and mutation-specific intracellular interactions
papers.abstract: Mutations in the microtubule-binding protein tau are considered causal for a diverse group of neurodegenerative diseases collectively referred to as primary tauopathies. Specific tauopathies are associated with different mutations, distinct tau isoforms, manifest in unique cellular and circuit-wide patterns of degeneration, and present with specific clinical symptoms and trajectories. The mechanisms that link variations in the primary tau protein structure to distinct forms of neural circuit dysfunction remain largely unknown. Here, we created an orthogonal viral resource to systematically examine the impact of expressing humanized tau isoforms harboring different disease-relevant mutations in excitatory pyramidal cells from the mouse prelimbic cortex. We used these reagents to show that expression of mutant humanized tau (hTau) as either of two isoforms produced very similar patterns of circuit-specific synaptic disconnection on cortical projection neurons. However, mass spectrometry revealed that the interactomes of these different tau species varied markedly as functions of isoform, mutation, and subcellular location. We validated the functional relevance of increased hTau interactions with mitochondrial proteins in induced neurons differentiated from Ngn2-iPSCs expressing different hTau constructs. These results suggest different disease-relevant hTau proteins likely use distinct mechanisms to drive a highly stereotyped form of synapse loss in cortical neurons.

papers.title: Amnesia Induced by Suppressing the Focus of Internal Attention
papers.abstract: Our thoughts can recede as we direct attention to the external world. This experience may reflect the suppression of thoughts about past events, future worries, or stray ideas that could otherwise disrupt focus. Such thoughts may arise spontaneously from replay mechanisms supported by the episodic memory system; hence, sustaining external focus may require suppressing these systems to stop internal distraction. Here, periods of high external focus disrupted diverse episodic content activated near in time, inducing an 'amnesic shadow'. This shadow occurred for both novel content and already formed memories and exhibited key markers of active suppression: forgetting beyond expectations from time alone, which generalised to an alternative reminder. External attention therefore automatically engages an active suppression mechanism that appears to broadly inhibit cognitive systems supporting the emergence of distracting thoughts. The findings raise the possibility that people may naturally gravitate toward activities demanding external attention, unwittingly, to regulate unwanted thoughts.

papers.title: Rapid Detection and Initial Treatment of Life-Threatening Subdural Hematoma in a Sheep Model
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is the leading cause of death and disability in people under 40 worldwide. There is an unmet need for detection and treatment of life-threatening TBI when computed tomography (CT) scanners and neurosurgeons are unavailable. We developed a new handheld frequency-domain multidetector infrared hemorrhage detection device. Using the new device, military pre-hospital medics required <4 minutes to detect life-threatening subdural hematoma in a sheep model. We developed a second device that allows non-neurosurgeons to safely create a burr hole and partially remove clotted subdural blood. In sheep, the treatment device reduced intracranial pressure within 20 minutes, and improved post-anesthesia blinded neurological outcomes. With human use adaptation, these devices could allow rapid detection and initial treatment of some life-threatening TBIs in challenging situations.

papers.title: MET inhibition exploits conserved regulatory dependencies in malignant rhabdoid tumors
papers.abstract: Malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs) are lethal, yet genomically simple childhood cancers characterised by universal SWI/SNF dysregulation. Despite this shared molecular framework, the regulatory programs sustaining MRTs and how they wire actionable dependencies, remain poorly defined. Here, we integrated single-cell multi-omic profiling and spatial transcriptomics across anatomically and molecularly diverse MRTs, generating a comprehensive multimodal MRT dataset at single-cell resolution. We leveraged this resource to identify candidate tumor-specific dependencies, which were subsequently functionally validated in vitro and in vivo in matched patient-derived models. We found that distinct malignant subpopulations are spatially patterned in complex environmentally shaped topologies, consistent with reciprocal interactions with stromal and immune compartments contributing to intratumoral transcriptional diversity. We identified recurrent transcriptional metaprograms conserved across patients and molecular subtypes, including a previously undescribed shared core rhabdoid program, as well as a metaprogram characterized by extracellular matrix interactions, and preferentially localized in tumor-stroma intermixed neighborhoods, supporting identification of niche conditioning cues. Mechanistically, we identified regulatory wiring driving these metaprograms, with the core shared rhabdoid programme coordinated by a circuit centred on TCF12, ZNF148 and CHD2. Guided by target nominations from our integrated analyses, we performed a curated drug screen using patient-derived MRT models and validated HGF/MET signaling as a selective vulnerability in extrarenal rhabdoid tumors. Pharmacologic MET inhibition was cytotoxic in sensitive models and induced a complete response in vivo using a clinically approved compound. Importantly, MET expression in primary tumors correlated with response, supporting biomarker-guided patient stratification for immediate clinical translation. Collectively, our findings define the molecular architecture of MRTs, reveal conserved regulatory programs beyond anatomical and molecular subtypes, and highlight a targetable signaling axis with immediate translational potential, establishing a framework for precision therapy in this lethal pediatric malignancy.

papers.title: Unprecedented urban freshwater microviral survey highlights shift from sewage to river water communities
papers.abstract: Microviruses are abundant yet still poorly resolved components of virosphere, particularly across urban freshwater continua. Here, we investigated complete microvirus genomes recovered from sewage water (SW), treated wastewater (TW), and river water (RW) along an urban SW TW RW continuum, providing an extensive genomic dataset of 18,449 complete genomes grouped into 825 genera. This catalog enabled a high-resolution assessment of microvirus diversity, taxonomy, and ecological distribution across anthropized aquatic compartments. All currently described microvirus orders were detected, with Gokushovirales dominating the dataset and Betagokushoviridae emerging as the most prevalent family in TW and RW samples. In contrast, Alpavirales were enriched in SW but strongly depleted after treatment, consistent with their association with gut-related bacterial hosts. Alpha- and beta-diversity analyses showed that water type was the main driver of microvirus community structure, whereas seasonal effects were weak and not robust under the hydrological conditions of the sampling year. Wastewater treatment plants thus acted as strong biological filters, reshaping viral assemblages and selecting compartment-specific microvirus populations. Finally, the pronounced and reproducible shifts observed across the continuum suggest that selected microvirus groups may serve as promising bioindicators of anthropogenic influence in freshwater systems.

papers.title: Neural Activation of Human Primary Intestinal Enteroendocrine L-cells
papers.abstract: Intestinal enteroendocrine L-cells play a central role in metabolic homeostasis by secreting the gut hormones GLP-1 and PYY, but whether and how neural signals regulate human L-cell function remains poorly understood. This gap reflects the limited availability of human model systems enriched for mature L-cells. Here, we establish a differentiation strategy that generates human donor-derived ileal organoids with markedly increased L-cell abundance, enabling functional interrogation of L-cell physiology in their basal state. Using this system, we show that cholinergic and adrenergic stimuli activate L-cells, triggering calcium influx and secretion of GLP-1 and PYY. Pharmacological analysis reveals that cholinergic regulation of human L-cells is mediated predominantly through M3 muscarinic receptors, while adrenergic regulation is mediated through the {beta}1 adrenergic receptor. Neurotransmitter-evoked activation also initiates gap junction-dependent calcium waves that propagate across the intestinal epithelium; however, disruption of epithelial coupling by abolishing calcium propagation does not impair hormone secretion. Together, these findings identify L-cells as integrative hubs that couple neural signals to gut hormone secretion and epithelial calcium waves, providing mechanistic insight into the gut-brain axis and how the nervous system regulates intestinal endocrine function in human intestine.

papers.title: From smartphone to gene: Automated image-based phenotyping captures flowering diversity of common buckwheat
papers.abstract: Common buckwheat (Fagopyrum esculentum Moench) exhibits an indeterminate flowering habit, resulting in the simultaneous occurrence of flowering, seed development and seed ripening. This contributes to yield losses and complicates mechanized harvesting. Therefore, the development of varieties with a desirable flowering pattern is a breeding priority in buckwheat. However, phenotyping of buckwheat flowering under field conditions remains challenging because manual assessments are time consuming and expertise dependent. Here, we show that imaging devices such as smartphones or cameras can be used for phenotyping of flowering traits in a buckwheat collection encompassing 169 accessions. Flowering traits describing flowering time (n=10), flowering intensity (n=6) and abscission (n=6) were extracted from 37,078 images captured over five growing seasons using a Mask R-CNN segmentation model combined with statistical modelling of flowering dynamics. The 22 extracted traits were highly heritable (0.5 < h2 < 0.93) and correlated well (0.84 <r< 0.94) with manually assessed flowering stages while providing additional information on flowering intensity. Genome-wide association studies revealed 171 genomic regions associated with flowering traits, including marker-trait associations for agronomically important breeding targets. Candidate genes had functional annotations including "Auxin response factor" and "Ethylene-insensitive protein", gene families involved in hormone signalling and developmental regulation, controlling flowering in other species. These results demonstrate how digital imaging combined with automated feature extraction can be leveraged to gain insight on buckwheat flowering patterns in large scale field trials across different phenotyping platforms. This paves the way to breed for desired flowering patterns using molecular tools in a targeted manner.

papers.title: De novo genome assembly of the floating-hook moss Warnstorfia fluitans
papers.abstract: The floating-hook moss Warnstorfia fluitans is a natural species dominant in subarctic and Arctic aquatic ecosystems. It is adapted to cold, acidic, and nutrient-deficient environments and possesses great potential for bioremediation by removing contaminants from polluted water in cold climate conditions. Here, we present the first de novo genome assembly of W. fluitans generated from pooled male and female gametophytes. The assembly is 725.04 Mb, has a N50 of 193.5 kb, a BUSCO completeness of 97.6% against the Viridiplantae lineage and 82% against the Embryophyta lineage. The whole assembly has Merqury quality value of 37 and Merqury completeness of 92%. A total of 30421 protein coding genes were predicted, with 78.62% completeness by compleasm and 87% OMArk completeness against the Embryophyta lineage. Repetitive sequences comprise 56.16% of the genome. We also present here the two complete circular chloroplast genomes and a linear mitochondrial genome of W. fluitans. This genomic resource will facilitate studies of ecological adaptation and a wide range of biological and evolutionary studies in bryophytes.

papers.title: Integrative Transcriptomic Meta-Analysis Reveals SIRT1-SNCA Correlation in Parkinson's Disease
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that affects midbrain dopaminergic neurons without any approved therapy. Candidate molecular targets identified in one model are not always traceable across the postmortem, induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC), and cell-based systems used to study PD, which complicates clinical translation. To address this gap, we performed an integrative transcriptomic meta-analysis of 33 publicly available datasets across postmortem human brain, iPSC-derived models, and dopaminergic cell lines of PD. Differential expression and functional enrichment analyses were combined with STRING protein-protein interaction networks, followed by drug-gene interaction screening against a polyphenol panel. Overall, resveratrol was recovered in all 33 comparisons, independent of model system, tissue, and genetic background. We associated resveratrol with 30 distinct target genes, and SIRT1 was itself a recovered target in 6 comparisons spanning all three model systems. Finally, we resolved the SIRT1-SNCA relationship into four directional patterns that differed by model, inverse in postmortem brain and positive in acutely toxin-exposed cells. These findings support a candidate, context-dependent resveratrol-SIRT1 axis in PD.

papers.title: PLATE: a global atlas of food metaplasmidomes
papers.abstract: Plasmids play a central role in the acquisition and spread of genes underlying important traits in food-associated microorganisms. Although shotgun metagenomics has greatly expanded opportunities to study food microbiomes, their plasmid diversity remains largely uncharacterized. Here, we present the Plasmid Atlas of Food Ecosystems (PLATE), a curated global resource of food metaplasmidomes. Built from 4,690 food metagenomes spanning 55 countries and 17 categories, PLATE comprises a broad catalog (bPLATE) of 3,904,895 putative plasmid contigs (PPCs) and a refined catalog (rPLATE) of 213,474 PPCs, corresponding to 181,871 unique sequences. Both catalogs are complemented by curated sample metadata, host predictions, taxonomic assignments, and functional annotations covering antimicrobial resistance (AMR), protein families and KEGG orthologs, CRISPR-Cas systems, carbohydrate-active enzymes, and bioactive peptides. We demonstrate PLATE's utility through a case study of AMR genes detected on PPCs from food microbiomes. PLATE is freely accessible and enables users to interactively search for and download sequences, annotations, and associated metadata. By organizing plasmid-associated sequence diversity and functional potential across food ecosystems, PLATE provides a foundation for analyses of food metaplasmidomes.

papers.title: Social ties are maintained through sensory adaptations in green chromides
papers.abstract: Sensory systems exhibit considerable plasticity in response to environmental changes, yet the functional implications of such plasticity remain poorly understood, particularly regarding how changes in visual gene expression influence social behaviour. To address this gap, we investigated how visual sensory plasticity relates to conspecific preferences in green chromides (Etroplus suratensis), an Indian cichlid that relies on vision for social preferences towards conspecifics. We first characterized retinal opsin and chromophore-related genes through transcriptomic analysis and subsequently examined behavioural and molecular responses under sequential white- and blue-light environments. We quantified visually mediated conspecific preferences, and the expression of rod and cone opsins and the chromophore-related gene Cyp27c1 at regular intervals.
