Pimpinellifolium) roots lie near the Pareto front, but existing models treat lateral roots as straight, misrepresenting curved architectures. - We extended the Pareto model to account for lateral-root curvature, estimating curvature parameter G and trade-off weight for 1,597 root systems from 240 accessions grown with or without 100mM NaCl. We also measured root angles and conducted a GWAS. This is the first Pareto model of root architecture to incorporate lateral-root curvature and the first study to demonstrate heritability of position on the Pareto front and identify an associated locus. - Curvature improved model fit in 80% of root systems after penalizing the additional parameter. Salt shifted root systems toward conduction-delay minimization (lower ) across all four architectural types. Lateral roots grew 10{degrees} closer to vertical, while main-root angle was unchanged. was more heritable under salt, and a chromosome~6 locus within an intron of the ISOAMYLASE~3 ortholog explained approximately 11% of its variation. - Salt reorganizes lateral roots, but not the main root, toward faster transport, with a heritable, mappable component.

papers.title: An endogenous retrovirus insertion disrupting bovine ALKBH8 causes a failure-to-thrive syndrome with immunodeficiency associated with juvenile mortality in Brown Swiss cattle
papers.abstract: The Brown Swiss (BS) cattle breed is one of the major Swiss dairy breeds. Intensive selection and the widespread use of few elite sires in artificial insemination have increased inbreeding and the occurrence of deleterious recessive alleles in the homozygous state. Analyzing life trajectories in large, genotyped cohorts can identify hidden recessive disorders that are difficult to detect using traditional case-control association testing. Long-read DNA sequencing enables precise detection of causal alleles, including structural variants. This study aimed to (1) identify cryptic recessive loci affecting rearing performance in Swiss BS cattle, (2) evaluate their impact on survival, (3) characterize the associated phenotype, (4) identify the causal variant using long-read whole-genome sequencing, and (5) assess its functional impact. Using Homozygous Haplotype Enrichment/Depletion (HHED) mapping, we identified a risk haplotype (BH39) on chromosome 15 spanning from 16,276,819 bp to 16,446,984 bp that was associated with increased juvenile mortality within the first 180 days of life when present in the homozygous state. The BH39 occurred at a frequency of approximately 4.5% in Swiss BS cattle and 5.3% in German and Austrian BS cattle, and homozygous carriers exhibited a significantly reduced first-year survival rate. Five females homozygous for BH39 underwent clinical examination. They all showed recurrent respiratory disease, impaired growth, poor body condition, rough hair coat, and brown-discolored teeth. Pathological examination revealed bronchopneumonia and eosinophilic enteritis. Clinicopathological findings indicated failure to thrive and immunodeficiency. Long-read WGS of two BH39 homozygous calves revealed a private homozygous coding variant that was in high linkage disequilibrium with BH39. The identified structural variant was an insertion of a large transposable element (10.4 kb ERVK[2-1-LTR]) into the third exon of ALKBH8 (NM_001080341.2 c.267_268indel). Full-length RNA sequencing of cerebellum and liver from a homozygous calf revealed that the endogenous retrovirus (ERV) insertion introduces a cryptic transcription termination signal, truncating ALKBH8 mRNA. This study demonstrates that exploring population-scale genomic data and mining thousands of life-history records, followed by veterinary follow-up evaluations and molecular genetic analyses, provides an effective strategy for identifying cryptic recessive disorders that shorten the lifespan of cattle. The findings provide strong evidence that the ERV insertion into the coding sequence of ALKBH8 represents a loss-of-function variant that causes a previously undescribed recessive disorder that results in increased rearing loss.

papers.title: Xeno-Free Peptide-Functionalized Hydrogels Support hiPSC Encapsulation and In Situ Differentiation into Cardiomyocytes with Enhanced Structural Maturation
papers.abstract: While defined synthetic substrates can replace Matrigel for human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) culture and hiPSC-derived cardiomyocyte (hiPSC-CM) production, existing approaches culture cells on two-dimensional surfaces and yield structurally immature cardiomyocytes, limiting their use in disease modeling and regenerative medicine. Here, we developed a xeno-free, fully-defined cyclic RGD (cRGD)-functionalized alginate platform in which we encapsulated hiPSCs to support their expansion and in situ cardiac differentiation. cRGD functionalization was essential for hiPSC survival and pluripotency, with maximal support achieved at a low ligand density (25 M). In the presence of cRGD, hiPSC encapsulation into softer gels made from lower molecular weight alginates led to enhanced hiPSC expansion and improved cardiogenesis. Strikingly, differentiation in situ with 3D gels led to hiPSC-CM with higher structural maturity, including a markedly increased proportion of cardiomyocytes positive for the structural maturation markers Desmin and MYH7. Finally, after enzymatic retrieval from hydrogels, cardiomyocytes derived from softer gels formed tissue-engineered myocardium with superior contractile stress compared to tissue fashioned from hiPSC-CM derived from more rigid gels. Together, these results demonstrate the promise of this defined, tunable platform for biomanufacturing of structurally more mature cardiomyocytes from hiPSC.

papers.title: SPARC Reveals Distinct Osteoclastogenesis-Associated Malignant States in Metastatic Osteosarcoma
papers.abstract: Single-cell studies of metastatic cancer have revealed extensive transcriptional heterogeneity and cellular plasticity as malignant populations establish themselves in distant organs. The growing availability of paired single-cell profiles from primary tumors and matched metastases offers new opportunities to investigate how malignant-cell states evolve during metastasis in relation to progression within the primary tumor. Static comparisons between these sites have identified differences in cellular composition and molecular programs, but can reduce heterogeneous populations to site-level summaries and overlook changes in gene-expression programs along possible routes of metastatic progression. Investigating these dynamics calls for trajectory inference that reconstructs state progression within each condition and transitions between conditions. However, existing trajectory inference tools have limitations in jointly modeling these relationships under biological ordering constraints. Traditional and widely used trajectory inference tools, such as Monocle 3 and Slingshot, do not impose direction constraints based on biological knowledge or the sampling design during graph construction. Optimal transport-based tools, such as moscot, incorporate temporal order to infer cross-condition correspondences, but these mappings alone do not reconstruct progression within each condition. More recent methods, including CStreet and CellRank 2, incorporate both transition types, but construct the two components separately through distinct modeling or graph-construction strategies. Here we introduce SPARC (Shortest Path Algorithmic Reconstruction of Cross-state Evolution), a unified graph-based optimization framework that evaluates both types of relationships under a common connectivity formulation to reconstruct complete, directionally constrained candidate trajectories. Across benchmarks, SPARC improved recovery of candidate metastatic precursors and complete progression routes in simulations, showed strong directed-trajectory reconstruction in conventional time-course settings, and performed competitively in real tumor lineage-tracing datasets. To examine metastatic progression in a model where lung lesions arise through spontaneous dissemination, we generated, to our knowledge, the first paired scRNA-seq dataset of primary osteosarcoma tumors and spontaneous lung metastases from the same mice, together with the first patient-derived osteosarcoma Visium HD dataset. The biological analyses revealed differences among metastatic tumor states in their association with osteoclast-like myeloid populations and candidate supportive signals, suggesting that certain malignant states may preferentially promote osteoclastogenesis. Together, SPARC provides a framework for investigating biologically ordered cell-state progression and identifying state-specific programs associated with metastatic disease.

papers.title: Protein language models learn the underlying accessibility of mutations alongside protein fitness landscapes
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) score the effects of amino acid replacements as pseudo-probabilities, which are widely utilised to map protein fitness landscapes. However, because their training data relies on natural amino acid sequences, these models conflate protein structural constraints with nucleotide mutation biases and codon accessibility. Using the rapid emergence of the divergent influenza A H3N2 K lineage as a stress test, we investigate how base PLMs (ESM-2 and ESM-C) versus fine-tuned versions of these models capture mutational processes. We systematically implement a parameter sweep to explicitly couple (or decouple) empirical nucleotide mutational supply from PLM-assessed amino acid substitution pseudo-probabilities across evolutionary forecasting tasks. We find that base PLMs implicitly learn generic nucleotide-level mutational constraints, an effect strongly amplified by virus-specific fine-tuning. Incorporating explicit mutational accessibility significantly improves the binary prediction of observed amino acid changes. Conversely, when predicting the final circulating frequency of variants that have already emerged, adding mutational supply degrades performance, confirming that selection dominates post-emergence dynamics. Additionally, we perform amino-acid-level epistatic scanning to investigate protein structural constraints in the context of genetic background. This indicates the improbable antigenic substitution I160K is dependent on co-occurring S144N and N158D mutations in the H3N2 K lineage. Ultimately, current PLM pseudo-probabilities are a composite metric that conflates protein structural fitness with historical biases in mutational supply. Explicitly decoupling these independent evolutionary processes optimises predictive accuracy for real-world pathogen forecasting and isolates pure protein fitness for synthetic design pipelines.

papers.title: Interspecies Differential Gene Expression Analysis with Regularized Phylogenetic Linear Models
papers.abstract: Comparative transcriptomic datasets are increasingly used to investigate the molecular basis of phenotypic diversification across species. However, finding genes that are differentially expressed (DE) between lineages remains challenging, for two main reasons. First, the random evolutionary drift can blur the signal left by lineage-specific shifts in mean expression, and induces phylogenetic correlations that, if ignored, can widely inflate the False Discovery Rate (FDR), i.e., the amount of spuriously detected genes. Second, DE analysis from RNA-Seq data involves multiple testing on many genes for a small number of individual measurements with high noise, and requires dedicated statistical tools. Traditional DE tools, such as limma, and classical Phylogenetic Comparative Methods (PCMs), such as the Expression Variance and Evolution (EVE) model, are both designed to tackle one of these two challenges alone, but both fail in the context of inter-species RNA-Seq data. In this work, we present phyloDE, a new tool for inter-species DE, that aims at taking the best from both approaches. On simulations based on a recently published four-species rodent dataset, we show that, contrary to other methods, phyloDE correctly controls the FDR in all settings, while keeping a reasonable power. When reanalyzing the empirical dataset, phyloDE discovers more DE genes that exhibit consistent changes in their cis-regulatory landscape compared to EVE in all the experimental settings. The method is implemented in R, with an interface inheriting from limma.

papers.title: Consequence and further analysis of the minor role of daylength in the floral initiation of sorghum crops
papers.abstract: Background and Aims Flowering time is assumed to be primarily controlled by daylength, but field observations disagree. For instance, mid-early sorghum varieties sown at the same time at tropical and temperate latitudes have similar flowering dates. We previously proposed an alternative framework integrating daily changes in sunrise and sunset times (dSR and dSS). Methods Variety trials of mid-late varieties from the Northern Hemisphere were carried out in Madagascar and in Argentina. Series of monthly sowings of 28 varieties were carried out in Mali between 2000 and 2009. Heading date and, in Mali, panicle initiation (PI) were recorded. Key Results In Madagascar and in Argentina mid-late varieties headed late or very late when sown in November and December, consistent with the higher dSR/dSS values of the southern hemisphere summer. In Mali, the high interannual variability in PI time in sowings between November and February revealed that up to four photoperiodic responses - two quantitative and two qualitative - may coexist within a single late photoperiod sensitive variety. Additionally, the qualitative responses may be triggered by an internal dSR/dSS phasic coincidence, which is set at the onset of the photoperiod-sensitive phase. These hypotheses were used to design a research model that incorporated only dSR and dSS cues. The model fitted the dataset well when two sets of parameters were calibrated for the first quantitative response, which covered two periods of over and under twelve hours per year. After daylength was added to the first qualitative response, the model also accurately predicted the duration to PI observed in three varieties sown at tropical and temperate latitudes. Conclusions The flowering time of sorghum crops mainly relies on dSR and dSS cues, while daylength plays a minor role. Two new hypotheses now require confirmation through further evidence, which is likely to come from genetic analyses.

papers.title: Homeostatic Plasticity Enables Stable, Flexible, and Tunable Assemblies
papers.abstract: Strongly interconnected neuronal populations, called assemblies, dynamically form through synaptic plasticity mechanisms and are thought to be a substrate for memories in the brain. Many assembly formation models use Hebbian excitatory-to-excitatory plasticity, where coordinated activity strengthens recurrent structure. However, these models typically yield binary assembly outcomes: networks with either weak (no assembly) or maximally strong (assembly) connectivity. We consider networks with a combination of Hebbian excitatory-to-excitatory plasticity and inhibitory-to-excitatory synapses with plasticity that homeostatically stabilizes excitatory neuron firing at a target value. When we set excitatory-to-excitatory plasticity to be homeostatically compliant, in that potentiation and depression are balanced at the homeostatic target firing rate, we find a stable continuum of synaptic strengths, and assembly structure is no longer binary. We use a recurrent network of spiking neuron models and an associated mean-field theory to identify this continuum as a line attractor in synaptic weight space. While along the attractor, homeostasis ensures that neuronal firing rates are invariant, the dynamical response properties of the network are quite malleable, with strongly coupled networks having high gain and longer timescale responses. Using our mean-field theory we show how correlated stochastic spiking activity among the excitatory neurons can destroy the line attractor, yet this can be mitigated when correlated inputs are shared across the excitatory and inhibitory neurons. Altogether, we provide an alternative learning framework based on homeostasis, where a tunable and flexible assembly structure is possible.

papers.title: Investigating the dynamic relationship between anxiety and spatial memory using autonomous ecological momentary assessment
papers.abstract: Anxiety has been extensively studied in relation to memory, yet its dynamic association with spatial episodic memory in naturalistic clinical settings remains largely unexplored. We developed an anxiety-spatial-memory EMA protocol (asm-EMA) and deployed it in 30 epilepsy patients undergoing inpatient EEG monitoring, delivering combined momentary anxiety ratings and a validated spatial memory task pseudo-randomly every 90-150 minutes across multiple days. Subject-level asm-EMA average and session-to-session variability correlated with standard neuropsychological assessments, supporting the clinical validity of the protocol. Momentary anxiety was not associated with reduced spatial memory accuracy. Higher within-person STAI-6 was associated with faster retrieval responses, but this association was attenuated after accounting for prior task exposure, suggesting that response-time effects may partly reflect task familiarity. Temporal analyses identified both gradual hospital-day change and short-term carry-over across anxiety, pain, and spatial memory measures. STAI-6 anxiety and spatial memory showed stronger hospital-day trends, whereas VAS anxiety showed the clearest carry-over from one session to the next. The asm-EMA protocol provides a feasible, autonomous framework for capturing moment-to-moment anxiety-memory dynamics in naturalistic settings.

papers.title: A genome-resolved atlas reveals lineage-specific activity patterns of prophages in cultured human gut bacteria
papers.abstract: Prophages dominate the gut virome, yet their basal activity landscapes remain elusive. Here, we developed ACTIVE (Activity Comparison Test for Induced Viral Elements), a robust coverage-based framework to accurately profile prophage replication activity based on sequencing data of individual bacteria. Applying ACTIVE across 31,150 gut bacterial isolates (875 species), we compiled these data into GPAC (Gut Prophage Activity Catalog) and found that 5.4% of prophages are detectably active under standard culture, with pronounced enrichment in Bacillota. Moreover, we uncovered distinct active viral lineages with broad host distributions. Comparative analyses identified 46 viral families significantly enriched for activity (SA-vFAMs). Notably, SA-vFAM7 represents a hyper-prevalent Candidatus Heliusvirales lineage whose host distribution expands into Bacteroidota (Tannerellaceae). Furthermore, we propose Candidatus Mubacviridae (SA-vFAM1), an active, hankyphage-inclusive transposable phage family associated with Bacteroidales, characterized by conserved MuA/B operons, diversity-generating retroelements, and multi-genus host distribution. Together, these findings establish GPAC as a resource linking prophage activity to host taxonomy and viral evolutionary lineages, providing a foundation for investigating prophage induction, host-phage interactions, and ecological dynamics of the human gut microbiome.

papers.title: Low-Dimensional Organization of Metabolic Phenotypes Underlies Recurrent Evolutionary Diversification
papers.abstract: Metabolic phenotypes vary within microbial species, yet how such variation is organized remains unclear. Diversification in carbon-source utilization often appears idiosyncratic, showing weak correspondence to phylogeny or simple gene content. Here, we combine quantitative growth phenotyping of natural Escherichia coli isolates across 32 carbon sources with diversification observed during de novo laboratory evolution, together with a reaction-level description of metabolic similarity. Despite deep phylogenetic divergence, growth-rate profiles varied independently of lineage. Instead, growth rates across carbon sources covaried in recurrent modular patterns aligned with flux-based metabolic similarity. Closely analogous modular relationships re-emerged during de novo evolution, indicating parallel diversification across evolutionary contexts. Growth-rate variation in natural and experimentally evolved datasets collapsed onto a shared low-dimensional variance structure. Together, our results indicate that quantitative metabolic phenotypes vary along a limited set of recurring, module-linked axes, providing insight into why similar metabolic states can repeatedly arise across independent evolutionary contexts.

papers.title: How the Azadithiolate Ligand Impacts O2-Stability of Group B -Hydrogenase ToHydA
papers.abstract: [FeFe]-hydrogenases are metalloenzymes that catalyze the reversible oxidation and production of H2, making them potential candidates for sustainable energy solutions. However, their practical application is restricted by their extreme O2 sensitivity, which leads to irreversible active site degradation. A newly characterized Group B hydrogenase, ToHydA from Thermosediminibacter oceani, has exhibited exceptional O2-stability even after long-term exposure to air. In ToHydA, the highly conserved proton-transporting cysteine (C212) safeguards the H-cluster from O2-induced degradation by formation of the Hinact state. In this study, we investigate the effects of replacing the azadithiolate (ADT) ligand of [2Fe]H with propanedithiolate (PDT), revealing that this substitution prevents the formation of the Hinact and Htrans states observed in ToHydA WT (bearing the ADT ligand). By combining ATR-FTIR spectroscopy and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we show that a favorable interaction between the nitrogen bridgehead of the ADT ligand and the C212 sidechain is crucial for stabilizing these states. The absence of this interaction in ToHydAPDT (bearing the PDT ligand) prevents the C212 sidechain from approaching the Fed center of [2Fe]H, thereby reducing Hinact accumulation. Moreover, as-isolated ToHydAPDT predominantly exhibits the Hhyd state, which is unusual for [FeFe]-hydrogenases with bound PDT ligand. These findings demonstrate how ligand substitution at the [2Fe]H site of ToHydA affects the structural dynamics, offering detailed molecular insights into the ligand-dependent modulation of [FeFe]-hydrogenases.

papers.title: V-SWITCH: A single-vector OFF-to-ON fluorescent reporter of live RNA virus infections
papers.abstract: Fluorescent reporters of viral infection are powerful tools for studying viral pathogenesis and host-pathogen interactions. Here, we present V-SWITCH, a highly modular, single-vector, cell-based OFF-to-ON fluorescent reporter that enables robust detection of viral infection in living cells. V-SWITCH is based on a split mNeonGreen (mNG) system employing a release-and-capture mechanism. In the "OFF" state, the mNG3A(1-10) fragment is anchored to the endoplasmic reticulum via a Sec61 transmembrane domain, while the mNG(11) fragment, fused to BFP, is constitutively expressed in the nucleus. Upon infection, the viral protease cleaves a protease cleavage site (PCS) adjacent to the mNG3A(1-10) fragment, liberating it for translocation into the nucleus. There, it complements mNG(11) to reconstitute fluorescence. The constitutive BFP serves as both an expression control and a nuclear segmentation marker for image analysis. Each module in this dual-cassette design is flanked by unique restriction sites allowing rapid swapping of virus-specific PCS, split fluorophores, membrane anchors, and promoters. We demonstrate the versatility of the V-SWITCH reporter for several viruses (Dengue virus, Zika virus, West Nile virus and Human Coronavirus OC43) in several cell lines (A549, BJ-5 fibroblasts, HEK293T and HeLa). Reporter activation enables clear discrimination of infected and uninfected cells by flow cytometry and reveals time-dependent and heterogeneous infection dynamics by live-cell imaging at single-cell resolution. Importantly, we demonstrate the potential of V-SWITCH to support both rapid functional screening for host factor dependencies, as well as high-throughput compound screening to enable antiviral discovery and comparative evaluation of therapeutic strategies across multiple viruses and cell types.

papers.title: Suppression of ITPK1 and IPMK activities impairs mTORC1 signaling due to accelerated signal termination and prevents pancreatic β-cell metabolic adaptation to excess glucose
papers.abstract: mTORC1 integrates growth factor and nutrient signals to regulate cellular metabolism, yet there are no metabolites known to directly regulate mTORC1 activity in cells. Cryo-EM studies revealed that inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6) associates with the FAT domain of mTOR, suggesting that inositol phosphates may directly modulate mTOR activity. We previously showed that higher-order inositol phosphates enhance mTORC1 kinase activity and stability in vitro. Here, we investigated whether inositol phosphate metabolism regulates mTORC1 signaling in HEK293 and pancreatic {beta}-cells. Suppression or acute inhibition of inositol phosphate multikinase (IPMK) selectively reduced cellular IP5 levels without altering IP6 and resulted in reduced basal and insulin-stimulated mTORC1 signaling, without decreasing mTORC1 complex stability or lysosomal localization. ITPK1 knockdown phenocopied IPMK inhibition by reducing IP5 and basal mTORC1. Combined inhibition of IPMK and ITPK1 nearly abolished IP5 and reduced IP6, demonstrating that these enzymes compensate to supply IP5 for IP6 synthesis. Importantly, depletion of IP5 did not impair PI3K/Akt activation but accelerated termination of the mTORC1 signal, indicating a role for IP5 in stabilizing the active mTORC1 complex. Reduction of IP5 levels did not prevent insulin- or glucose-induced mTORC1 activation, revealing that inositol phosphates primarily regulate signal persistence rather than initiation. Lastly, we show that suppression of IPMK or ITPK1 in {beta}-cells delayed the mTORC1-dependent metabolic acceleration in response to excess glucose. Together, these findings identify higher order inositol phosphates as metabolic regulators that prolong mTORC1 activity, providing a potential strategy for modulating mTORC1 signaling in cells.

papers.title: Disease-Causing Mutations Alter the Interplay Between Loop Dynamics and Catalysis in the Protein Tyrosine Phosphatases SHP-1 and SHP-2
papers.abstract: The protein tyrosine phosphatases (PTPs) SHP-1 and SHP-2 play complex roles in a variety of signaling pathways, including those involved in cancers and other diseases, making them important drug targets. These two PTPs have superimposable active sites, but different biological functions in vivo, including opposing roles in cancer development. Unique to these PTPs is the presence of two tandem Src homology 2 (SH2) domains, which regulate access to the phosphate-binding site in the catalytic domain through an autoinhibition mechanism. Studies of the allosteric regulation and dynamics of these PTPs, as well as associated drug discovery efforts, typically focus on autoinhibition rather than the dynamics of a catalytic loop in the phosphatase domain, the WPD-loop, which is essential for PTPase activity. However, recent deep mutational scanning data has demonstrated that oncogenic mutations also regulate WPD-loop motion in SHP-2. We provide here a detailed computational study of WPD-loop dynamics and catalysis in wild-type and mutant full-length and catalytic domain only SHP-1 and SHP-2, demonstrating that many oncogenic residues lie on the allosteric pathways regulating WPD-loop dynamics. Mutations at these positions alter WPD-loop dynamics, disrupting the active site and negatively impacting catalysis. Further, our simulations provide molecular insight into the link between the presence of the SH2 domains and loop motion in the catalytic domain, and, importantly, how it differs between the two PTPs. Taken together, our work showcases the impact of altered WPD-loop motion in disease-causing SHP-1 and SHP-2 variants, opening new strategies for selectively targeting these important therapeutic enzymes.

papers.title: Wetness modulates the effects of grazing on net ecosystem productivity in global grasslands
papers.abstract: Overgrazing has induced widespread grassland degradation globally. However, how grazing intensity affects ecosystem carbon dioxide (CO2) fluxes with wetness fluctuations in grasslands worldwide remains poorly understood. Here we measured ecosystem CO2 fluxes covering the 7th to 11th years of a continuous grazing experiment in a typical steppe, and conducted a meta-analysis of 585 observations by collecting relevant data in global grasslands. Our experimental results showed that mean gross primary productivity (GPP) and ecosystem respiration (ER) were decreased under heavy grazing (HG) compared with control without grazing (CK), whereas net ecosystem productivity (NEP) was not different between HG and CK in the typical steppe. The NEP was higher under light grazing in the wetter years, but it was not different between light grazing and CK under drier years in the typical steppe. The structural equation model showed that grazing affected NEP by increasing plant relative growth rate, while decreasing plant aboveground biomass (AGB). In contrast, grazing decreased GPP, ER and NEP, respectively, in global grasslands. Both our field experiment and the meta-analysis revealed that the response of NEP to light grazing, rather than heavy grazing, was linearly correlated with the wetness index. Higher wetness and AGB increased the response of NEP to grazing in global grasslands. However, heavy grazing reduced NEP and AGB even under higher wetness indices in global grasslands, resulting from a loss of their resilience in long-term heavy grazing. These findings indicate that light grazing appears to be a promising management to promote plant relative growth rate and carbon sequestration. Overall, the meta-analysis and field experiment jointly provide global perspectives on the response of ecosystem CO2 fluxes to grazing intensity and improve our understanding of the factors influencing the response of ecosystem CO2 fluxes to grazing intensity.

papers.title: Near perfect identification of half sibling versus niece/nephew avuncular pairs without pedigree information or genotyped relatives
papers.abstract: Motivation: Large-scale genomic biobanks contain thousands of second-degree relatives with missing pedigree metadata. Accurately distinguishing half-sibling (HS) from niece/nephew-avuncular (N/A) pairs--both sharing approximately 25% of the genome--remains a significant challenge. Current SNP-based methods rely on Identical-By-Descent (IBD) segment counts and age differences, but substantial distributional overlap leads to high misclassification rates. There is a critical need for a scalable, genotype-only method that can resolve these "half-degree" ambiguities without requiring observed pedigrees or extensive relative information. Results: We present a novel computational framework that achieves near-complete separation of HS and N/A pairs using only genotype data. Our approach utilizes across-chromosome phasing to derive haplotype-level sharing features that summarize how IBD is distributed across parental homologues. By modeling these features with a Gaussian mixture model (GMM), we demonstrate near-perfect classification accuracy (> 98%) in biobank-scale data. Furthermore, we show that these high-confidence relationship labels can serve as long-range phasing anchors, providing structural constraints that improve the accuracy of across-chromosome homologue assignment. This method provides a robust, scalable solution for pedigree reconstruction and the control of cryptic relatedness in large-scale genomic studies.

papers.title: Accelerating antibiotic discovery from Earth's isolated habitats through protein language models and microfluidics
papers.abstract: The antibiotic potential of Earth's isolated habitat microbiomes remains largely unexplored. Accessing this resource requires reliable prioritization across divergent peptide sequences and efficient experimental validation. Here we present MicroSPEAR, an end-to-end framework for antimicrobial peptide (AMP) discovery integrating SPEAR, a sequence-structure-aware ensemble predictor, with MicroGrad, a microfluidic testing platform. SPEAR generalized to low-homology peptides and prioritized potent candidates despite training on binary activity labels. MicroGrad simplified liquid handling and shortened susceptibility testing from approximately 18 h to 4 h. Applied to a catalogue derived from 4,480 metagenomes spanning 15 isolated habitat types, SPEAR identified 383,027 non-redundant candidate AMPs, 63.1% of which lacked detectable homologues in reference databases. Of 85 synthesized candidates, 79 exhibited antibacterial activity at [≤]64 M;. Mechanistic analyses revealed distinct modes of membrane disruption. Four broad-spectrum candidates with low toxicity significantly reduced bacterial burdens in a mouse thigh infection model. MicroSPEAR connects underexplored microbial diversity with experimentally validated antibiotic leads and provides a foundation for lab-in-the-loop discovery.

papers.title: Administration of short-chain fatty acids reduces bacterial translocation to peripheral organs and the brain, preserves gut barrier integrity, and mitigates brain injury following stroke.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Stroke remains a leading cause of death globally, with post-stroke infections (PSIs) representing its main life-threatening complication. While traditionally attributed to nosocomial infections or medical procedures, emerging research has revealed that PSIs primarily originate from bacterial translocation following gut barrier disruption. Yet, the phenomenon of bacterial translocation remains poorly characterized. Critical knowledge gaps persist regarding the exact spatiotemporal dynamics of this event, and whether bacterial dissemination actively drives stroke pathogenesis and worsens neurological outcomes. Consequently, the development of targeted therapies remains severely limited. In this context, short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) have emerged as key regulators of the brain-gut-immune axis, exerting neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory properties. However, their potential therapeutic modulation of bacterial translocation has remained unexplored. Methods and Results: Using a middle cerebral artery occlusion model in mice, we confirmed that stroke induces systemic bacterial dissemination to the liver, lungs, and spleen, and provided novel evidence of the presence of bacteria in the heart, brainstem, and ischemic lesion core. Interestingly, systemic bacterial load correlated with worse neurological outcomes but not with ischemic volume. Furthermore, we described for the first time the spatiotemporal kinetics of this process, demonstrating that translocation initiated as early as 6 hours post-stroke, peaked between 24 hours and 4 days, and had almost completely resolved systemically by 7 days, while strikingly persisting in the central nervous system. Importantly, SCFA treatment reduced both systemic and cerebral bacterial translocation, preserved gut barrier integrity, and reversed post-stroke immunosuppression. SCFAs also reduced infarct volume and blood-brain barrier leakage, ultimately improving survival rates. Conclusion: These findings provide crucial insights into the complex process of bacterial translocation and highlight SCFAs as a promising therapeutic strategy for both the ischemic event and its most lethal, yet least understood, complications.

papers.title: Split-luciferin Assay for Real-time Measurement of Cytosolic Molecular Accumulation in Live Mycobacteria
papers.abstract: Antibiotics against nontuberculous mycobacteria must cross a multilayered cell envelope before reaching their cytosolic targets, yet how much of a given compound arrives there is largely unmeasured. This gap matters because nontuberculous mycobacterial infections are rising among immunocompromised individuals and those with structural lung disease, and intrinsic and acquired multidrug resistance creates an urgent need for new agents. Existing methods quantify whole-cell association without resolving subcellular localization, and none report accumulation in live mycobacteria, in real time. Here we adapt a split-luciferin approach, the D-cysteine-linked accumulation profiling (D-CLAP), to luciferase-expressing Mycobacterium smegmatis and Mycobacterium avium. Compounds bearing a disulfide-linked D-cysteine tag release the tag upon entry into the reducing cytosol, where it condenses with an intracellular cyanobenzothiazole to form D-luciferin and generate a time-resolved luminescent signal. We applied D-CLAP to small-molecule antibiotics, polyarginine peptides, and griselimycin analogs, and found that masking carboxylates as methyl esters increased both cytosolic accumulation and antimycobacterial potency. A fluorescent polyarginine peptide also associated with M. smegmatis residing within macrophage phagosomes. D-CLAP provides a real-time readout of cytosolic entry in live mycobacteria and a route to structure-accumulation relationships.

papers.title: Aversive Learning Induces Context-Gated Global Reorganization of Neural Dynamics in Caenorhabditis elegans
papers.abstract: Learning generates experience-dependent changes to the brain. However, how neurons of diverse functions and connectivity reorganize and modulate their activities to generate coherent changes while preserving essential functions is not well understood. Here, we address this question using an aversive olfactory learning paradigm whereby Caenorhabditis elegans learns to reduce its olfactory preference for pathogenic bacteria. Using functional imaging during olfactory stimulation in naive and trained animals, we show that, at brain-wide scale, cell type-by-cell type, learning induces context-gated reconfiguration of the organization of neural activity throughout the brain to alter neural responses only during bacteria-discrimination task, while leaving intact bacteria-sensing functions. We found that the context-gated encoding of learning is globally distributed across layers of the nervous system, composed of neurons carrying information of context or learning experience. In particular, aversive training modulates multiple functional connections within the nervous system, including those between sensory neurons and interneurons, as well as those among interneurons, in a context-gated manner. At the systems level, training modulates correlated activity of neural populations; we found that low-dimensional temporal patterns of population activity correlate well with locomotory gaits that express olfactory preferences. Upon training, the rotation and contraction of the low-dimensional neural manifolds shifts the brain into predisposed states for the context-gated display of learned behavior. Because animals encounter unpredictable environments in life, efficient learning about relevant cues while maintaining other functions is essential for survival. Our findings uncover network-level mechanisms that help explain how the brain reorganizes its activity patterns to both encode new experience and preserve essential functions.

papers.title: Game structure shapes individuals' norms in collective decision-making
papers.abstract: Collective decision-making often requires individuals to reconcile private benefits with collective benefits of cooperation. Norms can sustain the cooperation by shaping how individuals evaluate consequences of actions and respond to shared behavioral standard. However, whether different game structures give rise to different norms, and the specific mechanisms underlying such effects, remain unclear. Here, we compared linear and threshold public goods games (LPGGs and TPGGs) in repeated four-person interactions, combining model-free behavioral analysis, agent-based modelling and fNIRS hyperscanning. LPGG produced more dynamic contribution updating and was more influenced by others' recent behavior, whereas TPGG showed more stable consensus and stronger punishment enforcement. Agent-based modelling revealed a corresponding dissociation: LPGG placed greater weight on consequence-based social norms, whereas TPGG showed stronger conformity-based norms. These normative differences were accompanied by distinct neural characteristics. TPGG elicited stronger rTPJ activation, which was positively associated with contributions. dmPFC--rTPJ connectivity tracked distinct consequence-based social parameters, namely the baseline weight in TPGG and context-dependent modulation in LPGG. At the group level, interaction-specific dmPFC inter-brain neural synchrony emerged only in TPGG but not in LPGG. Together, these findings show that game structure does more than alter incentives: it reorganizes the behavioral, computational and neural mechanisms through which norms sustain collective cooperation.

papers.title: Spiny mouse fibroblasts exhibit a baseline preference for glycolysis and are resilient to oxidative stress across lifespan
papers.abstract: Although metabolism was originally studied across an array of mammals, contemporary metabolic studies moved towards human and mouse cells. A newfound interest in how metabolism regulates cell state during homeostasis, tissue repair and disease has uncovered key roles for energy flux inside and outside of mitochondria. Fibroblasts are key mediators of wound healing outcomes and prior work uncovered that cells from highly regenerative mammals (spiny mice and rabbits) exhibit enhanced resistance to oxidative stress compared to those from non-regenerating laboratory mice and rats. Using a battery of cellular tests in primary ear pinna fibroblasts from spiny mice, rabbits, laboratory mice and rats, we show that cells from spiny mice and rabbits exhibit a baseline preference for glycolysis supporting lower ROS-production. Mitochondria from spiny mouse fibroblasts were generally low respiring and depolarized while exhibiting a large, spherical morphology. We observed this large, spherical phenotype consistently across lifespan in ear pinna fibroblasts from fetal, young and old spiny mice and cells from all ages were highly resistant to oxidative stress. While rabbit, mouse and rat fibroblasts had polarized tubular mitochondrial networks typical of adult mammalian fibroblasts, isolated rabbit and spiny mice fibroblasts shared lower oxygen consumption efficiency even in the absence of a potential gradient. Taken together, our results support that a shared metabolic signature exists in stromal cells from highly regenerative mammals, although possibly driven by different mechanisms, to converge on a ROS-resistant phenotype that increases cellular resilience.

papers.title: Disruption of theta-timescale spiking impairs learning but spares hippocampal replay
papers.abstract: The ability to rapidly learn and retrieve salient information about new environments is critical for survival. In mammals, the hippocampus plays a crucial role in that learning. Specialized features of hippocampal population coding, including network-level theta oscillatory activity, location-specific firing of principal cells, and reactivation of experience during immobility (replay), have been implicated in rapid storage and retrieval of spatial information. Disruptions of theta and replay jointly, or replay alone, are sufficient to impair learning; however, the specific contribution of theta-associated temporal structure during locomotion remains unknown. In this study, we manipulated hippocampal spiking activity in rats specifically during locomotion by optogenetically activating septal parvalbumin-expressing GABAergic neurons. We developed a closed-loop, theta phase-specific stimulation protocol that reliably reduced theta power shortly after stimulation onset. This manipulation preserved the place codes of individual cells but disrupted the fine temporal structure of endogenous spatio-temporal representations (i.e., theta sequences) at the pairwise and population level. Theta disruption during locomotion was also sufficient to cause pronounced deficits in learning the more cognitively challenging component of a spatial alternation task, even though disruption was applied on only [~]66% of trials. Notably, network effects accompanying theta disruption were restricted to locomotor periods; we did not observe changes in replay rate, length, or content during immobility. Together, these results demonstrate the importance of the precise temporal microstructure of locomotion-associated spatial representations in the hippocampus for learning.

papers.title: Environmental fluctuations trigger faster evolution and turnover
papers.abstract: Biodiversity patterns and species communities emerge from the interactions between organisms and their environment and from processes spanning across different spatial and temporal scales. Understanding the dynamics of these interactions remains diffcult as it requires mapping how microevolutionary processes scale up to macroevolutionary outcomes. Here, we use an individual-based simulation framework to model how populations respond to environmental fluctuations in a spatially explicit context. Our approach tracks evolutionary processes over thousands of generations to quantify the emerging macroevolutionary patterns under varying degrees of environmental instability modeled as shifting environmental gradients. We found that increased instability across time and space leads to elevated rates of species-level extinctions leading to homogenization of species communities, while promoting high rates of phenotypic evolution. Emerging extinction patterns indicate a selective process where species with low migration ability, narrow environmental tolerance, and limited evolvability are disproportionally affected by phases of rapid environmental change. Understanding the impact of environmental variation on organisms and species evolution remains challenging but can be explored through simulations to generate expectations and testable hypotheses about evolutionary processes across different scales.

papers.title: Characterization of intermolecular base pairing using AMT crosslinking in mammalian cells during oxidative stress
papers.abstract: Intermolecular base pairing is essential for normal gene regulation but can also cause neurodegeneration when dysregulated. Despite its importance, intermolecular base pairing remains poorly characterized in cells. We coupled AMT crosslinking with RNA pulldown to probe intermolecular base pairing in mammalian cells under oxidative stress, a state that drives G3BP1/2-dependent stress granule assembly, translational repression, and increased exposure of RNA sequences available for intermolecular interactions. AMT captured intermolecular base pairing interactions among reporter RNAs in vitro and the known interaction between the U3 snoRNA and pre-18S rRNA in cellulo. Although detection sensitivity was limited for endogenous mRNAs, we found that base pairing among inducibly expressed reporter mRNAs is sensitive to RNA sequence, oxidative stress, and G3BP1/2. Furthermore, chemical probing revealed that base accessibility to DMS within non-translated regions of candidate RNAs remains similar between stressed and unstressed cells, and those lacking G3BP1/2, indicating that RNAs remained state under these conditions. Our findings establish an approach for studying RNA base pairing in cells and suggest that intermolecular base pairing may act together with RNA structure to preserve RNAs during oxidative stress.

papers.title: Ridge Redundancy Analysis for High-Dimensional Omics Data
papers.abstract: Redundancy Analysis (RDA) is a popular reduced rank regression approach for modeling the relationships between two sets of variables. In omics studies, RDA provides a flexible framework for investigating associations between high-dimensional molecular data. However, omics datasets often exhibit strong multicollinearity and suffer from the "large p, small n" problem, where the number of predictor variables p exceeds the number of samples n. Ridge RDA addresses multicollinearity by introducing a ridge penalty in addition to the rank restriction. Despite these advantages, its application to high-dimensional omics data remains challenging due to i) difficulties in manipulating the large coefficient matrix of dimensions p x q, where q represents the number of response variables, and ii) the need to jointly select the rank and the regularization parameter that both influence the performance of the method. Results: We propose an efficient computational framework for ridge RDA that overcomes these challenges by leveraging the Singular Value Decomposition of the predictor matrix X. This approach eliminates the need for direct covariance matrix inversion, improving computational efficiency. Furthermore, we introduce a novel strategy that reduces the memory burden associated with the storage of the coefficient matrix from pq to (p+q)r, with r the chosen reduced-rank dimensionality. Our method enables an efficient grid search to jointly select the ridge penalty {lambda} and r via cross-validation. The proposed framework is implemented in the R package rrda, providing a practical and scalable solution for the analysis of high-dimensional omics data. Availability: The R package rrda is available on CRAN: https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=rrda. Scripts and data used for the analysis are available on GitHub: https://github.com/Yoska393/rrda.

papers.title: Cigarette smoke induces PPP1R15A via oxidative stress to modulate inflammatory cytokine production by bronchial epithelial cells
papers.abstract: Cigarette smoke is the principal cause of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in Western societies. It induces pulmonary inflammation and activates multiple stress signalling pathways in bronchial epithelial cells, including the integrated stress response (ISR). The ISR is triggered by phosphorylation of the translation initiation factor eIF2 in response to a variety of insults and is functionally antagonised by the eIF2 phosphatase subunit PPP1R15A. Deletion of PPP1R15A exaggerates the ISR and, in many models, protects against cellular stress. However, loss of PPP1R15A was also shown to exaggerate pulmonary fibrosis in bleomycin-challenged mice. We therefore wished to understand the role of PPP1R15A in the pulmonary response to cigarette smoke, which can cause both COPD and pulmonary fibrosis. Whole cigarette smoke rapidly activated the ISR in differentiated mucociliary human primary bronchial epithelial cells, with those from COPD patients exhibiting higher levels of ISR. Acute exposure to cigarette smoke condensate induced a pro-inflammatory cytokine response accompanied by PPP1R15A expression. In this model, PPP1R15A induction was independent of eIF2 phosphorylation but was suppressed by antioxidants, suggesting a response to oxidative stress. In vivo studies in mice revealed that PPP1R15A deficiency enhanced the secretion of proinflammatory cytokines in mice, suggesting a regulatory role for PPP1R15A in modulating the inflammatory response to smoke. Taken together, these data suggest that PPP1R15A is induced by cigarette smoke by an ISR-independent oxidative stress mechanism and ameliorates the pro-inflammatory cytokine response to cigarette smoke

papers.title: Disentangling the effects of Anxious, Autistic and Schizotypal Traits on Perceptual Inference
papers.abstract: Perception combines sensory information with prior knowledge, but people differ in how they do so. These differences may be associated with psychological traits; however, previous studies often focused on one trait at a time and yielded contradictory results. We measured how anxious, autistic and schizotypal traits relate to perception in two general population samples (original: n=277; replication: n=279, pre-registered). We combined tasks in which priors were either explicitly communicated or implicitly learnt with computational modelling to distinguish the decision and learning stages of perceptual inference. The three traits formed distinct but correlated dimensions. At the decision stage, higher trait anxiety was associated with more optimal choices and greater reliance on sensory information, without any alteration in the reliance on priors, whether explicit or implicit. On the other hand, state anxiety was associated with a reduced effect of sensory information on response speed. When traits were analysed separately, autistic traits showed similar associations, but these associations disappeared once anxiety was taken into account in multidimensional analyses. No other credible or consistent effects emerged for autistic or schizotypal traits, nor for learning parameters. These results highlight the importance of a multidimensional approach, including anxiety measurements, to characterise inter-individual differences in perception.

papers.title: Histone H3 cysteines as redox switches in the nucleosome: molecular modeling of S-sulfenylation and its structural consequences
papers.abstract: Oxidation of buried histone cysteines links cellular redox signaling to chromatin regulation. Histone H3 carries two such residues: C96, unique to the H3.1 variant, and C110, shared by most H3 variants. Oxidation of H3.1 C96 by H2O2 drives histone variant exchange and chromatin opening in cancer cells, and C110 undergoes S-glutathionylation, yet both thiols are shielded from the solvent. How they are oxidized and what the modification does to the nucleosome structure remain unknown. Combining all-atom molecular dynamics, QM/MM and free energy calculations, we reveal S-sulfenylation mechanisms at both cysteines within the nucleosome core particle, from oxidant access to its structural consequences. Reaching either cysteine costs ~12 kcal/mol, paid mostly for the desolvation of H2O2 independently of the entry route. The reaction is then enabled in the hydrophobic environment by the presence of a single neighboring base. Such a residue is already in place at C110 (H3D123), but must first reorganize at C96 (H3E97), with barriers of ~18 kcal/mol at both sites. Once formed, the modification acts well beyond its site. C96 S-sulfenylation acts on DNA-histone interfaces, on elements recognized by chromatin remodelers and chaperones (H2AE91 at the acidic patch, H2A C-term release), and on the H4K91-H2B'D68 salt bridge bridging the two halves of the nucleosome. C110 oxidation mainly favors unwrapping and DNA destabilization at the dyad. These results provide a structural framework for understanding histone-mediated redox signaling and its implication in chromatin remodeling.

papers.title: Insular opioid signaling and distinct claustral ensembles in hedonic feeding
papers.abstract: Stress triggers eating that is driven by palatability rather than energy need, but how stress-related signals act on the circuits that control hedonic feeding is unclear. The claustrum, a thin sheet of neurons reciprocally connected with much of the cortex, is enriched in {kappa}-opioid receptors (KORs), the receptors for the stress-related peptide dynorphin. Here we show that a single forced swim increases palatable-food intake in mice without food restriction. Deleting or blocking claustral KOR attenuated this increase. A KOR-based sensor reported a fall in claustral opioid tone at the onset of eating. Prodynorphin (Pdyn)-expressing neurons in the anterior insular cortex (aIC) projected to the claustrum and recruited both vGAT and CaMKII-expressing claustral neurons. Single-cell imaging showed that eating engages claustral populations in distinct ways: nearly all vGAT neurons were activated, whereas KOR-Cre neurons divided into activated and suppressed subsets of similar size, with or without prior stress. vGAT responses to both sucrose and quinine grew after longer water restriction and scaled with licking, linking them to consummatory engagement rather than taste valence alone. Mice lacking Pdyn in the aIC ate more palatable food even without stress, and KOR ligands changed how mice engage with palatable food. These findings identify an insular-claustral opioid circuit through which stress can shape hedonic feeding.

papers.title: Dissociating instructive from permissive roles of brain circuits with reversible neural activity manipulations
papers.abstract: The brain has a remarkable capacity to recover from damage. Despite the value of such recovery, it has made determining which areas are critically involved in a specific brain function challenging. Different types of manipulations to brain tissue - from mechanical or chemical lesions to genetic ablations or pharmacological agents - often yield conflicting conclusions. In some cases, ablating a brain area causes only a temporary disruption because a downstream region can homeostatically recover from its loss of input, while in others it leads to permanent impairment due not to the damaged area per se, but because of the degeneration of distant areas. We sought to address these issues by exploiting the flexibility and reversibility of optogenetic manipulations. We applied a three-stage optogenetic approach to the mouse's primary visual cortex (V1) in a contrast detection task, beginning with intermittent silencing, followed by sustained illumination across multiple days of task-related behavior, and concluding with a return to intermittent silencing. Initially, intermittent V1 inactivation strongly impaired task performance, while during persistent multi-session inactivation, the animals' visual detection entirely recovered to pre-silencing levels. However, this recovery was itself reversible, as returning the animals to intermittent V1 inactivation reinstated the behavioral deficit. Suppressing activity in the superior colliculus (SC) concurrent with persistent V1 inactivation reversed the animals' recovery, demonstrating that SC is a key area that drives behavioral compensation in the absence of V1 function, even while under normal conditions V1 activity is crucial. These results support a scenario where primary sensory cortex is in the default circuit mice use to detect visual stimuli, but in its absence, midbrain regions can compensate for it. More generally, this temporally controllable optogenetic perturbation paradigm could be useful to adjudicate whether a brain area instructs or is accessory to a specific brain function.

papers.title: Long-term biodiversity responses to anthropogenic change are spatially and taxonomically heterogeneous across coastal wetlands
papers.abstract: Coastal wetlands have undergone centuries of anthropogenic modification, yet their long-term biodiversity trajectories remain poorly understood because ecological monitoring rarely extends beyond recent decades. Sedimentary ancient DNA (sedaDNA) offers a historical perspective for evaluating how biodiversity patterns vary across environmental contexts and timescales. We combined COI and 18S sedaDNA metabarcoding with 210Pb and radiocarbon chronologies, sediment geochemistry and stable-isotope records from eight coastal wetlands across four regions of the Iberian Peninsula. We reconstructed changes in eukaryotic amplicon sequence variant (ASV) richness and taxonomic composition and examined their relationships with an Anthropogenic Enrichment Index (AEI) based on ten elements potentially associated with human activities. Richness-AEI relationships differed among sediment records and genetic markers. Higher enrichment was associated with lower richness for both markers in one Cadiz record, whereas COI richness increased with enrichment in the Ebro Delta. However, after accounting for calendar time, only the positive association in the Ebro Delta remained statistically significant, indicating that several initial relationships were partly explained by shared temporal trends. Exploratory rolling correlations further suggested that the direction of richness-enrichment associations varied across historical periods within individual records. Taxonomic profiles differed between markers and wetlands, while community composition was strongly differentiated among sediment records, highlighting ecological variation not captured by richness alone. Multiproxy changes also followed locally specific configurations rather than a common regional trajectory. Together, these findings show that long-term relationships between sedimentary enrichment and biodiversity are context-dependent and sensitive to the temporal perspective considered. Integrating molecular, geochemical and isotopic records can therefore improve the historical interpretation of biodiversity change and inform conservation approaches that account for taxonomic composition, environmental history and locally appropriate reference conditions.

papers.title: Loss of cell-identity DNA methylation tracks division history, not DNA damage
papers.abstract: One influential proposal holds that DNA damage drives aging by degrading the epigenome, so that a cell loses the information that specifies what it is. We test that specific proposed driver, not the broader idea that aging involves a loss of epigenetic information. Cell-type-unique CpGs are a direct place to test it. They are the sites where a cell's methylome differs most from every other cell type, so they are where its identity information can be accurately measured. We built such a panel for human skin fibroblasts against twenty primary cell types, and found that most of its 9,150 CpGs behave as a record of proliferation rather than identity. Their methylation state in fibroblasts is shared with continuously proliferating cell lines, consistent with the bulk hypomethylation of late-replicating chromatin that accumulates in culture, and this layer must be separated from identity marks before identity loss can be tested. We then expressed every perturbation as the fraction of the panel's identity information lost beyond baseline-matched background CpGs, using a Bernoulli cross-entropy between the fibroblast code and a generic comparator cell. In 24 matched fibroblast cultures, replicative exhaustion cost 24.3% of the identity information (95% CI 20.2 to 28.7) and RAS activation cost 5.4% (4.6 to 6.1), both at p = 1.2 X 10^-7;. A senescence-inducing dose of X-rays cost nothing: -0.5% (-0.7 to -0.2), with identity CpGs if anything moving slightly further from other cell types than matched background did. The design could detect a loss of 0.4%, about one sixtieth of the exhaustion effect, so the X-ray result is a bounded negative rather than an absence of power. Doxorubicin-induced and irradiation-induced senescence did not move the panel either. Clones that kept dividing after irradiation moved further from other cell types rather than collapsing toward them. In human fibroblasts, loss of identity information tracks prolonged division, not acute DNA damage.

papers.title: Resolving Gene-Metabolism Links through Multi-Metabolite mQTL Commonality Analysis
papers.abstract: High-throughput metabolomics detects so many compounds that most studies use only a fraction of them, focusing on the few metabolites with an annotated structure or substructure. Metabolite genome-wide association studies of specialized metabolism detect many metabolite quantitative trait loci (mQTLs), but most associated metabolite features remain unannotated, limiting gene discovery. In leaves of 362 tomato accessions under control and water-deficit conditions, only 13 of the 826 metabolite features associated with 77 reproducible mQTLs were annotated with good confidence. To study the mQTLs with the largest impact, we developed commonality analysis, an approach that does not depend on well-studied pathways. Commonality analysis uses biologically defined groups, such as the features associated with one mQTL, to infer relatedness between metabolites. By identifying the fragments, neutral losses or mass transformations that are common in a group, it links the group to a substructure, pathway or reaction, and can extend annotation within the group. Most high-impact mQTLs had a significantly distinct fragment commonality, whose outstanding fragments suggested the pathway involved and its candidate gene. We demonstrate the approach in three representative mQTLs: (i) common fragments pointed to a sinapoyl-hexose pathway and a serine carboxypeptidase-like candidate acyltransferase; (ii) common fragments marked the features associated with a purine permease as nitrogen-containing, which isotope labeling then supported; (iii) a common 2.02 Da transformation pointed to a double-bond reduction and a putative reductase. Overexpression of each gene reproduced the commonality patterns, supporting the candidate genes and showing that the approach also applies to experimentally defined metabolite groups.

papers.title: Local chromatin, 3D genome folding and transposon cargo shape Sleeping Beauty transposition
papers.abstract: The cut-and-paste DNA transposon Sleeping Beauty (SB) is widely used for genome engineering, mutagenesis and gene delivery. When mobilized from a genomic donor position ("launch site"), SB preferentially reintegrates locally (< 2 Mb), but factors governing its transposition from genomic sites remain incompletely understood. Here we analysed local transposition experiments in mouse embryonic stem cells to determine the influence of chromatin context and transposon cargo on SB transposition. Transposons in launch sites with transcriptionally active, accessible chromatin showed lower transposition efficiency. Large cargo and cargo with higher transcriptional activity also result in reduced transposition efficiency. After excision, local reintegration patterns closely resembled 3D contact frequencies of the launch site. This indicates that chromosome folding is a major determinant of the transposition pattern. Surprisingly, we did not detect any effect of the destination chromatin composition on reintegration efficiency. Cargo sequence modified the reintegration patterns: promoter-containing cargo increased both very proximal (<10kb) and interchromosomal transpositions, while CTCF binding sites in the cargo increased reintegration on the launch chromosome. Together, these results define key determinants of SB transposition in chromosomes and inform the design of SB-based genome engineering strategies.

papers.title: Engineering morphology of tetrasulfide-incorporated mesoporous silica nanoparticles for enhanced mRNA delivery
papers.abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are the most studied nanocarrier for mRNA delivery, yet their broader application remains limited due to suboptimal cellular uptake, low efficacy in mRNA delivery, and poor stability. In this study, we report a novel tetrasulfide-incorporated virus-like porous silica (VLPSi) nanoparticle as a safe and efficient platform to enhance LNP-mediated mRNA delivery. By systematically tuning the synthesis parameters, a series of nanoparticles with distinct morphologies and architectures were obtained, enabling the study of how tetrasulfide and particle morphology affect mRNA delivery. The performance of VLPSi was optimized by evaluating cellular uptake, cytotoxicity, and transfection performance with different lipid and mRNA payloads across multiple cell types. The results showed that increasing the length and number of spikes on the VLPSi surface significantly improved cellular uptake efficiency and subsequent mRNA expression. Mechanistically, the enhanced delivery arose from the combined effect from the nanospikes and intracellular tetrasulfide degradation. Furthermore, the nanoparticles significantly enhanced the stability of mRNA. Overall, these findings establish a structure-function relationship between virus-like topography, biodegradable silica chemistry, and mRNA delivery. This work provides a structurally tunable, biodegradable, and highly effective bioinspired nanoplatform to enhance mRNA delivery.

papers.title: Gut microbiome-associated adaptability of suckermouth catfish inhabiting the polluted Buriganga River: insights into heavy-metal-remediating microorganisms
papers.abstract: The suckermouth catfish (SMCF), known for its pollutant tolerance and high invasiveness, is prevalent in the heavily contaminated Buriganga River in Bangladesh. This waterway, contaminated with a variety of pollutants, including heavy metals, has experienced the near-complete disappearance of native fish populations; however, the suckermouth catfish demonstrates remarkable adaptability in this environment. One objective of this study is to elucidate the role of the gut microbiome in SMCFs' adaptation to this severely polluted habitat. We performed next-generation sequencing (NGS) of gut contents from SMCFs to analyze the gut microbial profiles of the fish samples. The results indicated that the suckermouth catfish's gut is enriched with microbial communities, including Paraclostridium, Klebsiella, Staphylococcus, Bacillus, and Pseudomonas, which have the potential to remediate pollutants, including heavy metals. The subsequent aim of this research is to isolate and identify bacteria from the SMCF gut capable of remediating multiple heavy metals. We isolated three isolates with the potential to remediate multiple heavy metals and identified them as Staphylococcus pasteuri SD, Morganella morganii SAS1, and Sporosarcina saromensis SAS using partial 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and conventional techniques. All isolates showed distinct capabilities for remediating multiple heavy metals. Notably, S. pasteuri showed the highest lead (Pb) bioaccumulation (36.28%), S. saromensis showed the highest chromium (Cr) uptake (39.22%), and M. morganii showed the highest nickel (Ni) uptake (35.90%). Furthermore, these isolates exhibited remarkable metal-tolerance profiles, with maximum tolerable concentrations ranging from 125 ppm to 1000 ppm, and sustained healthy growth under metal-supplemented conditions throughout a 48-hour incubation period. This validates their potential to remediate multiple heavy metals. Collectively, the results underscore the ecological adaptability of suckermouth catfish in polluted aquatic environments, which is associated with their gut microbiome, and highlight the bioremediation potential of these gut-derived microbes as effective agents for mitigating heavy metal contamination.

papers.title: Ranging and territoriality in African Apes
papers.abstract: Intergroup relations vary strikingly among African apes, with only chimpanzees showing intense, often lethal territoriality. The economic defendability hypothesis proposes that such territorial behaviour is favored where home ranges can be economically defended, as indexed by the ratio of daily travel distance to home range diameter. To test this idea, we compiled and analyzed comparable data on yearly home range size, daily travel distance and defendability indices from one population of each nonhuman African ape species and integrated these with comparable published data. We find that bonobos had substantially larger home ranges and longer daily travel distances than chimpanzees and gorillas, contradicting a prevailing assumption that bonobos experience higher or more reliable food abundance. Defendability indices were higher in chimpanzees and bonobos than in mountain gorillas, but did not differ significantly between chimpanzees, bonobos, and western gorillas. Overall, our results indicate that economic defendability alone cannot explain interspecific variation in territoriality and that our current understanding of ecological differences between the species of the genus Pan have to be revised. Possible additional factors shaping space use of neighboring groups include mate competition within groups.

papers.title: Mapping and Probing the Substrate Scope of a Ketoamide-Forming Splicease by Computational Design
papers.abstract: -Keto-{beta}-amide warheads are protease-inhibiting pharmacophores in peptidomimetic antiviral drugs and drug leads, but their diversity-oriented synthesis for library-based drug discovery can be challenging. The same moiety is installed enzymatically in gene-encoded peptides by tyramine spliceases from spliceotide natural products. However, their substrate scope remains poorly understood. We mined bacterial spliceotide pathways for multi-precursor spliceases and identified HypX from Hyella patelloides that modified 5 of 7 native precursors in E. coli. Single-point mutagenesis showed promiscuity for HypX and the previously identified PlpX but different substrate scopes, suggesting that splicease mining can provide enzymes for focused libraries of various substrate types. To evaluate multipoint variants without exhaustive screening, we combined AlphaFold3 models with Rosetta calculations to rank millions of variants. Top-scoring peptides were spliced more efficiently than single-point mutants. Structural modeling rationalized position-specific tolerance, including a cofactor constraint. This work establishes a mining- and structure-guided strategy to streamline library-based splicease applications.

papers.title: Antibiotics drive immunometabolic rewiring of human immune responses
papers.abstract: Antibiotics are routinely evaluated for their antimicrobial activity, potential host toxicity, and disruption of the microbiome. Certain antibiotics can also impact cell-intrinsic host processes, including evolutionarily conserved processes in the mitochondria. These raise the possibility that antibiotics can directly impact host immunity, which relies on mitochondrial function for their immunometabolic activation. However, the immunological consequences of most antibiotics in current use have not been systematically examined. Here, we performed a comprehensive analysis of the effects of clinically used antibiotics on activation of primary human immune cells. We uncovered an underappreciated antibiotic-specific modulation of immune function in healthy individuals and infectious disease patients. Focusing on the immunomodulatory antibiotic ciprofloxacin, we found altered mitochondrial gene expression across multiple immune populations, driving distinct, lineage-specific responses and heightened sensitivity of T-cells. Ciprofloxacin impaired primary human T-cell expansion and activation and altered mitochondrial function and metabolism. We further demonstrated immunomodulatory effects of selected antibiotics in response to inactivated bacteria and during live viral infection. Finally, to test the implications of our findings in vivo, we showed that immune activation is altered shortly after a single dose of antibiotic administration in mice. This work established a widespread impact of antibiotics on immune-cell function, and identified mitochondrial perturbation as one underlying mechanism, with implications for host-pathogen interactions and antimicrobial therapy.

papers.title: Species-specific WNT requirements shape somite morphogenesis in mammalian embryo models
papers.abstract: Somitogenesis establishes the metameric body plan of the vertebrate embryo and can be recapitulated in vitro using stem cell-based embryo models. Although these systems are well established in individual species, they have rarely been compared across species, leaving unresolved how conserved developmental programmes generate species-specific tissue organisation. Here, we compare somitogenesis in embryo models derived from human, pig, sheep and cow pluripotent stem cells and investigate how WNT signalling and the extracellular matrix regulate axis segmentation. Under identical induction conditions, human and pig models diverge in cell-type composition and morphology, revealing distinct modes of axial elongation. Increasing WNT stimulation restores somite formation in pig models but fails to restore ordered segmentation. Furthermore, each of the four mammalian species requires a different level of WNT stimulation and matrix embedding time for somite formation. Finally, comparative analyses identify species-specific differences in progenitor dynamics. Human models, showing ordered segmentation, retain a posterior mesoderm-producing domain, whereas pig models show rapid depletion of this domain, associated with simultaneous somite formation. Together, these findings reveal species-specific requirements for mammalian somitogenesis in stem cell-derived embryo models and suggest that maintenance of a posterior axial domain contributes to ordered segmentation.

papers.title: Neural discrimination of emotional prosody in natural sentences in 2- to 3-month-old infants using OPM-MEG
papers.abstract: From birth, infants are sensitive to the emotional prosody of speech, yet it remains unclear when the developing brain discriminates emotions conveyed by natural spoken sentences. Here, we recorded brain activity with optically pumped magnetometer magnetoencephalography (OPM-MEG) in 15 infants aged 2-3 months while they listened to semantically neutral sentences spoken with happy or angry prosody. Natural sentences elicited robust auditory evoked responses, with prominent components at 88, 216, 380 and 1,356 ms after sentence onset and sources centred on bilateral superior and middle temporal cortex. Time-resolved multivariate pattern analysis revealed that distributed neural activity discriminated recordings spoken with happy from angry prosody 346-454 ms after the onset of the prosodically prominent word (the first word carrying a pitch peak), despite no difference in global field power between conditions. This discrimination was transient, emerged before the end of the sentence, and was carried primarily by phase-locked delta-band activity, followed by later differences in induced alpha power. Angry prosody also delayed the late auditory response by approximately 15 ms with no detectable changes in amplitude. Our findings show that cortical responses to happy and angry prosody in natural speech differ by 2-3 months of age, and demonstrate that OPM-MEG combined with time-resolved decoding can reveal the temporal, spatial and spectral organisation of early emotional-prosody processing.

papers.title: ADRA2B genetic polymorphism modulates vagus nerve stimulation response
papers.abstract: Introduction. Given interest in vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) as a potential therapy for Alzheimer's disease, due to its hypothesized influence on the noradrenergic (NA) system, there is a need to understand the pronounced individual differences in responsiveness to VNS in aging. We tested whether a genetic polymorphism related to NA signaling, the {Delta}301-303 deletion in the ADRA2B receptor, modulates transcutaneous auricular (taVNS) effects on task-related pupillary responses or pupil-linked cortical activity in noradrenergic projection territory. Methods. Forty-one adults (61% deletion carriers; ages 19-79) performed a visual oddball task during a sham-controlled single-blind crossover taVNS trial. Of these people, 25 (68% deletion carriers) also performed the same task with simultaneous fMRI. Results. ADRA2B genotype predicted the taVNS effect on oddball pupillary responses (t(37) = 3.03, p = .004, d = 0.84). Deletion carrier responses were more likely to increase, while non-carrier responses decreased.
