Carriers showed stronger spatial alignment between pupil-BOLD coupling and cortical norepinephrine transporter (NET) expression (t(22) = 2.82, p = .010, adjusted d = 1.21). This difference was selective to NET among 19 PET maps (all other p > .11). The individual effect of taVNS predicted NET alignment of pupil-BOLD coupling ({rho} = .45, p = .023). Conclusions. ADRA2B {Delta}301-303 deletion status, which is thought to increase NA availability, predicts the direction of the pupillary response to taVNS and how tightly pupil-linked BOLD activity aligns with cortical noradrenergic projection territory.

papers.title: Predicting seabird-vessel interactions from bird-borne data alone
papers.abstract: Seabirds often follow fishing vessels to scavenge discards and bait, benefiting from access to food but also facing the risk of bycatch. Exposure to bycatch is commonly assessed by analysing seabird-fishing interactions, typically through the spatiotemporal alignment of seabird and vessel tracking data. However, this approach may underestimate interactions when vessel tracking information is incomplete or unavailable. We tested whether seabird-vessel interactions could be identified using seabird telemetry alone and whether fishing and nonfishing vessels could be distinguished. We analysed GPS, wet-dry, accelerometer and pressure data from 273 Scopoli's shearwaters in the Northwest Mediterranean. We identified 779 vessel-attendance events using seabird GPS, Automatic Identification System (AIS) data and simulation-based tests to distinguish vessel attraction or following from chance encounters. We then trained random forest models to predict vessel-attendance from bird-borne movement and environmental metrics, testing different sensor combinations. Finally, we selected the GPS and environmental model for its performance and compatibility with GPS-only tracking data from 17 radar-equipped shearwaters, whose detectors identified nearby vessels independently of AIS. Models predicting vessel-attendance from seabird movement metrics derived from GPS, wet-dry sensors and accelerometers achieved classification rates above 90% during training. However, when tested on new individuals, 42% of their positive predictions were false-positives. Models combining environmental metrics with either GPS or GPS and wet-dry data achieved classification rates around 75% during training and generalised consistently across individuals, maintaining classification rates of 70% or above. Attendance events involving fishing (n = 482) and nonfishing vessels (n = 297) could not be reliably distinguished. Across 45 trips of radar-equipped shearwaters, the GPS and environmental model discriminated vessel-attendance in hourly bins against AIS detections (AUC = 0.85), supporting assessment of spatiotemporal attendance patterns. At the event level, only 17% of 227 predicted vessel-attendance events were supported by AIS or radar detections. However, radar detected nearby vessels during 19 predicted events lacking AIS support, highlighting the value of complementary vessel detection. This study presents a vessel-independent framework for assessing seabird-vessel interactions based solely on bird-borne data, complementing fisheries monitoring programmes, helping to identify gaps in vessel-tracking systems across poorly monitored marine regions, and informing future assessments of bycatch risk.

papers.title: Influence of antibody-antigen interaction on fluorescence of Rhodamine 6G conjugated to the antibodies measured in human serum
papers.abstract: Fluorescent dyes conjugated to monoclonal antibodies specifically trastuzumab (TRAS) and pertuzumab (PERT) serve as sensitive reporters of changes in the local energetic environment arising from antibody-antibody and antibody-antigen interactions. Upon covalent conjugation, the antibody local environment perturbates the energetic state of the dye, resulting in changes of the fluorescence emission energy and emission width of the dye. The dependence of these spectral parameters on antibody concentration was measured in HBS-8, diluted and undiluted human serum. In addition, the emission energy and emission width of dye-conjugated TRAS were investigated as a function of recombinant human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) extracellular domain concentration in HBS-8 and in diluted and undiluted human serum. Antibody-antibody and antibody-antigen interactions produce remarkable contributions into the emission energy and emission width. These contributions depend on the composition of the surrounding medium. Our study showed that the samples containing 100 nM TRAS in serum exhibited the largest spectral changes upon interaction with HER2 suggesting that antibody-antigen interaction are not linear across concentration range of the antibodies. Moreover, our results demonstrate that interactions between dye-conjugated antibodies and their binding partners can be detected under physiologically relevant conditions. These findings establish fluorescence emission energy and emission width analysis as a potential approach for probing antibody interactions in complex biological matrices.

papers.title: Wearable Estimation of Knee Joint Contact Forces: SiMPLeSENSE, a Simulated-IMU Pipeline Validated Against In Vivo Loads
papers.abstract: Knee joint compressive forces (KCF) are central to understanding joint loading and degeneration, but they can be measured directly only with instrumented implants. Musculoskeletal models provide a non-invasive alternative, and inertial measurement units (IMUs) could make such estimates portable. However, no dataset combines IMU signals with in vivo implant forces, so the accuracy of IMU-based KCF remains unverified. We developed SiMPLeSENSE, a framework that derives virtual IMU orientations from optical motion capture using subject-specific SMPL meshes. Using the CAMS-Knee dataset, we reconstructed kinematics with OpenSense and estimated KCF in OpenSim with a Rapid Muscle Redundancy solver, comparing the estimates with in vivo measurements during level walking and stair descent. We also assessed robustness to sensor placement error by adding empirically derived thigh and shank orientation noise (for two cases). Across subjects and activities, the simulated-IMU estimates closely tracked the optical mocap-driven estimates and reproduced the in vivo force pattern, with the agreement against the optical reference being higher for stair descent. Overall, the estimated forces matched the in vivo measurements with a median RMSE of about 0.3 to 0.5 BW and correlations near 0.95. Adding realistic orientation error increased RMSE only modestly, whereas doubling it markedly overestimated peak force, most evident for stair descent. These results indicate that the approach is robust to substantial changes in input kinematics, supporting a laboratory-independent setup combining inertial motion capture, a small EMG set, and instrumented force shoes for home and clinical monitoring of knee loading.

papers.title: Transcriptional contingency in the early hematopoiesis of inherited bone marrow failure syndromes
papers.abstract: The inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (IBMFS) are a group of heterogeneous genetic diseases caused by germline pathogenic variants in genes involved in hematopoiesis and genomic integrity. Despite sharing common phenotypical manifestations that have aided opportune diagnosis, such as bone marrow failure, congenital malformations and an increased predisposition to develop cancer, little is known about the shared and distinctive transcriptional programs in their hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells compartment that underlie the clinical manifestations of each disease. In this work we have successfully integrated and analyzed the publicly available scRNAseq datasets of HSPCs from patients with Fanconi anemia (FA) and Telomere Biology disorders (TBD), as well as healthy controls. Once integrated, we performed quality control metrics, as well as batch effect correction using different methods. Through dimensionality reduction, cell clustering and cell type annotation we found distinctive gene expression profiles per syndrome and per cell type, as well as orchestrated gene expression profiles, including upregulation of inflammatory pathways and cell proliferation pathways. This work shows the integration of datasets from FA and TBD, two major IBMFS, and provides the basis for an accumulative, comparative, and integrated atlas of scRNAseq data from patients with IBMFS.

papers.title: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNS for Flexible Working Memory
papers.abstract: Oscillatory phase coding (OPC) is widely observed in neural systems and has been implicated in cognitive functions such as memory and sequence processing. However, its computational role and neural substrates remain largely unclear. Here, we studied OPC by training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with adaptation to perform sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. After training, we found that OPC emerges in the RNN spontaneously: the memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm, with oscillation amplitude encoding item identity and phase encoding serial order. Ablation studies identified three key elements required for OPC: adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information. Neuron-type analysis revealed the emergence of content and time cells in the trained RNN, and they process item identity and sequence order separately. Recurrent connectivity analysis revealed phase-organized connections among time cells and structured connections within digit-selective content-cell groups. Inspired by these findings, we proposed a neural circuit model which reproduces OPC through interactions between content units and an adaptive time ring. Together, this study reveals how OPC arises from network structures and task demands, offers insights into the implementation and computational mechanisms of OPC in biological systems, and inspires us to develop computational models for human-like cognitive functions.

papers.title: Serotype specific anti-capsular polysaccharide IgG associated with colonizing and invasive group B streptococcus in pregnant woman-newborn dyads
papers.abstract: Maternal IgG against group B streptococcus (GBS) capsular polysaccharide (CPS), is the principal placental mediator of neonatal protection, yet naturally acquired anti-CPS immunity has not been characterized in North African populations. To address this gap, we conducted a prospective study in a Moroccan mother-newborn cohort to quantify the serotype-specific anti-CPS IgG levels in relation to colonizing versus invasive GBS serotypes. Additionally, we assessed the transplacental transfer of anti-CPS IgG and identified potential correlates of invasive disease. We examined serotype-specific anti-CPS IgG (serotypes Ia-V) in the plasma from maternal and cord blood of 103 GBS-colonized pregnant women, 35 uncolonized controls and their paired newborns (90 paired colonized dyads, including five newborns with invasive GBS disease) using a standardized six-plex immunoassay. Transfer ratios were compared with 1.0 and cord concentrations with published serotype- and onset-specific risk-reduction thresholds. Maternal anti-CPS IgG concentrations varied by serotype, with the highest median for serotype II(1.36g/mL) and the lowest for serotype Ib(0.003g/mL). They were higher in GBS-colonized than uncolonized mothers for serotypes Ia, Ib and II. Maternal and cord blood IgG concentrations were correlated across serotypes, but placental transfer was incomplete, with median ratios of 0.50-0.80. Among 77 newborns, 13.0%(n=10) reached early-onset and 44.2%(n=34) achieved late-onset disease risk-reduction thresholds. The serotype IV was the most identified among neonatal infection disease cases, and this was associated with sub-protective anti-serotype IV antibody. This suggests that while naturally acquired anti-serotype II antibodies were predominant, the low level of anti-serotype IV antibodies could contribute to neonatal infection diseases in mother-newborn pairs.

papers.title: Edi-Set-Flow: detecting differential RNA-editing at scale
papers.abstract: Background: Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing is a post-transcriptional modification catalysed by ADAR enzymes that can alter codons, splicing patterns, and RNA secondary structures. RNA editing is essential for innate immunity and nervous system development, and its dysregulation is implicated in neurological disorders, cancers, and autoimmune diseases. Despite its biological importance, accurately detecting RNA editing from RNA-seq data remains technically challenging, and robust inference of differential editing across experimental conditions is not straightforward. Findings: We have developed Edi-Set-Flow, a reproducible and scalable pipeline for transcriptome-wide A-to-I RNA editing analysis of bulk RNA-seq data. Implemented in Nextflow, the pipeline takes raw FASTQ files as input, trims reads and filters for quality, aligns reads to the reference genome, and identifies editing sites with JACUSA2. Common genetic variants are excluded using the gnomAD population database. Identified sites are annotated for genetic feature context and predicted functional consequences, and results are summarised in a user-friendly HTML report. The pipeline scales efficiently to hundreds or thousands of samples and is suitable for large datasets such as GTEx. An accompanying R package enables advanced analyses, including model fitting, hypothesis testing, false discovery rate control, and visualisation, thereby facilitating reliable statistical comparisons of editing across experimental groups. Applying Edi-Set-Flow to GTEx brain RNA-seq data, we uncovered distinct RNA editing signatures across brain tissues and recovered known protein-recoding events. Conclusions: Edi-Set-Flow provides researchers with a robust, user-friendly, scalable, end-to-end solution for efficiently identifying and interpreting biologically meaningful RNA editing events across diverse transcriptomic datasets, for both mouse and human.

papers.title: Actin filament bundling by the Arabidopsis VILLIN4 C-terminus involves the basic segment of the IDR linker and is sensitive to temperature and ionic strength
papers.abstract: Plant villins are ubiquitous proteins involved in F-actin regulation in all plant organs. Villins consist of folded core and headpiece domains connected by an intrinsically disordered linker. In plant villins these linkers include up to 200 amino acid residues, which is substantially larger than their vertebrate counterparts (~40 residues). Moreover, the linkers in most types of plant villins exhibit a distinct charge partitioning pattern: a larger basic N-terminus and a smaller acidic C-terminus. The roles of these distinct, sizable and disordered linkers in plant villins are not well understood and are currently under active scrutiny. Here we demonstrate that the basic portion of the linker in Arabidopsis thaliana VILLIN4 (AtVLN4) is capable of actin filament bundling. These interactions are also affected by the presence of the adjacent headpiece domain and are altered by temperature and levels of potassium ions, major abiotic regulators that influence plant growth. Based on these findings, we propose that the F-actin bundling capacity of the basic segment in AtVLN4 is responsive to environmental changes and is a uniform property in closely related villins due to high sequence homology across multiple species.

papers.title: Development of appropriate sensorimotor recalibration for a de novo skill
papers.abstract: Implicit adaptation operates automatically to ensure that well-learned movements remain exquisitely calibrated. A long-standing puzzle is how this process is applied when learning a new skill: Prior work has highlighted that implicit recalibration is inflexible, even when its operation results in maladaptive behavior given the sensorimotor mapping required for the new skill. Here, we revisited this problem, training participants for up to a month on a range of tasks with novel mappings, including mirror reversals and large rotations. Contrary to previous findings, implicit recalibration was flexibly reconfigured after prolonged training in a manner appropriate for each novel mapping. Training that emphasized feedforward planning rather than feedback control was sufficient to induce this reconfiguration. Learning involved reconfiguration of the sensory predictions and error correction policy for the new mapping, and participants were able to switch between mappings with minimal interference. These results demonstrate that implicit recalibration is reconfigured during skill acquisition, enabling flexible, context-specific adaptation.

papers.title: Dual role of RBM3 in PEDV infection: stabilization of viral RNA and upregulation of the entry factor HSPA5
papers.abstract: RBM3, a member of the cold-shock protein family, functions as an RNA chaperone that stabilizes target transcripts by binding to their untranslated regions (UTRs). Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) is an enteric coronavirus that poses a serious threat to the swine industry, and its replication heavily depends on its genomic and subgenomic RNAs, making these RNAs potential targets for host RNA-binding proteins. In this study, we show that RBM3 promotes PEDV replication through a dual mechanism. On one hand, RBM3 exhibits a binding preference for the viral 3'UTR, which prolongs the half-life of viral RNA and thereby promotes PEDV proliferation. RBM3 also interacts with the PEDV nucleocapsid (N) protein and replication-associated double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) signals, suggesting that RBM3 may be associated with viral replication complexes, though its contribution to their functional integrity remains to be determined. On the other hand, RBM3 increases HSPA5 promoter activity and HSPA5 mRNA levels, linking RBM3 to HSPA5, a host factor known to facilitate PEDV attachment and internalization. These two mechanisms together provide a mechanistic basis for efficient PEDV infection. Our findings identify RBM3 as a positive host regulator of PEDV and establish, for the first time, a functional link between RBM3 and HSPA5, offering new insights into coronavirus-host interactions and suggesting RBM3 as a potential target for antiviral intervention.

papers.title: PSI photoinhibition and protection at low temperatures and in fluctuating light: An 30 ecophysiological vista
papers.abstract: In green leaves in vivo, photosystem I (PSI) was thought to be resistant to photoinhibition. In 1994, it was found that, in chilling-sensitive plants such as cucumber (Cucumis sativus L.), exposing leaves to moderate constant light at temperatures below 10 degrees C induces PSI photoinhibition with little effect on PSII. Since the beginning of this century, PSI photoinhibition induced by fluctuating light (alternating high and low light, FL) or repetitive saturating pulses (rSPs) has been reported in many species. In this review, we compare the causes and consequences of PSI photoinhibition in cucumber at chilling temperatures with those of PSI photoinhibition induced by FL or rSPs. Changes in chloroplasts during these photoinhibitory treatments are followed, focusing on where and how reactive oxygen species are produced and which parts of PSI are damaged. We also discuss the roles of two pathways of cyclic electron flow around PSI, the NDH and PGR5/PGRL1 pathways, particularly in suppression of PSI photoinhibition. Lastly, we discuss problems with methods for measuring PSI parameters and future research directions from an ecophysiological viewpoint.

papers.title: RyR2-Mediated Ca2+ Leak Drives Progressive Arrhythmogenic Cardiomyopathy
papers.abstract: Background Abnormal sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca2+ release through ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2) is a well-established mechanism of ventricular arrhythmias. Whether persistent RyR2 dysfunction can also initiate the structural remodeling characteristic of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM) remains unknown. We tested the hypothesis that chronic RyR2-mediated Ca2+ leak is sufficient to couple electrical instability to progressive cardiomyopathy. Methods We generated a rabbit carrying the severe gain-of-function RyR2-V2475F mutation and characterized disease progression using longitudinal cardiac phenotyping, continuous electrocardiographic monitoring, cellular electrophysiology and Ca2+ imaging, histopathology, biochemical analyses, and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq). Therapeutic potential was evaluated by continuous treatment with the selective RyR2 inhibitor ent-verticilide for two months. Results RyR2-V2475F rabbits developed spontaneous ventricular tachyarrhythmias, sudden cardiac death, and progressive right ventricular (RV)-dominant fibrofatty cardiomyopathy recapitulating major features of human ACM. Malignant ventricular arrhythmias preceded overt structural remodeling and were associated at the cellular level with early spontaneous Ca2+ release and early afterdepolarizations. Early disease was characterized by remodeling of excitation-contraction coupling with preserved SR Ca2+ load and contractile function despite RyR2 dysfunction; upon disease progression, these compensatory changes were accompanied by SR Ca2+ depletion, impaired RV contractility and reduced left ventricular filling. Single-nucleus transcriptomics identified early fibroblast expansion and predicted cardiomyocyte-centered paracrine signaling before advanced fibrofatty infiltration. Cardiomyocytes also exhibited an altered lipid-metabolic transcriptome and intracellular lipid accumulation, accompanied by enhanced mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake. Selective RyR2 inhibition markedly reduced ventricular tachycardia burden and preserved RV contraction and LV filling during disease progression. Conclusions Severe RyR2 gain-of-function can lead to both malignant ventricular arrhythmias and progressive arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy in a large-animal model, establishing persistent intracellular Ca2+ dysregulation as a mechanistic link between electrical and structural heart disease. The ability of selective RyR2 inhibition to suppress arrhythmias and preserve cardiac function identifies RyR2 as a potentially actionable therapeutic target in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

papers.title: KaryoTap-based scDNA seq assessment of aneuploidy induction by hydroquinone in hematopoietic stem cells
papers.abstract: Monosomy 7 is a frequent cytogenetic alteration associated with poor outcomes in myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukemia. The benzene metabolite hydroquinone (HQ) has been reported to induce chromosome 7 loss in cultured hematopoietic cells, suggesting a mechanism linking benzene exposure to these diseases. However, these findings were largely based on FISH analysis of selected chromosomes in relatively small numbers of cells. Here, we tested whether HQ increases aneuploidy in primary human CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) using KaryoTap, a single-cell DNA sequencing approach that measures copy number across all 22 autosomes, together with interphase FISH. We first identified 20 uM as the highest HQ concentration tested that preserved sufficient viable cells for single-cell analysis. We then examined cord blood and adult mobilized CD34+ cells, including the MPS1 inhibitor reversine as a positive control in the cord blood experiment. Reversine increased whole-chromosome gains and losses, including those of chromosome 7. HQ did not produce a reproducible increase in aneuploidy across three donors and two sources of CD34+ cells, including two concentrations and two timepoints in the adult donor. A modest increase in chromosome 7 loss in one cord blood donor was not reproduced in the other donors. In the other cord blood donor, the estimated upper bound on the HQ-associated increase was approximately 1.4 percentage points. HSPCs also showed a greater increase in chromosome losses than epithelial cells or melanocytes following the same reversine exposure. These findings do not support a substantial, reproducible increase in whole-chromosome aneuploidy after HQ exposure under the conditions tested. They are consistent with a model in which benzene exposure favors the expansion of pre-existing monosomy 7 clones, although this possibility requires direct testing.

papers.title: Comparative cryo-EM structures of CGMMV and ToMMV reveal divergent coat protein packing and electrostatics indicating Tobamovirus host specificity
papers.abstract: Tobamoviruses are a group of economically important plant viruses exhibiting extreme stability and persistence. Despite high morphological similarity, they show extensive host-family specificity, cause a range of symptoms, and cause significant global yield loss in fruit and vegetable plants. Composed of a rod-shaped helical assembly of identical coat proteins encasing a single-stranded RNA, Tobamoviruses have long served as fundamental models for understanding helical assemblies. Here we report the cryo-EM structures of two viruses from this genus, CGMMV and ToMMV, at 2.86 [A] and 2.71 [A] resolution, respectively. The structures reveal divergent packing strategies within the virion assembly. While ToMMV is genetically similar to the canonical Tobamovirus TMV and displays a structure closely resembling TMV, CGMMV employs a more hydrophobic packing strategy, particularly in the solvent-exposed inner loop region of the coat protein. Comparative biophysical and molecular dynamics analyses from the reconstructed structures reveal more stable and compact protein packing for CGMMV at both the subunit and assembly levels. Furthermore, this study reports a newly identified electrostatic patch existing at the lower alpha-helix region of the coat protein that serves as an additional RNA-stabilizing region, with host family-specific amino acid substitutions among Tobamoviruses. Our study elucidates the structural mechanics and evolutionary strategies driving virion stability and host diversity while maintaining a conserved helical assembly. These findings reveal how subtle electrostatic tuning and divergent packing strategies drive viral stability and host adaptation within a strictly conserved quaternary scaffold.

papers.title: Integrated Characterization of Proximal and Distal Nerve Stumps in a Model of Chronic Motor Nerve Transection
papers.abstract: Prolonged peripheral nerve discontinuity subjects the proximal stump to chronic axotomy and the distal stump to chronic denervation, resulting in pathological changes that may compromise regeneration following delayed repair. Although these changes have been investigated in both nerve stumps, much of the existing evidence derives from mixed sensorimotor nerve models, leaving the histopathological changes of chronic motor nerve injury incompletely understood. Addressing this gap requires a well-defined, reproducible model that maintains prolonged motor nerve discontinuity and enables concurrent characterization of both nerve stumps. This study aimed to establish a chronic motor nerve transection model and characterize the distinct structural and microenvironmental changes occurring in both nerve stumps. The buccal branch of the facial nerve was transected in Lewis rats, and the nerve ends were secured to adjacent muscle to prevent spontaneous reconnection. At 10 weeks post-injury (p.i.), proximal and distal stumps were compared with uninjured nerves using histological, immunofluorescence, and morphometric analyses. Persistent functional impairment was observed throughout the study period. The proximal stump exhibited traumatic neuroma formation, altered axonal morphology, and loss of myelin integrity, but largely preserved its underlying nerve architecture and microenvironment. In contrast, the distal stump exhibited reduced neurofilament expression, clusters of small-caliber myelinated axons, and increased myelinated axon density compared to both uninjured nerves and the proximal chronically injured segment. These changes were accompanied by endoneurial tube atrophy, increased collagen I deposition, vascular remodeling, and immune-cell accumulation, indicating extensive structural and microenvironmental remodeling. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that chronic motor nerve transection produces two distinct pathological compartments: a proximal stump characterized by persistent but disorganized regeneration-associated features and a distal stump characterized by pronounced degenerative and microenvironmental changes. This study establishes a reproducible model of chronic peripheral nerve injury and provides a foundation for investigating how these compartment-specific pathologies contribute to regenerative failure and for developing targeted therapeutic strategies to improve regeneration following delayed nerve repair.

papers.title: The mouse Cdh23ahl allele drives early cochlear dysfunction and phenotypic heterogeneity before progressive hearing loss
papers.abstract: The Cdh23ahl allele is present in many commonly used inbred mouse strains and is known to cause progressive hearing loss. However, increasing evidence suggests Cdh23ahl can also modify the severity and expressivity of other genetic phenotypes, extending its biological effects beyond the cochlea. Here, we define the phenotypic, physiological, and molecular consequences associated with Cdh23ahl by comparing C57BL/6N mice with a co-isogenic strain in which the allele was repaired by genome editing. We find the auditory phenotype begins earlier and is more variable than generally appreciated, with significant threshold elevations at 3642 kHz already present by 1-month of age and progressive involvement of lower frequencies thereafter. Before these threshold elevations, inner hair cells at postnatal day 14 (P14) exhibit tonotopically distinct alterations in mechanoelectrical transduction, with reduced maximal transduction currents apically, but increased currents basally, while resting open probability and adaptation kinetics remain preserved. Cochlear transcription is also altered shortly after hearing onset: by P16, Cdh23ahl and repaired cochleae occupy distinct transcriptional states. By P30, transcriptional differences have expanded substantially, and Cdh23ahl cochleae show significantly increased inter-individual transcriptomic dispersion coincident with the emergence of variable high-frequency auditory dysfunction. These findings demonstrate that Cdh23ahl is not physiologically benign in young mice, but is associated with an altered cochlear state that precedes hearing loss. The early and variable consequences of this common allele provide a potential framework for understanding its effects on phenotype expressivity and have important implications for the design and interpretation of studies using mouse strains that carry Cdh23ahl.

papers.title: Classical guinea pig coat phenotypes are associated with variants in FGF5 and CELSR1
papers.abstract: Classical Mendelian coat phenotypes in the domestic guinea pig, Cavia porcellus, were central to early studies of mammalian genetics, yet their molecular bases remain unresolved. Long fur is characterized by elongated hair, and rough coat by whorled patterns of fur orientation. Here, we performed genome-wide association mapping using exome and whole-genome sequencing data to identify the genetic basis of both phenotypes. Mapping of long fur identified a locus containing FGF5 and resolved the association to a premature stop codon, independently confirming a previously proposed candidate variant. Mapping of rough coat identified a locus containing CELSR1, an atypical cadherin and core component of the planar cell polarity (PCP) pathway, resolving the association to an in-frame proline insertion in its extracellular domain. The variant is associated with a dominant rough-coat phenotype, unlike previously characterized recessive mouse Celsr1 alleles, which produce a similar hair-patterning phenotype only when homozygous. The mouse alleles are also associated with severe developmental abnormalities, including open neural tube, which are not observed in rough-coat guinea pigs. This dominant, tissue-specific phenotype suggests that the insertion alters CELSR1 function in a previously undescribed manner. Consistent with this possibility, the rough-coat variant localized normally to cell-cell junctions in cultured mouse keratinocytes and retained its ability to recruit Fzd6 and Vangl2, demonstrating preserved molecular interactions involved in PCP junction assembly. These findings resolve the molecular basis of two classical guinea pig coat phenotypes and identify a naturally occurring, dominant CELSR1 allele associated with a mode of PCP disruption distinct from previously characterized alleles.

papers.title: RNA accessibility sequencing reveals transcriptome-wide RBP binding and RNA structure
papers.abstract: We introduce RAD-seq (RNA Accessibility via Deamination sequencing), a simple and scalable method that quantifies RNA accessibility by protein binding in vivo. RAD-seq uses TadA8.20-mediated adenosine deamination to report the local exposure of each adenosine to its molecular environment, integrating the combined effects of base pairing, RNA folding, and RNA-binding protein (RBP) occupancy in a single experiment. RAD-seq profiles recapitulate known structural signatures, reveal high-resolution RBP footprints, report on the influence of RNA modifications, and capture dynamic remodeling of RNA accessibility during oxidative and heat-shock stress. By integrating RAD-seq with RNA Bind-n-Seq motifs, we detected local enrichment of the RNA N6-methyladenosine (m6A) methyltransferase recruiter TRA2A following knockdown of the exon junction anchor protein EIF4A3, revealing a potential mechanism that links RNA accessibility to enhanced TRA2A recruitment and m6A deposition. Extending this framework, we introduce an unsupervised statistical model that combines RAD-seq with motif priors to infer binding landscapes for multiple RBPs, reproducing the information from numerous CLIP-seq datasets from a single RAD-seq experiment. These results indicate RAD-seq as a generalizable approach for joint profiling of RNA structure and protein occupancy, defining enzymatic RNA accessibility as a new dimension to investigate regulatory elements on RNA.

papers.title: A Deep Phylogenetic Split Between Short- and Long-Wavelength-Tuned Visual Systems in Surgeonfishes (Acanthuridae)
papers.abstract: The light environment, coupled with ecology, is widely thought to drive visual adaptation, creating species-specific visual niches. However, coral reef ecosystems experience continuous spatiotemporal variations in light conditions, and mechanisms such as phenotypic plasticity may be essential for coral reef animals to adjust to such changing sensory requirements. It remains unclear how widespread colour vision plasticity is, or the extent to which ecology and phylogeny drive plasticity in coral reef fishes. Using a comparative transcriptomic approach across 22 species, we aimed to investigate visual plasticity within a prominent coral reef fish family, surgeonfishes (Acanthuridae), in response to changes in the light environment throughout development and across seasons in adults. Surprisingly, we uncovered a deep phylogenetic split (~42 mya) in visual opsin gene expression profiles, with Nasinae expressing a shorter-shifted palette than Acanthurinae, which coincides with the divide between water-column and benthic-feeding modalities during the speciation of their last common ancestor. However, opsin gene expression showed little variation in response to seasonal or ontogenetic shifts in the light environment, nor in the broad functional feeding groups extant species from both subfamilies fall under. Thus, the invariable visual gene expression observed in present-day surgeonfishes appears to be dictated by phylogenetic inertia, despite rapid diversification into a range of ecological niches. This suggests that spectral tuning into two main modalities, short and long, reduces the need for visual plasticity, allowing larger and more mobile coral reef fishes to conduct visually guided behaviours across the entire range of light environments they encounter.

papers.title: BundleMorphometry: Spatially Resolved White Matter Bundle Shape Analysis Using Nonlinear Streamline-based Registration
papers.abstract: Diffusion MRI tractometry quantifies microstructural properties along white matter (WM) bundles but does not directly measure their geometry, potentially overlooking localized morphological alterations. Here, we introduce BundleMorphometry, a framework for quantifying local WM bundle shape using the analytical Jacobian of nonlinear streamline-based registration. Individual subject bundles are registered to a reference atlas bundle using BundleWarp, a streamline-based nonlinear registration method. We derive the analytical Jacobian of the resulting deformation field and compute its log-determinant (log det J) to quantify local expansion and compression at each streamline point. To enable spatially resolved group comparisons, these measurements are projected onto the two-dimensional grid, capturing variations along and across each bundle. We evaluated BundleMorphometry using two clinical datasets comprising patients with glioma and Parkinson's disease (PD). In the glioma dataset, BundleMorphometry revealed spatially extensive deformation patterns in lesion-affected WM bundles that were not captured by displacement magnitude alone. Additionally, in a group analysis of the PD dataset (32 patients and 32 healthy controls), we identified significant localized morphological differences in the corpus callosum forceps major, mid-body and right spinothalamic tract, with distinct patterns of expansion and compression. These findings demonstrate the potential of BundleMorphometry to advance conventional tractometry by enabling spatially resolved analysis of bundle morphology.

papers.title: Aging reshapes cardiac extravascular leukocyte transcription through bidirectional remodeling during LPS-induced endotoxemia
papers.abstract: Sepsis disproportionately affects older adults and is frequently complicated by cardiac dysfunction. However, how aging alters the transcriptional responses of cardiac extravascular immune cells during systemic inflammation remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated aging-dependent transcriptional remodeling of cardiac immune cells using an LPS-induced endotoxemia model in young and aged C57BL/6 mice. Mice received intraperitoneal LPS (5 mg/kg body weight) or vehicle, and cardiac extravascular leukocytes were isolated from ex vivo retrogradely perfused hearts 24 h later for single-cell RNA sequencing. Aging was associated with bidirectional transcriptional remodeling, characterized by both up- and downregulation of gene programs, particularly in cardiac macrophages, monocyte-like macrophages, T cells, and B cells following LPS challenge. A shared feature across these four cell populations was reduced representation of mitochondrial-associated transcriptional programs, indicating aging-dependent remodeling of mitochondrial biology across cardiac myeloid and lymphoid lineages during systemic inflammation. In parallel, cell type-specific transcriptional remodeling revealed distinct functional-associated responses. Macrophages and monocyte-like macrophages exhibited increased tissue-remodeling and repair-associated transcriptional programs. Both T and B cells showed reduced metabolic programs but increased actin cytoskeleton organization. T cells additionally exhibited reduced cytotoxicity-associated and enhanced Th17-associated transcriptional programs, whereas B cells showed reduced antigen-processing and presentation programs. Cell-cell communication analysis suggested aging-associated differences in immune cell interactions following LPS challenge and potential features of cardiac inflammaging at baseline. Together, these findings demonstrate that aging bidirectionally reshapes the cardiac immune response to systemic inflammation, characterized by shared remodeling of mitochondrial-associated programs and cell type-specific changes in inflammatory, metabolic, cytoskeletal, and effector-associated programs. These aging-dependent transcriptional changes occurred in the context of the greater severity of illness observed in aged mice following LPS-induced endotoxemia.

papers.title: Targeted cancer ablation via programmable sensing of amplified oncogenic RNA
papers.abstract: Selectively eliminating cancer cells based on their oncogenic drivers holds great promise but remains challenging for targeted cancer therapy. Here, we present ORCA (Oncogenic RNA-triggered Cancer Ablation), a programmable and modular platform that couples RADAR-based detection of oncogenic RNA with conditional expression of therapeutic payloads in cancer cells. We identify RADAR sensors targeting the transcripts of endogenously amplified oncogenes, including MYC, FGFR2 and wild-type KRAS in colorectal and gastric cancer cells. Focusing on colorectal cancer (CRC) driven by extrachromosomal DNA-amplified MYC, we demonstrate targeted ablation of high-MYC cancer cells using two orthogonal strategies: anti-CD19 CAR-T therapy and enzyme-prodrug therapy. In vivo delivery of ORCA using adeno-associated virus (AAV) suppresses tumor growth in a subcutaneous xenograft model and prolongs survival in a CRC liver metastasis model. ORCA establishes oncogenic RNAs as actionable inputs for targeted cancer therapy via programmable RNA sensing, thus offering a strategy to target tumors through the transcripts of otherwise difficult-to-drug oncogenes such as MYC.

papers.title: Metabolic complexity in the human brain supports metastable network dynamics and declines in normative ageing
papers.abstract: The adaptive capacity of the brain is tied to the complexity of its neural activity. While entropy of brain signals has been used to characterise this complexity in haemodynamic and electrophysiological systems, it remains unknown whether entropy contributes to the temporal dynamics of the metabolic signals of the brain (glucodynamics) and how metabolic entropy may relate to network organisation, brain ageing and cognitive decline. Here, we combined dynamic functional PET (fPET) with 18F-fluoroedeoxyglucose and simultaneously acquired functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in 84 adults to investigate multiscale entropy (MSE) in the brain. We report that metabolic complexity measured with PET MSE represents non-linear, high-frequency complexity, whereas hemodynamic complexity reflects non-linearly constrained neurovascular phase dynamics. Greater metabolic complexity was associated with greater network metastability, particularly in unimodal and higher-order associative networks. Greater regional metabolic complexity also correlated with greater cortical thickness, cerebral metabolic rates of glucose (CMRglc) and cerebral blood flow, and was lower in older than younger adults. In contrast, global and network haemodynamic MSE was not significant associated with network dynamics. Higher global metabolic complexity was associated with better cognitive performance, and voxel-level derived MSE clusters were \associated with cognitive performance in both modalities, with varied cluster sizes and spatial locations. However, these associations were largely accounted for by age variance. We conclude that temporal complexity in cerebral glucose is associated with the dynamics of the underlying metabolic signals, enables metastable network states and declines in ageing. Entropy of metabolic brain signals offers promise as a neurobiologically grounded metric of brain ageing.

papers.title: Norepinephrine inhibits Afferent activation of NTS Catecholamine Neurons in Mice
papers.abstract: The nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) integrates visceral sensory input to regulate feeding behavior, with catecholaminergic (CA) and neuropeptide Y (NPY)-expressing neurons playing key roles in energy homeostasis. Recent evidence suggests functional heterogeneity among CA-NTS neurons, including distinct subpopulations that either suppress or promote feeding. In this study, we investigated how norepinephrine (NE) modulates excitatory synaptic transmission from solitary tract (ST) afferents onto tyrosine hydroxylase-positive (TH) NTS neurons in mice. Using patch-clamp electrophysiology in horizontal brainstem slices, we found that NE inhibits ST-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (ST-EPSCs) in a concentration-dependent manner, with maximal effects at 10 microM and an EC of ~3.4 microM. This inhibition was mediated by alpha-adrenergic receptors and was independent of GABAA receptor activity. NE also suppressed asynchronous glutamate release and attenuated CCK-induced increase in spontaneous EPSC frequency, suggesting a presynaptic mechanism. NPY similarly reduced ST-EPSC amplitude via Y2 receptor activation, and co-application of NE and NPY produce additive or synergistic effects, even at subthreshold concentrations. Together, our results reveal a novel mechanism by which noradrenergic and peptidergic systems interact to regulate visceral sensory processing in the brainstem.

papers.title: Resolving how genetic perturbations act through gene regulatory paths
papers.abstract: Perturb-seq measures transcriptional responses to thousands of genetic perturbations, but each gene's response mixes the contributions of many regulatory paths, so how a perturbation acts cannot be resolved from expression alone, however large the model. Here we present REGA-perturb, which supplies this missing information rather than adding model complexity: reference epigenomes define a scaffold of possible transcription factor (TF)-regulatory element-gene paths, and perturbation responses, pooled through shared latent programs, determine how each path is used, requiring only RNA measurements. Across three CRISPR interference screens totaling 2.4 million cells, REGA-perturb inferred TF-target relationships that agreed with ChIP-seq binding with a gain over random more than four times that of the best existing method, separated candidate direct from indirect targets, and predicted targets of TFs withheld from training. It also inferred perturbation-induced changes in TF activity not reflected in TF transcript levels, and resolved perturbation-specific regulatory rewiring in which opposing regulatory changes cancel at the expression level.

papers.title: Proteolytic feedback of quorum sensing promotes infection by Pseudomonas aeruginosa
papers.abstract: Quorum sensing (QS) enables bacteria to coordinate collective behaviors in response to population density. However, the mechanisms by which QS circuits are reset or attenuated remain poorly understood. In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the LuxR-type transcription factor RhlR controls virulence gene expression at high cell density, requiring both its cognate acyl-homoserine lactone signal and the accessory protein PqsE for full activity. Here, we show that RhlR abundance is actively controlled by ATP-dependent proteolysis through a self-limiting negative feedback loop. We identify an N-terminal degron within RhlR that is protected from protease recognition by PqsE binding and is required for degradation by both the Lon and the ClpP1-ClpP2 protease complex. Removal of this degron stabilizes RhlR, advancing the timing of QS-regulated gene expression, enhancing biofilm formation, imposes a competitive fitness cost in vitro, and reduced virulence in an acute mouse lung infection. Mechanistically, RhlR directly activates transcription of clpP2, encoding a subunit of the protease complex required for its own degradation, establishing a self-limiting negative feedback loop. Disruption of RhlR DNA binding stabilizes the receptor through dual effects on reduced clpP2 expression and increased PqsE availability via the loss of RhlR-dependent repression of pqsE. Together, these findings reveal proteolytic turnover as an underappreciated regulatory layer of QS-activation and establish a mechanism for how receptor turnover may facilitate the transition away from high-cell density states.

papers.title: Removal of maternal compensation reveals retinal-specific roles for Pomgnt1 in zebrafish
papers.abstract: Genetic variants in Protein O-mannose N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase 1 (POMGNT1) result in a broad spectrum of disorders, ranging from severe congenital muscular dystrophy with brain and ocular malformations to non-syndromic retinitis pigmentosa. Despite POMGNT1's established role in the glycosylation of the transmembrane glycoprotein &alpha-dystroglycan (&alpha-DG), the mechanistic basis for this clinical variability remains poorly understood. Previous work in a zebrafish pomngt1 knock-out (KO) line identified retinal degeneration at 6 months post-fertilization (mpf). However, potential involvement of other tissues was not characterized, and compensation from maternal transcripts which can occur in the zebrafish oocyte was not tested. Here, we analyzed maternal-zygotic pomgnt1 KOs (MZKOs) to determine whether maternal compensation influences the onset and severity of pomgnt1-associated phenotypes. We assessed survival, gross morphology, locomotor activity, behavioral patterns, and retinal organization across multiple timepoints. MZKOs survived to adulthood and exhibited no morphological or locomotor deficits up to 5 mpf. Retinal abnormalities were found as early as 2 mpf in MZKOs, demonstrating that maternally provided factors of pomgnt1 delay the onset of retinal pathology. Additionally, MZKOs displayed a novel wall-hugging behavioral pattern that may be consistent with visual impairment or anxiety. These findings demonstrate a strong tissue-specific phenotype following loss of pomgnt1 in zebrafish showing evolutionary divergence in the necessity for Pomgnt1 function in the muscle. However, this strain provides a useful system for investigating the mechanisms underlying the retinal vulnerability observed in POMGNT1-related retinitis pigmentosa.

papers.title: Evolution Shapes Cortical Interneuron Migration
papers.abstract: The cerebral cortex comprises excitatory neurons and inhibitory interneurons originating from distinct forebrain regions. During migration, cortical interneurons (cINs) interact dynamically with neighbouring cells and their microenvironment, contributing to cortical architecture. However, how evolutionary changes in cIN migration shape species-specific cortical development remains unclear. Comparative analyses in mouse, ferret, and human models revealed a conserved migratory sequence but distinct behaviours: human cINs migrate slower, display increased leading-process branching, and exhibit more frequent homotypic repulsive interactions than their mouse and ferret counterparts. These features promote dispersed cortical invasion of cINs in humans and ferrets, contrasting with the stream-like migration observed in mice. Mechanistically, elevated expression of the cytosolic carboxypeptidase CCP1 in human cINs reduces microtubule glutamylation and doublecortin recruitment, thereby facilitating leading-process branching. These findings identify a CCP1-dependent mechanism regulating cIN dispersion and suggest that evolutionary changes in cIN migration contribute to divergent patterns of cortical morphogenesis across mammals.

papers.title: Monounsaturated fat prevent, whereas saturated fat promote, cholesterol crystals in cytoplasmic lipid droplets
papers.abstract: Objective: Metabolic dysfunction associated steatohepatitis (MASH) may, in part, result from excessive storage of cholesterol in hepatic lipid droplets that transition into a crystalline state. The mechanism by which crystals form in lipid droplets of hepatocytes and other cells such as macrophage is incompletely understood. Recently, we showed cholesterol must be esterified for crystals to form in lipid droplets. As the physicochemical properties of saturated cholesteryl ester render it more susceptible to crystallize than unsaturated cholesteryl ester, we investigated whether lipid droplet crystals are composed of saturated cholesteryl ester. Method: Lipid droplet crystals were measured in cholesterol-loaded Hep3B hepatocyte-like and RAW 264.7 macrophage-like cells co-treated with vehicle, monounsaturated fat, or agents that increase cellular saturated fat level. Lipidomics was used to quantify cholesteryl ester species. We also used Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectromicroscopy on livers of mice with MASH to determine the molecular identity of crystals in hepatic lipid droplets. Results: Cholesterol loading increased cholesteryl ester content and lipid droplet crystals. Monounsaturated fat treatment (e.g., oleate) increased the ratio of unsaturated to saturated cholesteryl ester and this corresponded with a substantial reduction in lipid droplet crystals. Treatments increasing saturated fat level did not exhibit this effect. (FTIR) spectromicroscopy identified cholesteryl palmitate as the prominent molecular constituent of hepatic lipid droplet crystals in mice with diet-induced MASH. Conclusion: Hepatic lipid droplet crystals in mice with diet-induced MASH are composed of saturated cholesteryl ester and unsaturated fat intake supports the cellular capacity to sustain non-crystalline liquid disordered cholesteryl ester in lipid droplets.

papers.title: Hmox1/CO regulates retina regeneration via modulation of Wnt/β-catenin signalling and induction of vaspb in zebrafish
papers.abstract: Muller glia (MG) in the zebrafish retina retain a latent stem cell capacity that is absent in mammals, yet the injury responsive signals that drive this reprogramming remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify heme oxygenase-1 (Hmox1), the stress-inducible, rate-limiting enzyme of heme catabolism, as a previously unrecognized regulator of this process. Following injury, hmox1a is selectively and rapidly induced among the heme oxygenase gene family, localizing to photoreceptors with expression peaking during the MG proliferation window. Pharmacological inhibition and morpholino mediated knockdown of Hmox1 dysregulate the acute inflammatory response, impair Muller glia-derived progenitor cell (MGPC) proliferation, and produce lasting deficits in retinal lamination, establishing Hmox1 as a potentially non-redundant, early-acting node required for structural recovery. Exogenous delivery of carbon monoxide (CO), a bioactive Hmox1 metabolite, partially rescues each of these phenotypes, functionally implicating CO as a key downstream effector. Mechanistically, Hmox1/CO signalling stabilizes {beta}-catenin likely via transcriptional repression of the Wnt antagonist dkk1b. This stabilized {beta}-catenin is enriched at a predicted Tcf7l2 site in the promoter of vaspb, which encodes an actin binding protein and is newly identified here as an injury-induced Wnt target gene. Bioinformatic and functional analyses further implicate Nfe2l2a (Nrf2) as a candidate intermediary bridging Hmox1/CO to Wnt regulation, with putative antioxidant response elements identified within the dkk1b locus. Together, these findings outline a putative Hmox1[->]CO[->]Nrf2[->]dkk1b[->]{beta}-catenin[->]vaspb relay coupling redox biology to Wnt-dependent glial reprogramming. Notably, HO-1 is similarly induced in stressed mammalian retina, yet Wnt/{beta}-catenin activation fails to sustain regeneration, positioning the Hmox1/CO axis as a candidate target for future investigation in mammalian retina regeneration.

papers.title: cGAS integrates Toll-like receptor signaling in platelets to promote thromboinflammation
papers.abstract: Thromboinflammation is driven by innate immune signaling and promotes tissue injury during sepsis. Activation of platelets by bacterial products and alarmins amplifies inflammation, coagulation, and thrombotic dysfunction. However, the mechanisms by which these diverse inflammatory signals converge to elicit common platelet responses remain largely undefined. Mitochondria are key integrators of cellular stress responses and can activate innate immune pathways through the release of mitochondrial DNA and engagement of the DNA sensor cGAS. We therefore hypothesized that stimulation of innate immune receptors generates endogenous cGAS ligands within platelets, providing a unifying mechanism by which distinct inflammatory cues converge on cGAS-STING signaling. Here, we demonstrate that activation of TLR4, TLR1/2, and TLR5 engages a platelet-intrinsic mtDNA-cGAS-STING axis that promotes platelet activation. In a model of endotoxemia, genetic deletion of cGAS reduced platelet activation, thrombocytopenia, pyroptosis and the early systemic inflammatory response. Platelet transfer experiments further established that platelet-intrinsic cGAS is sufficient to amplify inflammatory responses in vivo. Mechanistically, we demonstrated that cytosolic accumulation of mtDNA and activation of cGAS-STING signaling pathway in platelets are dependent on mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU) and correlated with the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential and the production of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species. In contrast, canonical platelet agonists activated platelets independently of cGAS and failed to induce substantial cytosolic mtDNA accumulation. Importantly, this signaling architecture was conserved in human platelets, where TLR1/2-mediated activation required MCU- and STING-dependent signaling, whereas responses to thrombin receptor-activating peptide and collagen-related peptide remained largely unaffected. Together, these findings identify cGAS as an intracellular signal integration node that allows diverse innate immune receptors to converge on a common platelet activation pathway through sensing of mitochondria-derived DNA, allowing a rapid platelet response to microbial products.

papers.title: A domain-general basal ganglia mechanism for inhibitory control during language comprehension
papers.abstract: Whether controlled language processing involves domain-general or language-specific neural circuits is subject of controversial debate. We tested whether the inhibitory control of linguistic activity shares a common neural process with motor inhibition in twenty humans undergoing intra- and extracranial neural field potential recordings and deep-brain stimulation. Engaging motor and linguistic inhibition simultaneously resulted in a significant behavioral cost, suggesting a shared underlying neural process. Indeed, neural decoders trained during motor inhibition were able to decode linguistic inhibition and vice versa. Depth-electrode recordings from the subthalamic nucleus (STN), a key basal ganglia area for inhibitory control, showed increased {beta}-band (13-30 Hz) activity during both linguistic and motor inhibition. Finally, disrupting the STN via deep-brain stimulation impaired behavioral and neural signatures of both linguistic and motor inhibition. Together, these findings show that the inhibitory control of language and movement share a domain-general mechanism implemented via the subthalamic nucleus of the basal ganglia.

papers.title: Exclusion from DNA double-strand breaks is a pervasive feature of the hnRNP family
papers.abstract: Heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (hnRNPs) are abundant RNA-binding proteins that have been linked individually to the DNA double-strand break (DSB) response, but their behaviour at damaged chromatin has only been examined one protein at a time and under disparate conditions. Here, we compare the core hnRNP family side by side by laser microirradiation and live-cell imaging. We find that 13 of 14 members are excluded from damaged chromatin, 10 directly and 3 after a transient phase of recruitment, establishing exclusion rather than accumulation as the predominant behaviour of this family. We characterised this behaviour in detail for hnRNPH1, which has not previously been linked directly to the DSB response. Its exclusion is sustained for several hours and also occurs at nuclease-induced breaks at a defined genomic locus. Importantly, exclusion is independent of the signalling pathways that drive protein recruitment to breaks and of transcriptional elongation, and instead requires the GYR low-complexity domain, with RNA binding contributing redundantly through three quasi-RNA recognition motifs. Finally, tethering hnRNPH1 to breaks through the RNF8 FHA domain selectively impairs 53BP1 accumulation without affecting {gamma}-H2AX, MDC1 or RPA, and hnRNPH1 is excluded from 53BP1 nuclear bodies in unchallenged cells. Together, these findings establish protein exclusion as an active component of the DSB response and show that the presence of an hnRNP at damaged chromatin can determine which repair factors assemble at DNA break sites.

papers.title: A Preventive Effect of Exercise in a Mouse Model of Essential Tremor
papers.abstract: The effects of exercise have not been widely studied for potential benefits in essential tremor (ET), while this has been growing for other neurodegenerative disorders. This study examines the effects of two types of exercise [high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and resistance training (RT)] on mice that were subjected to harmaline injections to trigger tremor. We employed a repeated-measures design with three groups: a HIIT group, a RT group, and a sedentary (SED) control group. Each group received an injection before and after the intervention. Tremor kinetics (power within the 8-14 and 14-29 Hz bands) were assessed using accelerometry. Tremor kinematics were also assessed using high-speed video analysis, for validation. As potential signalling molecules from exercise, we also tested for blood lactate and BDNF in each group. Compared to pre-intervention measurements, we found a significant decrease in power within the 8-14 Hz band combined with an increase in the 14-29 Hz band, for the HIIT group, but not in the RT or SED groups. We also found a change in BDNF concentration for the HIIT group. These results suggest that the HIIT protocol may have helped the animal to shift tremor frequency to higher bands, thereby offering functional resistance to harmaline-induced tremor. This study supports high intensity aerobic physical exercise as a potential therapeutic/preventive intervention for ET, with translational implications for human studies.

papers.title: Description of Alternaria kierstenii sp. nov. from invasive garlic mustard highlights agricultural biosecurity risks of foreign weeds as pathogen reservoirs
papers.abstract: Invasive weeds can increase agricultural biosecurity risks by serving as reservoirs for emerging or undercharacterized plant pathogens. Garlic mustard (Alliaria petiolata), an invasive brassicaceous weed in North America, occurs near agricultural landscapes and is susceptible to multiple crop pathogens. A previously undescribed Alternaria species was isolated from a diseased garlic mustard population in Maryland, USA, prompting investigation of its taxonomy, origins, and host range. De novo genome sequencing produced a near-chromosome scale assembly of 35.8 Mb comprising 17 contigs. Comparative genomic analyses with other crucifer-infecting Alternaria species revealed expanded repertoires of predicted CAZymes and peptidases, as well as unique effectors and biosynthetic gene clusters. Phylogenetic and comparative analyses supported recognition of this fungus as Alternaria kierstenii sp. nov., representing a distinct lineage within section Sonchi. Host range assays demonstrated that A. kierstenii was highly aggressive on diverse hosts in the Brassicaceae, including vegetable, ornamental, cover crop, and invasive species. The disease caused by this new pathogen manifested as foliar and stem lesions, chlorosis, necrosis, leaf death, and, in several hosts, rapid plant mortality. Amplicon sequence data from a nationwide garlic mustard microbiome study detected closely related taxa only in the plants from the eastern states of Maryland, Pennsylvania, and New York, suggesting a geographically restricted population consistent with expectations for a potentially emerging pathogen. The description of this phylogenetically unique, broad host range pathogen demonstrates the potential for widespread invasive weeds to harbor pathogens and pathogen genomic diversity with agricultural relevance, underscoring the hidden biosecurity risk of understudied invasive weeds.

papers.title: Synthetic MPRA perturbation supervision improves variant-effect prediction in sequence-to-function models
papers.abstract: Deep learning sequence-to-function (S2F) models learn to predict functional readouts, such as gene expression, from genetic sequence. However, these models are trained predominantly on the reference genome and struggle to accurately predict the effect of genetic variation on gene expression. Massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs) explore the direct impact of genetic variation on gene expression, but saturation-mutagenesis MPRAs that measure variant effects directly remain limited, thereby restricting their use for fine-tuning S2F models. In this work, we investigate fine-tuning Borzoi, a state-of-the-art S2F model, on model-generated synthetic MPRA variant-effect data as a scalable alternative to overcome limits on the availability of supervised training data for genetic variation. First, we trained an ensemble of 16 models on 110,359 K562 MPRA measurements. Then, we distilled their predictions into a single student model using MPRA elements associated with 1,000 genes. The distilled model was subsequently used to generate synthetic variant-effect labels across increasing numbers of genes (50 to 1,000), with 600 variants per gene, to fine-tune Borzoi. Performance improved as we included more genes in training. In data-limited settings, training on more genes with fewer variants per gene performed better than training on fewer genes with more variants per gene, given the same number of total variants. Compared to pre-trained Borzoi, Borzoi fine-tuned on 600,000 synthetic samples across 1,000 genes increased Pearson correlation from 0.28 to 0.54 on CAGI5 promoter variants and from 0.39 to 0.46 on 903 GTEx fine-mapped whole-blood expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs). Importantly, these improvements were achieved while preserving the pre-trained performance across all 7,611 output tracks. Furthermore, fine-tuned Borzoi recovered regulatory motifs identified by the MPRA model in genes unseen during training, suggesting that learned regulatory features can generalize across loci. Together, these results provide a proof of concept that model-generated synthetic supervision can improve variant effect prediction in S2F models while preserving their original pre-trained capabilities, offering a scalable strategy toward capturing the impact of genetic variation on gene regulation.

papers.title: Mapping AMPA and NMDA receptors at mouse brain hippocampal synapses by cryo-ET
papers.abstract: AMPA and NMDA receptors are fundamental to synaptic transmission through the detection of released neurotransmitter. These ion channels open in response to glutamate binding, resulting in depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane and influx of calcium. Receptor localization plays a key role in synaptic strength, and changes in receptor number and location underpin synaptic plasticity, learning and memory. Here we apply receptor subunit-specific antibody fragments and multiplexed gold nanoparticle conjugates, together with cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), to elucidate the in-situ molecular organization of AMPA and NMDA receptors at hippocampal synapses in adult mouse brain tissue. AMPA receptors are predominantly found in densely packed liquid-like clusters, with interspersed NMDA receptors and adjacent NMDA receptor clusters. By direct localization of individual receptors, we provide molecular-resolution insight into the distribution of AMPA and NMDA receptors across the synapse, at peri and extrasynaptic sites, and within endocytosed vesicles. Visualization of multiple presynaptic vesicle fusion events suggests that receptors are near, but not always directly adjacent to, transmitter release sites. By mapping AMPA and NMDA receptors, and glutamate release sites, we provide receptor-resolution insight into the structure and function of brain hippocampal synapses.

papers.title: Helicase family proteins promote antiviral ADP-ribosylation of DNA purines
papers.abstract: DarTG defense systems studied to date contain a DarT1 or DarT2 toxin that blocks phage replication by ADP-ribosylating DNA and a NADAR or macrodomain antitoxin, DarG, that reverses this modification at homeostasis. Here, we identify additional DarTG subfamilies, one of which comprises a DarT3 toxin, an ADP-ribosylhydrolase (ARH)-domain antitoxin, and a helicase family protein, DarH. The Escherichia coli DarHTG3 system confers broad phage defense, requires DarH and, unlike previously characterized DarTG systems, modifies adenine. Characterization of additional DarH-containing DarTG systems reveals that a subset also target guanine. Our data support a model in which ADP-bound DarH functions as a processivity factor by recruiting DarT to its single-stranded DNA substrate and allowing for ADP-ribosylation of multiple target sites. These findings reveal how a helicase family protein regulates an antiviral effector by promoting DNA engagement rather than unwinding and thereby expanding the functional repertoire of helicase family proteins in bacterial immunity.

papers.title: Knockdown of fibrillarin reveals cell- and virus- dependent restriction of henipavirus replication and enhanced antiviral immune signalling
papers.abstract: The henipavirus genus includes several highly pathogenic zoonotic viruses that lack medical countermeasures. The 2-O-methyltransferase fibrillarin (FBL) has been identified by genome-wide functional genomics studies as a henipavirus pro-viral factor. While FBL is a potential target for host-directed antiviral therapeutics, its impact on henipavirus replication in cell types relevant to henipavirus disease has not been explored. Here we demonstrate that depleting cellular FBL using short interfering RNAs (siRNAs) has varying impacts on henipavirus replication, depending on cell type and virus. FBL depletion in small airway epithelial cells (HSAEC1-KT) significantly impaired viral gene transcription for Hendra virus (HeV) genotypes 1 and 2 (HeV-g1, HeV-g2), and Nipah virus (NiV) Bangladesh strain (NiV-B), but not NiV Malaysia (NiV-M) strain or Cedar virus (CedV). Conversely, reduced FBL expression in bronchial epithelial (NuLi-1) cells, aortic endothelial (Telo HAEC) cells or neuroblastoma (BE(2)-M17) cells did not inhibit HeV-g1 replication. Transcriptomic analyses revealed that impaired virus replication in FBL knockdown cells was associated with enhanced activation of innate immune pathways and robust upregulation of interferon stimulated genes (ISGs). Together, these findings demonstrate a virus- and cell-type dependent impact of FBL on henipavirus replication and support a role for FBL in modulation of the antiviral innate immune response.

papers.title: CrJAMs are transcriptional repressors of the monoterpenoid indole alkaloid pathway in Catharanthus roseus
papers.abstract: Catharanthus roseus produces monoterpenoid indole alkaloids (MIAs) in response to the defense hormone jasmonate (JA). In Arabidopsis, JA regulates defense processes through MYC2 and JA-Associated MYC2a-like transcription factors (JAMs). Here we characterize two previously identified C. roseus JAMs, CrJAM2 and CrJAM3, as regulators of MIA biosynthesis. Functional screens using viral-induced gene silencing and transient promoter activity assays showed that CrJAMs repress the MIA pathway; silencing both CrJAM2 and CrJAM3 increased expression of MIA pathway genes and MIA levels while their individual overexpression repressed promoter activity. To assess their activity broadly across MIA regulatory and biosynthetic genes, we generated C. roseus hairy root cultures either constitutively overexpressing individual CrJAMs or CRISPR-Cas9 creating mutations in multiple CrJAMs, and profiled their expression by RNA-Seq. CrJAM2 overexpression decreased expression of most MIA biosynthetic genes relative to the GUS control, while double mutant lines showed increased basal expression of these genes relative to non-targeting controls. Notably, methyl JA treatment perturbs this equilibrium, reversing these trends at 24 hrs in both CrJAM overexpression and mutant lines relative to basal conditions. In summary, CrJAMs broadly repress MIA regulatory and biosynthetic gene expression and together with CrJAZ and CrMYC2a regulates MIA biosynthesis.

papers.title: A Systems Theory of Cardiac-Autonomic Trajectories and Equilibria
papers.abstract: Heart rate variability (HRV) is conventionally summarized with static indices computed over fixed windows, which cannot show how cardiac autonomic regulation persists, transitions, responds to perturbation, and recovers. We develop the Systems Theory of Cardiac-Autonomic Trajectories and Equilibria (STATE), in which autonomic regulation is a low-dimensional latent stochastic dynamical system observed only through RR intervals, and we derive what the theory can and cannot claim. First, we prove that for isotropic linear dynamics the sympathetic and parasympathetic coordinates are not separately identifiable from a scalar RR signal, whereas distinct time scales or coupling restore observability. Second, we derive exact properties of a minimal bistable system (stationary law, mean escape time, critical forcing), and a Monte Carlo simulation agreed with the exact escape time within 6%. Third, in 2000 simulated replicates of a monostable and a bistable system that share the same linearization at rest, baseline variability (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, AUC, 0.56) and peak displacement at the pulse used (AUC 0.42) did not discriminate the systems, yet sustained return after an identical pulse differed: 100% versus 7%. We define resilience as a multidimensional response profile, show that recovery descriptors depend on analyst-chosen tolerances that must be fixed a priori, and state four falsifiable hypotheses with the result that would refute each. The work is theoretical and computational; no empirical recordings were used.

papers.title: TRPV4 antagonist efficacy in a post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus pig model
papers.abstract: Hydrocephalus occurs across the age spectrum but is particularly prevalent in young and old individuals. One form of this disease is post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus (PHH), which is a life-threatening sequela of intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH). There are no effective non-surgical interventions for the treatment of PHH or other forms of hydrocephalus. Progress has been limited by the lack of gyrencephalic animal models that exhibit high fidelity to human conditions. Here, we establish a pathophysiologically relevant novel swine model of IVH that recapitulates key features of severe PHH, including sustained ventriculomegaly, elevated intracranial pressure (ICP), neuroinflammation and white matter injury. Using this model, we test the therapeutic potential of pharmacologic inhibition of the transient receptor potential vanilloid 4 (TRPV4) non-specific cationic channel. The orally bioavailable TRPV4 antagonist GSK2789917 penetrates the blood-brain barrier, and prevents progression to PHH when administered 2 days after IVH. Specifically, GSK2789917 prevents the development of ventriculomegaly, suppresses early ICP elevations and prevents or reverses inflammasome activation. These findings establish a clinically relevant large-animal model of PHH and identify TRPV4 antagonism as a promising treatment for hydrocephalus.

papers.title: GMP-Cor: Quantifying Transcriptional Dysregulation in Antibiotic Tolerance and Persistence
papers.abstract: When cells are exposed to stress, they typically activate stress-response pathways and enter a regulated growth-arrest. But what if the stress overwhelms these pathways? In such cases, cells may enter a disrupted growth-arrest - a poorly adapted, abrupt cessation of growth, characterized by a broad distribution of lag times upon stress removal. This distribution underlies antibiotic persistence during stress recovery. Therefore, gaining a deeper understanding of the disrupted growth-arrest is important for developing more effective antibiotic therapies. In this study, we perform single cell RNA-seq on bacteria in disrupted conditions. We develop GMP-Cor: a metric to quantify dysregulation and analyze gene-gene correlation patterns in sparse single-cell data. We find that gene-gene correlations are significantly reduced in disrupted cells compared to regulated cells, providing direct evidence that this tolerance-enhanced state, along with its increased membrane sensitivity, is associated with global-dysregulation. We demonstrate that GMP-Cor can extend to other biological systems, such as persistent cancer cells, where it separates proliferating from drug-arrested cells.

papers.title: Long-term dysregulation of histone acetylation, BDNF expression, and the hippocampal transcriptome in adult rats exhibiting a depressive-like phenotype following repeated chlorpyrifos exposure
papers.abstract: Epidemiological evidence indicates that occupational exposures to the organophosphate pesticide chlorpyrifos (CPF) in adults are associated with an increased risk for depression. In this study, we use a rat model of occupational-like CPF exposure associated with a chronic depressive phenotype to investigate underlying molecular mechanisms. Adult rats received CPF (5 mg/kg/day) for 21 days. When assessed three months later, blood and brain cholinesterase activity had returned to control levels despite the presence of depressive signs. Hippocampal tissue was collected at this endpoint for molecular analyses. Western blotting analysis showed significant upregulation of histone deacetylase protein levels of HDAC3 and HDAC5, whereas HDAC1 and HDAC2 were unchanged. HDAC5 regulates histone acetylation at the brain-derived neurotrophic factor (Bdnf) gene. We used chromatin immunoprecipitation to assay histone 3 lysine 9 acetylation (H3K9ac) occupancy at the Bdnf promoter IV. H3K9ac levels at the Bdnf promoter IV were significantly reduced in CPF rats, accompanied by a concomitant reduction in BDNF protein expression. Exploratory RNA-sequencing identified 100 significantly differentially expressed genes in CPF-exposed rats at a false discovery rate < 5%, including significant downregulation in genes such as insulin-like growth factor 2 (Igf2), fibroblast growth factor 14 (Fgf14), and slit guidance ligand 2 (Slit2) involved in neuronal growth, synaptic function, and axon guidance. Gene Ontology analysis revealed enrichment in pathways related to neurogenesis, neuronal projections, and myelination. Overall, this study indicates persistent epigenetic and transcriptional dysregulation associated with reduced hippocampal BDNF and alterations in neuronal plasticity-related pathways linked to a long-term depressive-like phenotype following CPF exposure.

papers.title: Molecular machines measure the nanomechanics of biological membranes
