papers.abstract: Mechanical properties such as elastic resistance to distortion define many materials and can routinely be measured with an indenting tip as simple as a finger. We have miniaturized the indentation principle by 8 orders of magnitude to analyze lipid bilayer nanomechanics, which are of relevance in biology and disease progression. Our nanoscale indenting tip is designed with DNA nanotechnology to be an integral part of a molecular machine which autonomously binds to membranes, actively indents localized membrane patches, measures the membranes elastic response to indentation, and converts the indentation degree into an optical readout signal. Compared to serially operated macro-to-microscale indentation probes, our miniaturization strategy enables deploying millions of the indenting machines for parallel analysis of membrane elasticity. The nanoscale molecular machines are also taken up by biological cells to reveal softer inner membrane compartments compared to stiffer cytoplasmic membranes, using indentation depths of solely up to 1 nm. We envision the DNA-based nanotools to contribute to the analysis of membrane mechanics of cells as well as soft polymeric interphases.

papers.title: Open filament tracks drive Bacteroidota gliding motility
papers.abstract: Bacteria of the phylum Bacteroidota glide across surfaces using adhesins that attach to the substratum and are propelled along the cell body by an underlying track. The track is currently thought to form a single closed loop around the cell. Here we use 3D super-resolution tracking of single adhesin molecules in Flavobacterium johnsoniae to characterize adhesin movements in unprecedented detail. Our data overturn multiple aspects of the single closed loop model by showing that adhesins follow non-repeating trajectories that cross, make sharp turns, and exhibit reversals and circular paths. We develop a new model for Bacteroidota gliding in which the track network comprises multiple independently moving, open filaments. This supramolecular organization resembles that of other moving bacterial filaments such as MreB and FtsZ, suggesting that open filaments are a common organising principle in the bacterial cytoskeleton.

papers.title: Reconstitution of lipid nanoparticle-mediated siRNA transfer across endosomal membrane mimics
papers.abstract: Endosomal escape limits RNA delivery by lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). If escape requires membrane rupture, productive delivery would be intrinsically coupled to membrane damage and its potential toxicity. Here, we establish a cell-free system based on giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs) with an early endosome-like lipid composition to dissect the mechanism of siRNA transfer and determine whether it can occur while membrane barrier function is preserved. Acidification promoted LNP-membrane association, lipid redistribution and siRNA translocation into the receiving lumen without detectable dissipation of transmembrane pH gradient. Complementary cryo-electron tomography revealed local interfacial lipid reorganisation without detectable membrane rupture. Fluorescence correlation spectroscopy revealed heterogeneous diffusion of translocated siRNA, consistent with free and lipid-associated species. Pre-formed RNA-lipid complexes exhibited pH-dependent dissociation and heterogeneous diffusion, supporting lipid association as a possible origin of slower luminal diffusion. Serum or apolipoprotein-E preincubation reduced siRNA translocation into the GUV lumen. Together, these findings support a model where siRNA-lipid association facilitates membrane crossing without sustained loss of barrier function. This platform provides a means to dissect LNP-mediated RNA delivery and develop formulations with improved efficacy while limiting membrane damage.

papers.title: Pain Matters: Nociceptive signaling drives neural encoding of inflammatory responses
papers.abstract: Pain is a cardinal sign of inflammation, constructed by the brain from peripheral nociceptive input. Yet, its role in the brain's response to inflammation remains unknown. Here, we demonstrate that nociceptive signaling is essential for the brain to represent and replay inflammatory states. Analysis of human fMRI and mouse activity mapping revealed that peripheral inflammation generates a distinct brain state. In mice, ablation of TRPV1+ sensory neurons or pharmacological analgesia disrupted this organization and prevented the insular cortex from forming retrievable immune representations. Conversely, augmenting nociceptive signaling during inflammation strengthened subsequent immune recall. These findings identify nociceptive input as a critical signal in brain-immune dialogue, enabling the encoding and retrieval of inflammatory events.

papers.title: HOT1 functions as a homodimer to promote ALT-permissive chromatin
papers.abstract: Telomere homeostasis is a tightly regulated and dynamic process sustained by a network of proteins that organize telomeric chromatin and safeguard chromosome stability. In ALT-positive cells, telomere maintenance relies on recombination-based mechanisms and is modulated by local chromatin states and epigenetic regulation. Here, we show that the telomeric binding protein HOT1 (HMBOX1) requires dimerization - depending both on interaction with the dimerization-mediators DYNLL1/2 and its intrinsic HNFp1 domain - for its stable association with telomeres in vivo. Loss of HOT1 leads to an epigenetic switch from H3K9acK14ac to H3K9me3 at telomeres accompanied by attenuated ALT activity as illustrated by reduced ALT recombination by-products (C-circles) and a decrease in telomere dysfunction-induced foci (TIFs). We further show via binding assays and cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) analyses that HOT1 directly interacts with telomeric nucleosomes, providing a molecular basis for its involvement in telomeric chromatin organization. Collectively, these findings suggest that HOT1 functions as a homodimer to promote a telomeric chromatin state that is highly permissive for ALT recombination.

papers.title: Establishing de novo microbial biosynthesis of anisole
papers.abstract: Anisole is a valuable aromatic ether and promising green solvent whose industrial manufacture relies exclusively on petroleum-derived phenol and hazardous alkali-mediated methylation. Here, we establish the first de novo microbial biosynthesis of anisole from glucose in Pseudomonas putida KT2440 by integrating retrosynthetic pathway design with growth-coupled directed evolution. Using a selection platform in an engineered double auxotroph, in which growth depends on S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methylation, we evolved a promiscuous plant chavicol O-methyltransferase to yield phenol O-methyltransferase 1 (POMT1; bearing a key D264N substitution), which improved anisole production by 2.3-fold over the wild-type enzyme. To overcome product volatility, we integrated an in situ two-phase extraction system using dodecane that achieved near-quantitative product recovery. Then, we compared two phenol routes from the shikimate pathway, selected the 4-hydroxybenzoate route, and raised precursor supply by deleting competing reactions and introducing feedback-resistant and reduced-flux variants in two shikimate pathway enzymes. The final strain produced up to 0.57 mM anisole (62 mg/L) from glucose.

papers.title: PERTURBATION OF THE AMINO ACID STRESS RESPONSE PATHWAY EXPOSES A METABOLIC VULNERABILITY IN MULTIPLE AGGRESSIVE CANCER SUBTYPES
papers.abstract: Cancer cells frequently experience nutrient limitation and depend on adaptive stress-response pathways to maintain metabolic homeostasis. Here, we show that pharmacological perturbation of amino acid stress signaling exerts broad anti-tumor activity across multiple aggressive malignancies, including acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia, triple-negative breast cancer, ovarian cancer, and neuroblastoma. Sensitivity to pathway modulation is associated with a chronic stress-adapted metabolic state marked by constitutive amino acid response signaling, elevated NFE2L2 expression, and reduced mitochondrial abundance despite evidence of efficient oxidative metabolism. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that the ATP-competitive compound GCN2-IN-6 does not phenocopy genetic GCN2 suppression and exhibits context-dependent effects on the amino acid stress response. Nevertheless, tumors experiencing chronic metabolic stress remain exquisitely sensitive to disruption of this adaptive network, regardless of whether signaling is perturbed through canonical inhibition or paradoxical activation. Collectively, our findings identify chronic metabolic stress adaptation as an actionable vulnerability and establish off-balancing amino acid stress signaling as a therapeutic strategy across multiple cancer types

papers.title: When perfect is a warning: explanations expose shortcuts that accuracy hides in cancer gene-expression classifiers
papers.abstract: When the classes in a training set come from different data sources, a classifier can score near-perfectly while learning where a sample came from. We show this for cancer classifiers trained on tumours from The Cancer Genome Atlas and normal tissue from the Genotype Tissue Expression project. Six model families, including a tabular foundation model, reached an area under the curve of 1.000 yet called 80 to 97% of tumour adjacent normal tissue cancer, and 100% in an independent cohort; a few matched normal samples per tissue removed most of this shortcut. Near-perfect accuracy could not tell a shortcut from an honestly easy task, flagging 87 to 92% of models trained on such tasks. We introduce a label free score, computed from model explanations, that uses the fact that a source difference looks the same in every tissue whereas cancer changes do not. It raised no false alarms, ranked models by their real reliance on the source, transferred to unseen model types and data, and failed where its theory predicts.

papers.title: Apelin signaling controls neuroendocrine homeostasis via Atoh8-dependent transcriptional regulation
papers.abstract: Apelin is a pleiotropic peptide hormone with established roles in cardiovascular function, angiogenesis, and metabolism, but its contribution to neuroendocrine development and function remains poorly understood. Here, using genetic loss-of-function and inducible gain-of-function approaches in zebrafish, we show that Apelin signaling is dosage-sensitive and required for normal development, reproductive capacity, and physiological homeostasis. Both apelin deficiency and apelin overexpression disrupted embryonic development and reduced adult lifespan, while exhibiting markedly reduced fertility in both sexes. Transcriptomic profiling revealed broad changes in neuroendocrine, hormonal, stress-response, and inflammatory genes with young adult mutant expression profiles resembling those of aged wild-type fish. Both loss and excess of Apelin also disrupted hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid (HPT) axis development, reducing hypothalamic thyrotropin-releasing hormone-expressing cells, pituitary gonadotropic cell populations, and thyroid gland volume. Transcriptomic analyses identified atoh8, encoding a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor, as a candidate effector of Apelin signaling. Apelin expression increased atoh8 expression during early embryogenesis, whereas atoh8 mRNA partially rescued developmental defects in apelin mutants, including hypothalamic and pituitary markers, and thyroid volume. Conversely, atoh8 crispants displayed thyroid and pituitary abnormalities, supporting a role for Atoh8 in neuroendocrine development. Together, these findings establish Apelin signaling as a dosage-sensitive regulator of zebrafish development and tissue homeostasis and identify Atoh8 as a functional downstream effector that partially mediates Apelin-dependent HPT axis formation. This work links peptide hormone signaling to neuroendocrine development and provides a framework for investigating its broader contributions to vertebrate physiology, reproduction and aging.

papers.title: Cargo levels control endosomal PI(3)P homeostasis through direct feedback between SNX17 and MTM1
papers.abstract: The sorting of internalised cell surface proteins through the endosomal network is crucial for cellular function. Phosphatidylinositol-3-phosphate (PI(3)P) is a critical lipid identity cue for organising endosomal sorting but there is limited understanding of how PI(3)P homeostasis is regulated. Here, we show that free PI(3)P is segregated into distinct endosomal subdomains and that depletion of the disease-relevant lipid phosphatase Myotubularin1 (MTM1) leads to its accumulation and mis-segregation, impairing cargo recycling. Complementary imaging and reconstitution approaches show that MTM1 recruitment and activity are controlled by binding to the endosomal cargo adaptor SNX17. This interaction is mediated by sorting motifs in the C-Terminal tail of MTM1 and is in competition with the same sorting motifs in cargo that bind to SNX17. This competitive binding mechanistically links cargo sorting to PI(3)P depletion and because SNX17 is itself a PI(3)P effector, establishes negative feedback regulating local PI(3)P levels. Importantly, we demonstrate that this feedback couples endosomal cargo levels to PI(3)P depletion. We propose that cargo levels thereby modulate endosomal phosphoinositide identity through cargo sensitive feedback between SNX17 and MTM1.

papers.title: GENOME ASSEMBLIES FOR 28 PHAEOSPHAERIACEAE ISOLATES FROM CANADA
papers.abstract: Glume blotch and Septoria Tritici Blotch (STB) are destructive crop diseases caused by fungal pathogens formerly classified under the genus Septoria. Recent taxonomical revisions have led to the reclassification and renaming of these fungi, some of which are now under the genus Parastagonospora, family Phaeosphaeriaceae, order Pleosporales, and class Dothideomycetes. In this study, we performed whole genome sequencing and assembly for 28 Phaeosphaeriaceae isolates from Canada. Sequencing was performed using a combination of Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read and Illumina short-read sequencing platforms. Most of the genomes were very complete, BUSCO >99%, with the genomes assemblies derived from ONT sequencing having very few contigs that likely encompass entire chromosomes or chromosome arms. To determine the relationship between these isolates and similar fungi that have been previously characterized, we performed whole genome alignments to 2,668 other Dothidiomycete genomes obtained from NCBI using NUCmer. Comparative genomic analysis revealed that 27 of the isolates clustered discretely with either Parastagonospora nodorum, or Parastagonospora pseudonodorum (Parastagonospora avenae f. sp. tritici), with one genome having no other similar genome in NCBI which we hypothesize to be the first genome assembly of Phaeosphaeria pontiformis. Both P. nodorum and P. pseudonodorum species were isolated from wheat and barley and only the latter was isolated from durum, while the P. pontiformis was isolated from wheat. In summary, we sequenced and assembled the genomes of 28 isolates of Phaeosphaeriaceae spp. from Canada and the genomes add to our foundational knowledge of these plant pathogens and efforts to better understand their diversity.

papers.title: Sensory neurons gate a cortical plasticity window for immune encoding
papers.abstract: Activity-dependent plasticity allows brain circuits to encode experience, but this has been established with brief stimuli. Immune responses develop over days and are represented in the insular cortex (IC). How the cortex encodes experiences with this temporal structure is unknown. Here we show that Trpv1+ sensory neurons open a multi-day cortical plasticity window matched to the immune response. Following peripheral immune challenges, Parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory interneurons are activated first, restricting plasticity. Vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing interneurons respond two days later, disinhibiting IC excitatory neurons. Weaker challenges trigger the first phase but not the second, and preventing the transition blocks immune encoding, whereas lowering inhibition beforehand does not. These results identify a body-to-brain mechanism that gates cortical plasticity on the timescale of slowly evolving physiological experience.

papers.title: Mucosal ACP subunit vaccine formulated with a small molecule STING agonist drives protective TH1/TH17 responses and serum bactericidal antibodies against Neisseria gonorrhoeae
papers.abstract: STING agonists are emerging vaccine adjuvants; however, only cyclic dinucleotides (low permeability and stability) have been tested against pathogenic bacteria. We examined diABZI, a non-nucleotide STING agonist active in human and murine orthologs, combined with the Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Ng) Adhesin Complex Protein, a conserved adhesin and human lysozyme C inhibitor, as a gonococcal vaccine. Intranasal administration of recombinant ACP (rACP)+diABZI accelerated gonococcal clearance, in contrast to rACP or rACP+CpG+MPLA, despite comparable antibody responses. While both diABZI and CpG+MPLA induced TH1, diABZI also induced TH17 polarization. Peptide mapping localized the immunodominant T cell epitopes to the ACP-lysozyme C interface. rACP+diABZI elicited higher human serum bactericidal activity (hSBA), that correlated with Ng clearance, and antibodies that reversed human lysozyme C inhibition and interfered with Ng adhesion and invasion in 3D human vaginal/urethral mucosal models. Passive serum transfer did not recapitulate protection, implicating mucosal antibodies and cellular immunity over circulating IgG.

papers.title: Species identity rather than colony size partitions shape variation in six Caribbean octocorals
papers.abstract: Caribbean reefs are increasingly dominated by arborescent octocorals as scleractinian cover declines. The physical structure of these octocoral forests is established by the manner in which octocoral species generate and modify colony form as they grow. We tested whether colony shape exhibited species-specific architecture and whether it changed allometrically with size. Two-dimensional projections of colony form were modeled as a series of stacked bands, whose areas were measured from scaled in situ images of colonies of six sympatric Caribbean octocorals from St John, US Virgin Islands. Principal component analysis (PCA) of relative band areas resolved a single dominant axis, accounting for 67.9% of the variation, that separated top-heavy from bottom-heavy colony profiles. Species identity explained 42% of the total variation in relative form, whereas colony height only explained 2% and had no detectable effect on either PCA axis. The proportion of the colony outline occupied by branches increased with height, from a predicted 41% at 20 cm to 52% at 100 cm. Colonies therefore grew without a detectable redistribution of area along their vertical axis, filling a species-specific outline more densely rather than moving along a common allometric trajectory. The vertical geometry of an octocoral canopy may therefore depend more on which species are present than on the sizes its colonies have reached.

papers.title: Continuous Topological Accessibility (RFA) as a 3D-Aware GRN Filter: Anticorrelation with eQTL and No Prediction of ΔRNA
papers.abstract: We formalize Relative Forest Accessibility (RFA), a topological accessibility index computed as the solution of (I - {gamma}P )x = v0, where P is a Markov transition matrix built from Hi-C contacts and v0 is a vector of TF peaks (or ATAC peaks). RFA yields a continuous accessibility profile across all genomic bins. We test RFA on three targets. First, on promoter TF counts (GM12878 chr1, 10 kb, 811 genes), RFA loses to 1D distance (AUC 0.836 vs 0.976); this is an artifact because the target and the 1D distance look at the same window. Second, on eQTL (GTEx v10 LCL, chr1+17+19, 10 kb, 1625 genes), RFA anticorrelates with eQTL: {rho}(RFA, - log10 pmin) = -0.09, AUC(RFA) = 0.386 (below chance), AUC(-RFA) = 0.614. High RFA corresponds to fewer eQTL, and dose-response analysis confirms that AUC(RFA) decreases with eQTL strength (mean trend -0.056, 19/20 TFs). A distance-preserving shuffle of the Hi-C matrix reproduces this anticorrelation ({triangleup}AUC vs real: [-0.074, +0.076] across 5 TFs, all CIs include 0), whereas a degree-preserving rewiring destroys it ({triangleup}AUC [isin] [-0.261, -0.003], CIs exclude 0 for 5/5 TFs); the anticorrelation therefore reflects distance-decay of Hi-C contacts (local 3D accessibility), not higher-order topology. The anticorrelation replicates on chr17 ({triangleup}{rho} = -0.13 for rewired, 0/5 for shuffled) and on chr19 with an inverted control pattern, consistent with local within-diagonal heterogeneity as the carrier on short gene-dense chromosomes. Third, on {triangleup}RNA (MCF10A vs MCF7, 40 kb, ATAC peaks), RFA does not predict {triangleup}RNA ({rho} = +0.005, permutation p = 0.87, bootstrap 95% CI [-0.040, +0.053], n = 1730); the CI includes zero and does not exclude the practical boundary |{rho}| = 0.05. Within-line sanity checks are also null. We conclude that RFA anticorrelates with eQTL via local distance-decay and does not predict {triangleup}RNA. The anticorrelation is carried by distance-decay, not by loops or TADs, and may reflect expression buffering: genes with strong eQTL are less dependent on local 3D accessibility. RFA is not a universal predictor but a filter with an inverted sign on eQTL and no signal on {triangleup}RNA.

papers.title: Molecular insights into the regulation of coenzyme selection in NADP-specific glutamate dehydrogenase from Saccharomyces cerevisiae
papers.abstract: Coenzyme specificity is one of the crucial aspects of the functional regulations in enzymes. Understanding the molecular basis of coenzyme specificity in glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) is highly essential as this is the only enzyme that fulfils various physiological demands in terms of energy production and/or nitrogen assimilation via its strict functional regulation by connecting carbon and nitrogen metabolic cycles in every living organism. We have studied S. cerevisiae GDH3 (ScGDH3), as a model system for NADP-specific fungal GDHs. K272R and S250E mutants of ScGDH3 exhibited remarkable alteration in coenzyme specificity, with 15-55-fold and 3-14-fold more preference towards non-specific coenzymes [NAD(H)], respectively. S250E exhibited higher NADH affinity (~ 1.3-fold) than that of towards NADPH. K272R showed ~ 10-fold increased coenzyme affinity (1/KM) and binding affinity (1/kd) towards NADH, compared to the wild type enzyme (ScGDH3-WT). We solved the crystal structure of ScGDH3-K272R complexed with NADP+ at 2.50 [A] resolution with a unique oligomeric arrangement having two distinct subunit conformations (''open'' and ''super-closed'') and it is the first structure of a GDH from S. cerevisiae. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide insights into NADH binding and its increased affinity to ScGDH3-K272R. Further structure-based sequence analyses unravelled that a lysine and an arginine are naturally preferred residues for providing NADP(H) and NAD(H) specificity, respectively for various amino acid dehydrogenases. Taken together biochemical and structural data, our study successfully illustrates the evolutionary conserved mechanism of coenzyme related regulation in fungal and other GDHs; as well as amino acid dehydrogenases.

papers.title: Chromosomally-Encoded Hok/Sok Toxin/Antitoxin SystemsInhibit Phage Infection
papers.abstract: The primary physiological role of toxin/antitoxin (TA) systems is phage defense; they are also used to stabilize mobile genetic elements. In the initial publication in 1996, plasmid-encoded Hok/Sok, a type I TA system (protein toxin, RNA antitoxin that inhibits toxin mRNA), was shown to inhibit T4 phage infection in Escherichia coli by reducing its efficiency of plating and burst size and by increasing the time for mature phage to form (latent period). This publication also identified that the mechanism of Hok/Sok inhibiting T4 was host transcription shutoff, arguably the most-general phage inhibition system since most phages impair host transcription. However, recently, the role of Hok/Sok in phage inhibition has been challenged. Therefore, here we investigated the role of four E. coli chromosomally-expressed, hok+/sok+ loci and the one orphan hok+ locus and found that the Hok proteins inhibit the infection of E. coli by BASEL phage 48, a Vequintavirus with myovirus morphology. Of the five Hok proteins, the greatest phage inhibition was by HokB, and infection by BASEL phages 34 and 39 were also inhibited by HokB. We also find BASEL phage 48 requires the WecB-generated receptor NGR for infection. Therefore, chromosomally-derived orphan Hok proteins, produced at physiological levels, are relevant for phage inhibition.

papers.title: Inflammatory proteostasis reprogramming creates a lysosomal bottleneck for microglial aggregate clearance
papers.abstract: Efficient clearance of extracellular protein aggregates by microglia is essential for maintaining brain homeostasis and limiting the accumulation of pathological proteins during neurodegeneration. However, how inflammatory activation affects the ability of microglia to internalize and degrade these aggregates remains incompletely understood. Here, we show that lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced inflammatory activation impairs the degradation of extracellularly-acquired -synuclein (-Syn) and Tau aggregates while largely preserving their uptake. Mechanistically, Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) activation induces translational reprogramming and increases intracellular proteostatic demand, while inhibition of protein synthesis restores -Syn degradation without preventing inflammatory Nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-{kappa}B) activation. Despite largely preserved canonical autophagic flux, inflammatory stimulation is associated with reduced expression of lysosomal proteins, including cathepsin D, suggesting insufficient lysosomal adaptation to increased intracellular demand. Consistent with this model, pharmacological activation of transcription factor EB (TFEB) restores aggregate degradation, indicating that the impairment can be overcome by enhancing lysosomal function. Supporting its potential relevance to human disease, microglial -Syn deposits in brain tissue from patients with dementia with Lewy bodies show limited spatial association with cathepsin D-positive structures. Together, our findings identify a demand-driven lysosomal bottleneck through which inflammatory activation compromises aggregate degradation without substantially affecting uptake, highlighting lysosomal adaptation as a critical determinant of microglial aggregate clearance during neuroinflammation.

papers.title: Cell-lineage selection interacts with development and life history to shape the rates and identity of heritable mutations
papers.abstract: Mutation rates determine the supply of heritable variation and are central to evolutionary theory, yet they are usually treated as properties of molecular mutational processes. We hypothesised that mutation rates are also shaped by selection among cell lineages within organisms and that the strength of this process depends on developmental and life-history traits. To test the extent of this idea, we combined mathematical modelling with experiments in Drosophila melanogaster and treated mutation rates as emergent properties of interactions among molecular mutagenesis, development, life history, and cell-lineage selection. The model predicts that even modest effects of mutations on cellular fitness can substantially alter the probability that mutations are transmitted, and that these effects depend strongly on developmental architecture, germline dynamics, and time to reproduction. In Drosophila, we experimentally demonstrate biased transmission of a mutation affecting cellular proliferation and show that this bias changes over the reproductive lifespan of the individual. Extending the model genome-wide reveals that the cellular distribution of fitness effects and its interaction with developmental parameters influence both the estimated mutation rate and the composition of transmitted mutations, producing transmission biases that favour mutations with particular cellular fitness effects. These results suggest that developmental and life-history parameters determine how cellular fitness effects translate into transmission bias; therefore, estimates of heritable mutational input can vary from species to species even under constant molecular mutagenesis. By filtering mutations before they enter populations, developmental and life-history evolution can modify both the rate and the nature of heritable variation and thereby influence evolutionary trajectories.

papers.title: Particle picking and centering in cryo-electron micrographs via a vanishing radial kernel
papers.abstract: A training-free procedure combines particle picking and approximate centering in cryo-electron microscopy through a single convolution of the micrograph with a compact radial kernel, whose weights increase with distance from the origin, saturate in an annulus, and vanish beyond it. Particles are darker than their surroundings and much weaker than the noise; each carves a well in the response, and local minima of the response are candidate centers. Constant background offsets leave these extrema unchanged away from image boundaries, and a local stability bound controls the displacement of a well's minimum under signed perturbations without assuming a symmetric particle. Grid seeds are iteratively updated, nearby endpoints are merged, and two-dimensional classification follows. On the \emph{Plasmodium falciparum} 80S ribosome and $\beta$-galactosidase data sets, reconstructions reach 3.68 and 4.30~\AA{}, compared with 3.77 and 4.36~\AA{} using reference coordinates, with picking at 0.20--0.26~s per micrograph.

papers.title: Shared and divergent features of the immune response to acute and chronic Trypanosoma cruzi infection in mice revealed by cardiac transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Chagas disease is caused by infection with Trypanosoma cruzi and can result in chronic cardiomyopathy. However, the molecular programmes that define infected cardiac tissue, and how they change as the host-parasite relationship moves from acute pathogenic infection to long-term persistence, remain incompletely understood. Here, we used RNA sequencing to characterise host transcriptional responses in cardiac tissue during both acute and chronic infection in a mouse model. Cardiac parasite distribution was defined using bioluminescence imaging and histology, and RNA sequencing was performed on anatomically standardised cardiac tissue samples collected at both stages. Acute infection was associated with a broad interferon-driven immune activation, whereas during chronic infection this network contracted, with preservation of a tightly connected antigen presentation core centred on major histocompatibility complex genes and immunoproteasome components. Genes associated with extracellular matrix remodelling and fibrosis were not broadly activated. These findings indicate that reduced, but sustained immune activation, rather than widespread fibrotic transcriptional remodelling, represents a prominent feature of cardiac tissue in chronically infected mice. They identify a transition from an overtly inflammatory, pathogen-driven acute response to a more restricted chronic host-parasite equilibrium in which immune surveillance remains transcriptionally active despite very low and spatially intermittent cardiac infection. We identified a conserved 20-gene signature shared between acute and chronic stages. This overlap is consistent with continued or episodic parasite-derived stimulation and/or intrinsic host mechanisms that maintain cardiac immune surveillance. Thus, chronic T. cruzi infection can be viewed as a persistent host-parasite association in which biological coexistence does not imply benignity: immune containment and parasite persistence can occur alongside cumulative cardiac injury.

papers.title: Bispecific VSV-G Engagers: A Platform for Cell-Type-Specific Delivery of Viral Vectors
papers.abstract: VSV-G-pseudotyped lentiviral vectors (LVVs) enable highly efficient ex vivo gene delivery through the broadly expressed LDL receptor (LDLR) but lack the cell-type specificity required for in vivo applications. To provide cell-type specificity, we developed reversible engagers consisting of a cell-specific ligand or antibody fused to the ~40-amino-acid VSV-G-binding domains of LDLR. Following endocytosis, the engager dissociates, releasing unmodified VSV-G for efficient delivery of the vector cargo. An engager comprising the CEACAM8 N-terminal domain enables selective transduction of CEACAM6-positive epithelial cells. A trimeric CEACAM8-based engager matching the VSV-G homotrimeric spike blocked non-specific VSV infection through LDLR with an IC50 of 16.7 pM, while enabling effective VSV-mediated lysis of CEACAM6-positive tumor cells. An anti-CD3-based trimeric engager selectively transduced non-preactivated T cells in human PBMCs with high transduction efficiency. Engager-mediated in vivo CAR T cell generation resulted in sustained control of human OPM2 multiple myeloma tumors in NSG mice. This platform may further advance in vivo gene therapy, including in vivo CAR T-cell therapy and tumor-directed oncolytic virotherapy.

papers.title: Peripheral Axons Form Endoplasmic Reticulum-Rich Conduits With Breast Cancer Cells
papers.abstract: Peripheral nerves are active components of the tumor microenvironment, but the physical routes by which sensory axons communicate with cancer cells remain incompletely defined. Here, we show that primary dorsal root ganglion neurons form thin membrane conduits with EMT6 breast cancer cells that contain endoplasmic reticulum (ER). ER-Tracker labeling and neuron-restricted expression of the ER proteins CNPY2 and ATL3 identified ER-rich axonal extensions terminating on cancer cells. Serial-section scanning transmission electron microscopy resolved ER-like membranes within these conduits and at axon-cancer cell interfaces. Scanning electron microscopy and live holotomographic imaging further revealed dynamic contact formation and associated remodeling of the cancer cell surface. These observations define an ER-containing structural interface between sensory axons and cancer cells and provide a framework for testing whether neuronal ER contributes to direct intercellular signaling or material transfer.

papers.title: Proteomic signatures of cold adaptation and sponge host adaptation in marine Archaea
papers.abstract: Temperature shapes the biochemistry of microbial proteins, and several amino acid compositional indices have been proposed to detect cold adaptation in microbial proteomes. Whether these indices capture cold adaptation in Archaea, which are abundant in cold marine environments such as the Arctic Ocean, has not been tested. We calculated six amino acid compositional indices (arginine to lysine ratio, acidic residue proportion, aliphatic index, aromaticity, grand average of hydropathicity, and proline residue proportion) across global protein families for 142 Marine Group I (MG-I; Thaumarchaeota) and 146 Euryarchaeota genomes from the Bacterial and Viral Bioinformatics Resource Center (BV-BRC), together with three MG-I metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) recovered from the Western Arctic Ocean. The Arctic MAGs fell within the range of index and phylogenetic distances of the wider MG-I population, and no signature of cold adaptation was detected. Instead, index values differed between the two main MG-I phylogenetic groups and between freshwater and marine genomes, and the Euryarchaeota formed five index-based clusters consistent with phylogeny. A group of 19 MG-I MAGs associated with sea sponges had significantly higher arginine to lysine ratios than other MG-I, differed in the usage of all amino acids except alanine and lysine, and had distinct codon usage and higher GC content; their anomalous placement in the MG-I phylogeny is consistent with long-branch attraction. These results indicate that amino acid compositional indices developed for Bacteria have limited power to detect cold adaptation in Archaea, but reveal strong proteomic signatures associated with host adaptation in sponge-associated Thaumarchaeota.

papers.title: Functional ultrasound imaging in free-moving marmosets reveals that intra-call prosodic features modulate large-scale cortical dynamics
papers.abstract: Vocal turn-taking relies on sequential structure and rhythmic timing, yet how primate brains integrate these features across timescales in naturalistic, free-moving contexts is unclear. We developed functional ultrasound imaging for free-moving marmosets, combining an exogenous marker-based workflow for robust registration from non-standard imaging planes with preprocessing pipeline optimized to reduce locomotion artifacts. We systematically perturbed sequential and rhythmic features of interactive phee calls across hierarchical timescales. Cortical networks showed selective sensitivity to intra-call structure: disrupting phrase sequences increased activity in auditory and para-insular cortices and strengthened inter-subject functional connectivity within this network. Rhythmic manipulations primarily affected core auditory cortex: shortening inter-phrase intervals enhanced responses, whereas lengthening intervals suppressed them. These findings establish a practical framework for free-moving primate neuroimaging and identify intra-call prosodic features as promising targets for mechanistic investigation.

papers.title: Metagenome-assembled genomes reveal water-mass-associated distribution ecotypes of marine Archaea in the Western Arctic Ocean
papers.abstract: Archaea are important contributors to marine biogeochemical cycling, yet their ecology remains poorly characterized in the Arctic Ocean. The three dominant marine archaeal lineages, Marine Groups I, II, and III (MG-I, MG-II, and MG-III), are generally reported to have distinct, clade-consistent vertical distributions that are attributed to light penetration and temperature. Here, we used shotgun metagenomic sequencing of seawater collected during the 2015 U.S. Arctic GEOTRACES expedition (GN01) to recover archaeal metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from the Western Arctic Ocean and to relate their relative abundances to water mass structure. Temperature, salinity, silicate, and N* distinguished four water mass layers: the summer surface layer, the Polar Mixed Layer, Atlantic Water, and Arctic Ocean basin water. Of 155 MAGs recovered from a metagenomic co-assembly, 17 were archaeal and represented all three marine groups (four MG-I, eleven MG-II, and two MG-III). Abundance-based clustering of samples from two deep central Arctic stations separated microbial communities according to water mass. Mapping MAG relative abundance across several hundred samples revealed surface, mid-depth, and deep distribution ecotypes; members of every marine group displayed more than one ecotype, and ecotype was not consistent with MAG phylogeny. These results indicate that archaeal distributions in the Western Arctic Ocean are more closely tied to water mass stratification than to clade identity, and that previously reported clade-specific depth distributions of marine Archaea may partly reflect the limited resolution of amplicon-based surveys and shallow sampling.

papers.title: Direction-Dependent Encoding of Forward and Inverse Models in the Same Purkinje Cells
papers.abstract: Saccadic eye movements are too fast to be guided by sensory feedback and therefore depend on precisely calibrated internal models. The cerebellum is widely thought to compute both forward and inverse models, yet how these two computations coexist in the same circuit remains unclear. We hypothesized that the same Purkinje cells (PCs) can serve as a forward model for saccades in one direction and as an inverse model for saccades in the opposite direction, because target neurons on either side of the cerebellar nuclei contribute differently to leftward and rightward saccades. To test this hypothesis, we recorded from PCs in the oculomotor vermis of macaque monkeys during repetitive saccade paradigms that induce adaptation and fatigue. Using the preferred error direction of each PC conveyed by increased complex spike (CS) activity (CS-on direction) as a proxy of the side of the cerebellar nuclei it projects to, we compared population activity for saccades directed against the CS-on direction (CS-on opposed) and along it (CS-on aligned). CS-on opposed saccades, (toward the PC's projection side) were accompanied by a precisely timed, sharp burst of simple spike (SS) activity at saccade onset that scaled with peak velocity, and CS error sensitivity was highest after the saccade. SS activity also changed systematically after adaptation, reflecting the altered kinematics of the adapted saccade. These properties are consistent with a forward model that estimates ongoing movement and updates itself based on post-movement error. In contrast, the CS-on aligned saccades, (away from the PC's projection side) were accompanied by broader SS modulation around saccade offset, and the CS error sensitivity was highest before the saccade. CSs around saccade onset encoded target location and initial eye position, and their occurrence was associated with reduced saccade amplitude. This reduction likely adjusts the motor command to the starting eye position, as expected for an inverse model that pre-programs the motor command before movement begins. Together, these findings provide neural evidence that the same PC population can contribute to both forward and inverse model computations, depending on saccade direction.

papers.title: Fibronectin-Assisted Coating of Low-Molecular-Weight Fucoidan Creates a Biomimetic Interface for Endothelialization of Cobalt-Chromium Stents
papers.abstract: Incomplete or delayed endothelialization after stent implantation compromises vascular healing and increases the risk of restenosis and late thrombosis. To address this limitation, Cobalt-Chromium (Co-Cr) stents were modified with a biomimetic coating combining Low-Molecular-Weight Fucoidan (LMWF), a sulfated polysaccharide with glycocalyx-mimetic properties, and fibronectin, to promote endothelial repair while preserving vascular homeostasis. The morphology, chemical composition, wettability and stability of the coating were characterized using complementary physicochemical approaches. The behavior of human endothelial cells cultured on this dual fibronectin-LMWF-coated stent was then assessed. Our results showed that fibronectin-LMWF-based coating achieved a ten-fold higher surface density on the stent than LMWF alone (0.29 {+/-} 0.04 vs 0.03 {+/-} 0.01 {micro}g/mm2) and retained 0.27 {+/-} 0.03 {micro}g/mm2 of the coating after 168 h, compared with 0.01 {+/-} 0.01 {micro}g/mm2 for LMWF alone. Although wettability remained similar to that of uncoated stents, the combined coating markedly enhanced endothelial cell adhesion, spreading, lamellipodia formation, proliferation, and MMP-2 secretion. These effects were accompanied by enhanced F-actin organization and redistribution of membrane-associated VE-cadherin, integrins {beta}1 and 6, and syndecans-1 and -4, without major changes in their total expression. Importantly, the coating induced these responses without detectable cytotoxicity or significant inflammatory activation. Overall, the fibronectin-LMWF-based coating provides a stable biomimetic interface that enhances endothelialization through coordinated remodeling of adhesion, cytoskeletal, and glycocalyx-associated structures, while maintaining endothelial homeostasis on Co-Cr stent. This strategy offers a promising platform for next-generation glycocalyx-like stent coatings designed to improve vascular healing and limit restenosis.

papers.title: A validation approach for RNA structures based on deep-learning 3D-structure predictions
papers.abstract: Understanding the molecular mechanisms of life depends on accurate macromolecular structures. RNA, in particular, poses a particular challenge for structural biology due to its inherent flexibility and dynamic nature. The challenging nature of structure determination experiments and their interpretation have led to the development of validation approaches to prevent or fix errors in solved structures. Existing methods for RNA structure validation can, as with proteins, be broadly split into two types. Map-based validation tools seek to detect discrepancies between the experimental data and the determined structure. They are excellent for fixing all types of errors, but only when high-resolution experimental data are available.Model-only validation methods, which usually focus on molecular geometry, are excellent for fixing short-length-scale issues even when experimental resolution is low. Conkit-validate is a mapless method for protein validation, which is not based on chemical plausibility, but rather on the similarity between experimental models and structure predictions for the same protein. By comparing contact patterns, this tool leverages evolutionary covariance information, learned by state-of-the-art structural prediction models, into a mapless validation method capable of detecting sequence assignment issues, with notable success in detecting register errors. Here, we extend the conkit-validate method to work on RNA.The results show performance similar to that previously achieved for proteins. %We also show how this new method can detect errors missed by map-based approaches when the experimental data is of low resolution. In a scan of the PDB, its detection rate does not depend on the local resolution of the density, so it remains applicable where map-based approaches are not, and case studies show it can identify register errors where the density alone cannot decide between models.Together, this highlights the complementary value of a contact-prediction based validation approach using information orthogonal to map- and geometry-based approaches to ensure the quality of deposited RNA structures against varying criteria.The performance of the method can be expected to track ongoing improvements in RNA structure prediction methods.

papers.title: Prokaryotic Community Structures in the Bering and Chukchi Seas
papers.abstract: Bacteria are essential to marine ecosystems as they remineralize organic matter, cycle carbon, nitrogen, and other key elements, and support higher trophic levels through food webs. The Bering and Chukchi Seas off the coast of Alaska are among the most productive regions in the world, with intense seasonal algal blooms, yet their bacterial communities remain poorly characterized, and the region is warming rapidly as heat transport from the Pacific Ocean increases. Here, we used 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing of 181 samples collected on 0.2 {micro}m filters at three depths (surface, middle, and bottom) across 62 stations during the Arctic Shelf Growth, Advection, Respiration and Deposition Rate Experiments (ASGARD) cruise in June 2017, when sea surface temperatures were anomalously warm. Hierarchical clustering of amplicon sequence variant (ASV) relative abundances resolved 11 sample clusters in three divisions, all dominated by Alphaproteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria, and Bacteroidia. Community structure was related to water mass, salinity, and bloom stage, but not to depth. Clusters ranged from Gammaproteobacteria-dominant, Bacteroidia-poor assemblages in warm and cool Shelf Water (Division A) to Bacteroidia-rich assemblages spanning pre- to post-bloom conditions (Divisions B and C). In distance-based redundancy analysis, temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen, nitrate, and fluorescence together explained 14.8% of the variation in community composition, with salinity the strongest contributor. These results indicate that water-mass origin, physicochemical conditions, and bloom stage jointly shape bacterial communities, and that changes in temperature, salinity, and the magnitude and timing of blooms could substantially alter bacterial communities of this Pacific gateway to the Arctic.

papers.title: Msp300 Links Autophagy to Nuclear Morphodynamics
papers.abstract: Autophagy is a fundamental cellular process that maintains homeostasis and enables adaptation to stress by degrading damaged or superfluous components. While its core machinery is well characterized, the interplay between autophagy and nuclear architecture remains poorly understood. In this study, we identify the LINC complex protein Msp300 as a novel interactor of the autophagy protein Atg8a in Drosophila melanogaster. Msp300 belongs to the KASH (Klarsicht/ANC-1/Syne Homology) domain protein family, known for its role in nuclear positioning through interactions with the cytoskeleton. The KASH domain anchors Msp300 in the outer nuclear membrane, where it pairs with SUN domain proteins across the nuclear envelope to form the LINC complex, a mechanical bridge between the nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton. Yeast two-hybrid screening revealed an interaction between Atg8a and Msp300 isoforms E and G, mediated by a canonical LC3-interacting region (LIR). Localization studies show Msp300 associates with Atg8a within the cytoplasm and at the nuclear periphery under both basal and elevated autophagy conditions. Functional perturbations through stress assays indicate that this interaction influences event in and around nucleus, establishing a link between autophagy and nuclear architecture. By exploring the role of Msp300 isoforms E and G in shaping not only nuclear organization but potentially endoplasmic reticulum, through autophagy machinery, this study introduces a new dimension to nuclear envelope biology and opens opportunities to explore how steady state homeostasis, stress adaptation and cytoskeletal connectivity are coordinated at the nuclear periphery.

papers.title: Pubertal timing is a critical dimension of adolescent brain vulnerability
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a period of rapid brain development, during which biological maturational timing varies substantially between individuals. This variability may drive specific developmental vulnerabilities to adverse experiences with long-term consequences, warranting early identification of at-risk individuals. We utilized ultrasonic bone age measurements to track pubertal maturity, classifying participants by adolescent biological maturity relative to chronological age (accelerated, average, decelerated). Brain hierarchy was quantified as the irreversibility of brain signals in resting state electroencephalography, providing a brain-based method to detect vulnerability patterns. The COVID-19 pandemic presented a unique opportunity to also assess alterations in brain hierarchy following external disruption. We mapped maturity-defined trajectories and rates of hierarchical organization, and their post-pandemic deviation from expected development, capturing two distinct vulnerability forms. First, early maturing adolescents showed persistent reduction in brain hierarchy. Second, those undergoing their fastest phase of development - specifically, decelerated adolescents - showed the strongest disruption in brain hierarchy following the pandemic. These findings suggest that pubertal timing is a critical dimension of individual variation in adolescent brain development and vulnerability. They also emphasize the need for objective maturity measurements to tailor support to individual pubertal timelines, particularly given the secular trend toward earlier puberty and ongoing global ecological crises.

papers.title: WhaleSonic: Recordings of cetacean vocal behaviour with hydrophone arrays in Northern Norway
papers.abstract: Killer whales, humpback whales, fin whales, and sperm whales converged in a fjord system in Northern Norway during the 2023-2024 winter, where whale watching and fishing vessels add to the acoustic scene. Cetaceans are intensely studied for their acoustic behaviour and communication, and the co-occurrence of four species in confined waters offers a unique opportunity to record them with hydrophone arrays. We present WhaleSonic, a raw acoustic dataset recorded with two synchronised array systems. Four drifting buoys, each carrying a tetrahedral hydrophone array, captured 78 hours of calibrated recordings; seven bottom-mounted hydrophones yielded 52 days of continuous data. Both systems are synchronised to UTC (<1 us and 3-7 ms) and positioned to 2 m accuracy. Transmission experiments and sound velocity measurements provide in-situ ground truth. All data are in physical units and a unified coordinate system, self-documented in HDF5 files, and published with open-source tools. WhaleSonic supports the development of multichannel algorithms for source separation, localisation, sound field analysis, and group communication in free-ranging cetaceans.

papers.title: The ecological niche and seasonality of Theileria equi in Portugal
papers.abstract: Equine piroplasmosis, caused by the tick-borne protozoan Theileria equi, is an evolving concern in Europe. In recent years, it has been associated with substantial economic costs and with transmission showing signs of pushing into previously free or marginal northern regions. While piroplasmosis is endemic in Portugal, not much is known about the interplay of seasonally varying and spatial abiotic drivers that may modulate infection. In this study, we leveraged unique field-surveillance data based on equine PCR testing together with publicly available data to unravel and characterize the spatio-temporal dynamics and ecological niche of Theileria equi. Infection probability was estimated to increase with local bovine abundance, temperature and the presence of planosol soils, and to decrease with local equine density due to an intraspecific dilution effect of vector exposure. At an individual level, the highest infection probabilities were estimated among female and pasture-kept equids. We estimate strong seasonal signatures in local and national infection probability, maximized in August and minimized in February, and a spatially heterogeneous ecological niche landscape. Far northern and north-eastern regions combined low infection probability both in- and off-season with prolonged off-seasons, whereas centre and north-western regions combined high probability both in- and off-season with brief off-seasons. The former plausibly function as unsuitable reservoirs, and the latter as suitable year-round reservoirs. Our results provide a first quantitative, risk-stratified basis for regional and individual targeted Theileria equi surveillance, awareness and control in Portugal.

papers.title: Long-range allosteric restraint by the Spiral-Pincer scaffold gates oxidative activation of the ATM kinase
papers.abstract: ATM is a master regulator of the DNA-damage response, activated either by DNA double-strand breaks through the MRN complex or, independently, by oxidative stress, which drives disulfide bond formation between Cys2991 residues on the two halves of the ATM dimer. Although both pathways involve release of the PIKK regulatory domain (PRD) from the kinase active site, how the distant Spiral--Pincer scaffold regulates access to this state remains unclear, partly because the PRD--FAT-TRD3 interface is unresolved in available experimental structures. Here, we combine an AlphaFold3-completed full-length ATM dimer model with well-tempered metadynamics to map its conformational landscape. We find that an oxidation-competent conformation already exists in the resting dimer, although it is rarely populated, supporting conformational selection rather than induction of a new state. Removing Spiral--Pincer eliminates this restriction: the conformation becomes dominant, and the landscape narrows to a few well-separated states. The dimer's two halves respond unequally, one loop of the PRD rearranging substantially while the other remains unchanged, via specific domain contacts rather than a direct route to the reactive cysteines. This identifies Spiral--Pincer as a release-controlled brake on ATM activation, a mechanism that may extend across the wider PIKK kinase family.

papers.title: Emergence and robustness of 3D complex tissue architectures from simple physical forces
papers.abstract: Although at central stake in biology and biological engineering, our understanding of how biological tissues acquire their architectures during morphogenesis and which mechanisms have been selected through evolution remain limited. Using adipose tissue as a biological model, we build a 3D mathematical model with simple mechanical rules between cells and fibers, and show that the model reproduces, in-silico, not only the emergence of complex and heterogeneous 3D architectures, but also the intra and inter-individual heterogeneities of shapes as observed in vivo. The model reveals that specific rules for cell differentiation are not necessary for tissue structuring, but could have been selected through evolution for robustness and efficiency. This study therefore suggests a paradigm shift where tissue architecture is an emerging process surprisingly more driven by mechanical processes than by complex predetermined molecular or genetic programs.

papers.title: Myelin Governs Hippocampal Network Function through the Extracellular Space it Occupies, Not Only the Axons it Insulates
papers.abstract: Myelin, the multilamellar sheath wrapping neuronal axons, enables saltatory conduction. Beyond electrical insulation, myelin occupies volume, and therefore shapes the extracellular space (ECS) through which interstitial fluid flows and neurotransmitter diffuses. How these two roles interact is unknown. We built a multi-scale model of hippocampal CA1 coupling lattice Boltzmann simulations of ECS flow to detailed networks of reconstructed neurons and glia. Demyelination enlarged the ECS volume fraction from 28 to 43 per cent up to 43 to 70 per cent across layers, lowered tortuosity from about 1.7 to 1.4, raised effective diffusivity from 0.35 to 0.50 of free solution and shortened solute breakthrough times by roughly a third, while raising flow speed yet lowering viscous dissipation. Because transmitter concentration scales inversely with that volume, synaptic driving force fell: postsynaptic potential amplitude declined with wrap count and transmission failed entirely below four of sixteen wraps. In 200-cell networks, demyelination halved firing (pyramidal 7.9 to 4.4 Hz), rendered discharge burst-dominated, reduced band power by up to 8.7-fold and displaced the population state, which a classifier separated at 100 per cent accuracy, whereas an inflammatory glial census left every functional measure unchanged. Driving myelin continuously from intact to 12.5 per cent and back recovered the same threshold near four wraps, and firing rate and spectral power returned fully to baseline. Myelin thus governs circuit function through the space it vacates as well as the axons it insulates, with opposite consequences for clearance and for signalling, a dissociation that may matter in demyelinating disease.

papers.title: AMD1-driven MTA production sustains chemoresistance by rewiring PMN-MDSC immunosuppression
papers.abstract: Chemoresistance reflects both tumor cell-intrinsic adaptation and remodeling of the immune microenvironment. However, the mechanisms by which chemoresistant tumor cells orchestrate and sustain an immunosuppressive microenvironment remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that chemoresistant tumors exhibit marked accumulation of polymorphonuclear myeloid-derived suppressor cells (PMN-MDSCs), which exert potent immunosuppressive effects on CD8+T cells and are critical for drug resistance. Metabolomic profiling reveals that resistant tumor cells release the metabolite 5'-methylthioadenosine (MTA). MTA enhances the immunosuppressive function of PMN-MDSCs by bolstering JAK-STAT3 signaling. Mechanistically, MTA binds to the protein tyrosine phosphatase PTPN2 to block its phosphatase activity, thereby potentiating activation of JAK-STAT3 signaling pathway. Moreover, we uncover that adenosylmethionine decarboxylase 1 (AMD1) is the key metabolic determinant of MTA accumulation in chemoresistant tumor cells. Genetic or pharmacological AMD1 inhibition significantly decreases MTA level, diminishes PMN-MDSC immunosuppressive function, and re-sensitizes the resistant tumors to chemotherapy and immunotherapy. Our findings identify MTA as an important metabolic link between chemoresistant tumor cells and PMN-MDSCs to sustain immunosuppression and therapeutic resistance. Targeting AMD1-dependent MTA production represents a valuable strategy for overcoming chemo-immunotherapy resistance.

papers.title: The self-renewing lymphoid-biased hematopoietic stem cells support long-term lymphopoiesis in mice
papers.abstract: Lymphopoiesis is profoundly impaired during ageing largely due to ageing-susceptible changes of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). How to maximize the preservation of lymphopoiesis during ageing remains unknown and whether there exists a specific population with life-long lymphoid potential not intensively affected by ageing is of substantial scientific and translational significance. Here, we identified a self-renewable, lymphoid-biased hematopoietic stem cells (Ly-biased HSCs) subset within the EPCR+CD150-CD48-LSK (HSC2) population, phenotypically termed EPCR+MPP6 (CD34-CD135-HSC2), that not only displayed comparable multi-lineage potential with HSC in young mice, but also maintained similar lymphoid-biased reconstitution during aging. The lymphoid-biased characteristics of EPCR+MPP6 were also supported by immune associated program at transcriptome and proteomic levels. Notably, EPCR+MPP6 and HSCs rarely generated one another following the first cell division in vitro and under homeostasis in vivo indicating the most likely independent relationship between them and an earlier-than-thought bifurcation of the lymphoid differentiation pathway, which may function as a backup source to support lymphopoiesis. Collectively, this newly defined Ly-biased HSCs represent a promising cellular target for both mechanistic studies and therapeutic strategies concerning age-related immune decline.

papers.title: Putative biosurfactants from polar microbial consortia
papers.abstract: Biosurfactants (BS) are amphiphilic microbial metabolites that are biodegradable, low in toxicity, and environmentally compatible, making them attractive for applications in food, pharmaceutical, and bioremediation industries. This study investigated the phylogenetic composition and biosurfactant-producing potential of marine oil snow (MOS)-associated microbial consortia from the Churchill Marine Observatory, western Hudson Bay. MOS aggregates were cultivated in mineral Bushnell-Haas (BH) medium supplemented with 3% (w/v) NaCl, using motor oil as the sole hydrocarbon source. Enrichment cultures capable of growth in BH medium were subsequently evaluated for biosurfactant production using qualitative and quantitative assays at 4 {degrees}C and 20 {degrees}C. All cultures were maintained as enrichment consortia throughout the study. A total of eight enrichment cultures were identified as biosurfactant-producing consortia. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that Pseudoalteromonas dominated all consortia, while Paraglaciecola, Marinomonas, and other taxa were present at varying relative abundances. Although none of the consortia exhibited high emulsification activity (E24 > 40%), biosurfactant yields were significantly higher at 4 {degrees}C. Additionally, three consortia tested positive for rhamnolipid-type biosurfactant production.

papers.title: Oil biodegradation and marine oil snow formation in Arctic seawater microcosms at 4 °C
papers.abstract: Hudson Bay is a sub-Arctic inland sea characterized by seasonal sea-ice cover, which governs marine circulation, biological productivity, and ecosystem structure. In recent decades, the duration of sea-ice cover has declined, resulting in longer ice-free seasons that are expected to elevate marine activity and environmental exposure to anthropogenic disturbances. As such, the potential for oil spill incidents associated with increased marine operations is expected to rise. To understand microbial biodegradation dynamics associated with marine oil snow (MOS), seawater microcosms amended with diesel fuel were incubated at 4 {degrees}C for 6 weeks. We amended all our microcosms with UV-weathered Churchill diesel fuel at 1% (v/v). 16S rRNA sequencing of the incubations revealed a decline in overall microbial diversity and a dramatic increase in specialized oil-degrading taxa, with Pseudomonas and Pseudoalteromonas being the main taxa involved, as both effectively degrade hydrocarbons under ambient and stimulated conditions. Biostimulation with nutrients (NaNO3, KH2PO4) and an alternative dispersant at 0.1% (v/v) resulted in a greater abundance of MOS aggregates and rapid enrichment of oil-degraders. Simple n-alkanes exhibited the highest biodegradation loss relative to complex polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs); however, biostimulation did not substantially enhance their degradation. Additionally, UV weathering resulted in a 22% loss of PAHs, which is three times higher than the UV loss observed for n-alkanes. Biostimulated samples exhibited an elevated transfer of high molecular weight alkanes and PAHs from the oil into the aqueous phase, accompanied by a rapid enrichment of oil-degrading taxa.

papers.title: Draft genome of Paraperlucidibaca sp. CMO1 isolated from marine oil snow in the Churchill Marine Observatory, MB, Canada
papers.abstract: An oil-degrading enrichment culture was inoculated from Marine Oil Snow (MOS) collected during an oil-spill experiment at the Churchill Marine Observatory in winter 2024. The complete metagenome-assembled genome for Paraperlucidibaca sp. CMO1 was reconstructed, exhibiting the genetic potential to degrade hydrocarbons, including alkanes and aromatic compounds, as well as the ability to produce surfactants.

papers.title: Marine oil snow formation in microcosm incubations of artificial seawater at 4 °C
papers.abstract: An oil spill in the Arctic would have far-reaching impacts on the environment, the biota, and the Inuit communities that depend on this unique ecosystem for their livelihoods. Due to the rapid retreat of sea ice in the region, the Arctic is becoming more vulnerable to oil spills. Since microorganisms are the first responders to oil contamination, understanding their behavior is critical for designing bioremediation approaches tailored to Arctic conditions. In this study, we conducted microcosm experiments at 4 {degrees}C in the dark to simulate an Arctic oil spill, using crude oil and diesel as hydrocarbon sources. Biostimulation was tested with the addition of nutrients NaNO3 and KH2PO4, and soy lecithin-Tween 80 dissolved in ethanol as an alternative dispersant. Microcosms were placed on tube rollers at 3 rpm to mimic natural wave action and run with appropriate controls to assess microbial community shifts. Our objectives were to characterize the early microbial succession associated with oil degradation and marine oil snow (MOS) formation, and to determine how nutrients, dispersants, oil type (crude vs. diesel), photochemical aging (fresh vs. weathered), and oil concentration influence these processes. We observed that the combined effect of nutrients and dispersant resulted in rapid MOS formation, occurring as early as 30 minutes after the initial setup. Microbial taxa exhibited varying tolerance to different concentrations of the same oil, and the dominant hydrocarbon degraders in fresh diesel treatments were distinctly different from those in weathered diesel. Furthermore, the nutrient-dispersant treatment promoted an earlier succession of oil-degrading taxa compared to nutrient-only or dispersant-only treatments. Together, these results highlight the importance of cold-adapted microbial communities in driving early oil degradation and MOS formation in Arctic waters, and they provide insights relevant to the development of Arctic-specific bioremediation strategies.

papers.title: NPlasmid-seq: Cas9-encoded terminal signatures enable molecule-level nanopore quality control of vector and IVT-template plasmids
papers.abstract: Consensus-based plasmid quality control can overlook structural heterogeneity within a preparation. We developed NPlasmid-seq, a Cas9-guided nanopore workflow that encodes sample identity through paired terminal signatures generated at predefined backbone positions, without sample-specific oligonucleotide barcodes. We cleavage-validated 24 sgRNAs. In five representative assigned read bins, each bin showed its strongest sequence agreement with its cognate reference. Contaminant detection was evaluated with a single class-specific classifier applied both to computational read mixtures and to physical DNA mixtures, placing the two designs on a common scale. In computational read mixtures of 5,000 reads, a contaminant was detected in all 20 independent subsamples at each of 0.2%, 0.5%, 1% and 5% abundance and in 13 of 20 subsamples at 0.1%; precision was 1.000 in all 100 subsamples, with no false-positive calls among 493,200 reads from the declared target plasmid. In physical DNA mixtures carried through cleavage, pooled library preparation and sequencing, a contaminant was detected in all six samples prepared at 0.5 mol% input and all six at 1 mol%. Observed read fractions did not distinguish the 0.5 and 1 mol% input levels. Instead, they differed systematically by 4.0-fold between preparation pools, a larger effect than the difference between the two input levels. We therefore interpret the workflow as a detector, not a quantifier, of sub-percent contamination. Read-level analysis identified a recurrent 93-bp deletion in 61.7% of reads from a preparation that had passed consensus-based quality control. Sanger genotyping of 24 colonies identified deletion-type profiles in 10 colonies and intact-type profiles in three. The remaining 11 colonies showed double peaks at the diagnostic locus, consistent with coexistence of both sequence forms within individual clones. In in vitro transcription template plasmids, longer poly(A) tracts were associated with higher multimeric-read fractions. Across ten matched A90 culture pairs, propagation at 30 degree reduced these fractions relative to 37 degree (paired t-test, P = 0.0098). These measurements describe recovered read populations, not absolute molecular abundances. NPlasmid-seq therefore complements consensus validation by revealing sequence and structural heterogeneity within a preparation and by identifying a culture condition associated with a lower multimeric-read fraction.

papers.title: Locus Coeruleus activity correlates with transient elevations in breathing during opioid-induced respiratory depression
papers.abstract: A history of use remains a key risk factor for opioid-related overdose deaths in the ongoing opioid epidemic. The locus coeruleus (LC) is the principal source of noradrenergic tone and a site for opioid neuromodulation and tolerance. How a history of opioid use affects LC activity and shapes opioid-induced respiratory depression (OIRD) remains poorly understood. Using plethysmography and fiber photometry, we assessed how fentanyl affects LC activity and OIRD before and after five days of repeat opioid use (ROU). Fentanyl increased the frequency of LC bursts independent of exposure history and was coupled to transient elevations in breathing. LC coupled ventilation (LC-Ve) persisted through ROU. After ROU, OIRD magnitude diverged across mice. Mice developing an adaptive ventilatory response (AVR) showed a smaller OIRD that coincided with improved ventilation outside LC bursts and reduced LC-Ve gain. Mice with the non-adaptive response (NVR) show no improvement in OIRD or ventilation outside LC bursts, resulting in an unchanged reliance on LC-Ve. While LC-Ve reflexively counters OIRD acutely, it may also drive oscillations to destabilize blood gas homeostasis, perpetuating pathophysiology with repeat use. Thus, LC-coupled breathing appears to be a physiological signature of divergent respiratory responses with a history of fentanyl exposure.

papers.title: The IFN-γ-inducible GTPase IIGP1 regulates mitochondrial remodeling and immunometabolic reprogramming during inflammatory macrophage polarization
papers.abstract: Macrophages are key effector cells of the innate immune system that undergo dynamic polarization into functionally distinct phenotypic states, ranging from classically activated inflammatory (M1) to alternatively activated (M2) macrophages. Inflammatory macrophage polarization requires coordinated integration of cytokine signaling, metabolic reprogramming, and mitochondrial remodeling. However, the molecular effectors that control inflammatory signaling for mitochondrial metabolism and remodeling remain poorly defined. Using quantitative mass spectrometry-based proteomics, we identified Interferon-inducible GTPase 1 (IIGP1) as one of the most robustly induced proteins during inflammatory macrophage polarization. Its expression is governed by the IFN-{gamma}-JAK-STAT1 signaling axis and is crucial for this polarization process. IIGP1-deficient macrophages exhibited significantly impaired iNOS induction, nitric oxide production, pro-inflammatory gene expression, co-stimulatory surface marker expression, and morphological remodeling. Further, IIGP1 associates with mitochondria and its absence impairs key characteristics of inflammatory macrophages, including glycolytic metabolic reprogramming, mitochondrial redox adaptation, membrane potential regulation, and structural remodeling. Consistent with these defects, IIGP1-deficient macrophages displayed impaired intracellular killing of Escherichia coli and Salmonella Typhimurium. Collectively, these results point to IIGP1 as an IFN-{gamma}-inducible effector that facilitates efficient inflammatory macrophage polarization and antibacterial immunity by linking inflammatory signaling to mitochondrial homeostasis and immunometabolic reprogramming.

papers.title: Defining nutrient dependencies of intestinal Klebsiella pneumoniae guides rational probiotic engineering
papers.abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a major cause of antibiotic-resistant infections, yet the ecological determinants enabling its intestinal expansion remain poorly defined. Here, we combined in vivo transcriptomics and metabolomics to identify carbon sources exploited by K. pneumoniae during colonization of the antibiotic-disrupted gut across strains and dietary contexts. Despite its metabolic breadth, K. pneumoniae consistently exploited a restricted set of substrates, including arabinose, raffinose, oligogalacturonate, arabitol, xylose, and gluconate, that contributed to intestinal fitness, with related metabolic signatures also observed in antibiotic-treated human samples. Guided by these findings, we engineered Escherichia coli Nissle to enhance consumption of these nutrients and assembled a defined consortium, NICHE, designed to reinforce colonization resistance through nutrient competition. NICHE restricted intestinal expansion of multidrug-resistant and hypervirulent K. pneumoniae in preventive and therapeutic settings, with efficacy influenced by dietary nutrient availability. Together, this work defines exploitable K. pneumoniae nutrient dependencies and a framework for rational probiotic engineering.

papers.title: DarHTG is a tripartite phage defence system for purine DNA base ADP-ribosylation
papers.abstract: Bacteria evolved a variety of phage defence strategies to combat the constant onslaught of viral threats. DarTG toxin-antitoxin systems provide phage defence by ADP-ribosylation of bases in single-stranded DNA which interferes with viral replication and aborts phage infection. Here, we describe DarHTG, a system widespread among bacteria, that combines DarTG with a non-processive superfamily I helicase functioning as co-toxin for DarT and thereby enabling the ADP-ribosylation of double-stranded DNA. We identified two such DarHTG subclasses which catalyse the ADP-ribosylation of adenosine and guanosine bases, respectively, and reverse these modifications with structurally unique ARH superfamily antitoxins. Thus, DarHTG antitoxins expand the known macromolecular target spectrum of the ARH enzyme class to nucleic acids. These DarHTG systems confer resistance to a broad range of bacteriophages and can be triggered by the highly charged tails of viral single-stranded DNA-binding proteins, which occlude the active site of the ARH antitoxin.

papers.title: Res ipSAE adhuc loquuntur: What the directionality of predicted aligned error in cofolding models can tell us about scoring diverse molecular complexes
papers.abstract: AlphaFold 3 (AF3) and Boltz-2 estimate confidence in predicted biomolecular complexes using the interface predicted template modeling (ipTM) score, which is derived from probability distributions of predicted aligned errors (PAEs) between molecular tokens. These errors are directional: the predicted position of tokens in one molecule is evaluated relative to coordinate frames defined by tokens in another. The PAE matrix is therefore asymmetric, but AF3 reports the maximum of the two directional pairwise ipTM scores, whereas Boltz-2 reports them separately. In both programs, the TM-score scaling parameter, d0, depends on molecular system size rather than solely on the component being scored. In protein-protein complexes, including disordered regions and domains unrelated to the interface can further lower ipTM. I previously introduced the interaction predicted score from aligned errors (ipSAE) to address these limitations for protein-protein complexes. Here, I extend ipSAE to interactions involving proteins, nucleic acids, small-molecule ligands, and atomic ions. The framework makes three explicit choices for each molecular pair: which component supplies the alignment frames, which tokens are scored, and how d0 is defined. For different molecular types, I propose aligning on the more complex molecule and scoring the simpler one. For protein-ligand complexes, this entails aligning on protein residues, scoring all ligand heavy atoms without a PAE cutoff, and using a fixed d0 of 2 [A]. In benchmarks of 102 protein-ligand complexes predicted by AF3 and Boltz-2, this ipSAE formulation yields a substantially wider range of confidence scores than native ipTM. On a held-out set of 82 complexes, ipSAE thresholds of 0.5 for AF3 and 0.8 for Boltz-2 classified ligand placements with balanced accuracies of 0.938 and 0.862, respectively, using a ligand RMSD threshold of 5 [A]. Protein-DNA benchmarks support the same directional scoring scheme, while smaller protein-RNA benchmarks provide a preliminary assessment. These results establish a framework for interpreting predicted structural confidence across different classes of biomolecular interactions and suggest that directional scoring may also be useful for computationally designed protein binders.
