Principal component analysis (PCA), when visualized using only leading components, can obscure fine-scale structure, while nonlinear neighbor-based methods such as uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) often fragment geographic and admixture gradients into discrete clusters. Here, we introduce a framework for constructing ancestry coordinates using potential of heat-diffusion for affinity-based trajectory embedding (PHATE), a diffusion-based method that preserves relationships across scales. Across synthetic benchmarks and large genomic datasets, we show that appropriate scale tuning and population balancing allow PHATE to recover geographic organization and admixture gradients. We show that incorrectly tuned neighborhood scale and population imbalance can distort the resulting representations of population structure. These results therefore provide a methodological framework and practical guidance for constructing ancestry visualizations that better reflect continuous human genetic diversity.

papers.title: Mapping brain networks underlying abstract perceptual decision formation and its EEG signatures
papers.abstract: Perceptual decisions have been proposed to involve a common mechanism of evidence accumulation operating across sensory modalities and motor contexts. In human EEG, the centroparietal positivity (CPP) tracks evidence accumulation in such a supramodal motor-independent manner, but its cortical sources are uncertain. Here we combined fMRI and EEG, acquired in separate sessions of the same supramodal change-detection paradigm, with individualized finite element head modeling to identify decision-related networks. A conjunction analysis across visual and auditory modalities and across motor and non-motor required tasks revealed consistent activation of bilateral postcentral, supramarginal, and superior parietal lobules, precentral gyrus, central operculum, middle frontal gyrus, and cerebellum. Forward modeling of fMRI-defined sources indicated that parietal-opercular regions were the dominant contributors to the response-locked and non-motor-required peak-locked CPP signal. These results implicate a network of brain areas in supramodal, motor-independent target-detection decisions, whose specific functional roles can be interrogated in more complex decision tasks in future.

papers.title: DoAggregate: a pipeline for aggregation testing for rare-variant on a gene and pathway level
papers.abstract: Motivation Aggregation tests overcome the classical limitation of rare variant analysis in cohort study design. Choosing the right statistical test remains one of the biggest challenges. Existing tools fall short in offering a comprehensive solution that includes automatic data processing, testing across all genes, as well as exploration of broader genetic regions such as pathways and Gene Ontology (GO) terms. Most aggregation tests only report p-values and basic statistics, lacking in the presentation of cohort level statistics and comparison of results across whole genome or exome scales. Results We introduce DoAggregate, an innovative, scalable pipeline designed to address these challenges. DoAggregate enables users to perform aggregation tests across genes, pathways, and GO terms. It leverages Excalibur, an ensemble approach combining 36 distinct aggregation methods. The pipeline enhances data analysis by presenting over-representation analysis and aggregation results in detailed Excel sheets, complete with annotations and plots to facilitate nuanced interpretation and comparison. Applied to public exome data from the 1000 Genomes Project, DoAggregate tested 10,447 genes, 49 over-represented pathways and 36 over-represented GO terms in a single run, returning annotated, cohort-level results for each region. Availability and implementation DoAggregate source code, documentation and installation instructions as well as test data sets and results are freely available at https://github.com/boutrys/DoAggregate and released under the MIT license. The repository contains the serial implementation (R package), the parallel implementation for Slurm-based computer clusters and the web application.

papers.title: Unsupervised prioritization of gene-regulatory variants with isolation forests
papers.abstract: Most common variants occur in non-coding genomic regions. Numerous expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) can influence nearby gene expression. Across diverse traits and diseases, many genome-wide association study (GWAS) loci have been shown to colocalize with eQTLs, supporting gene-regulatory causal mechanisms. However, linkage disequilibrium (LD) obscures the identification of the causal variant(s), necessitating prioritization by functional annotations. Previously published variant prioritization tools relied on the machine-learning-based combination of diverse feature types like evolutionary conservation and chromatin information, whereas more recent deep learning tools learn and describe gene-regulatory DNA sequence grammar. However, the latter approaches often generate a large number of scores per variant. We designed a novel unsupervised machine-learning approach based on isolation forests to integrate the predictions from the broadly used Enformer deep learning model into a single gene-regulatory predictive score for each common variant. Our novel approach eQTL prediction with isolation forests (eQIF) demonstrates strong performance in predicting eQTLs and gene-regulatory GWAS variants. We show that top eQIF variants are located in evolutionarily conserved transcription factor binding site (TFBS) footprints, and that the frequency of top eQIF variants within overrepresented TFBS motifs recapitulates the motif information content. eQIF predictions are precomputed for 9,431,969 common variants and publicly available.

papers.title: Compost-associated microbiota modulates root transcriptional responses and enhances tomato drought resilience
papers.abstract: Compost is a promising sustainable alternative to mineral fertilization because it supplies nutrients and organic matter while hosting diverse microbial communities. However, even if its application to plants has been proven to alleviate different biotic and abiotic stresses, it remains unclear whether its benefits arise from its physico-chemical properties, its associated microbiota, or both. In this study, we compared the impact of compost, sterile compost and an NPK treatment providing equivalent macronutrient inputs on tomato plants cv. Micro-Tom. After assessing physiological parameters of the leaves and molecular responses of the roots under optimal conditions, we performed a drought stress experiment under the three fertilization treatments, complementing the analysis with the investigation of substrate water-retention properties. Although all fertilized treatments improved plant performance relative to nutrient-poor soil, RNA sequencing revealed distinct root transcriptional profiles among compost, sterile compost and NPK, with the compost treatment upregulating several pathways related to plant growth and health, such as hormone signaling, nutrient metabolism, and stress responses. When subjected to severe water stress, compost-treated plants retained the highest photosynthetic efficiency and compost showed the highest available water content compared to the other treatments. These findings suggest that compost may enhance tomato drought resilience through combined effects of substrate water availability and compost-associated microbiota.

papers.title: SDHB deficiency silences ABCB1 expression and confers therapeutic vulnerability across multiple cancer types
papers.abstract: Succinate dehydrogenase B (SDHB)-deficient cancers, including pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL), renal cell carcinoma (RCC), and gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST), exhibit aggressive clinical behavior with limited treatment options. To identify novel therapeutic vulnerabilities, we performed high-throughput drug screening using co-cultured human SDHB-deficient and SDHB-reconstituted UOK269 human renal cell carcinoma cells with dual fluorescence labeling. Several compounds displaying preferential cytotoxicity toward SDHB-deficient cells were known substrates of the ATP-binding cassette B1 (ABCB1) transporter, also known as Multidrug Resistance Protein 1 (MDR1). Accordingly, SDHB-deficient cells demonstrated markedly reduced ABCB1 expression, a phenotype confirmed across human SDHB-deficient PPGL, RCC, and GIST samples, but absent in IDH- or FH-deficient tumors. Mechanistic investigation revealed that KDM4A histone demethylase is downregulated in SDHB-deficient tumors, and KDM4A loss (or inhibition) is sufficient to reduce ABCB1 expression, globally increase H3K9me3 levels, and sensitize cells to cytotoxic ABCB1 substrates. TCGA analysis confirmed correlated KDM4A-ABCB1 expression in SDHB-deficient cancers, with ABCB1 levels predicting drug sensitivity across cancer cell lines. Clinical analysis demonstrated that SDHB-mutant PPGL patients treated with vincristine-containing chemotherapy exhibited significantly longer progression-free survival compared to non-SDHB patients. These findings establish a novel metabolic-epigenetic pathway linking SDHB deficiency to ABCB1 silencing and provide rational basis for repurposing vincristine, and related ABCB1 substrate vinca alkaloids, across SDHB-deficient cancer types; offering an alternative precision treatment approach for these challenging malignancies.

papers.title: A noncanonical function of Dicer fuels self-dsRNA-driven inflammation
papers.abstract: Self-derived double-stranded RNAs (self-dsRNAs) can drive autoinflammation, but how structurally constrained self-dsRNAs become immunostimulatory remains unclear. We identify a noncanonical role for Dicer and a broad requirement for LGP2 in this process. Dicer is required for responses to self-dsRNAs, but not exogenous dsRNAs, that arise from defects in RNA editing, splicing, epigenetic silencing, or mitochondrial RNA degradation in multiple cell types, including a human stem cell-derived model of neuroinflammation. Independently of microRNA biogenesis, Dicer promotes activation of MDA5, PKR, and OAS-RNase L. Dicer binds immunostimulatory dsRNAs and uses its catalytic activity to generate shorter duplexes with accessible ends that are available for LGP2 end-binding, enabling MDA5 filament assembly. Thus, Dicer converts short, structurally constrained self-dsRNAs into inflammatory ligands, thereby facilitating their recognition as danger-associated signals.

papers.title: Distinct antischistosomal profiles of antimalarials and TRP agonists
papers.abstract: Schistosomiasis control relies on praziquantel mass drug administration, but reports of field treatment failure and laboratory-selected resistance highlight the need for alternatives. Praziquantel activates a schistosome transient receptor potential (TRP) channel, TRPMPZQ. Alternative leads or chemotherapies include meclonazepam, which activates a distinct schistosome TRP channel, and the antimalarials artemether and mefloquine, whose flatworm targets are unknown. To compare molecular responses and assess cross-resistance, we conducted comparative RNA-seq and efficacy studies in infected mice. We profiled adult Schistosoma mansoni recovered 48 hours after artemether or mefloquine treatment and compared responses with existing datasets for TRP agonists praziquantel and meclonazepam. Transcriptional profiles clustered by drug class but showed largely distinct changes, with only 33 upregulated and 63 downregulated transcripts shared across treatments. Plexin domain-containing genes were strongly induced by both TRP agonists and, to a lesser extent, by antimalarials. Artemether downregulated gene families expressed in intestinal cells (saposins, cathepsins, and Bax inhibitor-like proteins), consistent with potential heme-dependent activity in the schistosome gut. Genes involved in glutamine metabolism, iron homeostasis and responses to oxidative damage were upregulated across multiple treatments. We evaluated all four treatments in mice infected with praziquantel-susceptible or resistant parasites. Praziquantel (200 mg/kg) reduced resistant male worm burdens by only 39.3%, versus 99.0% in susceptible parasites. Meclonazepam (83.0% versus 91.6% in susceptible parasites), mefloquine (99.1% versus 98.8%), and artemether (98.2% versus 99.4%) retained activity. The distinct transcriptional responses and retained activity against praziquantel-resistant parasites support further investigation of these compound classes as praziquantel alternatives or potential combination partners.

papers.title: Unfamiliar conspecifics increase freezing and shift movement towards immobility in zebrafish, most clearly in males
papers.abstract: Familiar companions can buffer stress in zebrafish (Danio rerio), but whether an unfamiliar shoal is itself a stressor, and whether the sexes respond alike, is unclear. We exposed adult zebrafish to a familiar or an unfamiliar shoal for at least 75 min, video-tracked their behaviour over the last 60 min and then measured whole-body cortisol. In males, an unfamiliar shoal increased freezing (+14.5 percentage points), reduced swim bouts and shifted movement towards a frozen state (8% to 49% of frames). In females, the changes were smaller and not significant. With the sexes pooled, whole-body cortisol was 1.6-fold higher after exposure to the unfamiliar shoal. Sex differences were only found for swim bouts and movement states, not for freezing or cortisol. We conclude that an unfamiliar shoal is a likely stressor for zebrafish, with behavioural effects clearest in males. Thus, who a zebrafish shares its tank with is not a neutral background, and the familiarity of conspecifics should be considered whenever fish are placed in new social settings in the lab.

papers.title: Visual-cortex-projecting neurons in mouse auditory cortex show distinct audiovisual responses independent of motor-related activity
papers.abstract: Cells in mouse primary visual cortex (V1) not only respond to visual stimulation, but also to sound. Part of this auditory modulation likely originates from auditory cortex (AC). Yet, the circuit-level functionality of the AC-to-V1 projection remains poorly understood. Here we performed acute in vivo high-density recordings in mouse AC during auditory, visual, and audiovisual stimulation, identifying AC-to-V1 projecting neurons by optogenetic tagging. Compared to non-tagged neurons, AC-to-V1 neurons more often responded to auditory, visual, or audiovisual stimuli. Furthermore, most AC-to-V1 neurons responded to specific sound frequencies; a modest but significant fraction was selective for visual orientations. These results could not be explained by motor responses or single-neuron variations in firing rate, cortical recording depth, or waveform type. These findings show that AC-to-V1 neurons carry sensory-specific signals, as opposed to nonspecific modulations, and exhibit distinctive response profiles compared to non-tagged AC neurons.

papers.title: ARCADE disentangles cell abundance from continuous transcriptional state in spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics is widely used to infer both cell-type abundance and within-type transcriptional variation, but these signals are difficult to separate in mixed spot-level measurements. Here, we present ARCADE, a computational framework that addresses two major sources of uncertainty in spatial analysis: unstable single-cell references and entanglement between abundance and cell state. ARCADE first builds a robust reference through hyperparameter optimization and consensus filtering, then performs spatial inference in two stages by estimating cell-type composition before modeling continuous intratype transcriptional programs around this compositional anchor. Across simulated and semi-synthetic benchmarks, ARCADE improves deconvolution accuracy and yields more stable state inference than existing approaches. In matched human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex datasets with spatial proteogenomic readouts, ARCADE distinguishes localized cell enrichment from astrocyte and microglial activation programs. These results show that decoupled modeling can improve the interpretability of spatial transcriptomic signals in complex tissues.

papers.title: Anti-TGFβ peptide P144 augments CAR-T cell efficacy through neutrophil recruitment and TME remodeling in malignant mesothelioma
papers.abstract: Malignant mesothelioma is a rare, aggressive and highly desmoplastic cancer characterised by a profoundly immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment (TME). Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of hematological malignancies, but its activity against solid tumours such as mesothelioma remains limited, in part through transforming growth factor-beta (TGF{beta})-mediated immunosuppression. To address this barrier, we engineered murine CAR-T cells that simultaneously target tumour antigen and deliver TGF{beta} blockade to the tumour. We first compared two anti-TGF{beta} peptides, the beta glycan-derived P144 and the phage-display-derived P17, in vitro; both attenuated TGF{beta}-induced epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and reporter activity, but P144 suppressed canonical Smad3 phosphorylation more effectively and was selected for downstream work. Murine CAR constructs targeting either mesothelin (M11) or fibroblast activation protein (FAP) were modified to secrete P144, and the resulting products were assessed in co-culture assays and in the syngeneic AE17m model of mesothelioma. P144 secretion did not alter transduction efficiency, expansion or antigen-specific cytotoxicity, but markedly increased antigen-driven IFN{gamma} production, most notably at low effector-to-target ratios. In vivo, both M11-P144 and FAP-P144 CAR-T cells-controlled tumour growth better than their parental, peptide-free counterparts, although complete tumour resolution was not achieved. Flow cytometric profiling of the tumour immune infiltrate showed that P144 delivery increased intratumoral neutrophil frequency approximately three-fold, and neutrophils recovered from these tumours were substantially more cytotoxic ex vivo than those from control tumours. Antibody-mediated neutrophil depletion attenuated the additional benefit conferred by P144 while leaving parental CAR-T activity largely intact, indicating that neutrophils contribute functionally to the effect. Local, CAR-T-delivered TGF{beta} blockade therefore remodels the mesothelioma TME and engages a tumoricidal neutrophil response, offering a modular strategy for enhancing adoptive cell therapy in desmoplastic solid tumours.

papers.title: Real-time reorienting during episodic retrieval rescues memories from suboptimal arousal-attentional states
papers.abstract: Successful knowledge expression varies with one's arousal-attentional (A-A) state at the moment just prior to attempting to remember. Yet, whether such states causally affect retrieval remains unclear. Here we introduce PRISM (Pupil-based Real-time Intervention System for Memory), a closed-loop paradigm that continuously monitors pupil size to track A-A states in real time and, during suboptimal states (SOS), delivers a visual reorienting cue in the moment before a retrieval attempt. In 67 participants performing a goal-directed source memory and item recognition task, we show that pupil-defined SOS just prior to retrieval impair both item recognition and source recollection relative to optimal state (OS) trials. Critically, delivering a brief visual reorienting trigger cue on SOS trials in real time rescues item memory, but not source memory, raising item memory to a level not credibly different from real-time OS trials and providing causal evidence that phasic attentional reorienting during A-A-defined suboptimal states facilitates memory access at retrieval. Offline spline-detrending analysis confirms that the A-A state-memory relationship is robust to slow physiological drift. It also shows that the trigger benefit was credible for marginally suboptimal (drift-driven) SOS trials and smaller and less certain for deeply suboptimal (drift-resistant) SOS trials, consistent with a zone-of-recoverability account, although the difference between the two SOS subtypes was not credible. Furthermore, among deeply suboptimal trials the A-A-boosting trigger cue improved memory for low-A-A SOS (i.e., pupillary constriction) but not high-A-A SOS (i.e., pupillary dilation) trials, consistent with the classic inverted-U relationship between arousal and performance, although the difference between the two directions was not credible. Together, these findings causally link phasic arousal-attentional reorienting at retrieval to memory rescue and suggest that the depth and direction of suboptimality shape whether such rescue succeeds, connecting the readiness-to-remember framework to the classic arousal-performance inverted-U relationship. Moreover, these findings provide a further foundation for adaptive closed-loop technologies that would tailor intervention to the depth and direction of momentary arousal-attentional states, facilitating memory expression in real time.

papers.title: Ultradeep optical coherence tomography
papers.abstract: Deep optical imaging of intact brain tissue is limited by scattering and absorption, restricting our ability to study subcortical structures. Here, we introduce ultradeep optical coherence tomography (OCT), which combines hardware and computational approaches to enhance the signal from deep tissue regions. Ultradeep OCT utilizes a longer illumination center wavelength of 1575 nm, spectral-domain balanced detection and imaging in the conjugate configuration with the zero optical path difference positioned deep in the tissue. Autocorrelation artifacts are measured and subtracted, and multiple frames are coherently averaged to improve the signal-to-noise ratio further. These techniques, along with computational refocusing and bandwidth control, allowed us to extend structural imaging depth in biological tissues. Ultradeep OCT demonstrated physical imaging depths of 2.3 to 2.8 mm (mean 2.5 mm) in the ex vivo mouse brain and 2.5 to 3.0 mm (mean 2.8 mm) in chicken tissue. The resulting volumes in the ex vivo mouse brain samples depict the dorsal hippocampus and its two major subregions with sufficient contrast to allow segmentation and three-dimensional reconstructions. Features in the thalamus could also be discerned. These findings demonstrate the potential of ultradeep OCT as a label-free approach for visualizing deep-brain structures at a spatial scale complementary to magnetic resonance imaging and microscopy. This approach could enable optical imaging studies of hippocampal structural changes in mouse models of neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: Establishing an assay for visual desensitization in larval zebrafish for understanding synaptic plasticity
papers.abstract: Synaptic plasticity, the ability of neurons to modify the strength of their connections, is essential for learning. Desensitization is a type of synaptic plasticity during which a behavioral response to a stimulus is reduced after repeated presentations of a weakened version of the stimulus which does not produce the behavioral response and thus is deemed a subthreshold stimulus. Here we explore whether the larval zebrafish escape response from visual threats, such as an expanding dark spot, can act as a potential model to study desensitization. We developed a novel experimental setup to investigate visual desensitization, exposing larvae to looming visual threats of varying contrast, and used high-speed cameras to verify rapid escape movements. First, we established stimuli which reliably acted as subthreshold and suprathreshold stimuli. Next, we quantified the response rate before and after desensitization and compared those data to control larvae who were not desensitized. We observed desensitized larvae reduced their response rate to threatening looming stimuli. By providing an opportunity to explore the plasticity mechanisms governing sensory-motor transformations and behavioral adaptation, this research contributes to our understanding of fundamental principles of learning and neural plasticity across vertebrates.

papers.title: Circuit regulation along an activity continuum shapes flexible and stable representations during learning
papers.abstract: Learning requires neural representations to flexibly incorporate new information while progressively stabilizing to support enduring memories. How neural circuits balance these demands remains unclear. Here, we identify complementary mechanisms supporting representational flexibility and stability in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), a key component of the cognitive map for memory-guided navigation. Longitudinal calcium imaging in mice learning novel virtual environments revealed a persistent axis of excitatory neuronal activity associated with distinct representational dynamics. Low-activity neurons exhibited intermittent activation that varied with learning stages and greater learning-dependent representational refinement, flexibly shifting their encoding from landmarks toward reward locations. By contrast, high-activity neurons exhibited more persistent activation and maintained more stable spatial representations. Dopaminergic pre-reward ramping was associated with the emergence of reward encoding in low-activity neurons, whereas interactions with inhibitory interneurons contributed to the stability of high-activity neurons. Notably, interneurons exhibited activity changes opposing those of excitatory neurons during learning, and their transient activation upon novelty exposure delayed excitatory representational remodeling, stabilization, and behavioral learning, suggesting that inhibitory circuits gate learning-dependent representational dynamics. Together, these findings reveal how activity-dependent excitatory neuronal organization and circuit-level regulation enable complementary forms of representational flexibility and stability to coexist, facilitating the incorporation of novel experiences into stable, context-specific cognitive maps that support learning.

papers.title: scSTEC: Annotating Chromatin Subcompartments from Individual Single-Cell Hi-C Data via Direct Two-Dimensional Embedding and Chromosome-wise Consensus
papers.abstract: \textbf{Motivation: }Single-cell Hi-C (scHi-C) technologies enable the study of three-dimensional (3D) genome organization at individual-cell resolution. Many computational methods have been developed to infer hierarchical structures from scHi-C data. However, annotating chromatin subcompartments from sparse scHi-C data remains a challenge. The recently developed scGHOST provides a framework for single-cell subcompartment annotation, but relies on a deep learning-based architecture, a multi-step upstream pipeline involving cell embedding and matrix imputation, and cross-cell information sharing. These features complicate algorithmic interpretation and make the annotation of an individual cell dependent on information from other cells in the dataset. Hence, methods are needed that annotate subcompartments directly from an individual cell's own contact matrix, without complex upstream processing or cross-cell information sharing. \textbf{Results: }We developed scSTEC, a computational framework that annotates subcompartments directly from an individual scHi-C matrix without data imputation, complex upstream processing, or cross-cell data sharing. We show that the estimated inter-chromosomal matrix constructed by scGHOST is intrinsically of rank 2, revealing that the geometry relevant to clustering can be represented in two dimensions. Leveraging this low-dimensional structure, scSTEC performs direct subcompartment annotation through 2D genomic embedding and chromosome-wise consensus. Across bulk Hi-C, downsampled simulations, and real scHi-C datasets (four human cell lines, adult mouse cortex, developing mouse embryos, and developing olfactory sensory neurons), scSTEC achieves subcompartment annotations comparable to scGHOST despite operating on each cell independently, while providing greater algorithmic interpretability. Furthermore, subcompartments identified by scSTEC effectively resolve cell types, capture developmental dynamics, and show consistent associations with gene expression and epigenetic profiles. \\textbf{Availability: }scSTEC is freely available at \url{https://github.com/Ge-lab-pku/scSTEC}.

papers.title: GFRAL neurons remodel intestinal structure and type 2 immunity
papers.abstract: The brain has emerged as a key regulator of immune functions, but the underlying neural mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here we show that brainstem GFRAL-expressing neurons prime type 2 immunity and shape intestinal epithelial structure in mice. Type 2 inflammation results in activation of GFRAL neurons and potentiation of their excitatory synaptic inputs. Enhancing GFRAL neuron excitability is sufficient to remodel intestinal type 2 immunity through a polysynaptic vagal brain-gut circuit, expanding tuft and goblet cell populations and increasing intestinal type 2 cytokine expression; while inhibiting GFRAL neurons leads to largely opposite changes. Accordingly, manipulating GFRAL neuron function reshapes intestinal structure and pathophysiology in food allergy, helminth infection and colitis models. Thus, GFRAL neurons orchestrate type 2 immune responses to facilitate recovery from intestinal diseases.

papers.title: CNVision: a computational framework for functional interpretation of intragenic copy number variants
papers.abstract: Background Intragenic copy number variants (CNVs), including exon-level deletions and duplications within a single gene, represent an important class of pathogenic genomic variation. Their functional consequences depend on the precise relationship between the CNV breakpoints, exon structure, coding sequence boundaries, transcript orientation, and reading frame. Although intragenic CNVs contribute substantially to Mendelian disease, their interpretation remains difficult because many existing workflows rely on manual transcript review or annotation pipelines that do not consistently resolve exon-level and base-pair-level consequences. Results We developed CNVision, a containerized computational framework for standardized interpretation of intragenic CNVs. CNVision accepts multiple input formats, including exon-based entries, genomic coordinates, and HGVS genomic notation, and converts each into a unified internal representation for transcript-aware analysis. The system maps CNVs to coding sequence regions, calculates affected coding sequence length at base-pair resolution, and classifies predicted reading-frame consequence. CNVision was evaluated using a dataset including 200 curated intragenic CNVs spanning multiple genes, genome builds, variant structures, and input types. Across the dataset, CNVision produced predictions concordant with manual transcript-level analysis and correctly processed exon-based, coordinate-based, and HGVS-formatted inputs. Beyond basic evaluation, CNVision also identified discrepancies in previously published CNVs. Of 131 reported CNVs evaluated, 15 yielded classifications that differed from the original published interpretation; independent manual transcript-level analysis using the UCSC Genome Browser supported CNVision's classification in all 15 variants, indicating the discrepancies were attributable to differences in transcript interpretation or coordinate calculation rather than computational error. In terms of processing speed, CNVision was tested by two board-certified laboratory geneticists who compared the runtime of CNVision versus manual analysis across 18 CNVs, 6 of each input type. CNVision consistently outperformed manual analysis by both geneticists across all variants by a significant margin. Conclusion CNVision provides a reproducible framework for functional interpretation of intragenic CNVs by automating input parsing, transcript mapping, coding sequence overlap calculation, and reading-frame classification. The framework reduces manual burden, improves consistency, and provides a foundation for future expansion into batch CNV processing and graphical variant interpretation.

papers.title: Noise-referenced multi-shell diffusion-weighted imaging for regional cerebrospinal fluid thermometry
papers.abstract: We developed a multi-shell diffusion-weighted imaging approach for separate ventricular and subarachnoid cerebrospinal fluid thermometry. The approach uses measured image noise to assess agreement among temperature estimates. In 12 participants, temperature was estimated from four non-zero diffusion weightings. For each voxel, disagreement between these estimates was compared with that expected from image noise, accounting for their shared reference image. Voxels meeting this consistency criterion were retained for regional analysis. Mean diffusion-derived temperature ({+/-} SD) was 38.4 {+/-} 0.4 {degrees}C in the lateral ventricles and 36.0 {+/-} 1.1 {degrees}C in the subarachnoid space. Ventricular estimates were consistently higher than subarachnoid estimates across all participants, with a mean difference of 2.4 {+/-} 1.2 {degrees}C (95% confidence interval 1.6 -3.1 {degrees}C). This difference persisted under alternative noise models and temperature estimators. Subarachnoid estimates increased with retained voxel count; in a post hoc analysis of the six participants with the largest retained counts, ventricular estimates remained higher by 1.6 {+/-} 0.7 {degrees}C. Absolute temperature accuracy and the physiological origin of the regional difference require independent validation. This approach provides an internal consistency check for CSF thermometry and supports separate assessment of ventricular and subarachnoid temperatures.

papers.title: NeuralFieldManifold: Uncovering the Manifold Geometry of Local Field Potentials
papers.abstract: Manifold geometry has become a powerful framework for understanding how the brain organizes high-dimensional neural activity into compact, interpretable structure. To date, however, most theoretical and methodological advances in neural manifold analysis have focused on spiking activity, leaving unresolved a fundamental question: What are the geometric principles governing the dynamics of local field potentials (LFPs); population level signals reflecting integrated subthreshold and suprathreshold neural activity that are broadly integral to clinical and brain-computer interface settings. Here, we establish, analytically and empirically, that the lag-embedded dynamics of LFP signals lie on a low-dimensional K-torus, where K directly relates to sustained oscillatory modes present in the signal. Modeling LFPs as bounded autoregressive processes, we show that each oscillatory component contributes an independent circular degree of freedom, while aperiodic 1/f structure and noise contribute only geometric thickness around the manifold without altering its topology. To apply this theory to real nonstationary recordings, we introduce DeepLagField, a physics-informed network that jointly estimates time-varying AR structure and effective model order, with formal guarantees that local toroidal geometry is preserved despite non-stationary nature of neuronal processes. Persistent homology analysis on real recordings reveals topological signatures consistent with the predicted toroidal Betti numbers in primate V1 LFP, rodent hippocampal LFP, and mouse cortical EEG, with varying degrees of agreement across recordings and temporal windows. Crucially, decoding analyses across three distinct neural datasets demonstrate that these geometric structures are not merely descriptive but capture behaviorally relevant information rivaling conventional spectral features. Together, these findings establish a theoretically grounded and empirically validated geometric framework for neural field analysis, extending the manifold perspective beyond spiking activity and offering a complementary language to spectral analysis for understanding and translating population dynamics across neural modalities.

papers.title: Serial intravascular labeling resolves dynamic decidual NK residency and gestational remodeling toward T-bet-Low states
papers.abstract: Decidual natural killer (dNK) cells are the predominant immune population at the maternal-fetal interface during early pregnancy. However, how vascular trafficking, tissue residency, proliferation, and apoptosis-associated activity are coordinated to establish and maintain the dNK population throughout pregnancy remains unclear. We hypothesized that gestational remodeling of the dNK compartment reflects coordinated changes in these cellular processes in association with progressive T-bet downregulation. We combined serial intravascular labeling (SIVL), flow cytometry, BrdU incorporation, active caspase-3 detection, spatial imaging, and Tbx21 fate mapping to examine NK cells in virgin mice and across gestation. Pregnancy altered CD49a/CD49b-defined dNK-cell composition and redistributed dNK cells among SIVL-defined vascular-accessibility states, supporting a model of dynamic dNK-cell tissue residency. Trafficking-associated marker scores displayed continuous gradients of tissue retention, circulatory/egress potential, and chemokine responsiveness rather than defining a single resident state. Spatial imaging demonstrated greater dNK-cell density in the mesometrial decidua and preferential CD31 vessel contact by recently intravascular dNK cells during early and mid-gestation. BrdU incorporation and active caspase-3 positivity peaked during early pregnancy and varied across SIVL-defined states. Tbx21 fate mapping identified a progressive and selective shift from current T-bet expression toward ex-T-bet and non-fate-mapped Eomes dNK states. T-bet-low states preferentially maintained proliferation at mid-gestation, whereas current T-bet expression was associated with greater circulatory/egress potential. However, active caspase-3 was not selectively increased in current T-bet-expressing cells. Collectively, these findings identify pregnancy-induced dNK-cell remodeling as a coordinated process integrating dynamic tissue residency, vascular accessibility, local proliferation, and apoptosis-associated activity, alongside a progressive shift toward T-bet-low dNK states.

papers.title: LabWeaver: reliable agentic data analysis grounded in laboratory knowled
papers.abstract: Agentic systems powered by large language models are rapidly automating biological data analysis. However, their reliability remains questionable because they often overlook experimental context, such as disease domain and experimental protocol. Existing agentic systems organize context around individual users and projects, whereas research is organized around laboratories whose projects share experimental context. As a result, experimental context learned in one project remains unavailable to related projects. We introduce LabWeaver, an agentic data analysis framework with a laboratory-organized architecture of three tiers: laboratory, user and project. Further, LabWeaver distills experimental context into laboratory memory and skills, which are shared across users and projects after human-gated review. To isolate the contribution of experimental context, we analyzed a synovial sarcoma single-cell RNA-seq dataset in two sessions that differed only in whether laboratory memory and skills were available. The context-free session lost the fusion reporter at read alignment and misannotated the tumor cells. In contrast, the context-enabled session recovered reporter expression and resolved five fusion-anchored tumor cell states.

papers.title: A mouse model of metastasis-induced breast cancer cachexia with non-cachectic controls bearing isogenic primary tumors
papers.abstract: Background Patients with advanced cancer frequently develop cachexia, an involuntary weight-loss condition that correlates strongly with metastatic burden. Despite this clinical association, metastasis is rarely considered in preclinical research of cancer cachexia, which is in part due to the lack of rigorously established animal models to investigate metastasis-associated cancer cachexia. Methods To establish an animal model of metastasis-associated cancer cachexia, here we focused on syngeneic mouse models of breast cancer. Using the metastatic 4T1 murine breast cancer cell line and its isogenic non-metastatic 67NR cell line, we generated primary tumors via orthotopic injection into the mammary fat pad and surgically resected the primary tumor to allow sufficient time for spontaneous metastatic outgrowth, or generated experimental lung metastases by direct intravenous injection into the tail vein. Across these tumor-bearing groups, we systematically characterized the metastatic burden and cachectic phenotypes of the mice, including body weight, food intake, body composition, muscle mass, grip strength, locomotor activity, energy expenditure, and respiratory exchange ratio. To isolate the contribution of reduced food intake to the cachectic phenotypes, we pair-fed orthotopic 4T1 tumor-bearing mice (which were non-cachectic) to mice with 4T1 lung metastases (which were cachectic). We further measured muscle atrophy gene expression and profiled circulating cytokines and metabolic hormones for the mouse groups. Results Body weight loss occurred exclusively in mice bearing lung metastases from 4T1 tumors, with no weight loss observed in mice bearing either primary 4T1 tumors or 67NR lung tumors, thus presenting a model of cancer cachexia that is driven by 4T1 lung metastasis. Comprehensive cachexia characterization demonstrated that the 4T1 metastasis model recapitulates all key features of cachexia, manifesting as reduced food intake (or anorexia), depletion of adipose tissues, loss of lean mass including muscle mass loss, and reduced grip strength. Pair-feeding non-cachectic primary 4T1 tumor-bearing mice to 4T1 metastatic mice led to the same losses in body weight, fat, and lean mass as in cachectic mice, but no change in grip strength, indicating that anorexia is the primary driver of tissue wasting whereas muscle weakness arises through a food intake-independent mechanism. Moreover, we identified distinct circulating cytokines and metabolic hormones associated with the metastasis-driven cachexia. Conclusions Our results establish a metastasis-induced breast cancer cachexia model with a tightly matched control group, providing a platform for the field to identify metastasis-derived cachectic mediators and pathways.

papers.title: Graph neural network approach for inferring neuronal connectivity
papers.abstract: Understanding the connectivity of neuronal networks is essential for understanding brain function. Current anatomical mapping techniques, such as serial section microscopy and viral tracing, are resource-intensive and cannot capture the efficacy of connectivity. A complementary approach is to infer effective connectivity from single-neuron-resolution population activity. We developed a graph neural network (GNN)-based tool, CircuitGNN, that accurately infers neural effective connectivity from population activity. CircuitGNN accurately inferred the connectivity of several small circuits and detected both the strengthening and weakening of connections, such as those that occur during learning. CircuitGNN outperformed other methods when applied to simulated population activity generated by an invertebrate central pattern-generating circuit and a cortical microcircuit. CircuitGNN was evaluated on networks of varying size, recording duration, and proportion of hidden neurons. Although performance improved with longer recordings, CircuitGNN achieved high precision with recordings as short as 4 min, scaled to large circuits of up to ~750 neurons, and remained robust when 20% or 40% of neurons were hidden. These results establish CircuitGNN as an accurate and robust technique for inferring neural connectivity from activity.

papers.title: SCN- induces prestin contraction through reduced intermonomer angles and a modified transporter like movement of each monomer.
papers.abstract: Prestin is the membrane based molecular motor responsible for outer hair cell electromotility that expands and contracts in response to transmembrane voltage. How voltage brings these about is unknown but cryoEM structures in the presence of ligands has led to the extrapolation of structures with the transporter cycle and its expansion contraction coupling. We find prestin to adopt novel increasingly contracted states that are brought about by a reduced intermonomer angles in the obligate dimers and a transmembrane contraction of each monomer at its cytoplasmic half in the presence of SCN-. These changes are associated with a loss in the intermonomer beta sheet at its N terminus. There is a hyperpolarizing shift in Vh along with increased affinity for SCN-. SCN- binding at the internal binding site likely cause the structural changes since they are reversed by SCN- displacement by salicylate.

papers.title: AI-based structural modelling and pathogenic variant mapping across the human protein interactome
papers.abstract: Spanning the complex landscape of the human proteome, physical interactions between proteins coordinate cellular organization, signaling, regulation, and homeostasis. Yet the three-dimensional structures of most of these interactions remain unresolved. Here, we performed AI-based modelling of 109,282 human protein interaction structures, generating a structural resource for large-scale analysis. The predicted structures were systematically characterized through analysis of interface residue involvement, buried surface area, intermolecular bonding, and energetic properties. Additionally, we mapped pathogenic variant data onto the predicted structures, identifying interface-localized mutations for over 4,000 annotated disease categories. Acute myeloid leukemia, Alzheimer's disease, and cardiomyopathy were examined as representative disease contexts for exploring the distribution of interface mutations within disease-associated protein interaction networks. Strengths and limitations of predictive capabilities were also assessed, including through experimental structure comparisons. Collectively, this structural resource and accompanying analyses offer a basis for developing novel hypotheses and informing experimental studies involving human protein interactions in physiological and disease contexts.

papers.title: Imipramine binds to amyloid-β and extends the survival of Alzheimer's disease patients
papers.abstract: Background Apolipoprotein E (apoE) plays numerous roles in the pathogenic pathway to Alzheimer's disease (AD). We previously performed a high-throughput screen and identified the antidepressant imipramine as an inhibitor of the interaction between apoE and amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}). We also found that imipramine use to treat depression in AD patients was associated with better Mini-Mental State Exam (MMSE) scores. Here we studied the mechanisms by which imipramine inhibits the AD pathogenic pathway and investigated its effect on mortality in AD patients. Methods Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy was used to characterize the interaction between imipramine and A{beta} monomers. Human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived AD cerebral organoids (COs) and transgenic AD rats treated with imipramine underwent neuropathological evaluation, while rat learning and memory were assessed in the Morris Water Maze. AD patient mortality in the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center's database was analyzed by Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards models. Results Imipramine inhibits the apoE-A{beta} interaction by binding directly to A{beta} monomers. Imipramine reduces A{beta} accumulation and neuronal cell loss in AD COs. Imipramine-treated female AD rats had enhanced reference memory and increased hippocampal cellularity and cholinergic neurotransmission. AD patients prescribed imipramine had reduced all-cause mortality over 10 years relative to those prescribed other tricyclic antidepressants (TCA), non-TCA antidepressants, or no antidepressants. Conclusions The findings support the conclusions that: a) the mechanism by which apoE confers risk for AD is by catalyzing the polymerization of A{beta} into neurotoxic species, b) targeting apoE is a promising, underappreciated strategy for the prevention of AD, c) imipramine should be used more frequently to treat depression in AD clinical practice, and d) imipramine should be evaluated in prospective trials, particularly in APOE4 carriers, as a potential method to improve cognition and reduce mortality in AD.

papers.title: Protein Pocket Coengagement Prioritizes Drug-Drug Interactions
papers.abstract: Drug-drug interactions (DDIs) are largely catalogued empirically, with limited structural explanation of why two drugs interact. We asked whether a purely structural mechanism - competing or cooperating engagement of the same protein pocket - is sufficient to recover documented DDIs without any training on clinical interaction labels. Using composite protein multiple-ligand (COLIG) assignments, which classify co-bound ligand pairs as attractive or repulsive, we scored 21,945 pairs of 210 drugs by predicted engagement of each proteins top-ranked pocket. Confidence-summed COLIG ranking achieved top-5% precision of 49.3% against DDInter and 25.1% against KEGG, versus background prevalences of 29.6% and 14.7%, respectively; pooled top-pocket engagement reached 50.3% DDInter precision. These results support pocket-based DDI screening and class-dependent hypotheses about direct and noncontact ligand engagement, while leaving causal mechanisms to be established.

papers.title: Phylogeny-Guided Global-Local Shrinkage for Microbiome Feature Selection
papers.abstract: Microbiome feature selection is challenging because sequencing counts are sparseand compositional, while evolutionarily related taxa may exhibit similar associations with an exposure. We propose phylogeny-guided global--local shrinkage (PGL), a Bayesian regression method for identifying exposure-associated differences in the relative abundances of individual amplicon sequence variants (ASVs). A multinomial logit-normal working model analyzes relative abundance among ASVs detected in each sample. A zero-sum constraint gives the regression coefficients a log-ratio interpretation relative to the mean across retained ASVs. Global--local shrinkage accommodates weak and large associations, while an estimated weight controls information sharing along a supplied phylogenetic tree. Simulation ablation studies showed that phylogenetic borrowing improved detection power and estimation of nonzero coefficients when associations aligned with the tree, with little change under a tree-independent generator. Estimated borrowing decreased as the supplied tree was corrupted. Comparisons with benchmark methods revealed different trade-offs between detection power and false discovery rates across simulation settings. In an HIV oral microbiome application, ablation analysis showed that phylogenetic borrowing preserved the overall pattern of estimated associations while changing posterior uncertainty and selecting three additional ASVs. PGL provides ASV-level inference with adaptive information sharing across evolutionarily related features.

papers.title: Effects Of Lymphocyte Trafficking on Antiretroviral Drug Distribution within the Lymph Node
papers.abstract: The lymph node (LN) lobule is physically isolated by selective transport barriers, including high endothelial venules and sinusoidal endothelium, that restrict free diffusion of many antiretroviral (ARV) drugs used to treat HIV, especially non-lipophilic compounds. Recent spatial pharmacokinetic analyses have suggested that passive diffusion alone cannot explain observed ARV concentrations in lymphoid tissues, raising the possibility that lymphocytes may act as incidental drug carriers. To investigate the relative contributions of free and cell-mediated drug trafficking, we conducted murine experiments in which drug was delivered intravenously to a murine model, with lymphocyte entry into the lobule blocked by a functional antibody. The experimental results show that blocking lymphocyte entry into the LN increases raw intracellular drug concentration within the LN for tenofovir and efavirenz, but not raltegravir. To understand the mechanism behind this observation, we developed a computational transport model. The model consists of a mechanistic physiologically based pharmacokinetic framework with four compartments: plasma, peripheral blood mononuclear cells, LN extracellular fluid, and LN intracellular space, while dynamically accounting for changes in LN extracellular fluid volume driven by lymphocyte trafficking. Our simulations predicted that blocking lymphocyte trafficking increases extracellular fluid volume and, counterintuitively, elevates intracellular drug concentration within the LN, with the effect size depending on the drug's intracellular equilibration kinetics. Raltegravir, which equilibrates rapidly between extracellular and intracellular compartments, is insensitive to this mechanism, a model prediction confirmed by the experimental null result. In conclusion, our study identifies extracellular fluid volume dynamics within the lymph node as a previously unrecognized, drug class-dependent modulator of intranodal ARV distribution. This mechanism operates independently of barrier-level penetration and has direct implications for drug efficacy in patients with altered immune trafficking.

papers.title: DEEPNET-LLM: Highly accurate structure prediction of unknown metabolites from mass spectra via their molecular neighborhoods
papers.abstract: Most molecular features detected by untargeted mass spectrometry-based metabolomics remain unannotated. This so-called 'dark matter' currently comprises more than 90% and likely holds uncharacterized bioactive chemistry. Structure prediction from fragmentation spectra remains an outstanding challenge, because a spectrum does not uniquely determine a structure and the space of candidate structures is mostly unbounded; correspondingly, existing methods rarely return the correct de novo structure as their top prediction. Here we describe De novo Ego network-Enabled Propagation and Neighborhood Extrapolation of Topology using Large Language Models (DEEPNET-LLM) reasoning approach, which uses Molecular Community Networking (MCN) to restrict the search of a query spectrum to its local neighborhood within the global metabolome, and applies AI reasoning to propagate structural information from neighbors to the query. For a collection of 900 authentic standards (2,249 spectra) that have never been publicly released to exclude possibility of data leakage, DEEPNET-LLM returned the correct structure as its top prediction for 84.7% of spectra. Accuracy was independent of precursor mass across a range over which the number of candidate structures grows by 30 orders of magnitude, and was comparable across ion polarity, adducts and in-source fragmentation. On a random subset of the public MassSpecGym benchmark, DEEPNET-LLM reached 85.9% top-1 accuracy excluding stereochemistry. We showcase the use of DEEPNET-LLM with an example of a discovery of tryptamine amidate of a bile acid in mouse gut, confirmed against a synthetic standard. The DEEPNET-LLM approach is orthogonal to existing in silico methods and can be combined with them.

papers.title: Caudate nucleus aging and its association with brain disorders
papers.abstract: The caudate nucleus supports cognition and goal-directed behavior, undergoes age-associated changes, and is implicated in substance use, psychiatric, and neurodegenerative disorders. However, how aging alters its diverse cell types and how such changes relate to diseases remains poorly understood. To address these questions, we assembled single nucleus transcriptomic atlases of the caudate tissue, comprising 963,842 nuclei from 178 human donors, including controls and individuals with alcohol use disorder (AUD) or opioid use disorder (OUD), and 83,699 nuclei from six healthy rhesus macaques. We also curated 3,139 bulk RNA-seq profiles from the caudate and other brain regions spanning controls and multiple diagnostic groups, as well as paired RNA and chromatin accessibility profiles from 257,524 caudate nuclei across 161 control and AUD donors. These datasets enabled comparisons across age, species, brain regions, and diagnostic groups. We found shared glial aging features in humans and macaques, whereas neuronal changes were more divergent. Inferred neuron-to-neuron communication declined with age, with greater declines in AUD. Both transcriptional and chromatin accessibility profiles showed nonlinear age-associated patterns, with pronounced changes in later adulthood. In donors with AUD, age-associated changes appeared earlier, with altered trajectories in lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function, and neuronal signaling. Across comparisons involving AUD, OUD, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and Alzheimer disease, mitochondrial function and fatty acid metabolism emerged as consensus features linking caudate aging to diseases, although the direction and extent of overlap varied by disorder and brain region. Together, these findings define cellular and regulatory features of primate caudate aging and reveal shared and context-dependent relationships between aging and brain disorders.

papers.title: Circadian multimodal physiological, ocular and behavioural data from a 40-hour forced-desynchrony protocol
papers.abstract: We present a multimodal dataset from twelve healthy adults (aged 19-30 years, 50% female) who completed a 40-hour ultra-short sleep-wake forced desynchrony protocol which scheduled 2 h 30 min of wakefulness in dim light and 1 h 15 min of sleep in darkness (2:1 wake:sleep ratio), with the protocol ending after the last wake period. This schedule compressed the typical 24-hour day into an ultradian 3 h 45 min cycle to decouple circadian and homeostatic influences on physiology and behaviour. During each wake interval, participants completed repeated assessments of visual psychophysics (chromatic temporal contrast sensitivity), pupillometry with silent-substitution stimuli, ocular structure (optical coherence tomography) and physiology (intraocular pressure), psychomotor vigilance, salivary hormones, and standardised questionnaires, alongside continuous actigraphy, electrocardiography, and recordings of core and peripheral temperature, blood pressure, and interstitial glucose. Two supplementary evening sessions under experimental light exposure and dim-light conditions provide comparison data on circadian phase (salivary melatonin concentration, dim-light melatonin onset). Data collected from one pilot participant and screenings of two excluded candidates are additionally included. This dataset supports reuse for investigating circadian dynamics across multiple domains beyond the retinal-function hypotheses of the original study.

papers.title: Discovery of P1-P2 depeptidized boronic acid based Plasmodium falciparum SUB1 inhibitor
papers.abstract: The Plasmodium falciparum subtilisin-like serine protease 1 (PfSUB1) is an essential enzyme required for parasite egress from host red blood cells and represents a promising target for antimalarial drugs. Peptidic boronic acids are potent reported PfSUB1 inhibitors, however their drug-likeness is limited by their pronounced peptidic character. Based on molecular docking studies using peptidic boronic acids, we designed a series of partially depeptidized PfSUB1 inhibitors by replacing the P1-P2 dipeptide fragment with a 3-aminomethylphenylboronic acid core. Structure-activity relationship (SAR) investigations targeting interaction with active-site residue Lys138 revealed that introducing a meta-carboxylate group (compound 3a) markedly enhanced inhibitory activity, yielding a low-nanomolar PfSUB1 inhibitor (IC50= 10.2 nM). Bioisosteric replacement of the carboxylic acid demonstrated that an N-acylsulfonamide group (compound 4k) retained high enzymatic potency (IC50= 13.5 nM)). In cellular assays against blood-stage P. falciparum (3D7 strain), the leading depeptidized boronic acids exhibited growth inhibition with values in the low-micromolar range suggesting that further structural modifications are needed to enhance membrane permeability across host and parasite membranes to reach exonemes prior to egress. Overall, this study validates the P1-P2 depeptidization of boronic acid scaffolds and provides key SAR insights for the rational design of non-peptidic PfSUB1-targeted antimalarials.

papers.title: A medial entorhinal connectome reveals compartmentalized microcircuit architecture
papers.abstract: The medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) transforms multimodal inputs into spatial representations, but the synaptic architecture underlying its computations remains unclear. Here we generated a synapse-resolution connectomic dataset spanning all six layers of mouse MEC and the adjacent parasubiculum with serial electron microscopy, providing a continuous volume for mapping cellular organization and connectivity across layers and regions. We found that clustered pyramidal neurons in MEC layer II extended oblique apical dendrites with a dorsolateral bias and long-range myelinated axons within the layer. Exhaustive reconstruction of one cluster revealed a central exclusion core (ExC) that spatially partitioned basal dendritic architecture and synaptic connectivity. A spatially constrained growth model reproduced the position-dependent dendritic patterns. Within the ExC, pyramidal neurons formed a compact recurrent excitatory network and converged onto shared inhibitory partners. Basket cells (BC) and recurrent Martinotti cells provided perisomatic and apical-dendritic feedback, respectively. Dense, compact reciprocal connectivity between L2P neurons and BCs within the ExC, together with BC axonal bands extending beyond the ExC, suggests a potential circuit mechanism for generating temporally structured inhibitory output from the pyramidal-cell cluster along directionally extended axons. Together, these findings link cellular-scale geometry and synaptic wiring to emergent circuit dynamics that extend from dense computation within individual clusters to region-wide modulation, providing a connectomic foundation for understanding the circuit basis of spatial navigation.

papers.title: ssGSEA3.0: Feature-Level Bootstrap Resampling for Robust Assessment of Statistical Significance
papers.abstract: Motivation Single-sample Gene/Post-Translational Modification Set Enrichment Analysis (ssGSEA/PTM-SEA) methods assess pathway or signature activity per sample using permutation-based significance testing. ssGSEA2.0's weighted scoring (ssGSEA2.0-orig) uses a correlation-vector reordering that inflates false positives at nonzero weight; directly fixing this (ssGSEA2.0-fixed) restores null-distribution calibration but sacrifices detection power at nonzero weight. Results ssGSEA3.0 replaces feature-label (gene- or site-level) permutation with feature-level bootstrap resampling, which remains calibrated across weighting schemes. On published lung adenocarcinoma and phosphoproteomic perturbation datasets, ssGSEA3.0 shows greater detection power than ssGSEA2.0-fixed, with an additional gain for directional (PTM-SEA) scoring. Previously published findings remain robust across methods, including at nonzero weight. Bootstrapping adds a ~1.5- to 2-fold computational cost. Availability and Implementation ssGSEA3.0 is implemented as an open-source R package (github.com/broadinstitute/ssGSEA3.0, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23734262) and includes the worked examples on biological data presented here.

papers.title: Identification of Cryptococcus neoformans capsule-associated protein antigens that mediate B cell-dependent vaccine protection in mice and elicit antibody responses in humans with cryptococcosis
papers.abstract: Infection with the encapsulated fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans causes substantial global disease burden in persons with compromised T cell function. Previously, we demonstrated that vaccines containing adjuvanted recombinant cryptococcal proteins protected mice against lethal infection by mechanisms dependent on CD4+ T cells. For the present study, we hypothesized that vaccines containing protein antigens naturally located on the surface of the cryptococcal capsule would contribute protective B cell responses. We found that B cell-deficient mice exhibited reduced survival following vaccination with any of four capsule-associated antigens: Blp4, Cpd1, Lhc1, or Krp1. To further elucidate the role of antibodies in protection, we tested serum from mice vaccinated with a live-attenuated strain (cda123) and then challenged with a virulent C. neoformans strain for IgG responses to a panel of 26 cryptococcal recombinant proteins. Strong reactivity was detected against Blp4, which we focused on because it is capsule-associated and protects mice when administered in adjuvanted subunit vaccines, by mechanisms partly dependent on B cells. Blp4 antibodies were consistently present in surviving mice, including those vaccinated with unrelated proteins or those challenged with diverse clinical isolates. Additionally, serum from Blp4-vaccinated mice promoted macrophage opsonophagocytosis of C. neoformans. Finally, IgG antibodies against Blp4 were detected in 20 of 21 serum samples from patients who survived cryptococcosis, compared with only 4 of 14 samples from healthy controls. Together, these data identify Blp4 as an antigen that elicits protective B cell responses and is a strong candidate for inclusion in subunit cryptococcal vaccines.

papers.title: Agentic Discovery Transfer Enables Cross-Cancer Discovery at Scale
papers.abstract: Cancer research generates tens of thousands of studies each year, yet whether a published finding holds in another cancer type or patient population is rarely tested as doing so is labor-intensive and difficult to scale. We define this task as discovery transfer and present SMART, a multi-agent large language model framework for discovery transfer in single-cell RNA-sequencing studies. Given a source manuscript and a target dataset, SMART extracts major clinical and mechanistic findings, generates and executes analyses for the testable findings, reports which findings transfer, and suggests follow-up. Applied to 121 studies across six cancer types, SMART identified findings that transfer across cancers, including a lung cancer prognostic signature that we confirmed to be associated with survival in liver cancer, pancreatic cancer and pleural mesothelioma. SMART also generated new mechanistic hypotheses, demonstrating how agentic discovery transfer can extend published findings beyond their original setting.

papers.title: Gentamicin impairs nephron development in iPSC-derived kidney organoids and disrupts proximal tubular lysosomal function
papers.abstract: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic used to treat Gram-negative bacterial infections. However, its clinical use is limited by nephrotoxicity, affecting approximately 10 - 20% of treated patients. Nevertheless, gentamicin remains widely used due to its high potency, low cost, and low incidence of bacterial resistance and hypersensitivity. Importantly, gentamicin crosses the placental barrier and is administered to neonates, including preterm infants in whom nephrogenesis is still ongoing, raising concerns about its effects on kidney development. Current knowledge of this risk relies largely on rodent studies, which fail to fully recapitulate human kidney physiology. Here, we developed human-relevant in vitro models to investigate the impact of gentamicin on kidney development and to unravel the dynamic cellular responses underlying gentamicin-induced impairment. Kidney organoids differentiated from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC) and magnetically sorted proximal tubule cells were used to model immature kidney and immature proximal cells, respectively. Organoids were continuously exposed to gentamicin (0.25 - 1.5 mM) throughout development (d7+18), while megalin-expressing proximal tubule cells were exposed for 24 hours to explore the cellular mechanisms underlying gentamicin toxicity. Intracellular concentrations of the gentamicin congeners C1, C1a, and C2/C2a/C2b were quantified by LC-MS/MS. Gentamicin exposure impaired organoid growth, and nephron formation and maturation. Additionally, gentamicin induced lipid accumulation and reduced lysosomal area in proximal tubule cells, indicating disrupted cellular metabolism and homeostasis. In conclusion, iPSC-derived kidney organoids provide a suitable platform to further investigate gentamicins impact on kidney development and studying co-treatments to mitigate its adverse effects.

papers.title: Role of the gut microbiota in the remodelling of the jejunal, colonic, hepatic and blood proteomes in a mouse model of Anorexia Nervosa
papers.abstract: Background: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a typical form of eating disorder characterized by a severe body weight loss, a fear of gaining weight and dysmorphophobia. This disorder is associated with both psychiatric comorbidities and multi-organ dysfunctions. Increasing evidence suggests a role of the gut microbiota in the onset or maintenance of AN. Although a dysbiosis has been reported in patients with AN, the physiological consequences of this dysbiosis remain poorly documented. To gain further insight into the role of the gut microbiota in the pathophysiology of AN, we used the murine Activity-based Anorexia (ABA) model and compared the remodelling of the jejunal, colonic, hepatic and blood proteomes occurring in male mice with intact gut microbiota, as well as in gut microbiota-depleted animals. Results: We observed a significant proteome remodelling in several organs in response to the ABA model. More than 250 proteins involved in energy metabolism, catabolic processes, lipid metabolism, ghrelin regulation, and immune functions were found to show altered abundance in ABA mice compared to control mice. We observed in addition in the blood of ABA mice a significant increase in the level of circulating proteasome. By comparing mice treated or not with antibiotics, we identified 75 proteins whose regulation in ABA mice is gut-microbiota dependent. The other identified proteins were similarly affected in ABA mice with intact or depleted gut microbiota, suggesting that these factors are mainly regulated by food starvation and physical activity, and not directly by the gut microbiota. We finally confirmed that ORM2, a protein identified as significantly decreased in the plasma of ABA mice, is also decreased in the blood of patients suffering from AN. Conclusion: Our results demonstrate that the Activity-Based Anorexia model is associated with an extensive proteome remodelling in several organs and tissues. We highlight in addition that some of these targets are regulated in a gut microbiota-dependent manner, thereby reinforcing the hypothesis of a role of the gut microbiota in Anorexia Nervosa. Together, our study provides a valuable resource to better delineate the impact of undernutrition and maladaptive physical activity on the proteome of various organs and the role of the gut bacteria in the pathophysiology of Anorexia Nervosa.

papers.title: Spatial transcriptomics of pediatric tuberculosis lymph nodes reveals a conserved hypoxia_SPP1 niche
papers.abstract: Pediatric tuberculosis (TB) often presents as primary disease involving the mediastinal lymph nodes; however, its granuloma microenvironment remains poorly characterized because these population patient tissues are rarely available for study. Here, we use spatial transcriptomics to profile 60 granulomas from four children aged 4 to 36 months. We identified nine recurrent transcriptional microenvironments shared across granulomas, despite their marked histological heterogeneity. One macrophage-rich microenvironment showed strong hypoxia-associated activity and secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1) enrichment. This microenvironment was present in both non-necrotic and necrotic lesions and overlapped with a Mtb-persistence macrophage signature previously identified in murine TB lymph nodes. Pathway analysis revealed the enrichment of both antimicrobial and regulatory programs within this microenvironment, suggesting partial immune control rather than uniform inflammatory or suppressive activity in this region. SPP1 expression was associated with regions enriched for both M1- and M2-like macrophages, suggesting a macrophage program that extends beyond conventional polarization classifications and may be influenced by the local granuloma microenvironment. We further observed a similar spatial association between hypoxia-associated activity and SPP1 expression in an independent adult TB dataset (pooled Spearman {rho}=0.65) and validated this association at protein level by multiplex immunofluorescence in our pediatric TB granuloma sample. Overall, this study identified a hypoxia-associated SPP1-enriched microenvironment that may contribute to incomplete bacterial clearance and could provide a framework for evaluating host-directed strategies to enhance sterilizing immunity without exacerbating tissue damage.

papers.title: Oligodendrocyte precursor cell death does not contribute to lifelong population homeostasis
papers.abstract: Oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) proliferate and differentiate into myelinating oligodendrocytes throughout life, but it is unclear if their continuous self-renewal is balanced by cell death. We find that OPCs do not die during development or adulthood, nor during remyelination, acute systemic inflammation, or aging. These findings challenge the assumption that spontaneous OPC death is common and reveal that OPC homeostasis does not depend on programmed cell death.

papers.title: Multi-scale place fields provide a predictive basis for hierarchical control
papers.abstract: Hippocampal place cells typically exhibit unimodal spatial selectivity in small enclosures, but express multiple, irregularly spaced fields in environments of naturalistic scale. However, existing predictive-map theories of the hippocampus do not scale well to large environments and do not account for these heterogeneous place field characteristics. Here, we introduce the factorised hierarchical successor representation (fHSR), a predictive map that supports hierarchical control using subgoal-directed subroutines. We show that the fHSR allows efficient generalisation across tasks, scaling favourably with environmental size, and it reproduces key statistical and topological characteristics of multi-scale CA1 place cell activity in rats and bats. Analyses of experimental data further confirmed a novel prediction of the fHSR: population firing rates exhibit spatial periodicity with a characteristic wavelength independent of environmental size. These results identify the integration of hierarchical control and predictive representations as a normative principle that unifies efficient navigation with the spatial organisation of hippocampal activity.

papers.title: Optimizing non-invasive assessment of gastric activity: a fully automated channel-wise pipeline for multi-electrode electrogastrography
papers.abstract: Electrogastrography (EGG) is a non-invasive, and affordable technique for investigating gastric physiology. However, its broader adoption is hindered by low signal-to-noise ratios and the lack of standardized, objective procedures for channel-wise artifact rejection and signal quality assessment. To address these limitations, we developed a fully automated, data-driven pipeline (Gastric Signal Processing Toolbox, GSPT) for channel-wise EGG preprocessing and analysis, designed to preserve physiologically-relevant information even under high-noise conditions. GSPT exploits high-resolution time-frequency representations, to automatically identify and remove motion-related and electronic artifacts through entropy-based analysis of the signal's instantaneous energy and robust outlier detection through integration of multiple anomaly-detection strategies. The resulting signals are characterized through a channel-wise gastric fingerprint, comprising established EGG measures, such as dominant frequency, together with novel descriptors such as Renyi entropy. Channel quality relays on Monte Carlo surrogate analysis, while recording-level quality is evaluated through dominant frequency consistency across channels. GSPT further provides ridge-based estimates of instantaneous amplitude and phase and quantifies inter-channel interactions through Total Correlation, enabling the construction of a global gastric fingerprint. Validation on datasets containing controlled motion artifacts demonstrated robust signal recovery with improved signal-to-noise ratios at the dominant frequency. Artifact identification, assessed using precision and recall, was comparable or better than existing approaches. Gastric fingerprints showed high stability within subjects and across recording sessions. As a freely available, one-click MATLAB toolbox, GSPT reduces manual bias and standardizes EGG preprocessing and analysis, even in low-density recordings, potentially providing a reproducible framework for investigating gastric functions in psychological, neurological and pathological conditions.

papers.title: Ark-ADMET: endpoint-specific selection of molecular representations and hyperparameters for gradient-boosted ADMET models under the Therapeutics Data Commons benchmark protocol
papers.abstract: Typical submissions to the Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC) absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) benchmark leaderboard apply a single architecture and a single feature representation across all 22 endpoints, despite substantial heterogeneity in evaluation metric, training-set size, and class balance. Rather than proposing a new architecture, we show that endpoint-specific selection of molecular representations and CatBoost hyperparameters, carried out under the official TDC ADMET benchmark protocol, is a competitive alternative to that uniform recipe. For each endpoint, a fixed CatBoost backbone was paired with configurations chosen from a common candidate set comprising published fingerprints and physicochemical descriptors, truncated three-dimensional PaDEL descriptors, frozen graph isomorphism network (GIN) and MiniMol embeddings, and a convex combination with a shallow network trained on the MiniMol embedding alone. All feature and hyperparameter choices were made on an internal scaffold validation split under a prespecified strict-improvement rule. Against a frozen snapshot of the public leaderboard, the resulting Ark-ADMET family of 22 endpoint-specific models matched or exceeded the best previously listed score on 7 of 21 rankable endpoints and strictly exceeded it on 3. All selected configurations retain the baseline fingerprint-and-descriptor block; optional components differ across endpoints.
