In northern pike, which lacks this duplication, cyp27b1 was not detected in the kidney either. The catabolic enzyme cyp24a1 was only weakly expressed in the kidney and the head kidney. These transcript data suggest that vitamin D3 activation in Atlantic salmon may not depend on renal cyp27b1 expression under the conditions sampled, and that albumins or lipoproteins may carry vitamin D metabolites. Both hypotheses need to be tested with protein, enzyme activity, and metabolite measurements. The curated gene set provides a basis for studies of vitamin D3 metabolism and dietary vitamin D3 requirements in salmonids.

papers.title: Striatal and frontal signatures of social context and cost-benefit decision making in developmental stuttering
papers.abstract: Developmental stuttering is usually framed as a sensorimotor disorder, yet it manifests in communicative situations that engage motivational, self-referential, and regulatory processes. In this case-control study, we combined a socio-economic decision task outside the scanner with a socially modulated speech task during functional MRI to test how listener presence and self-referential speech shape neural activity in 34 adults who stutter and 32 controls. Both groups valued talking with another person about themselves more than talking with another person about someone else or talking to themselves. On the neural level, listener-directed (vs. private) speech and self-disclosure (vs. guessing the preferences of a famous other) elicited stronger responses in the ventral striatum and medial prefrontal cortex, with no significant group differences in the central listener-directed versus private contrast. Within the stuttering group, individual differences revealed a systematic reweighting of socially modulated activation as a function of symptom burden: higher anticipation of stuttering and greater self-reported impact of stuttering on everyday life were associated with stronger engagement of motivational circuitry, greater recruitment of frontal evaluative-control regions, and reduced contextual differentiation within speech-language cortex. Stuttering anticipation and lived experience gradually shift the balance between control, language, and motivational salience-processing systems, contributing to the disorder's marked heterogeneity and context sensitivity. These findings indicate system-level signatures of the interaction between social context and symptom severity in developmental stuttering, extending accounts based on sensorimotor deficits.

papers.title: Cholinergic-dopaminergic synergy and antagonism shape prediction-error broadcasting
papers.abstract: Cholinergic and dopaminergic pathways control reinforcement learning, yet how their basal forebrain and midbrain populations interact remains unresolved. We simultaneously monitored both systems using dual-cell-type optogenetic tagging and neurotransmitter measurements in mice engaged in psychometric learning. Their activity contributed synergistically to reward prediction-error signaling. However, punishment-inhibited dopaminergic neurons showed antagonistic interactions with cholinergic neurons as well. Optogenetic stimulation and channelrhodopsin-assisted circuit mapping revealed a cholinergic-to-dopaminergic disynaptic inhibitory pathway through basal forebrain GABAergic neurons consistent with this antagonism. Chemogenetic suppression of cholinergic activity reduced dopaminergic responses to reward-predicting stimuli, attenuated punishment-induced dopamine suppression, and impaired learning. These findings reveal how a common underlying circuit architecture can flexibly shape prediction-error signaling through synergistic and antagonistic interactions, with implications for adaptive learning and neuropsychiatric disease.

papers.title: A predictive mechanochemical modeling framework for the deformation and remodeling of the nuclear lamina
papers.abstract: Nuclear envelope (NE) deformation and rupture are common in cell spreading and migration in a variety of microenvironments and lead to marked changes in nucleocytoplasmic transport. Predicting responses to different mechanochemical cues that are transmitted to the nucleus remains an open problem in the field of mechanomedicine. We have developed a predictive modeling framework to examine how nuclear deformation on substrates with different nanotopographies influences nucleocytoplasmic transport and rearrangement of the nuclear lamina. Using the finite element method, we simulated nuclear compression by the perinuclear actin cap on substrates with arrays of nanopillars, modeling the NE-lamin composite as a nonlinear elastic structure and coupling deformations to a biochemical model of lamin remodeling and nucleocytoplasmic transport. Our simulations generated nuclear morphologies that agreed well with our experimental measurements and predicted that the regions of highest NE stretch are adjacent to cell-nanopillar contacts, leading to maximized NE tension on nanopillars spaced by 5-7 microns. We then considered the effects on transport of YAP/TAZ and remodeling of the nuclear lamina. In our model, increased nuclear flattening facilitated YAP/TAZ nuclear localization due to NPC dilation. We validated these predictions by measuring nuclear YAP and lamin localization in subsequent experiments. Finally, we considered the implications of our model for NE rupture. We found that substrate nanotopography and lamin abundance were both strong predictors of the force load in the nuclear lamina and the resulting rupture likelihood. We validated this prediction in subsequent experiments with lamin-depleted U2OS cells, establishing the central importance of lamin transport and microenvironment nanotopography in nuclear mechanotransduction.

papers.title: A VTA-pontine GABA pathway biases locomotor direction via local and distal inhibition
papers.abstract: Locomotor direction in mammals is implemented by descending circuits, yet how midbrain selection systems bias directional motor output remains unclear. Here we define a projection-defined inhibitory pathway from the ventral tegmental area to the oral pontine reticular nucleus (VTAPnO) whose activation is sufficient to drive backward locomotion. These TH- VTA neurons form monosynaptic GABAA synapses locally while projecting to PnO, establishing a dual local-projection inhibitory architecture. Somatic activation reliably induced backward locomotion, and selective stimulation of VTAPnO terminals reproduced the effect. Pathway recruitment produced a rapid transient increase in dopaminergic single-unit activity and frequency-dependent increases in dopaminergic population calcium signals in awake mice. During forced locomotion, chronically recorded VTAPnO neurons were preferentially engaged during reverse compared to forward rotations. Together, these findings reveal a projection-defined midbrain pathway that biases locomotor direction through coordinated local inhibition and distal engagement of a brainstem premotor node.

papers.title: A hypothalamo-septo-hippocampal circuit for REM sleep-dependent consolidation of social memory
papers.abstract: REM sleep constitutes a critical window for memory consolidation, yet the brain circuits orchestrating this process remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify a lateral supramammillary nucleus (SuM)-medial septum (MS) projection as a REM sleep-specialized pathway essential for hippocampal memory consolidation. Fiber photometry and optrode recordings revealed that lateral SuM-MS projecting neurons were selectively active during REM sleep. REM-specific optogenetic silencing of this projection impaired consolidation of both social and contextual fear memories. Crucially, silencing of its downstream target, the MS-CA2 pathway, during REM sleep selectively disrupted social memory while sparing contextual fear memory. This functional dissection establishes a hypothalamo-septo-hippocampal circuit (lateral SuM-MS-CA2) dedicated to social memory processing, in parallel to the recently-described direct SuM-CA2 pathway. These results also position the SuM as a REM sleep-hub that routes information via parallel septal pathways to consolidate distinct memory modalities.

papers.title: Diet-Related Molecular Evolution Differs between Vertivores, Invertivores, and Combined Carnivores
papers.abstract: Mammals have repeatedly evolved specialized diets, including a variety of predatory diets targeting different prey animals. Prior research has found differences in positive selection, gene family evolution and gene functional loss linked with diet, but has focused primarily on trophic level classifications of herbivory, carnivory, and omnivory. Here we divide "carnivores" into vertivores and invertivores, due to the differences in nutrient composition of those food sources. We find significant differences in evolutionary conservation of multiple genes and GO categories between vertivores and invertivores. Conservation relative to herbivores differs among vertivores, invertivores, and the combination of all carnivores. Lineages with predatory diets have increased conservation in lipid and amino acid metabolism relative to herbivores. Notably, we find that results in the combined carnivore-herbivore comparison are much more similar to those of the invertivore-herbivore comparison than the vertivore-herbivore comparison, which suggests that prior studies on carnivory may have been detecting signatures of selection related to invertivory.

papers.title: Association between white-matter lesion volume and heart-rate variability: A comparison of T1w, T1w+T2w and T1w+FLAIR-based segmentations using FreeSurfer SAMSEG
papers.abstract: Background Heart disease is a crucial risk factor for brain degeneration, but the specific mechanisms of this association are still under investigation. Notably, the development of white-matter lesions, a hallmark of cerebral small-vessel disease with connections to progressive neurodegeneration and cognitive decline, has been linked to cardiovascular disease. As such, measures of cardiovascular function such as heart-rate variability may represent accessible indicators of white-matter lesion burden. Methods This study used data from healthy adults drawn from the Leipzig Study for Mind-Body-Emotion Interactions (LEMON) dataset to examine heart function through measures of heart-rate variability, as well as their relationship to cerebral small-vessel disease as quantified through white-matter lesion volumes, using FreeSurfer SAMSEG. White-matter lesion volumes were segmented using 3-Tesla T1w+FLAIR, T1w+T2w or T1w images alone. Results Unadjusted exploratory results suggested that lower heart-rate variability was associated with higher lesion volume, a cerebral hallmark of hypertension. After controlling for the effect of age on lesion volume, low-frequency heart rate variability specifically was found to interact with age-related lesion volume. Moreover, we showed that the relationship between white-matter lesion volume and heart-rate variability is apparent using T1w+FLAIR or T1w+T2w based lesion estimates could be observed with T1w-based lesion estimation alone, opening new avenues for studying cerebral small-vessel disease. Discussion These results suggest heart rate variability as a factor in the translation between cardiovascular risk and white matter degeneration, as well as an accessible and non-invasive indicator of white-matter lesion burden and associated cognitive impairment in later life. The unique association between reduced low-frequency band heart-rate variability and age-related lesion burden may help to establish the link between autonomic control of cardiac function and brain health in aging.

papers.title: Active vision modulates early cortical stages of visual processing: Evidence from MEG and eye-tracking
papers.abstract: Vision is fundamentally active. Humans and other mammals make several saccadic eye movements per second. This feature of mammalian vision has received increasing interest across the last decades and many behavioural and neurophysiological studies have investigated how the visual system accounts for the effects of self-generated motion (efference copy) in perceptual processing. Still, it is often believed that, besides accounting for the efference copy and for the rhythmic modulation of activity due to perpetual saccade-fixation cycles, active vision does not further modulate neural processing of visual input obtained during periods of fixation. In contrast, using a gaze-contingent trans-saccadic change design with concurrent MEG and eye-tracking data recording from human participants, we find sequential history effects in visual cortices. Harnessing the preview effect, we show that primary visual and ventral occipital cortices respond differently when eye-movements bring objects into focus compared to when the same objects appear during steady fixation. Specifically, we find that sequential modulations of cortical processing across saccades, in the form of preview effects, are increased during active vision compared to steady-gaze control conditions. Our data also show that these sequential modulations cannot be explained by any type of adaptation alone. Our study, therefore, provides an update on the role of active vision in modulating cortical function.

papers.title: Guanosine tetraphosphate (ppGpp) promotes tolerance to 2 excess light in Arabidopsis thaliana.
papers.abstract: Guanosine tetraphosphate (ppGpp) is a hyperphosphorylated nucleotide originally discovered in prokaryotes and found in the chloroplasts of plants and algae. In plants, ppGpp regulates photosynthetic activity, which is important in acclimation to environmental stresses such as nitrogen limitation. However, the full range of stresses involving ppGpp signalling is not yet known. Here, we investigated the role of ppGpp accumulation in the acclimation of plants to excess light. We found that the over-accumulation of ppGpp in transgenic lines that overexpress RSH3 (OX:RSH3) increases tolerance to excess light. Although ppGpp leads to higher non-photochemical energy dissipation (NPQ) than in wild-type plants, we show that NPQ is not critical for the enhanced excess light tolerance. Rather, our results show that ppGpp accumulation leads to broad changes in plant physiology that prime plants to resist and subsequently recover from excess light exposure. ppGpp levels themselves also increase in response to excess light exposure, suggesting that ppGpp may play a physiological role in excess light acclimation. Our work adds to a growing body of evidence for the importance of ppGpp in plant stress acclimation.

papers.title: Patient-specific metabolic fluxes reflect molecular subtype and heterogeneity in breast cancer
papers.abstract: Tumor metabolism is dynamic and context-dependent, yet gene expression provides only an indirect view of metabolic activity. We combined patient-specific genome-scale metabolic models with supervised and unsupervised machine learning to infer metabolic fluxes for 1,223 TCGA breast tumor and normal samples under a uniform physiological medium. Flux profiles distinguished tumor from normal tissue under patient-grouped nested cross-validation (ROC-AUC up to 0.989) and predicted receptor status and molecular subtype (e.g., Basal-like versus other tumors, AUC = 0.966), but not stage, nodal status or age. Within tumors, metabolic variation was continuous rather than organized into discrete groups and aligned only partially with clinical classifications. These findings support a view of breast cancer metabolism as a structured but continuous landscape that reflects molecular subtype and receptor status, and provide a reproducible framework to characterize tumor heterogeneity.

papers.title: Genetic diversity and population structure of Phytophthora infestans in Guatemala and Honduras
papers.abstract: Phytophthora infestans,the causal agent of late blight, remains a major constraint to potato production worldwide. In Central America, particularly in Guatemala and Honduras, information on the pathogen's population structure is limited despite its economic importance and reliance on imported seed potatoes. This study characterized the population structure of P. infestans from potato fields in Guatemala and Honduras using microsatellite markers, mitochondrial haplotypes, and mating type analyses. Four SSR-defined groups were identified, corresponding to the clonal lineages EU_13_A2, US_25, US_8, and a distinct group designated CeA (Central America). EU_13_A2 was predominant, accounting for 141 of the 154 isolates analyzed, whereas US_25, CeA, and US_8 were represented by eight, four, and one isolate, respectively. Reference isolates from Nicaragua previously designated as NI_1 clustered with US_25, while reference isolates from Honduras designated as HN_1 clustered with EU_13_A2. A total of 89 multilocus genotypes were identified, indicating substantial SSR genotypic diversity despite the predominance of EU_13_A2. All successfully characterized isolates exhibited the Ia mitochondrial haplotype. Hierarchical AMOVA showed that most SSR variation occurred within departments (69.86%, p=0.002), whereas variation among departments within countries (15.97%, p=0.092) and between Honduras and Guatemala (14.17%, p =0.108) was not statistically significant. The predominance of EU_13_A2 together with the occurrence of additional genetically distinct groups highlights the importance of continued monitoring of P. infestans populations and their movements across Central America.

papers.title: A Biologically Inspired Attention Model for Neural Signal Analysis
papers.abstract: Understanding how the brain represents sensory information and triggers behavioural responses is a fundamental goal in neuroscience. Recent advances in neuronal recording techniques aim to progress towards this milestone, yet the resulting high-dimensional responses are challenging to interpret and link to relevant variables. Although existing machine learning models propose to do so, they often sacrifice interpretability for predictive power, effectively operating as black boxes. In this work, we introduce SPARKS, a biologically inspired model capable of high decoding accuracy and interpretable discovery within a single framework. SPARKS adapts the self-attention mechanism of large language models to extract information from the timing of single spikes and the sequence in which neurons fire using Hebbian learning. Trained with a criterion inspired by predictive coding to enforce temporal coherence, our model produces low-dimensional latent embeddings that are robust across sessions and animals. By directly capturing the underlying data distribution through a generative encoding-decoding framework, SPARKS matches or exceeds state-of-the-art decoders across diverse electrophysiology and calcium imaging datasets from the motor, visual and entorhinal cortices. Crucially, the Hebbian coefficients learned by the model are interpretable, allowing us to infer directed functional interactions and recover the known functional hierarchy of the mouse visual cortex. Overall, SPARKS unifies representation learning, high-performance decoding and model interpretability in a single framework by bridging neuroscience and AI, providing a powerful and versatile tool for dissecting neural computations and marking a step towards the next generation of biologically inspired intelligent systems.

papers.title: JUMP Cell Painting chemical dataset: Morphological map of 115,796 compounds in human cells
papers.abstract: Image-based profiling decodes complex cellular states for high-impact biological and therapeutic applications, yet a large, public reference dataset of chemical perturbations has been lacking. We present Cell Painting images and 1.53 billion single-cell profiles for 115,796 compounds in human osteosarcoma cells, generated by the Joint Undertaking for Morphological Profiling (JUMP)-Cell Painting Consortium of 18 industry and non-profit partners. Despite technical variability across 12 data-generating laboratories, more than 15% of compounds show statistically significant phenotypic activity, reproducibility drops only 34% versus single-laboratory data, and compounds sharing biological targets often show similar image-based profiles. JUMP establishes a validated public reference resource that brings image-based profiling on par with genomics and transcriptomics. The dataset, shared alongside previously released genetic perturbation data in the Cell Painting Gallery, is a powerful predictive engine for the impact, mechanism, targets and activities of compounds, fundamentally accelerating chemical and cell biology and early-stage drug development.

papers.title: An oral protein cocktail therapeutic for C. difficile infection
papers.abstract: Here we show that transgenic spirulina may solve key challenges of developing effective monoclonal protein therapeutics for diseases afflicting gastrointestinal (GI) tissues. We describe, as a paradigm for this novel approach, LMN-201: an investigational four-component treatment for Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) infection comprising four monoclonal protein therapeutics produced and delivered within spirulina biomass. Three antibody-like moieties within LMN 201 were rationally designed using a multiplicative potency framework, termed synthetic avidity, that increased in vitro toxin neutralization potency by >200-fold relative to the individual components. The fourth moiety, a lysin enzyme protein, adds direct, toxinotype-agnostic antibacterial activity. In rodent challenge models, species-relevant LMN-201-like cocktails reduced disease burden and mortality. In a human GI pharmacokinetic study, LMN-201 was present at concentrations 100- to 1,000-fold above the estimated minimally effective therapeutic threshold at the distal intestine. In Part A of a Phase 2 study, participants with C. difficile infection (CDI) were treated for seven days with LMN-201 plus standard-of-care antibiotics. The primary endpoints of safety and tolerability were assessed favorably. An interim analysis of efficacy in pre-planned coordination with the data and safety monitoring board showed an initial clinical cure rate of 21/21 (100%) and sustained clinical cure rate through four weeks of 19/21 (90.5%). These findings support LMN-201 with standard-of-care antibiotics as a viable treatment option for CDI, validate spirulina as a scalable platform for oral biologics, and establish a generalizable strategy for engineering high-potency combination protein therapeutics for diseases with a GI tissue nexus.

papers.title: Redesigning the Eterna100 RNA design benchmark for the Vienna 2 folding engine
papers.abstract: The rational design of RNA is becoming important for rapidly developing technologies in medicine and biochemistry, spurring development of numerous RNA secondary structure design algorithms and benchmarks to evaluate their performance. However, the problem of RNA design is dependent upon the inverse problem of RNA structure prediction through "folding engines" that predict structure from sequence. We hypothesized that differences in RNA folding engines could impact design algorithms, and recruited an online community of RNA design experts to modify the widely used RNA secondary structure design benchmark Eterna100 to address target unsolvability when changing the folding engine used (ViennaRNA 1 updated to 2). We tested this new Eterna100-V2 benchmark with six RNA design algorithms, and found that the performance of RNA design algorithms changed depending on which folding engine was used in training or evaluation. We further explored algorithms reported to have solved the original Eterna100 and found that incorrect folding engine settings were used in their prior evaluation. As a result, currently, both the original Eterna100-V1 and the modernized Eterna100-V2 benchmark remain unsolved with their intended folding engine settings. This work demonstrates that the design difficulty of RNA structures is intrinsically linked to thermodynamic models and suggests that future RNA design algorithms that can adapt to updated thermodynamic models may result in improved performance. Eterna100-V1 and Eterna100-V2 benchmarks and example solutions are freely available at https://github.com/eternagame/eterna100-benchmarking.

papers.title: Expertise modifies neural responses to causal inference during language comprehension
papers.abstract: Linguistic communication relies on shared common ground, yet different individuals in a community have specialized semantic knowledge. As a key example, physicians acquire rich knowledge about the causes of illness. An open question is whether such "causal expertise" influences the neural basis of language comprehension. Here we tested the hypothesis that when understanding everyday language like, "Holly used a grimy faucet during her overseas plane ride. Now she has the stomach flu," medical experts retrieve richer representations in semantic networks of the brain. Physicians (n=16) and age- and education-matched controls (n=16) undergoing fMRI read two-sentence vignettes that elicited implicit causal inferences about illness or object mechanics as well as control vignettes that did not elicit causal inferences. Vignettes were linguistically matched across conditions and were accessible to experts and non-experts alike. Across both groups, causal vignettes about illness engaged a temporoparietal semantic network previously implicated in thinking about animates, i.e., people and animals (precuneus and left temporoparietal junction), whereas causal vignettes about object mechanics engaged a semantic network associated with places and objects. Critically, physicians' responses in the animacy network were more robust and self-similar, suggesting the activation of richer semantic knowledge. Medical expertise effects were specific to biological inferences rather than mechanical or mental state inferences. By contrast, individually localized frontotemporal language and frontoparietal reasoning networks did not respond preferentially to causally connected sentences or show effects of expertise. Our findings suggest that causal expertise alters neural responses to causal inferences that unfold automatically during language comprehension.

papers.title: Polygenic evolution towards a morning chronotype in modern humans
papers.abstract: Chronotype is a behavioural phenotype, and its phenotypic trend is considered to change at higher latitudes. In the current study, we performed a polygenic assessment of chronotype trend using associated single nucleotide polymorphisms identified by a genome wide-association study. We found that the phenotypic trend towards morningness increased drastically during the migration of anatomically modern humans above 20 degrees north. Furthermore, two types of latitudinal selection of morningness alleles contributed to establishing the trend towards the morning chronotype at higher latitudes. We propose that the trend towards morningness is stronger in present-day modern humans living above 20 degrees north than in Neanderthals.

papers.title: XRN1-dependent RNA homeostasis regulates hepatitis D virus
papers.abstract: Hepatitis delta virus (HDV) infection causes the most severe form of viral hepatitis, yet the host mechanisms restricting HDV replication remain poorly understood. Although HDV infection activates the MDA5-LGP2 pathway and induces robust interferon (IFN) responses, these antiviral programs have limited impact on viral replication. Here we identify the 5-3 exoribonuclease XRN1 as a key regulator of HDV infection. Loss of XRN1 in hepatoma cells increased double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) levels and induced interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs), including MDA5 and MAVS, and limited HDV infection. XRN1 deficiency enhanced ADAR1-mediated RNA editing, revealing a dynamic interplay between endogenous dsRNA metabolism and antiviral sensing. Inhibition of type I IFN signaling restored MDA5 expression and rescued HDV replication in XRN1-deficient cells. To identify the downstream effectors responsible for this restriction, we combined transcriptomic profiling with functional siRNA screening and identified DUSP5 and SIRPA as previously unrecognized ISGs with anti-HDV activity. Together, our findings establish XRN1 as a gatekeeper of dsRNA homeostasis that controls HDV replication through innate immune activation and reveals host antiviral effectors that may provide therapeutic opportunities for chronic hepatitis D.

papers.title: Microbial plankton in southern Hudson Bay and James Bay in late summer
papers.abstract: Hudson Bay and James Bay, on the southern margin of the Arctic, are warming and freshening as river discharge increases and surrounding permafrost thaws, yet their microbial plankton remain poorly described, and James Bay and the waters around the Belcher Islands have never been surveyed with environmental DNA. We conducted the first dedicated DNA-based survey of eukaryotic and prokaryotic plankton in southern Hudson Bay and James Bay, sequencing 18S rRNA (V9) and 16S rRNA (V4) gene amplicons from 72 samples collected at 51 stations in August 2022 and 2023. Hierarchical clustering resolved nine distinct communities; the primary division separated surface James Bay from Hudson Bay, with further structuring by year, distance to coast, depth, and riverine influence. Temperature, salinity, depth, and distance to coast together explained 31% of community variation (distance-based redundancy analysis), and threshold indicator taxa analysis placed an abrupt community-level change in offshore surface waters at 55.3 N and a salinity of ~24.5. Across this boundary, primary producers shifted from large Chaetoceros diatoms in Hudson Bay to the picoplanktonic green alga Picochlorum and the cyanobacterium Cyanobium in James Bay, while large Gyrodinium dinoflagellates and Calanus copepods gave way to Gymnodinium, Pseudocalanus, and small cercozoans and ciliates. Heterotrophic bacteria in Hudson Bay were dominated by Proteobacteria, Bacteroidota, and Verrucomicrobiota, likely using diatom- and dinoflagellate-derived organic matter, whereas Actinomycetota and Planctomycetota dominated James Bay, likely using cyanobacterial and terrestrial dissolved organic matter. Prokaryotic diversity was highest in riverine, estuarine, and James Bay waters and declined northward and seaward. We also report the first strong presence of marine Synechococcus CC9902 in Hudson Bay and identify cosmopolitan bacteria that provide a baseline for future monitoring. These results suggest that continued freshening of the Hudson Bay Complex will favour smaller primary producers and a stronger microbial loop, and that ecosystem shifts may occur abruptly once surface waters cross a salinity threshold.

papers.title: Single-molecule bouncing at a liquid interface governs presynaptic enrichment
papers.abstract: Many cellular processes rely on accumulating highly diffusive cytoplasmic proteins to a specific location within the cell. This spatial enrichment is generally thought to rely on locally immobilizing proteins or slowing diffusion through binding and molecular crowding. Paradoxically, cytoplasmic proteins that are enriched within nerve terminals remain highly diffusive, raising questions about the mechanisms that govern presynaptic enrichment. Here, using in vivo single-molecule microscopy, we tracked the diffusion of a model cytoplasmic protein, -Synuclein (-Syn), and synaptic vesicles (SVs), in motor neuron presynapses of live Drosophila larvae. We demonstrate that -Syn undergoes rapid and frequent "bouncing" events at a presynaptic interface, locally impeding escape from the presynapse. We measured escape probabilities at the interface, and show that impeding escape, without dramatically slowing diffusion, is sufficient to govern presynaptic enrichment. The interface is liquid-like and coincides with the boundary of the SV cluster, which is a necessary scaffold for the presynaptic enrichment of -Syn. Our results provide direct evidence of interfacial reflectivity at the interface of liquid-like compartments, and that this phenomenon can govern the subcellular enrichment of proteins and small organelles at the level of individual particles.

papers.title: Nanobodies against Plasmodium vivax AMA1 block parasite invasion
papers.abstract: Plasmodium vivax is the most widespread malaria species to infect human populations. P. vivax invades young red cells called reticulocytes to replicate and proliferate. An essential protein in parasite invasion is the Apical Membrane Antigen 1, PvAMA1, which forms the tight junction between parasite and red cell membrane through its interaction with Rhoptry Neck Protein 2, PvRON2. Here we report the identification of PvAMA1 nanobodies using phage display in combination with Sanger sequencing, next-generation sequencing and structure prediction tools. We show that these nanobodies bind with high affinities and across several different epitopes on PvAMA1. Several nanobodies recognize PvAMA1 in merozoites of late-stage schizonts and inhibit parasite invasion of red blood cells. These growth inhibitory nanobodies bind to conformational epitopes of PvAMA1 and most bind to a site distinct from a known potent human monoclonal antibody 826827. Crystal structures of two inhibitory nanobodies in complex with PvAMA1 show that they bind novel neutralizing epitopes which are outside the hydrophobic groove that contacts PvRON2. Furthermore, we show that two other PvAMA1 nanobodies also inhibit Plasmodium falciparum invasion. These results demonstrate the potential of PvAMA1 nanobodies to inhibit malaria parasite invasion across multiple Plasmodium species.

papers.title: The transformer as a candidate canonical cortical microcircuit
papers.abstract: Neuroscience hypothesizes a canonical microcircuit subserving cortical computation across brain systems. In artificial intelligence, neural networks have become a universal computational substrate. Here, we leverage newly available large-scale data and mapping techniques to compare neural network motifs to the brain. We embedded a spectrum of candidate microcircuit architectures within a common spatial macrocircuit, measuring alignment with an extensive battery of cortical signatures. We find that one specific circuit type--the transformer--uniquely captures fine-grained unit-level circuit details, population-level functional maps and neuronal activity patterns, and systems-level wiring efficiency and behavioral demands. The key ingredient enabling the transformer's success is a learned multiplicative component making relational information available without extensive long-range wiring. These results suggest striking convergence between computational motifs in natural and artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Comparative genomics of canonical antifungal dsRNA target genes across fungal plant pathogens: conserved siRNA-length windows define the scope for broad-spectrum spray-induced gene silencing
papers.abstract: Background. Spray-induced gene silencing (SIGS), in which double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) sprayed onto a crop is taken up by a fungal pathogen and silences an essential gene, is advancing as a biopesticide strategy. A recurring ambition is a broad-spectrum dsRNA: a single construct, directed at a conserved housekeeping gene, that controls several pathogens at once. Because silencing is driven by Dicer-processed small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) of roughly 21 nucleotides, the feasibility of this ambition depends on whether the target gene is conserved between pathogens at siRNA-length resolution, not merely at the level of overall gene identity. That resolution has not been mapped across the fungal plant-pathogen tree. Results. We screened eleven canonical antifungal dsRNA target genes of Fusarium graminearum (three CYP51 sterol 14-alpha-demethylases, six chitin synthases and two beta-tubulins) for perfect 21-nucleotide identity against the transcriptomes of twelve fungal plant pathogens spanning four taxonomic classes (Sordariomycetes, Leotiomycetes, Dothideomycetes and Basidiomycota). Of 27,116 candidate siRNA start positions across the eleven genes, only 2,108 (7.8%) were conserved as a perfect 21-mer in even one other pathogen, 148 in at least three, twelve in at least seven, and none in eight or more. Conservation decayed steeply with phylogenetic distance: the congeneric F. oxysporum shared 1,209 sites, other Sordariomycetes 262-313, Leotiomycetes and Dothideomycetes 62-204, Basidiomycota 41-48, and the reduced-genome obligate biotroph Blumeria graminis just one. The beta-tubulins carried the most broadly conserved individual sites (shared by up to seven pathogens), whereas CYP51C was the least conserved (shared by at most one). Even for the congener, perfect-match conservation covered only 4.5% of target positions and was concentrated in discrete windows rather than spread along the gene. Conclusions. At the siRNA-length resolution that governs silencing, perfect-match conservation of canonical antifungal targets is scarce and strongly clade-limited. A perfect-match broad-spectrum dsRNA is therefore realistic only within a narrow clade, in practice around the genus level; genus- and class-spanning broad-spectrum SIGS cannot rely on perfect siRNA identity and would require mismatch-tolerant design or pathogen-specific constructs. The conserved windows mapped here identify where clade-level broad-spectrum constructs can be placed, and the gene ranking (beta-tubulins most cross-targetable, CYP51C most pathogen-specific) provides a genome-guided basis for choosing antifungal dsRNA targets.

papers.title: Molecular and Structural Characterisation of the MERS-Coronavirus Polymerase
papers.abstract: MERS-CoV (Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus) belongs to the Betacoronavirus genus, which also includes SARS-CoV-2, the causative agent of the COVID-19 pandemic. MERS-CoV is the pathogen responsible for Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS), a respiratory disease with a 36.5% case fatality rate. Given the capacity of coronaviruses for genetic recombination and mutation, MERS-CoV remains a pathogen of significant pandemic potential, with viral evolution potentially facilitating enhanced adaptation and transmission in humans. There are no approved treatments for MERS-CoV infection. The MERS-CoV replication-transcription complex (RTC), a multimeric protein complex key to genome amplification, has no cellular analogues and a highly conserved sequence, making it a useful target for antiviral compounds; however, structural and biochemical characterisation of the MERS-CoV RTC is limited. Here, we characterise the minimal MERS-CoV RTC using in vitro and single-molecule assays and show that it is susceptible to the RNA-dependent-RNA-polymerase inhibitor suramin. We present a structure of the minimal MERS-CoV RTC in complex with an RNA duplex, which shows strong structural similarity to the SARS-CoV-2 RTC. We use cross-subunit swapping experiments to show that the MERS-CoV NSP12 core can efficiently utilise SARS-CoV-2 cofactors NSP7 and NSP8, whereas SARS-CoV-2 NSP12 exhibits reduced in vitro activity with the MERS-CoV NSP8. This asymmetric cross-species compatibility highlights both the evolutionary conservation and virus-specific adaptation of coronavirus polymerase-cofactor interactions. Together, these findings provide a structural and mechanistic framework for understanding MERS-CoV RNA synthesis and establish its conserved RTC as a potential target for the development of broadly acting coronavirus antivirals.

papers.title: Bottom-heaviness stabilizes pelagic fish eggs and generates advective transport at their surface
papers.abstract: Pelagic fish eggs are small spheres (~1 mm) that drift in the open ocean, carried by large-scale currents. Embedded in these currents are egg-scale turbulent eddies that impose local rotational forcing on the eggs. Accordingly, eggs are considered passive tracer particles that move with these eddies, implying that mass transfer of oxygen and waste are controlled only by molecular diffusion. However, eggs are bottom heavy, characterized by a dense embryo and a buoyant oil globule at opposing poles. We hypothesized that such internal structure generates a gravitational restoring torque, stabilizing the egg and generating relative egg-water motion. To test this hypothesis we exposed fish eggs to controlled flows with shear levels typical of upper mixed-layer and estuarine environments, and analyzed their dynamics. Eggs displayed one of two repeatable behaviors: (i) steady orientation, with a near-constant egg angle, and (ii) revolving motion, with egg rotation at time-varying angular speed. Both behaviors generated relative motion between the eggs and the surrounding water. A rigid-body rotational model balancing external flow-induced torque and gravitational restoring torque showed that transitions between these states depend on local flow fields and developmental stage, with older eggs shifting to revolving behavior at lower external fluid torque. Together, these findings suggest that advective transport is important and that diffusion-only models underestimate exchange rates, which are a major component in predicting the effects of environmental factors on embryo survival.

papers.title: MaxCAT-Net: Hybrid Transformer-Based Skin Lesion Classification and Lightweight Segmentation with Calibration and Cross-Dataset Validation
papers.abstract: Class imbalance, poor confidence calibration, and limited generalization under varying imaging conditions are major challenges in automated dermoscopic skin lesion analysis. We propose a hybrid classifier, MaxCAT-Net (MaxViT + CBAM + Attention Transformer), consisting of a pretrained MaxViT-Tiny backbone combined with CBAM and a lightweight two-layer Transformer encoder. We also evaluate four encoder-decoder networks for lesion segmentation as a separate task using ISIC 2018 Task 1. After removing exact and near-duplicate images, the remaining 10,012 images were divided into lesion-wise training, validation, and test sets using a 72/14/14 split, ensuring that images from the same lesion did not appear across multiple subsets. On the test set (n = 1,405), MaxCAT-Net outperformed the ResNet152-CBAM, MobileNetV3-CBAM, GhostNet-hybrid, and standalone MaxViT-Tiny-CBAM baselines, achieving an accuracy of 0.869 (95% CI: 0.847-0.890), balanced accuracy of 0.742, macro-F1 of 0.751, and macro-AUC of 0.944. However, ablation-related macro-F1 improvements (0.017-0.022) were not statistically conclusive. Temperature scaling reduced the expected calibration error (ECE) from 0.099 to 0.038. On the PAD-UFES-20 dataset, accuracy decreased to 0.341 and melanoma recall to 0.096, while melanoma recall on HAM10000 was only 0.587. For segmentation, a Swin-T-encoder U-Net achieved a Dice score of 0.903 on 520 test images, whereas a FasterNet-T0 U-Net, with approximately one-tenth the number of parameters, achieved a Dice score of 0.901 (Holm-adjusted p < 0.002). A standard U-Net achieved a significantly lower Dice score of 0.888. All results are based on a single random seed and should therefore be interpreted as preliminary trends rather than definitive evidence of improvement.

papers.title: Decoding stress-induced adaptation of cancer cells in spatial confinement by integrating live-cell imaging and mathematical modeling
papers.abstract: The adaptive strategies employed by cancer cells to combat stress when grown in 2D cultures have been extensively studied, including applying evolutionary game theory. However, relatively little is known about these strategies when the cells are grown in confinement that resemble the tumor microenvironment more closely. Here, we used cisplatin-sensitive and -tolerant lung cancer cells that were grown as monotypic or heterotypic spheroids in a microfluidics system and monitored in real time. Competition and cooperation between these cells were modeled by estimating the parameters through the best fit of observed measurements using a modified version of the Cellular Potts model. The results indicated that the two sensitive and tolerant populations exhibited different cooperative and competitive strategies under changing environmental conditions. Importantly, we found that in addition to initial cell type composition, the population fitness was governed by the spatial organization, intercellular interactions, and dynamic remodeling of the local microenvironment by these cells. Further, tolerant cells exhibited similarities to a persister trait and appeared to cooperate with sensitive cells, enabling them to evade chemotherapy.

papers.title: Cumulus cells mediate the protective effect of the marine carotenoid fucoxanthin against postovulatory oocyte aging via NRF2 signaling
papers.abstract: Background Oocytes awaiting insemination undergo postovulatory aging, an oxidative stress-driven loss of developmental competence. Fucoxanthin (FX), the major carotenoid of the brown alga Undaria pinnatifida, acts through NRF2, which requires a nucleus and transcription; the metaphase-II oocyte has neither, so its site of action is unresolved. Purpose To determine whether FX delays postovulatory aging of mouse oocytes and identify the mediating compartment of the cumulus-oocyte complex. Study design Ex vivo study of intact cumulus-oocyte complexes from superovulated ICR mice aged for 12 h, or 24 h for spindle analysis. Astaxanthin (AX) served as benchmark and the NRF2 inhibitor ML385 tested pathway dependence. Methods Complexes were held in M16 medium with FX (1-10 {micro}M) or AX (5 {micro}M). Mitochondrial membrane potential, reactive oxygen species (ROS) and glutathione were measured with JC-1, DCFH-DA and monochlorobimane; spindle organization and cumulus-cell NRF2 localization by immunofluorescence. Results At the optimal 5 {micro}M, FX raised the JC-1 aggregate-to-monomer ratio eight-fold over untreated aged oocytes (1.24 {+/-} 0.10 versus 0.15 {+/-} 0.02; p < 0.05), lowered ROS to 0.18 {+/-} 0.04-fold and raised glutathione to 1.80 {+/-} 0.02-fold of control (both p < 0.01), comparably to AX. ML385 abolished all three effects concentration-dependently. FX increased the cumulus-cell NRF2 nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio (p < 0.05) and, after 24 h, nearly halved abnormal spindles (p = 0.059). Conclusion FX preserves mitochondrial and redox status in postovulatory-aged oocytes through NRF2, which translocates in cumulus cells rather than the oocyte, identifying the cumulus cell as a target for extending oocyte usability in assisted reproduction.

papers.title: Isolation and characterization of diverse Veillonella phages reveal novel lineages and distinct host interactions
papers.abstract: The human oral microbiome is diverse and home to many species of bacteria, archaea, microeukaryotes, fungi and viruses. Homeostasis in the oral microbiome is important for health and dysbiosis in these communities leads to periodontal and systemic diseases. Veillonella are gram-negative, anaerobic, lactate-fermenting early colonizers of the mouth and are abundant in healthy oral microbiomes. Although considered commensals, Veillonella serve as bridging species in dental biofilms, promoting later colonization by pathogens, with mounting evidence supporting their roles as accessory pathogens in dental caries and periodontal disease. Bacteriophages are key regulators of bacterial community composition and are important drivers of microbial diversity, evolution, and ecology of the oral environment. Despite the ecological importance of Veillonella in the oral microbiome, phages infecting Veillonella remain largely uncharacterized. Here, we report the isolation of ten phages infecting natural isolates of three Veillonella species, representing seven distinct phage genomes. These phages exhibit diverse morphologies, genome organizations, and host ranges, with infection restricted to strains within the species of isolation. Several phages establish stable lysogeny, confer resistance to superinfection, and differ substantially in spontaneous production of infectious phage progeny. Genetic analysis of resistant mutants implicates lipopolysaccharide O-antigen as the receptor for one phage. Although none of the isolated phages had close matches in existing oral virome catalogs, related sequences were detected in oral metagenomes from geographically diverse populations. Together, these findings establish an experimentally characterized collection of Veillonella phages and connect previously uncharacterized oral viral diversity to bacterial hosts and infection phenotypes.

papers.title: The genetic architecture of human DNA methylome variation
papers.abstract: Population DNA methylome analyses remain largely confined to reference-defined genomic space despite extensive human genetic diversity. A central challenge is therefore to define comparable methylation phenotypes across diverse genomes and map the genetic architecture of methylome variation. Here, using 460 haplotypes from the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium Release 2, we develop two complementary pangenome-based frameworks: one compares methylation within homologous regions while retaining haplotype-specific structural configuration and CpG content; the other represents CpG island (CGI) variation at homologous loci as sequence-resolved alleles. We identified 47,039 CGI alleles, including 8,040 absent from CHM13; 62% were attributable to structural variants and 31% to small variants. Through local genealogies, we reconstructed CGI gain, loss and turnover, revealing how present-day methylation differences align with CGI evolutionary trajectories. We found that genome-wide, methylation variability was buffered against genetic diversity across more than 90% of the genome, with exceptions at extreme nucleotide diversity and locally around structural variants. Our methylation framework enabled population-scale allele-aware methylation quantitative trait locus (mQTL) mapping into non-reference and structurally complex sequence, where mQTL-associated intervals were enriched. mQTLs linked methylation to transcriptomic phenotypes, population differentiation and complex traits, supporting 8% of population differentially methylated regions and colocalizing with more than half of genome-wide association study loci. Together, our study redefines human methylome analysis and our findings reveal a genome-wide architecture of genetic-epigenetic coupling, reshaping how methylation variation is interpreted across human development and disease.

papers.title: NAD Metabolism Drives CTCF-Cohesin Chromatin Regulation in EBV-Transformed B-Cells
papers.abstract: Chromatin architecture regulates gene expression, and it is maintained by architectural proteins such as CTCF and the cohesin complex. In Epstein Barr virus infected cells, viral chromatin organization is stabilized through the interaction between PARP1 and CTCF, ensuring maintenance of latent gene expression. EBV B cells exhibit elevated PARP1 activity, which imposes a substantial metabolic burden due to NAD consumption by PARP1 itself. We demonstrate that efficient EBV infection and B-cell transformation rely on the NAD salvage pathway to sustain PARP1 activity and CTCF and cohesin chromatin folding. Pharmacologic inhibition of the rate-limiting enzyme NAMPT with FK866 phenocopies the chromatin architectural disruption induced by PARP1 and changes in NAD levels affects CTCF/cohesin chromatin architectural remodeling and loop extrusion. Moreover, NAMPT inhibition reduces tumor burden in EBV xenograft models. These findings identify a critical metabolic dependency linking NAD homeostasis to CTCF-cohesin mediated chromatin architecture and reveal a therapeutic vulnerability in EBV-associated malignancies.

papers.title: Endothelial protein C receptor is an entry receptor for Langya and related parahenipaviruses
papers.abstract: Langya virus is a zoonotic parahenipavirus with pandemic potential that causes acute febrile illness in people. We identified endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR) as an entry receptor for Langya, Wenzhou, and Mojiang parahenipaviruses. A 3.1 [A] cryo-electron microscopy structure reveals that Langya attachment glycoprotein engages EPCR through a site distinct from that of the ephrin binding site of Nipah G. This binding mode resembles those of protein C and a malarial adhesin, demonstrating convergent evolution. Interface substitutions abolish entry, whereas natural variation explains differential human EPCR use and predicts receptor compatibility across 26 animal species. These findings establish EPCR as a receptor for the Langya clade and provide a structural framework for understanding cross-species transmission and human infection potential.

papers.title: Fentanyl and fentanyl-xylazine co-exposure influence mitochondrial transcriptional programs in human trophoblasts
papers.abstract: Introduction: Illicit fentanyl exposure during pregnancy is associated with adverse outcomes. Yet its direct effects and their underlying molecular mechanisms in human trophoblasts remain largely unknown. Xylazine and medetomidine, two [a]2-adrenergic agonists, were recently detected as adulterants in illicit fentanyl-containing products, and have been linked to worsened clinical outcomes. Methods: We assessed the transcriptional responses of human trophoblast stem (TS) cells in their cytotrophoblast state (TS-CTBs) and derived syncytiotrophoblasts (STBs) after 4-day and 9-day exposure to fentanyl alone or combined with medetomidine and xylazine (FMX). Results: Fentanyl alone produced modest gene expression changes in TS-CTBs, but consistently induced suppression of mitochondrial and ribosomal transcriptional programs in STBs regardless of exposure duration, an effect absent in parental TS-CTBs. 9-day FMX co-exposure influenced mitochondrial respiratory chain gene expression in derived STBs, resulting in discordant regulation of nuclear versus mitochondrial genome-encoded respiratory chain genes. Temporal pathway analysis reveals progressive trophoblast remodeling and dysregulation of mitochondrial transcriptional programs following fentanyl and FMX co-exposure. Discussion: Together, these findings illuminate trophoblast pathways affected by fentanyl alone and by FMX co-exposure, and establish a basis for future studies examining the functional and clinical relevance of these transcriptional responses.

papers.title: Consensus methods for trees of blobs and level-1 phylogenetic networks
papers.abstract: Phylogenetic networks are increasingly used to represent evolutionary histories involving hybridization, introgression, and other reticulate processes that cannot be captured by a single tree. Recent advances have produced numerous methods for inferring networks from genomic data. These methods may produce multiple plausible networks due to optimality ties, bootstrap analyses, Bayesian posterior samples, or differences in tools, datasets, and parameters. While consensus methods are well established for trees and some approaches exist for rooted networks, no consensus framework currently exists for semi-directed (unrooted) networks. We address this gap by introducing a new consensus framework for phylogenetic networks, rooted or semi-directed. We first develop a method for constructing a consensus tree of blobs, taking as input networks of any complexity. Building on this approach, we construct a consensus for level-1 networks (i.e., networks with non-overlapping cycles). This method, called 'L1N consensus', takes a collection of level-1 networks as input and returns a level-1 network. The different components of this consensus network (e.g., blobs, hybrid clades, and edges) have support values that correspond to the frequency of the given component among the input networks. These methods are implemented in PhyloSummaries, building on the foundation of PhyloNetworks. We evaluate the performance of L1N consensus using large-scale simulated data. Our results demonstrate that L1N consensus outperforms existing methods in the rooted setting in terms of informativity and accuracy. Similar results are obtained in the semi-directed setting. Applying L1N consensus to Leopardus and HIV datasets confirms these findings and demonstrates the usefulness of the method.

papers.title: Suitability of clove oil for the euthanasia of four ornamental fish species: Goldfish (Carassius auratus), Bristlenose catfish (Ancistrus sp.), Midas cichlid (Amphilophus citrinellus) and Three-spot gourami (Trichopodus trichopterus)
papers.abstract: Euthanasia of ornamental fish is usually performed by immersion in an anaesthetic bath. However, it may be difficult for private fish owners to access anaesthetics, and alternative methods are limited. Clove oil is commonly available in drugstores and its use for fish euthanasia has been reported. However, there is a lack of scientific literature supporting its suitability for this purpose and of available species-specific protocols. Our study aimed to assess the suitability of clove oil to euthanise goldfish (Carassius auratus), bristlenose catfish (Ancistrus sp.), Midas cichlid (Amphilophus citrinellus) and three-spot gourami (Trichopodus trichopterus). Time to loss of reflexes and to cessation of opercular movements were recorded. Aversive reactions and histological gill lesions were compared with positive and negative controls, and reversibility of euthanasia attempts was assessed. Opercular movements did not reliably cease in goldfish, even under high clove oil concentrations (1000 mg/L). Clove oil caused loss of indicators in Midas cichlid at a concentration of 1000 mg/L, and in bristlenose catfish and three-spot gourami at a concentration of 400 mg/L. Five Midas cichlid recovered after treatment with clove oil. Clove oil caused severe gill lesions to goldfish and Midas cichlids. The results show that clove oil is not suitable for humane euthanasia of goldfish and Midas cichlid. Additionally, some studies have questioned the ability of clove oil to induce loss of consciousness in fish. Therefore, we recommend avoiding euthanasia with clove oil when suitable alternatives are available and using a secondary killing method, as euthanasia attempts are not always irreversible.

papers.title: Strategies of mechanical adaptations of circulating tumor cells and properties of their cellular microenvironment have predictive and prognostic biomarker value
papers.abstract: Mechanically demanding conditions in the blood circulation damage and kill majority of tumor-shed circulating tumor cells (CTCs). Mechanical fitness: a set of mechanical properties detected with atomic force spectroscopy based force spectrometry supports survival of CTCs. We propose that live CTCs isolated from peripheral blood of prostate cancer patients represent distinct strategies of fitness promoting mechanical adaptations to the fluid shear stress. Some of the cells mimicked properties of erythrocytes (high stiffness) or leukocytes (high deformability). The clustering strategy characterized by exceptionally high adhesion is ingenious to CTCs and not found in blood cells. The abundance of CTCs with elevated adhesion has a predictive value for prostate cancer patients starting first round of androgen deprivation therapy. Moreover, a high adhesion score based on individual cells or average patient-specific adhesion is instrumental to stratify recurrent patients that underwent diagnostic imaging by PSMA-PET/CT and clarify inconclusive PSMA scan results. Including contribution of erythrocyte-like strategy broadened the predictive power of CTC mechanophenotyping. Improved biomarking opportunities to predict early castration resistances were noted when the composition of CTC microenvironment was included alongside the mechanical properties. We demonstrated previously that the CTC microenvironment is formed by large cells co-purifying by microfiltration of the blood of cancer patients. Analysis of the association of particular components of CTC microenvironment with the clustering strategy led to pointing at highly adhesive CTC-EMT. However, in the advanced patients adhesiveness of CTC-EMT was surpassed by tumor hybrid cells (THCs), a distinctive kind of invasive species formed by incomplete phagocytosis of CTCs by macrophages. THCs changed their mechanical phenotype and strategy preference with disease progression pointing at the dynamic nature of adaptations of tumor-shed cells to circulation conditions.

papers.title: A developmentally scheduled inhibitory polarity circuit centers the stomatal pore
papers.abstract: Symmetry in living systems often arises from coordinated asymmetries at smaller scales. The guard cells of stomata--bilaterally symmetric epidermal valves that mediate plant-atmosphere gas exchange--show coordinated asymmetries in pore placement and wall modification. Stomatal form and function are deeply conserved, yet molecular mechanisms defining coordinated cellular asymmetry are unknown. Here we show that pore position arises from a combination of pole avoidance and gradient centering in the membranes and wall dividing sister guard cells. Boundaries are established by spatiotemporal restriction of the receptor-like kinase MUSTACHES (MUS), which directs the disordered polarity protein OCTOPUS-LIKE2 (OPL2) to pore-forming regions. OPL2 peaks correspond to a focus of microtubules, and, from this position, the pore emerges. Experimental rewiring of the MUS-OPL2 polarity module profoundly impacts stomatal morphogenesis, eliminating, shifting, or even redirecting the pore to the opposite wall. These findings reveal a stomata-specific integration and elaboration of core polarity and centering programs, and challenge previous models of stomatal morphogenesis.

papers.title: The DNA demethylase TET1 recognises chromatin via nucleosome engagement of its N-terminal region
papers.abstract: TET1 is a DNA demethylase critical for mammalian embryonic development, yet how it is recruited to its chromatin substrate remains poorly understood. Here we identify a previously uncharacterized N-terminal region of TET1 that directly binds nucleosomes and promotes chromatin binding in mouse embryonic stem cells. Robust chromatin association was evidenced by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching during interphase and chromosome retention throughout mitosis. A 2.47 angstroms cryo-EM structure of the TET1-nucleosome complex reveals recognition of the nucleosome acidic patch through a canonical arginine anchor centred on R75, with additional contacts extending along the H2B surface. Biochemical and cellular analyses validate this interaction and demonstrate its contribution to TET1 chromatin engagement. The region is absent from TET2 and TET3 and displays strong conservation within mammals, indicating that direct nucleosome recognition is a specialized feature of TET1. Together, these findings uncover a previously unknown chromatin-binding module in TET1 and establish a structural basis for its interaction with nucleosomes.

papers.title: One-step glycan photoaffinity probe synthesis enables identification of human milk oligosaccharide-interacting microbiota
papers.abstract: Glycans are found on the surfaces of all living cells and engage in cell signaling through the binding of various molecular targets. However, chemical probes to detect and identify carbohydrate interactions remain difficult to produce, due in large part to the challenges of late-stage, site-specific functionalization of oligosaccharides. Here, we report the synthesis and application of a minimal bifunctional diazirine/alkyne linker utilizing an N,O-dialkylhydroxylamine (NODHA) moiety that can readily be installed on the anomeric position of unprotected sugars. Our linker functionalizes glycans with complete {beta}-stereoselectivity, appends less mass than a single hexose unit, and maintains the closed-ring structure of the reducing end sugar. With this molecule, we generate glycan photoaffinity probes in a single step using unprotected human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs). We then validate binding selectivity of our compounds using lectins with known affinity towards our sugars. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of these glycan photoaffinity probes by performing photocrosslinking on a complex microbiota community and use cell sorting paired with metagenomic sequencing to identify potential new HMO-interacting microbes. Together, our work provides a one-step route to synthesize photoaffinity probes from unprotected, reducing glycans for interrogating carbohydrate interactions at the host-microbiota interface.

papers.title: Therapeutic vulnerabilities of the drug-resistant fungal meningitis pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans
papers.abstract: Treatment options are limited for the priority fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans. We describe CRISPR-insert, a scalable gene inactivation method for global interrogation of drug targets. Genome-wide screens using this methodology combined with machine learning predict 1,297 essential genes under liberal criteria. Unexpectedly absent from this list is FKS1, encoding the target of echinocandin drugs to which C. neoformans is resistant. Contrary to longstanding literature, targeted deletion shows that FKS1 is not essential. Solid-state NMR reveals that fks1{triangleup} mutants lack {beta}-1,3-glucan, arguing against compensation by another synthase. We experimentally test essentiality predictions for genes lacking human orthologs, identifying high-priority drug target candidates. To uncover targets for combination therapies, we establish genome-scale quantitative genetic interaction mapping. We use this method to uncover synthetic lethal dependencies of echinocandin resistance determinants, including the druggable calcineurin and Cdc50-Apt1 pathways. CRISPR-insert illuminates therapeutic vulnerabilities of an invasive fungal pathogen.

papers.title: SENgEAR: an interactive visualization platform for comparative analysis of senescence signatures and cellular communication
papers.abstract: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets provide tremendous potential to identify the cellular states and communication networks associated with senescence. Annotating senescent cells in these datasets is hindered by the lack of universal markers for senescent cells and their context-dependent variability. To overcome this, several groups have developed gene signatures to annotate cells with distinct senotypes. However, comparing these signatures and their biological contexts to determine the specificity of senescence signatures remains complicated by the separate data platforms for signatures and datasets. We present SENgEAR, a no-code web platform for senescent cell annotation, visualization of cell-cell communication networks, and comparison of senescence signatures across studies, tissues, species, and data modalities. SENgEAR provides a unified framework to explore contextual signature specificity, cellular communication pathways, and senotype heterogeneity. We demonstrate the use of SENgEAR for applications spanning aging, fibrosis, and wound healing and its ability to interrelate these states.

papers.title: Uncovering the Multifaceted Role of the Kinetochore Scaffold 1 (KNL1) in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: Integrative Bioinformatics Analysis and CRISPR-Cas9 Experimental Study
papers.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a highly aggressive malignancy characterized by pronounced heterogeneity, chromosomal instability, and limited therapeutic options. Kinetochore scaffold 1 (KNL1), a core mitotic checkpoint component, is implicated in multiple cancers, but its role in HCC remains unclear. Here, we integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses with functional in vitro validation to elucidate the biological and clinical significance of KNL1 in HCC. KNL1 was markedly overexpressed in HCC tumors, particularly those harbouring TP53 mutations, and correlated with increased tumor break load, suggesting a link to structural chromosomal instability. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) and hallmark gene set enrichment identified a KNL1-associated G2M checkpoint network, in which KNL1 ranked among the top 10 hub genes. A KNL1-G2M network score, stratified patients into high- and low-score groups, with high scores correlates with poorer overall survival, increased proliferation, and higher chromosomal instability. Immune deconvolution (CIBERSORTx) revealed that high-score tumors were enriched in T-regulatory cells and M0 macrophages, and had elevated TIDE and exclusion scores, indicating potential resistance to immune checkpoint blockade. Single-cell RNA-seq confirmed preferential activation of the KNL1-G2M module in malignant hepatocytes and highlighted increased extracellular matrix remodeling and immunomodulatory interactions. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated KNL1 downregulation in HepG2 cells induced modest G2/M arrest, suppressed proliferation, reduced survivin and Bcl2 expression, and produced ultrastructural changes consistent with early apoptosis. Collectively, our results implicate KNL1 and its associated G2/M network in tumor progression-related processes, including chromosomal instability, proliferative activity, and immune modulation in HCC. While further mechanistic and clinical studies are required, KNL1 and its associated network may represent a biologically relevant vulnerability and a potential biomarker of aggressive disease behavior in hepatocellular carcinoma.

papers.title: TREM2 encodes plaque macrophage plasticity to mediate atherosclerosis regression
papers.abstract: Cholesterol lowering therapies stabilize atherosclerotic plaque and reduce ischemic events, but the molecular mechanisms governing plaque remodeling or regression remain poorly defined. The lipid sensor TREM2 is a key modulator of plaque-associated foam cell development and was upregulated by plaque macrophages in atherosclerosis regression. We examined macrophage- or monocyte-specific Trem2 deletion during regression in mice and found that TREM2 expression on plaque macrophages, not newly recruited monocytes, was required for plaque regression. Trem2 deletion impeded necrotic core resolution, leading us to interrogate the efferocytic capacity of TREM2+ cells during lipid lowering. An in vitro model of cholesterol-experienced ex-lipid associated macrophages (Ex-LAMs) demonstrated that prior lipid priming enhanced efferocytic ability after unloading lipids and maintained expression of lysosomal and cytoskeletal remodeling genes. Augmented TREM2 signaling through genetic models or agonist treatment accelerated efferocytic ability in vitro and plaque regression in vivo. Thus, we posit that a TREM2-dependent ExLAM programming drives atherosclerosis resolution and facilitates beneficial plaque remodeling through enhanced efferocytosis. Overall, targeting the TREM2 pathway may be a viable strategy for stabilizing atherosclerotic plaques in patients treated with aggressive cholesterol control.

papers.title: A RecBCD-like enzyme regulates expression of bacterial defense operons in response to DNA damage
papers.abstract: Bacteria must quickly respond to stress signals including bacteriophage (phage) infection, invasion by mobile genetic elements, and other threats. DNA damage is a stress-signaling nexus in bacteria, initiating global responses such as the SOS response and triggering expression of specific defense and immune pathways through DNA damage-sensing transcriptional regulators. Here we identify a three-protein pathway termed Cerberus that senses dsDNA ends that become available during DNA damage or inhibition of the key DNA repair complex RecBCD, and controls expression of an associated defense/immune operon. The central player in Cerberus is a large peptidase-helicase-nuclease fusion protein, CerC, that is architecturally similar to the RecBC complex itself. Upon DNA damage or RecBCD inhibition, CerC binds and unwinds free DNA ends to allosterically activate its fused HExxH metallopeptidase domain. CerC specifically cleaves the adjacently encoded anti-sigma factor CerB to release its cognate sigma factor CerA, allowing CerA to mediate transcription of a defense/immune operon encoded nearby. Cerberus therefore represents a pathway that has co-opted a key DNA repair machine for DNA damage sensing, and linked that activity to transcriptional control through anti-sigma factor cleavage.

papers.title: How Well Does Structural MRI Classify Autism? A Leakage-Free, Site-Aware and Externally Validated Machine-Learning Evaluation in Two ABIDE Cohorts
papers.abstract: Background: Many studies report high accuracy for classifying autism spectrum disorder (ASD) from structural MRI, but small samples, single train-test splits, site effects and information leakage can inflate performance. We evaluated how well brain morphometry distinguishes autistic from typically developing (TD) individuals under rigorous, leakage-free validation. Methods: FreeSurfer-derived features (n = 280: regional thickness, area and volume; subcortical volumes; Yeo-network composites; asymmetry indices; global measures) from ABIDE II (804 participants; 341 ASD; 12 sites) were used to train logistic regression, linear support vector machine, random forest, XGBoost and multilayer perceptron classifiers. Confound regression (age, age2, sex, brain volume), site-wise centring and standardisation were learned within training folds only. Performance was assessed with nested 10-fold cross-validation, leave-one-site-out validation and external validation in ABIDE I (917 participants; 20 sites), and compared with full-pipeline permutation tests and a confound-only baseline. Results: Cross-validated discrimination was modest: the best model (regularised logistic regression on all features) reached an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.60 [0.56, 0.64], significantly above chance (permutation p = .002) but far from clinically useful and below a confound-only baseline using age, sex, brain volume and site (AUC 0.63); non-linear models did not perform better (AUC 0.45-0.60 across models and feature sets). Pooled leave-one-site-out AUCs were 0.54-0.61, with large between-site variation, and AUCs in the external ABIDE I cohort were 0.52-0.58. Age-stratified models did not exceed AUC 0.60. Across 300 random 80/20 splits in young adults, test-set AUCs ranged from 0.21 to 0.90, showing that single-split estimates such as 0.74 can arise by chance. Conclusions: Under leakage-free, site-aware and externally validated evaluation, structural MRI morphometry classifies autism only slightly better than chance. Reports of high accuracy should be interpreted with caution, and the heterogeneity of autism argues for stratification and normative approaches rather than binary diagnostic classifiers.

papers.title: GDF15 modifies NAD+ salvage pathway and dampens immune response in mitochondrial disease
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial integrated stress response (ISRmt) is a main mammalian metabolic stress pathway, with local ISRmt and a systemic response via circulating metabokines GDF15 and FGF21 as early signs of the response in mitochondrial diseases. FGF21 has been reported to regulate ISRmt progression and nutrient homeostasis, but the roles of GDF15 have remained unclear. Here, we explored the effects of inactivation of FGF21 or GDF15 or them together in Deletor mice. These mice endogenously activate the full ISRmt and metabokines as part of their mitochondrial muscle disease. GDF15 inactivity upregulated the skeletal muscle enzyme NMRK2, which converts nicotinamide riboside (NR) to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) and NAD+. FGF21 was required for glutathione homeostasis. GDF15 inactivation also induced immune cell invasion in the muscle, aggravated by FGF21 loss, suggesting synergistic anti-inflammatory effects. Our findings indicate that in addition to their systemic effects, FGF21 and GDF15 are autocrine controllers of redox homeostasis in mitochondrial disease muscle.

papers.title: Beyond a single threshold: calibration of CADD v1.7 and AlphaGenome for ACMG/AMP computational evidence across variant classes, model versions, and reference data
papers.abstract: Clinical laboratories use computational predictors as supporting evidence for or against pathogenicity under the ACMG/AMP guidelines, but this evidence is reliable only when score thresholds are calibrated. Genome-wide predictors such as CADD are often applied using a single cutoff across all variant types and model versions, and the new AlphaGenome Variant Impact score (AVI) has not been calibrated. Following a prespecified plan and the ClinGen calibration method, we calibrated CADD v1.7 and AVI on rare ClinVar missense variants. Both predictors provided moderate evidence of pathogenicity and strong evidence of benignity, and their thresholds held for variants classified after calibration. AVI performed better than CADD in each comparison and approached the missense-specific predictors. Thresholds available in 2024 gave AVI evidence in the final direction for 72.5% of the variants of uncertain significance (VUS) resolved by 2026, compared with 60.5% for CADD. Applied to 1.2 million current missense VUS, the calibrated predictors agreed on pathogenic or benign evidence for four in ten, and on strong pathogenic evidence for 186 VUS reviewed by expert panels, which can be reassessed first. Outside missense variants, the same thresholds failed, producing false-benign evidence for pathogenic noncoding variants. A change in CADD version altered the evidence level for a third of variants without improving discrimination. Our results suggest that computational evidence is most reliable within the variant class and model version in which it was calibrated. In practice, laboratories may prioritize missense-specific predictors, use AVI when a genome-wide predictor is needed, and reassess thresholds after model updates.

papers.title: Spatial Decoupling of the Endodermal Functions Establishes the Innermost Cortex as the Gravity Sensor in Rice Stems
papers.abstract: Gravitropism is a remarkable example of coordinated growth, enabling plants to perceive gravity and generate asymmetric cell expansion that restores organ orientation. In Arabidopsis, gravity sensing in shoots occurs within starch-rich endodermis cells. In rice, however, the stem must accommodate gravitropic bending while preserving integrity of tissues surrounding emerging crown roots, raising the possibility that gravity sensing relies on distinct structural and physiological adaptations. Here, using high-resolution imaging together with auxin-response analyses, we identify a specialized cell layer at the inner boundary of the rice stem cortex, operationally defined by its position adjacent to the lignified endodermis and associated with gravitropic responses. This layer is characterized by circumferentially elongated cells, starch sedimentation, a confined auxin-response domain, and expression of gravity-sensing markers. Following gravistimulation, starch granules realign and the auxin response domain expands asymmetrically within this layer, coinciding with differential growth during stem bending. Our results further indicate that this response depends on polar auxin transport and conserved components of the gravitropic regulatory network.
