papers.abstract: The Saccharomyces genus present as a genetically diverse set of microorganisms capable of tolerating a range of environmental stressors, demonstrating high fermentation capacity and producing interesting flavour compounds. Such diversity can be exploited in a single organism by producing interspecies hybrids, overcoming the limitations of a single species. Here, as proof of principle, we exploited a library of F12 interspecies diploid hybrids between Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Saccharomyces jurei (Sc/Sj), to identify new strains harbouring traits of oenological relevance, such as ethanol and glycerol production, superior tolerance to acetic acid, limited production of H2S, and optimal growth on fructose. Moreover, we calculated robustness across strains tested on solid media comparing the trade-off between performance on a single conditions and overall robustness. Progeny from a range of robustness values with favourable H2S production profiles were isolated for further analysis via micro and small-scale fermentations. Micro-scale fermentations in synthetic grape must containing individual wine-associated stressors were performed, and the robustness of the selected strains was confirmed. The wine characteristics of the hybrids were tested in small-scale fermentations in synthetic grape media. We found that both ethanol and glycerol production across our selected progeny matched or exceeding that from the commercial wine strain, and most hybrids produced less acetic acid and more fatty-acids, including higher quantities of associated esters. Overall, we were able to identify suitable Sc/Sj hybrids with interesting aroma profiles to develop further for wine fermentation.

papers.title: Homoplastic evolution of proximal podomere patterning across Arthropoda
papers.abstract: The jointed arthropod leg is often credited as a key innovation spurring the evolutionary success of the phylum. Across lineages, each territory of the appendage has served as the substrate for myriad adaptations and structural innovations. While much of the available data has supported a conserved suite of transcription factors responsible for the initiation and patterning of the arthropod appendage, recent works have begun to highlight instances of lineage-specific shifts in expression dynamics, particularly amongst the chelicerates, correlated both with the emergence of novel structures and developmental system drift in the specification of plesiomorphic structures. These works confound efforts to align or homologize the leg segments across arthropod lineages, an effort already challenged by ground plan differences in segment number between the subphyla. An even more unusual architecture of leg segments occurs in sea spiders (Pycnogonida), which alone among Arthropoda are considered by systematists to bear three coxae (proximal segments), in contrast to the single coxa of the remaining arthropods. Here, we examined proximal podomere patterning in the developing appendages of a sea spider and an arachnid. We find that a particular spatial arrangement of Lim1 and SoxNeuro characterizes the developing coxa and trochanter of the harvestman Phalangium opilio (Opiliones) throughout appendage formation, with RNAi depletions of Lim1 yielding deletions of coxa and trochanter. Comparison of expression patterns across taxa shows that Lim1 and SoxNeuro have a similar spatial arrangement in the harvestman and sea spider, but these suggest conflicting interpretations of leg segment homology. We show that this is attributable to homoplastic patterns of evolution in SoxNeuro across Arthropoda. Expanding our surveys of prominent PD axis-patterning transcription factors supports additional instances of homoplasy in the domains of Sp6-9 and Irx2. The pervasiveness of homoplasy in gene expression patterns demands measured skepticism of homology statements and careful comparisons of multiple patterning genes, toward achieving falsifiability in the homology of structures.

papers.title: Harmonizing Repeated Multi-Platform Optical and LiDAR Observations for Continental-Scale Terrestrial Carbon Cycle Data Assimilation.
papers.abstract: Accurate monitoring of terrestrial carbon has attracted considerable attention due to the impacts of rapid climate change, disturbance, and land use on carbon storage and the growth of new global carbon markets and reporting requirements. While uncertainties in C estimates remain nontrivial, crucial opportunities exist to reduce uncertainty by rigorously harmonizing models and monitoring through data assimilation (DA). LiDAR has received considerable attention for its potential to inform carbon monitoring, and while there have been a number of papers on how to initialize models using LiDAR data, it has yet to be integrated into DA systems. In this study, we integrate GEDI LiDAR into an established DA system that already assimilates optical observations of aboveground biomass (AGB) and leaf area index (LAI), microwave soil moisture (SM), and ground-based soil organic carbon (SOC) to constrain C cycling processes across the entire North American continent. Notably, this is the first time both optical and LiDAR AGB products have been iteratively harmonized within a DA system. Results show that by assimilating both optical and LiDAR observations, we reduced the uncertainty in woody biomass by 63.7% relative to unconstrained model simulations and 18% relative to our previous DA system, and achieved an average RMSE reduction of 38.3 kg/m2 across five AGB products. Importantly, LiDAR reduces DA biases in high AGB regions where optical AGB estimates were exhibiting saturation. Analysis further identified the leading factors driving spatial error patterns within the DA system to be data quality, cloud coverage, and elevation. Overall, by bridging the spatial and temporal limitations of individual satellite products, this approach offers a practical, generalized workflow for high-resolution terrestrial carbon MRV in complex, dynamic ecosystems.

papers.title: Inferring scaling laws of branching networks from their geometry by global optimization
papers.abstract: Optimality principles are widely used to understand branching networks, yet they are tested on individual branchings that cannot reliably distinguish competing scaling laws. We formulate the missing link between the laws and measurements by mapping each law to its predicted branch points through global optimization. Vascular branch points closely match weighted-length optima when each vessel is allowed its own fitted weight. Inferred scaling laws reveal type-specific geometric signatures hidden from local analysis. They beat all tested laws, including Murray's law in 1,679 of 1,744 held-out hepatic and pulmonary trees. For coronary arteries on the heart surface, an exact discrete optimization model extends the framework beyond convex geometry and supports area-preserving scaling. The framework also identifies distinct laws for airways and plant shoots while rejecting weighted-length optimality for neuronal axons. Global optimization turns network geometry into a quantitative test of the principles that govern branching networks.

papers.title: Fluidized Bed Cathodes Enable High-Rate CO2 to Formate Production and In Situ Microbial Growth
papers.abstract: Electrochemical CO2 Reduction Reaction (eCO2RR) to formate offers a sustainable and promising route for storing renewable electricity in a microbial energy substrate. Conventional CO2 electrolyzers rely on flat electrodes with limited catalytic surface area, mass-transfer constraints, and electrolytes that are incompatible with microbial growth, preventing direct coupling of electrochemical formate production with biological conversion. Here, we developed a biocompatible CO2 electrolysis configuration that uses fluidized particles of Sn, Bi, and In as electrocatalysts to enhance CO2 to formate conversion while supporting microbial utilization in the same chamber. The fluidized configuration enabled high formate production rates up to 0.24 mmol cm2 with Faradaic efficiencies of 86 to 92%, representing a two fold improvement over static electrodes. The system also achieved a carbon conversion efficiency of 42%, approaching the theoretical limit for co-generation of formate and bicarbonate. Importantly, electrolysis was performed in a biocompatible medium that supported direct in situ cultivation of Cupriavidus necator within the cathode chamber using only electricity and CO2/O2 as fed substrates. C. necator continuously consumed electro-generated formate for 5 to 6 days under aerobic conditions, demonstrating integrated CO2 to biomass conversion. This work establishes a fluidized electrocatalytic platform for simultaneous electrosynthesis and microbial upgrading in a single reactor, providing a scalable strategy for renewable carbon fixation and sustainable biomanufacturing.

papers.title: Ancient environmental DNA reveals the distinct fingerprints of whaling and climate change on Antarctic marine biodiversity
papers.abstract: The Southern Ocean is a disproportionately large contributor to Earth system processes, playing a crucial role in the global transport of carbon, oxygen and heat. It also hosts enormous seasonal biological productivity that supports diverse endemic marine biodiversity. Industrial whaling in the first half of the 20th century and recent human-driven climate change have both profoundly altered Antarctic ecosystems, but ecological surveys of these impacts are limited to well-known taxa in the short period since monitoring began. Here, we analysed five sediment records to reconstruct more than two centuries of ecosystem change across the Western Antarctic Peninsula, spanning periods before and during major human impacts. Environmental DNA metabarcoding of these records revealed substantial biodiversity shifts, with change accelerating in recent decades. We find a significant role for both climate change and whaling in restructuring communities, identifying unique variance in whole-community change explained by each driver. Moreover, we find a negative association between whaling and metazoan families which feed from the water column, suggesting that pre-whaling ecosystems had greater pelagic productivity. Overall, our results reveal baseline Antarctic biodiversity from long before observational records and identify a distinct fingerprint of human drivers in this fragile, rapidly changing ecosystem.

papers.title: No Effect of Exercise Timing on Daily Glycaemia Despite Shifts in Acute Glucose Dynamics in Participants with Normal Glucose Tolerance: A Randomised Crossover Trial
papers.abstract: Exercise is a well-established modulator of glucose regulation, but whether the time of day it is performed matters for healthy, free-living adults remains unresolved. In a randomised crossover trial, 29 healthy adults completed a single 30-minute bout of moderate-intensity exercise in the morning (07:00-10:00) and in the evening (16:00-19:00), with continuous glucose monitoring and wrist-worn activity tracking used to capture responses over an 8-day free-living protocol. Evening exercise produced a significantly greater acute reduction in blood glucose (P < 0.001) compared to morning exercise, but this did not translate into consistent differences in overall daily mean glycaemic exposure, whether measured over the calendar day or over a window aligned with exercise onset. Evening exercise was linked to greater within-day glycaemic variability than morning exercise, with the clearest evidence coming from the circadian-aligned analysis (day x timing interaction, SD: P = 0.00939; CV: P = 0.00766). Appetite rose after exercise in both conditions, with no difference by time of day. Taken together, these results show that exercise timing does not change how much glucose exposure a healthy adult accumulates over a day, but it does change the shape of the glucose response around the exercise bout itself, a distinction only visible when glucose is examined at a finer temporal resolution than daily averages allow.

papers.title: Ambivalent roles of nonsense-mediated mRNA decay in heat stress tolerance
papers.abstract: RNA homeostasis is essential for gene regulation and cellular survival; however, how RNA degradation pathways contribute to stress adaptation remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the role of the nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) in regulating heat stress (HS) memory in a long-term acquired thermotolerance assay. NMD-deficient Arabidopsis thaliana mutants upf1-5 and upf3-1 exhibited a biphasic phenotype: they displayed transiently elevated heat tolerance during early recovery but became more sensitive to heat during late recovery. Genetic analysis of upf3;hsfa2 and upf3;hsfa3 double mutants demonstrated that the early heat tolerance occurs independently of both HsfA2 and HsfA3 HS-memory transcription factors. Under non-treated conditions, the upf3-1 transcriptome exhibited baseline priming of heat-shock responsive transcripts, likely accounting for the initial heat tolerance. Further transcriptome profiling revealed that upf3-1 mutants exhibited reduced levels of the functional HsfA2 isoform (HsfA2-I) and attenuated expression of the HsfA2-dependent thermomemory regulon following the triggering stress. NMD deficiency also upregulated immune-response genes while repressing developmental and cell-wall-associated pathways. Together, impaired HsfA2-dependent thermomemory and a compromised growth defense balance underlies the late heat sensitivity of NMD deficient plants. Overall, NMD acts as a dual-action post-transcriptional regulator that coordinates the transition from stress response to growth resumption.

papers.title: Mechanotransduction tuned by intermediate filaments promotes DNA repair in stiff environments
papers.abstract: High mammographic density increases breast cancer risk. Dense tissues are rich in fibrillar collagen, forming a rigid extracellular matrix around the epithelium. Although cancer initiation and progression are closely tied to DNA damage and to the DNA damage response, if and how tissue stiffness affects genome maintenance is not fully elucidated. We found that repair factor recruitment is more efficient, and that DNA breaks are repaired faster by cells on rigid substrates. Mechanistically, hemidesmosomal integrins, intermediate filaments, the LINC complex, and YAP are key mediators of this mechanogenomic response. Rigid tissue contexts favor survival of cells with DNA damage, which may lead to the accumulation of somatic mutations, as identified here with RNAseq analyses of normal breast tissue. Our findings provide new insights into how tissue rigidity influences cancer risk.

papers.title: SpaceBlocks: an expert-supervised workflow for cohort-level spatial transcriptomics analysis
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has become a central tool in tissue biology, with multiple technologies addressing the issue from a different angle. Each platform imposes its own raw data format conventions, and few workflows address reproducible, scalable, cohort-level analyses while integrating expert-supervised decisions to strengthen computational and biological provenance. In this work, we present SpaceBlocks, a Snakemake workflow for reproducible cohort-level analysis of single-cell resolution-ST data that prioritizes expert supervision over full automation. SpaceBlocks homogenizes heterogeneous platform outputs into a common data format, whose structure is validated to ensure downstream processing. Comprehensive expert supervision is facilitated through per sample quality control and cell type annotation diagnostic visualizations, after which downstream analyses automatically follow. SpaceBlocks also allows the ingestion of technology-agnostic externally formatted data and provides interoperability with existing tools and technologies. We demonstrate the use of SpaceBlocks through the reanalysis of 37 samples from public Visium HD, Xenium 5K and MERSCOPE datasets. SpaceBlocks exhibited processing scalability across the three platforms. This reanalysis identified previously missed cell types in Visium HD and heterogeneous marker gene expression in MERSCOPE, highlighting the need for expert-supervised annotations. Moreover, SpaceBlocks facilitated the identification of differentially expressed genes associated with previously defined multiple sclerosis (MS) spatial domains in MERSCOPE, and transcriptional differences between healthy and malignant colorectal tissues in Visium HD. Together, these findings establish SpaceBlocks as a flexible and reproducible workflow for expert-supervised spatial transcriptomics analysis across technologies and biological cohorts.

papers.title: Heterogeneous primary nucleation determines Aβ42 fibrilstructure.
papers.abstract: The current developments in the field of amyloid fibril structure determination has revealed multiple structures for peptides of identical sequence. This may reflect variations in sample environment or similar nucleation barriers for multiple folds. Here we investigate the influence of aggregating surface and during fibril formation from monomeric amyloid {beta} peptide (A{beta}42). The fibril structures formed in identical solutions in glass vials / bottles and PEGylated polystyrene 96-well plates display very different monomer fold within the fibrils. This is a clear indication of extremely slow homogeneous primary nucleation. Instead, heterogeneous primary nucleation at vessel walls or at the three-line interface between air, water and vessel wall dictate the outcome in each solution, where the initially formed structure is propagated through elongation and secondary nucleation. The results further imply that the conversion towards the thermodynamically stable fibril structure one is slow for A{beta}42.

papers.title: Quantifying heritability in functional regions of the coding and non-coding genome across diverse individuals
papers.abstract: Most heritability studies have focused on common genetic variation and have largely excluded non-European or highly admixed populations. Here, we estimated the whole-genome heritability (h2WGS) of seven complex traits using 73,600,953 autosomal and chromosome X variants for 198,931 unrelated individuals from three genetic similarity groups. Adjusting for population stratification, we showed that rare variants (minor allele frequency<0.01) explain 30.6-67.7% of h2WGS. We used simulations to show how functionally-stratified heritability can be inflated due to linkage with missing or lower-quality variants. Finally, after accounting for confounding effects, we found substantial heritability enrichment from variants in non-coding RNA exons (maximum fold enrichment, FE=8.7, P=3.56e-7), UTRs (23.0, P=3.46e-30), distal regulatory regions (33.8, P=3.26e-42), and protein-coding exons (58.0, P=7.78e-15). Our study provides a framework for investigating the genetic architecture of complex human phenotypes using diverse whole-genome sequencing data and highlights the contribution of rare and non-coding genetic variants to the heritability of complex traits.

papers.title: CMVAE: Contrastive Supervision Improves Single-Omic Latent Manifold for Breast Cancer Survival Prognosis
papers.abstract: High-dimensional omics data are vital for fore- casting patient prognosis in oncology. While deep multi-omics learning methods are increasingly popular, they suffer from data missingness and low patient overlap across modalities. Consequently, advancing single-omic representation learning re- mains a critical yet challenging research problem. Standard generative dimensionality reduction methods rely on recon- struction objectives that optimize the global manifold topology; however, overlook downstream clinical outcomes. To address these limitations, we introduce a Contrastive Masked Denois- ing Variational Autoencoder (CMVAE), a self-supervised dual- optimization framework designed to map single-omic information into a clinical outcome-aware latent space. A stochastic feature masking strategy corrupts the input omic profiles, and CMVAE is optimized to simultaneously infer missing molecular data and contrastive alignment of patient survival trajectories. We evaluate CMVAE using leak-proof five-fold stratified cross-validation on the TCGA Breast Invasive Carcinoma (BRCA) cohort. The method outperforms traditional unsupervised methods, achieving an AUROC of 0.7397 {+/-} 0.0239 on patient prognosis. Further analysis demonstrates a highly significant (p < 0.0001) risk stratification among low vs. high risk groups. Beyond comparing within single-omic methods, CMVAE outperforms six state-of- the-art multi-omics survival baselines by a minimum of 3%. Availability: All codes including data preparation scripts, training and validation recipes, and experimental configurations are available at: https://github.com/kabir-ai2bio-lab/CMVAE. Note: Accepted at the IEEE BIBM 2026 workshop RLPD-Bio (Representation Learning and Pattern Discovery for Bioinformatics and Biomedicine).

papers.title: Evaluation of immunotoxic effects and metabolism of enniatins and beauvericin using in vitro models of the human intestinal epithelium
papers.abstract: Enniatins (ENNs) and beauvericin (BEA) are mycotoxins produced by Fusarium species. They are frequently detected in cereal-based foods such as maize and wheat. Consequently, the gastrointestinal tract is a primary site of exposure for consumers of grain-containing foods. This study examined intestinal effects of four major ENNs: ENNB, ENNB1, ENNA, and ENNA1, and the structurally related mycotoxin BEA, using the primary human intestinal model EpiIntestinal (TM) tissues and a Caco-2/TH29-MTX-E12 co-culture. None of the compounds induced cytotoxicity or impaired the barrier integrity at concentrations ranging from 1 to 10 microM. Furthermore, all ENNs and BEA stimulated IL-6 secretion, with ENNA and ENNA1 inducing the strongest responses, while IL-8 secretion was only triggered by ENNA and ENNA1. Transport studies revealed that approximately 32% of ENNB and 25% of ENNB1 crossed from the apical to the basolateral side of the intestinal tissue within 4 h, whereas the other ENNs and BEA had transport ratios below 10%. Further findings suggested that uptake and intracellular accumulation of ENNs and BEA were influenced by their affinity to the efflux transporter P-glycoprotein (P-gp). In addition, several ENNB and ENNB1 metabolites were generated in the EpiIntestinal (TM) tissues and transported. Lastly, it was demonstrated that ENNB can disturb the metabolism of the sex hormone estradiol in human liver microsomes. Overall, ENNs and BEA showed limited acute toxicity in human intestinal models but elicited distinct inflammatory responses and differed in transport and metabolism. These findings may be of relevance when evaluating health risks from chronic, low-level dietary exposure

papers.title: A Unique Promoter Architecture Defines Menin-KMT2A Complex Selectivity
papers.abstract: Selective occupancy of chromatin-regulatory complexes is central to developmental gene regulation, yet the sequence determinants of this selectivity remain poorly understood. Using interpretable machine learning, we identify a composite promoter architecture comprising CpG islands flanked by several-kilobase A/T-rich domains (AT-flanks) that denotes high occupancy of the Menin-KMT2A histone-modifying complex at developmental and leukemia-associated genes. Genetic deletion and chromatin-contact analyses show that AT-flanks support KMT2A retention at linked CpG islands. We identify LEDGF as an A/T-rich DNA-associated protein required for Menin engagement at AT-flanks and sustained KMT2A promoter occupancy. AT-flank extent is associated with differential KMT2A loss following pharmacologic disruption of the Menin-KMT2A interaction, providing a genomic basis for heterogeneous target sensitivity to recently approved Menin inhibitors in acute leukemia. Beyond Menin-KMT2A, the same architecture distinguishes promoters with high canonical PRC1 occupancy across diverse cell types, revealing a shared sequence organization associated with distinct chromatin-regulatory states.

papers.title: DECAPPING PROTEIN 5 regulates the circadian clock in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: The Arabidopsis transcriptome must be continuously reshaped to integrate endogenous and environmental cues, including the circadian clock and ambient light. This reprogramming relies on the coordinated synthesis and degradation of mRNAs, yet the contribution of RNA decay factors to circadian regulation remains poorly characterized. Here, we show that nearly all core clock genes are high-amplitude clock-controlled genes (HA-CCGs). A meta-analysis of transcriptome-wide mRNA decay datasets revealed that HA-CCGs have consistently shorter half-lives across multiple studies. We further identify the mRNA decapping activator DECAPPING PROTEIN 5 (DCP5) as a key regulator of circadian RNA stability. Using iCLIP, we show that DCP5 binds preferentially to HA-CCG transcripts at AU-rich motifs in their 3' UTRs, thereby modulating their stability. Accordingly, the dcp5 mutant displays an extended circadian period at both physiological and molecular levels. Our findings establish mRNA decay as a post-transcriptional regulatory layer that fine-tunes the decay of multiple key transcripts within the circadian system.

papers.title: Social foragers rely more on dynamic cues than prior beliefs in unpredictable natural environments
papers.abstract: Foraging is a prime example of adaptive decision-making in uncertain and changing environments. Foragers need to continuously integrate their direct experiences and observations of what others are doing with what they already know about the distribution of prey. Yet little is known about the importance of prior knowledge relative to dynamically sampled information in social foraging settings. Here, we investigated the role of prior beliefs in five large-scale ice-fishing competitions involving 49--53 highly experienced ice-fishers in 251 foraging trips. To quantify their prior spatial beliefs, participants marked areas they believed to have high resource abundance on topographic maps containing isoclines (i.e., depth curves) before each competition. GPS devices and headcams tracked behavioural states and foraging success. We found that prior beliefs about the fish distribution are to a large extent driven by lake topography and therefore converge across individuals. However, these prior beliefs were not systematically linked to foraging success. While prior beliefs predicted spot choices, especially in the beginning of competitions, they were heavily outweighed by dynamic personal and social information sources. Exploring how the use of prior beliefs differed between foraging trips, we found that high reliance on prior beliefs was associated with reduced avoidance of unsuccessful locations which resulted in limited spatial exploration. We conclude that dynamic information sampling and accumulation are key processes in social foraging decisions, with prior spatial beliefs playing only a minor role in natural environments where resources are hard to predict in advance.

papers.title: MaCADEMIA: a software toolbox for single-molecule fluorescence image quantification
papers.abstract: Single-molecule localisation microscopy (SMLM) is a powerful tool in molecular and cellular biology and part of the broad umbrella of super-resolution microscopy. A distinct feature of SMLM, is its capacity for deep quantification, beyond just spatial information, to copy number, stoichiometry, molecular interaction and dynamics in living cells. The hardware required is increasingly straightforward to implement. However, complexity remains in the image analysis where much remains fragmented across specialised software tools. Here, we present MaCADEMIA (Matlab Computational Analysis of Diffusion, Emitter Molecular Intensity and Abundance), a simple yet powerful toolbox of MATLAB functions and associated documentation to enable straightforward extraction of quantitative single-molecule information. MaCADEMIA performs ensemble particle detection achieving localisation accuracies down to 0.5 pixels Root mean squared error (RMSE) across wide signal-to-noise (SNR) ranges on standardised particle tracking benchmarks, consistently matching or exceeding the performance of 14 leading methods. Our integrated workflow enables molecular counting and stoichiometry determination through stepwise photobleaching analysis, mobility measurement via mean squared displacement, colocalisaton analysis and absolute protein copy number quantification using three-dimensional cellular models.

papers.title: Selective binders of a cotranslational folding intermediate
papers.abstract: Drug discovery efforts typically target mature, folded proteins, primarily to inhibit their function or induce their degradation. An alternative strategy would be to target incompletely folded states that are transiently populated during protein biogenesis, but whether these states contain druggable pockets was unclear. Here, we used an mRNA display approach to discover cyclic peptides that recognize a nascent polypeptide at an intermediate point during its synthesis on the ribosome. We identified peptides that bind with low-nanomolar affinity to a model nascent protein, {beta}-galactosidase, but do not detectably bind either the fully-folded protein or ribosomes synthesising different sequences. Hydrogen/deuterium exchange-mass spectrometry and cryogenic electron microscopy revealed the molecular basis for selective binding. We found that the nascent chain folds into an -helix against the ribosome surface during ongoing translation, creating a cryptic pocket together with ribosomal proteins uL23 and uL29 that is exploited by the hit peptides. Our results establish proof-of-concept for selective targeting of protein biogenesis intermediates, and provide a platform for future drug development.

papers.title: Mitotic centromeres organize in repeat-subunits with specialized histone landscape and multi-domain architecture as revealed by expansion microscopy
papers.abstract: Centromeres ensure faithful chromosome segregation during cell division, yet their underlying architecture and spatial arrangement of centromeric proteins remain incompletely resolved. Here, we apply Ten-fold Robust Expansion Microscopy (TREx) to human diploid hTERT RPE-1 cells to visualize mitotic centromeres at nanoscale resolution. We find that the centromeric histone variant CENP-A and the kinetochore protein KNL1 form discontinuous, repeating substructures. We further resolve centromeric chromatin into four spatially distinct domains: an inner kinetochore domain marked by CENP-A, a mantle domain marked by RAD21, an outer core domain marked by CENP-B, and a distinct, RAD21-associated inner centromere domain. Core and pericentromeric regions share a specialized chromatin landscape, extending the concept of centrochromatin, with enrichment of H3S10ph and H3K9me3, depletion of H3K27me3, and low-level enrichment of the euchromatic marks H3K4me3 and H3K36me3. Together, we uncover a discontinuous repeat-subunit organization and multidomain architecture of the human centromere that combines euchromatic and heterochromatic modifications.

papers.title: Diffusion-Based Synthetic Pretraining for Root Segmentation in Rhizotron Images
papers.abstract: Rhizotrons allow root system architecture to be studied non-destructively in soil. However, automated analysis of rhizotron images remains difficult: roots have low contrast against soil, soil particles resemble fine roots, and deep learning models need many manually annotated images that are slow and subjective to produce. Synthetic images could provide paired images and annotations at scale, but rhizotron images are largely absent from the data used to train generative models. We built a pipeline combining Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), ControlNet and inpainting to generate synthetic rhizotron images with paired root masks. We compared training on synthetic data only, real data only, and synthetic pretraining followed by fine-tuning on real images, using three segmentation models: nnU-Net v2, YOLO26 and Mask2Former. Synthetic-only training reached a Dice score of up to 0.60. Synthetic pretraining followed by fine-tuning on the full real training set (two annotated rhizotron images) reached 0.80, and nnU-Net v2 and Mask2Former reached 0.62 with only two annotated image patches containing visible roots. When real annotations were limited, pretraining also improved segmentation of unseen crops, including lettuce, barley, wheat, maize, tomato, cucumber, French bean and field bean. We also introduced a Soft Dice score that compares predictions with probabilistic consensus maps from seven independent annotators, accounting for annotator disagreement. Models matched average human agreement on low-ambiguity patches but remained below it on high-ambiguity patches. In conclusion, diffusion-generated images can complement real annotations and help scale root segmentation, although their effect on downstream root trait measurements still needs to be validated.

papers.title: De novo design of mini-proteins as specific binders to PACAP-38, a key mediator of migraine
papers.abstract: Pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating peptide 38 (PACAP-38) is a vasoactive peptide that is attracting attention as a potential target for next-generation migraine treatments. Antibodies against PACAP-38 have recently shown promising results as a ligand trap medicine in clinical trials. In this study, we investigated the de novo design of miniproteins to evaluate the potential for developing a medium-molecular-weight drug that binds to PACAP-38. Using Bindcraft, we designed binders against PACAP-38 and identified ICLIST-2, a 63-residue peptide with affinity for PACAP-38 (KD = 26.5 nM). Furthermore, by alanine scanning and structural analysis of ICLIST-2, we determined residues that were suitable for further optimization using ProteinMPNN. This resulted in the design of ICLIST-11, which incorporates nine amino acid substitutions relative to ICLIST-2, resulting in a KD of 4.51 nM. Interaction analysis based on a structural model suggested that three mutations in ICLIST-11 may be important for enhancing affinity. Moreover, ICLIST-11 exhibits a Tm value that is 14 {degrees}C higher, and MD simulations suggest that the substitution of three residues with hydrophobic residues (E30F, M31L, and R54W) is one reason for this. In cell-based functional assays, ICLIST-11 demonstrated potent, concentration-dependent neutralizing activity against PACAP-38-induced PAC1R activation (IC50 = 10.6 nM), significantly outperforming the parental ICLIST-2. Taken together, these results provide a framework for protein drug discovery targeting PACAP-38.

papers.title: Stimulus Sampling Shapes Estimated Perceptual Geometry in Psychophysical Scaling
papers.abstract: We used simulations and mathematical analysis to investigate how simultaneous estimation of transducer nonlinearity and perceptual geometry affects bias in maximum likelihood difference scaling (MLDS). Uniform sampling in the stimulus domain disproportionately sampled slowly varying regions and inadequately sampled rapidly varying regions of nonlinear transducers, leading to biased estimates of transducer shape. These biases were substantially reduced when stimuli were sampled uniformly in response space, distributing observations more evenly across the transducer. Likelihood-surface analysis revealed substantial confounding between sampling-induced distortions and effects attributable to changes in perceptual geometry. Uniform stimulus-domain sampling produced a pronounced trade-off between the parameters governing transducer nonlinearity and perceptual geometry, which was substantially reduced under uniform response-space sampling. Although response-space sampling generally improved the local conditioning of the likelihood surface, parameter identifiability remained dependent on its intrinsic geometry and thus on the underlying transducer. These results show that stimulus sampling can influence whether departures from a Riemannian perceptual metric are detected, highlighting the importance of sampling designs that adequately represent perceptual space. More generally, they demonstrate how appropriate sampling can help disentangle the effects of nonlinear transduction from those of nonlinear contributions of perceptual differences to judgments.

papers.title: A novel methodology for assessing reinforcement choice in primates under human care
papers.abstract: Positive Reinforcement Training is a technique commonly employed in zoological collections to elicit a desired behaviour from an animal under human care. Typically, a food item is offered as a reward for performing that behaviour. Three non-human primate species (Mandrillus sphinx, Pan troglodytes, and Hylobates lar) were offered four different foods (banana, grape, apple, and sweet potato) in a series of choice experiments. Latent variable models were employed to investigate which foods were the best selection to use as reinforcement items. Results show that food preference varies between the three primate species. Pan troglodytes and H. lar showed strong preferences for grape and banana, whereas M. sphinx showed a very strong preference for sweet potato. This study indicates that foraging ecology might play an important part in fruit selection and preference in primates. The findings highlight that understanding a species' natural behaviour and dietary preferences is key to informing reinforcement and training decisions.

papers.title: APR-246 and DNA polymerase theta inhibitor Novobiocinsynergize to eliminate TP53 mutant AML cells
papers.abstract: Patients with TP53-mutant myelodysplasic syndromes (MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) are usually elderly and frail with highly resistant malignant clones and a median survival of less than one year. The molecule APR-246 targets mutant p53 but also perturbs redox homeostasis. APR-246 showed favorable safety in a phase 3 trial in TP53 mutant MDS/AML but did not meet efficacy endpoints in combination with azacitidine (AZA), highlighting the need for more effective combination strategies. Conversion of APR-246 to the active compound MQ releases formaldehyde which generates DNA-protein crosslinks. AML cells depend on DNA polymerase theta (Pol[O]) to repair such lesions and Pol[O] protects cells from ferroptosis. Using a panel of isogenic MOLM13 AML cell lines each carrying a common TP53 variant, we show that the Pol[O] inhibitor Novobiocin (NVB) synergizes with APR-246 to induce AML cell death. We demonstrate strong synergy with this combination in all TP53 mutant cell lines and to a lesser extent in the TP53 wildtype and null cells, indicating both p53-dependent and p53-independent mechanisms behind the synergy. APR-246 provides selectivity for TP53-mutated cells while NVB enhances p53-independent apoptosis and p53-dependent ferroptosis. Levels of ferroptosis induction correlate with the observed synergy in TP53-mutant and WT cells. Combination of APR-246 and NVB induces potent in vitro growth inhibition of primary TP53-mutated AML/CMML patient samples, with significant activity achieved at low micromolar or nanomolar concentrations of APR-246. Our findings hold promise for combination of APR-246 and NVB as a new therapeutic strategy tailored for TP53-mutated AML patients with high efficacy and low toxicity.

papers.title: Host identity drives distinct prokaryotic and microeukaryotic microbiomes across four cold-water coral species in a near-pristine Mediterranean reef.
papers.abstract: Cabliers is the widest Mediterranean cold-water coral (CWC) mound province exhibiting active growth. This area, a ridge-like CWC mound located in the Alboran Sea (SW Mediterranean) is characterized by thriving CWC reefs and accompanying mega-benthic communities (i.e.: gorgonians, black corals, sponges) found in near-pristine conditions and undergoing an almost null human pressure. We provide in this study the first characterization of the prokaryotic and microeukaryotic microbiomes of four key deep corals structuring the Cabliers province: Madrepora oculata, Desmophyllum pertusum, Leiopathes glaberrima, and Acanthogorgia hirsuta. We used DNA metabarcoding of the 16S and 18S rRNA gene V4 regions via Illumina MiSeq technology to elucidate symbiotic relationships that enable the holobiont to thrive. We found that host identity was the primary driver of microbial community structure, identifying specific signature microbiomes within coral species. The octocoral A. hirsuta showed reliance on microbes for organic matter processing such as the BD1-7 clade, while scleractinians M. oculata and D. pertusum displayed distinct symbionts, including Endozoicomonas (involved in the sulfur cycle) and the SUP05 clade, respectively. We suggest that coral microbiomes are vital for the continuous growth of Cabliers, with physiological needs and host identity shaping unique microbial communities within these deep coral ecosystems.

papers.title: Delta/Notch signaling level is decoded through transcriptional burst duration during muscle progenitor specification
papers.abstract: The ability of progenitor cells to interpret different levels of signaling pathway activity is fundamental to the generation of cellular diversity during development. Muscle progenitors, for example, are exposed to different levels of signals from their microenvironment. However, how they decode these quantitative differences to regulate their cellular behaviors during myogenesis remains poorly understood. Here, we addressed this question during the specification of two populations of Drosophila adult muscle progenitors (AMPs). We found that, despite being spatially adjacent, indirect flight muscle (IFM) and direct flight muscle (DFM) progenitors receive distinct levels of Notch signaling. We further show that the spatial distribution of epithelial Delta contributes to differential Notch activation. Higher Delta levels adjacent to IFM progenitors promote stronger Notch signaling. To investigate how these quantitative differences are translated into transcriptional responses, we developed a Notch-responsive MS2 reporter to monitor transcription in living AMPs. Our measurements reveal that Notch-dependent transcription occurs in stochastic bursts, with IFM progenitors displaying longer but less frequent bursts than DFM progenitors. Strikingly, equalizing epithelial Delta levels abolished differences between the two populations in both Notch-dependent transcriptional activity and the protein levels of Notch target genes. Together, our findings suggest that quantitative differences in signaling may be translated into distinct transcriptional outputs through modulation of transcriptional bursting. This may represent a mechanism by which a single signaling pathway can be deployed to regulate diverse cellular responses during development.

papers.title: Macrophages use sub-micron actin ridges in phagocytosis of encapsulated fungal pathogens
papers.abstract: Ingestion and killing of pathogens by phagocytic cells is a key aspect of animal immunity. Cryptococcus neoformans is a major pathogen of AIDS patients that has a polysaccharide capsule that is critical for virulence. Phagocytic function is necessary for normal immunity to cryptococcal infection, and we sought to determine how Cryptococcus capsule prevents phagocytosis. In doing so, we discovered a new sub-micron actin structure, the ridge, that is present on macrophages, neutrophils and amoebae. Macrophages preferentially bind cryptococci via ridges and suppression of ridges is sufficient to prevent phagocytosis. Ridges are present on macrophages in vivo and are lost in interleukin 10 stimulated macrophages. The discovery and functional description of macrophage surface ridges fills a critical gap in our understanding of how phagocytes ingest encapsulated fungal pathogens, a crucial step in treating infection.

papers.title: Tripartite toxin-antitoxin system regulates the production and release of pneumolysin by Streptococcus pneumoniae.
papers.abstract: The production of toxins is critical to the success of bacteria, with their targets and outcomes varying widely. Pneumolysin (Ply), produced by the major human pathogen Streptococcus pneumoniae, is a cytolytic pore forming toxin that plays many diverse roles including inducing tissue damage and inflammation, evasion of many aspects of the human immune system, invasion of the bacteria into deeper tissue, and transmission to new hosts. Despite its importance, many aspects of the biology of this toxin have to date remained unknown, in particular, what role of the three other genes that form part of the ply operon play in Ply production. Here we demonstrate that these genes encode a complex regulatory system, that includes a putative membrane destabilising protein (PlyA) and a MazEF-like toxin-antitoxin system (PlyB and PlyC), the toxin of which (PlyC) destabilises the Ply transcript. We propose a tripartite model whereby when the operon reaches relatively high levels of expression PlyA destabilises the S. pneumoniae membrane creating a stress that triggers a necessary negative feedback loop which results in the degradation of the PlyB antitoxin, release of the PlyC toxin and degradation of the ply transcript, thereby providing a means by which Ply production can be tightly regulated. Given the importance of Ply to the ability of S. pneumoniae to cause infection, identifying the factors that result in the shutdown of Ply production and release by the bacteria would seem promising target for future therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: JAK1/2 Inhibition Restores Tissue Integrity by Rewiring Type 1/2 Immunity Toward Targetable IL-17 Responses
papers.abstract: Effective immune responses require coordinated communication between immune and epithelial cells to eliminate pathogens while limiting tissue damage. Disruption of this balance drives chronic inflammation and progressive tissue destruction. The Janus kinase (JAK) pathway coordinates cytokine signaling across these compartments and has emerged as a therapeutic target in inflammatory diseases. However, the consequences of JAK inhibition within a complex inflammatory environment remain incompletely understood. Here, we dissect the molecular, cellular, immunological and phenotypical effects of topical JAK1/2 inhibition in a chronic model of tissue-destructive skin inflammation driven by barrier dysfunction and bacterial superinfection. Single-cell transcriptomics and functional profiling revealed that JAK1/2 blockade selectively suppressed pathogenic CD8 T cells and their IFN-{gamma} production while shifting Th2-polarized CD4 T cells toward a Th17 phenotype, preserving type 3 immunity consisting of IL-17A-producing {gamma}{delta}-T cells and neutrophil responses. This immune rebalancing occurs rapidly and concomitantly with the restoration of epithelial barrier integrity through tight junction reinforcement, followed by recovery of antimicrobial defenses and reduced bacterial burden. Combination of JAK1/2 and IL-17A blockade further improved tissue homeostasis by targeting residual type 3-driven pathology. Thus, JAK1/2 inhibition acts as selective immunomodulator rather than a broad immunosuppressant, targeting pathogenic type 1/2 responses while preserving type-3-associated antimicrobial defense programs. These findings reveal how JAK1/2 inhibition coordinates immune rebalancing with epithelial repair and support its therapeutic potential in chronic type 1/2-driven inflammatory disease, while identifying residual IL-17A-mediated pathology as a target for combination therapy.

papers.title: Cross-regulatory sRNA networks shape adaptive stress responses in Staphylococcus aureus: RsaC and RsaOI regulate galactose metabolism and cell wall homeostasis
papers.abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is a major human pathogen whose adaptability relies on network of regulators, including two-component systems, transcription factors and small regulatory RNAs. Yet most of these regulators are dispensable for growth, suggesting cooperation or redundancy between them. To explore this hypothesis, we performed a yeast one-hybrid screen of 43 TFs against the promoters of seven sRNAs, which identified 27 novel TF-sRNA promoter interactions. We then focused on three sRNAs. We showed that srn_9342 is repressed by VraR and MntR, which also control rsaOI and rsaC, respectively. We found that rsaC, like rsaOI, is induced by acidic pH and vancomycin exposure, whereas srn_9342 expression remained unchanged. We also demonstrated in vitro that Srn_9342 interacts with both RsaOI and RsaC. Its role toward these two sRNAs remains unknown, but this interaction raises the possibility that it modulates their availability or activity. RsaOI and RsaC both act on the tagatose pathway for galactose utilization, through different genes: lacD for RsaOI, as previously reported, and lacC for RsaC, newly identified here. We showed that both sRNAs are required for surface charge remodeling and for growth under subinhibitory vancomycin. They also modulate the virulence factors PSM and protein A. Both sRNAs reduce PSM production, whereas protein A is decreased by RsaOI, likely through Rot, and increased by RsaC through an unknown, probably indirect mechanism. Together, our results suggest that a single cell wall stress can engage several regulators that could cooperate on shared targets or pathways, which may explain why individual regulators are dispensable.

papers.title: Leakage-Controlled Benchmarking of Variant Effect Predictors and Development of Gradient-Boosting Consensus Model
papers.abstract: Single amino acid mutations are among the most common forms of genetic variation, with effects ranging from negligible to severe disruption of protein function. Accurate quantitative evaluation of protein variants therefore represents a key challenge in medicine and protein engineering. Computational variant effect predictors (VEPs) are widely used to prioritize missense variants, yet their fair comparison is hindered by data circularity, benchmarks restricted to human clinical annotations, and limited availability of code and training data, all of which can inflate apparent performance. Here, we reviewed 18 recent and 3 older, widely adopted variant effect predictors for reproducible benchmarking and assembled a rigorously curated, leakage-controlled Benchmark dataset by integrating clinically annotated human variants from ClinVar and Humsavar as well as cross-species variants with functional annotations. The evaluation on this dataset revealed a narrow overall performance range for the benchmarked tools (AUC 0.631-0.758) and a consistent drop from clinical to functional data. Surprisingly, several tools published two decades ago demonstrated comparable performance to mid-ranked modern predictors. Building on these results, we developed a gradient-boosting consensus model, PredictSNPprot, which achieved an AUC of 0.82 on a held-out test set, outperforming the original PredictSNP meta-predictor and the best individual state-of-the-art tool by 13.6 and 5.7 percentage points, respectively. The Benchmark dataset, including the predictions from the evaluated tools, is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23597130 and PredictSNPprot consensus predictor is available at https://github.com/loschmidt/PredictSNPprot.

papers.title: The Almond Expression Atlas: A comprehensive multi-tissue transcriptomic resource for almond gene expression
papers.abstract: Background: Improving crop adaptation and enhancing agronomic and quality traits requires a deeper understanding of gene expression regulation, for which expression atlases are valuable tools. Almond (Prunus dulcis (Mill.) D.A. Webb) is one of the most economically important tree nut crops worldwide. However, an integrated transcriptomic resource for this species is still lacking. Available data remain fragmented across independent studies, limiting their comparability and reuse. Results: Here, we present the first almond gene expression atlas: a comprehensive multi-tissue transcriptomic resource integrating publicly available RNA sequencing data. A total of 142 high-quality untreated and control samples from 17 independent projects were curated through a metadata standardization process and analyzed using a unified bioinformatics pipeline. Standardized expression profiles were generated for 25,225 annotated genes in the Prunus dulcis Texas v2.0 reference genome. The atlas integrates two complementary expression approaches: a median TPM approach capturing quantitative expression levels and a rank-based strategy implemented using the Bgee expression calling method, designed to improve comparability across heterogeneous datasets. This design enables the identification of tissue-specific candidate genes and the exploration of expression patterns across tissues and developmental stages. Its applicability is demonstrated through two use cases, highlighting its ability to identify biologically meaningful gene sets associated with bud dormancy transitions and to prioritize candidate reference genes for RT-qPCR normalization in almond. Conclusions: The Almond Expression Atlas v1.0 is publicly available through FruitDBase (fruitdbase.csic.es), providing an interactive platform for gene expression exploration and visualization. This resource supports functional genomics studies and facilitates candidate gene discovery in almond, while ensuring data traceability and promoting data reusability.

papers.title: Resource competition controls the length-dependence of synaptic protein synthesis
papers.abstract: Synaptic plasticity is dependent on the availability of specific proteins at the synapse with distinct requirements for potentiation and depression. Specifically, experimental evidence suggests an upregulation of short proteins and a downregulation for long proteins during long-term depression (LTD). The mechanism of this length-dependent protein synthesis regulation is yet unknown. In this work, we propose an computational model of ribosomal regulation of protein synthesis than can reproduce the length-dependent shift in protein expression seen during ribosomal elevations. By analysing the model dynamics, we discover that this effect is due to a shift from initiation-restricted to elongation-restricted protein synthesis. This works offers a novel explanation for the loss of ribosomal control of protein synthesis due to saturation in pathological ribosome enriched conditions. This new theoretical model of ribosomal regulation of protein synthesis is capable of explaining length-dependent shifts in protein synthesis.

papers.title: An adjuvant for in vivo CAR-T therapy potentiation against solid tumors
papers.abstract: In vivo CAR-T therapy offers rapid and controllable T-cell engineering but has yet to achieve durable efficacy against solid tumors. Rather than focusing solely on CAR-T cells, we harness the intact immune system via an in vivo CAR-T adjuvant (iCTA). Composed of aluminum-manganese hydrogel, iCTA can form a spatially confined antigenic and immunostimulatory niche in-situ. By coupling controlled antigen exposure with STING-type I interferon signaling, iCTA not only recruited and reactivated CAR-T cells, but engage the CAR-negative immunocytes with enhanced dendritic-cell antigen presentation and mobilized endogenous antigen-specific T-cell responses. Combined with mRNA-LNP-mediated in vivo CAR-T generation, a single administration of iCTA increased CAR+ T-cell abundance in draining lymph nodes and blood by 2-fold. It also increased T and NK cell infiltration, established an IFNgamma-enriched tumor microenvironment, and reduced exhaustion-associated T-cell states. iCTA improved tumor regression and survival, establishing an adjuvant strategy to enhance in vivo CAR-T therapy.

papers.title: Recognition of the centromere-binding protein Ndc10 by Scm3HJURP directs Cse4CENP-A deposition at native centromeres
papers.abstract: Kinetochores connect centromeres to spindle microtubules, ensuring accurate chromosome segregation. Kinetochore assembly at centromeres depends on deposition of CENP-A, a histone H3 variant. Despite considerable progress, how CENP-A is specifically assembled on native centromeres remains an open question. Centromere-specific assembly of CENP-A occurs spontaneously in a cell-free extract system from the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, but with low efficiency, suggesting that one or more factors are limiting. Here, we show Scm3HJURP, a specific chaperone for the centromeric histone Cse4CENP-A, is one such limiting component. The addition of a complex of Scm3, Cse4 and histone H4 strongly stimulates Cse4 assembly in a centromeric DNA sequence- and dose-dependent manner; in addition, improvements in both Cse4 and kinetochore assembly were more prominent in mitotic versus interphase (G1) extracts. Using the complemented cell-free reconstitution system, we show that distinct Scm3 interfaces with Cse4 and with the Ndc10 subunit of the yeast centromere DNA sequence-recognizing CBF3 complex are essential for centromere-specific Cse4 assembly and cell viability. Thus, recognition of Ndc10 directs Scm3-dependent and locus-specific centromeric histone deposition.

papers.title: Minimal requirements and evolution of polar membrane targeting in the land plant SOSEKI protein family
papers.abstract: Accurate spatial distribution of polar proteins is essential for cell function, but mechanisms underlying polar protein targeting in plants are poorly understood. Here, we dissect the molecular mechanisms underlying the polar targeting of the SOSEKI1 (SOK1) protein in Arabidopsis thaliana. Using extensive mutagenesis and truncation analyses of the polarity domain, we mapped the minimal polarity fragment necessary and sufficient for stable polar targeting to a 25-amino-acid region. This region likely forms an amphipathic helix, and mutations reveal that both its polar and apolar faces are essential for membrane association and polarity. Using phylogenetic analysis, we reconstruct the evolutionary history of the minimal polar targeting region across land plants. Using cross-species expression and protein localization, we infer the ancestral polar SOK localization pattern and show how it remained remarkably conserved, only to diversify upon gene duplication. This work identifies a polar targeting peptide in plants, reveals a mechanism for polar membrane targeting of a plant protein family, and demonstrates both conservation and diversification within this family.

papers.title: Molecular crowding differentially regulates magnetic field-dependent fluorescence, recovery kinetics, and photostability of the magnetosensitive protein MagLOV2
papers.abstract: Macromolecular crowding and solvent composition can alter protein conformation, diffusion, hydration, and cofactor photophysics, yet their influence on magnetically sensitive flavoproteins is poorly understood. We tested seven molecular environments in MagLOV2-overexpressing Escherichia coli lysate using a custom-built, high-intensity magnetofluorescence platform. Five-point concentration series of Dextran 70, Ficoll PM70, PEG6000, PEG3350, glycerol, ethylene glycol, and bovine serum albumin (BSA) were measured at 22 mT under continuous 6.12 W/cm2 blue-light excitation. Dextran 70, Ficoll PM70, and PEG6000 progressively attenuated the negative magnetic field effect (MFE), whereas PEG3350 shifted toward mild enhancement at higher concentrations. Glycerol and ethylene glycol enhanced the negative MFE despite producing the strongest slowing of recovery upon the field being switched off (OFF-recovery), while BSA modestly enhanced MFE and accelerated OFF-recovery. Across 105 treatment cuvettes, the change in MFE was not globally correlated with changes in the OFF-recovery time constant (r = -0.07, p = 0.449). The initial pre-field illumination period revealed a second phenotype: Dextran and Ficoll increased late fluorescence loss, whereas glycerol and BSA were photoprotective. Pre-field fluorescence loss correlated moderately with MFE change across the full dataset (r = 0.474, p = 3.28 x 10-7) but not consistently within crowder classes. These findings show that MagLOV2 spin-dependent magnetofluorescence is shaped by crowder chemistry, polymer size, solvent environment, recovery kinetics, and photostability rather than by a single generic crowding or viscosity mechanism.

papers.title: Substrate-induced asymmetry coordinates lipoprotein handover and abaucin trapping in Acinetobacter baumannii LolDF
papers.abstract: The homodimeric lipoprotein transporter LolDF supports outer-membrane biogenesis in Acinetobacter baumannii. How homodimeric LolDF generates directional lipoprotein transport, and how the reported two- and four-abaucin states are related, remain unclear. Using defined lipidated AbLolB and AbLolA, we show that substrate binding breaks LolF symmetry: LolFB primarily accommodates the lipid anchor, LolFA positions the adjacent polypeptide, and LolA docks asymmetrically through the LolF hook and an AbLolA-specific loop. C1 reconstruction of the wide abaucin state reveals non-equivalent central ligands, whereas C2 processing of the same particles averages this asymmetry; the two peripheral ligands form a stable inhibitory core, while the central sites are conditionally occupied in the expanded cavity. Abaucin inhibits ATPase activity and LolA-mediated transfer from substrate-associated LolDF, supporting a unified mechanism in which substrate-induced asymmetry organizes productive handover and its conformational plasticity is redirected during inhibition.

papers.title: HNRNPC-mediated RNA processing promotes VHL-associated excessive vasculogenesis in von Hippel-Lindau syndrome revealed from patient-derived blood vessel models
papers.abstract: Von Hippel-Lindau Syndrome (VHLS) is an inherited disorder characterized by excessive vascularization, which contributes to the development of hemangioblastomas and benign or malignant tumors, as well as renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and cysts in multiple organs. VHLS is caused by mutations in VHL tumor suppressor gene, which encodes a component of an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex. Although therapeutic agents targeting hypoxia-inducible factor 2 alpha (HIF2A), which is stabilized by VHL loss and promotes tumor angiogenesis, have been approved for clinical use, their therapeutic response remains limited in RCC patients associated with VHLS. Therefore, there is an unmet need for the development of alternative therapeutic approaches independent of HIF2A. Here, we establish a human iPSCs-based model of VHLS-associated excessive vasculogenesis using induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from VHLS patients and VHL-edited isogenic iPSC lines. Vascular cells (VCs) differentiated from these VHLS-specific iPSCs exhibited excessive blood vessel formation compared to healthy donor-derived VCs, leading to vascular lesion formation characterized by abundant blood vessels and abnormal cellular growth in vivo. Mechanistically, RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) were preferentially stabilized in the patient-VCs. Among these RBPs, the stabilization of heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein C1/C2 (HNRNPC), which is a substrate for pVHL-mediated protein degradation independent of HIF2A expression, was critical for the dysregulated vascularization caused by VHL inactivation in this model. These findings provide an iPSCs-derived vascular platform to elucidate VHLS mechanisms and identify HNRNPC as a potential therapeutic target for VHL-driven vascular lesion formations through an HIF2A-independent mechanism.

papers.title: Cannabidiol Impairs Glucagon Trafficking and Secretion Through the Lysosomal System in Murine αTC1-6 cells
papers.abstract: Glucagon secretion by pancreatic cells is regulated by nutrient, paracrine, and neural inputs, and emerging evidence suggests that the islet endocannabinoid system (ECS) may also regulate -cell function. While phytocannabinoids such as cannabidiol (CBD) have been shown to interact with the ECS, and negatively regulate insulin secretion from pancreatic {beta} cells, whether CBD alters cell function in ways that disrupt glucagon trafficking and secretion remains unclear. This study investigates how acute CBD exposure affects transcriptional and secretory networks governing cell function. Using the TC1-6 glucagon-secreting cell line, we exposed the cells to 0.3 and 3 M CBD for RT-qPCR analysis, 3 M CBD for bulk RNA sequencing, and 3 M CBD or its inactive metabolite 7-COOH-CBD for imaging and secretion experiments. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that treatment with CBD did not alter the expression of ECS receptors and enzymes. However, pathways involved in cellular excitability, peptide hormone trafficking, and secretion were significantly downregulated. Using confocal microscopy, we found that CBD exposure increased the colocalization of glucagon with LAMP1 (a lysosomal marker), and that CBD rerouted peripheral glucagon, and glucagon-containing lysosomes towards the intracellular region of the cell. In conjunction with these findings, we observed reduced glucose-stimulated glucagon secretion under high glucose conditions. Overall, our data supports a model in which acute CBD exposure downregulates processes governing cellular excitability and peptide secretion and negatively regulates glucagon trafficking and secretion by rerouting peripheral glucagon into lysosome-associated intracellular compartments in TC1-6 cells.

papers.title: Species-Dependent Limitations of Murine Myocardium for Investigating the Combined Inotropic Effects of SERCA2a Stimulation and Myofilament Ca2+ Sensitization
papers.abstract: Impaired sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ handling and myofilament function both contribute to contractile dysfunction in heart failure. A previous study in failing human myocardium showed that combining the SERCA2a activator istaroxime (ISTA) with the Ca2+ sensitizer levosimendan (LEVO) produces greater positive inotropy than either drug alone. However, human multicellular preparations did not allow comprehensive investigation of the underlying cellular mechanisms. We therefore assessed contractile performance and Ca2+ dynamics in murine multicellular myocardial preparations and ventricular cardiomyocytes treated with ISTA (20 M), LEVO (0.5 M), or their combination. ISTA improved developed force, contraction-relaxation kinetics, and mechanical restitution. These effects were associated with increased Ca2+ transient amplitude, accelerated Ca2+ rise and decay, and enhanced sarcoplasmic reticulum reloading. Adding LEVO produced no further mechanical benefit and only minor changes in Ca2+ handling. LEVO alone elicited heterogeneous contractile responses and increased myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity in only a minority of cardiomyocytes, while consistently accelerating Ca2+ transient decay. This effect was reproduced by the phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor cilostamide, after which LEVO caused no significant additional change, consistent with a contribution of downstream cAMP-PKA signaling to the acceleration of Ca2+ removal. Thus, limited murine responsiveness to LEVO-mediated myofilament sensitization prevented mechanistic reconstruction of the additive inotropic effect observed in human myocardium, highlighting a species-dependent limitation of the mouse model for studying this combined therapy.

papers.title: Dissection of the contribution of bushy cell delays to sound localization in juvenile and adult Mongolian gerbils
papers.abstract: Sound sources along the azimuth generate interaural time differences in arrival (ITDs) at the ears. According to Jeffress hypothesis, ITDs are detected by coincidence-sensitive neurons of the medial superior olive (MSO) for which a differential axonal delay from each ear to the MSO compensates for the ITDs. The origin and development of these delays remain poorly understood. To this end, we made recordings from bushy cells (BCs), which project to both MSOs, in adult and in 2-4-week-old Mongolian gerbils of either sex. First spike latency revealed a frequency-dependent delay likely originating in the cochlea. Latencies were markedly larger for pure tone stimulation than for complex sounds. Combined with our published recordings from the MSO, we observed a developmental decrease in most delays, including the contralateral BC-to-MSO axonal delay. Unexpectedly, the ipsilateral BC-to-MSO axonal delay did not decrease. Anatomical brainstem reconstructions revealed that the inter-MSO distance was stable whereas the cochlear nucleus-to-MSO distance increased during development. Together, this indicated an increase in axonal propagation velocity, particularly for the contralateral projection. The variability in the averaged firing onset between BCs was found to be as large as the variance in bITDs, suggesting that BCs with matching firing onset are selected to converge onto the same MSO neuron. Together, our results indicate that the developmental speedup of ear-to-MSO delays contributes greatly to bringing the bITDs within their ecological range, but that the difference in path length is not overcome, keeping the ITD tuning biased to contralateral sound sources.

papers.title: Individual-specific recovery of the healthy human gut microbiota after antibiotics
papers.abstract: Following disruption by broad-spectrum antibiotics, the human gut microbiome undergoes a prolonged recovery where coarse ecological features, such as species richness and diversity, are largely restored. However, as these features are shared by most healthy individuals, it remains unclear whether, even after strong perturbation, individuals preferentially return toward their own pre-treatment composition ('individual-specific recovery') or instead switch to alternative equally healthy states. Resolving this question is fundamental for evaluating the long-term impacts of antibiotics, because an individual's health is affected by their unique microbiome composition, affecting immune regulation and metabolic processing, so a state switch, even to a broadly healthy configuration, could carry unintended consequences. Here we compare each subject's post-antibiotic endpoint with their own baseline and with the baselines of every other subject, across four cohorts (n = 121) whose regimens ranged from a five-day fluoroquinolone course to a four-day three-drug combination given to deplete the gut community. The recovered community was significantly closer to the subject's own baseline than to the alternative healthy baselines in more than 90% of individuals under the mildest regimen and in two thirds of those under regimens that broadly target the gut anaerobes, remaining above chance in every cohort and the majority outcome even where most baseline taxa fell below detection during treatment. This specificity is not merely the persistence and fast regrowth of survivors: it persists among baseline taxa that remain undetected for weeks to months, and the same taxon re-establishes more readily in a host where it was previously detected than in one where it was not. Newly established taxa are consistently more functionally similar to the pre-treatment community than transient arrivals, and their identity correlates with the surviving community's composition in a substantial fraction of subjects. State switching, in contrast, was uncommon and occurred almost exclusively among subjects with the largest reduction in detected taxa during the treatment. Together, these observations reveal the individual-specific nature of the microbiome resilience to broad-spectrum antibiotics, whereas the compositional changes are not random but rather functionally and ecologically associated with the subject's baseline.

papers.title: Cell-resolved pharmacodynamic profiling reveals tissue- and cell-population-specific activity of antisense oligonucleotide chemical conjugates in vivo
papers.abstract: Chemical conjugation can modulate antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) pharmacology and improve organ-specific delivery, yet whole-tissue measurements provide limited information on cell-specific activity. Here, we used metastasis-associated lung adenocarcinoma transcript 1 (Malat1) knockdown as a pharmacodynamic readout to compare whole-tissue and cell-resolved activity of chemically conjugated ASOs in platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha-enhanced green fluorescent protein (PDGFR-eGFP) mouse model to assess their in vivo uptake in PDGFR-expressing (GFP+) cells. This reporter mouse model uses PDGFR as an exemplar cellular marker and provides an accessible tool for evaluating ASO conjugate activity within mesenchymal stromal and progenitor populations, mainly tissue fibroblasts. Following subcutaneous administration, Malat1 was quantified in whole tissues and cell-sorted PDGFR+/GFP or PDGFR-/GFP- populations. ASO-mediated Malat1 reduction varied by tissue and conjugate chemistry, with palmitate conjugation producing the broadest extrahepatic activity and pronounced whole-tissue activity in heart and skeletal muscle. Cell-resolved analysis further revealed preferential palmitate-ASO activity within PDGFR skeletal-muscle populations. Preliminary safety assessment also showed conjugate-dependent differences, with body-weight loss and ALT elevation in tocopherol-ASO-treated male mice and spleen enlargement in both sexes. These findings present an in vivo modelling system for evaluating cell-specific ASO activity and demonstrate the advantages of cell-resolved assessment over whole-tissue measurements.

papers.title: MillionTrees: A global benchmark for tree detection across geography, sensor, and annotation geometry
papers.abstract: Airborne tree monitoring using remotely sensed data, combined with the growth of computer vision models for object detection and segmentation, can facilitate broad scale assessment of tree health, ecology and ecosystem function. However, datasets for airborne tree detection have been largely limited to a single geography, resolution, or annotation approach, making it difficult to develop general models and benchmark their utility for broad applications. We compile existing and newly published annotation datasets to create a comprehensive dataset for training and evaluating airborne tree detection in RGB imagery. The MillionTrees dataset has over a million individual trees from a broad range of forest types, tree species, and geographic locations. In addition, it has six million weakly supervised annotations from a range of sources including airborne LiDAR and photogrammetry, arborist surveys, and simulated landscapes. An evaluation standard is provided to facilitate rapid model development. We benchmark several existing tree detection algorithms and demonstrate that while current open-source models do not generalize across the diverse datasets in the benchmark, training on MillionTrees improves both within-domain and out-of-domain performance. Held-out validation datasets using ground truth derived from terrestrial LiDAR paired with overhead RGB show that overfitting to test data is common and hyperparameter tuning is an underappreciated challenge towards a global zero shot tree detection method. We discuss the limitations of the currently available data for airborne RGB tree detection, how to create more robust evaluation data and the need for better understanding of the uncertainty and utility of tree detection from airborne remote sensing.

papers.title: Feedback reliability modulates learning-related dynamics of midfrontal error monitoring
papers.abstract: Learning from feedback requires the brain to evaluate both performance outcomes and the reliability of the information used for learning. This study examined the dynamics of neural performance monitoring during deterministic (100% reliable) and probabilistic (75% reliable) associative learning using two within-subject tasks with different stimulus materials. Behavioral performance improved under both feedback regimes, but learning was consistently more successful under deterministic feedback. Error-related negativity, feedback-related negativity, and phase-locked midfrontal theta became progressively more pronounced across deterministic learning, particularly in the image-image task, whereas corresponding changes were attenuated under probabilistic feedback. Induced theta showed the opposite pattern, decreasing across deterministic learning while remaining comparatively stable under probabilistic learning. These opposing theta trajectories suggest that phase-locked and induced activity reflect distinct components of learning-related neural adaptation that may be obscured when total theta power is considered alone. Overall, the findings indicate that feedback reliability shapes the progressive tuning of midfrontal performance-monitoring responses during learning.

papers.title: Age-based shifts in multicellular community organization and abundance in HPV-Negative Head and Neck Cancer
papers.abstract: Aging represents a fundamental driver of cancer risk and progression, yet the mechanisms by which aging reshapes the tumor microenvironment remain incompletely understood. To interrogate how aging alters cellular and microenvironmental organization in cancer, we developed an integrated single-cell atlas of HPV-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) encompassing 73 patients aged 18-91 years. Using a multi-layered computational framework combining NMF-based module discovery and partial correlation network analysis, we reveal that age-associated differences in tumor composition are driven primarily by selective shifts in cell type abundance and organization rather than widespread age-dependent transcriptional rewiring. We identify an age-enriched cellular community centered on basal-like squamous epithelial states linked to epithelial-mesenchymal transition, matrix-associated myofibroblast-like CAFs, and FOLR2+ macrophages, which secrete immunosuppressive and ECM-remodeling factors. Cross-dataset in-silico validation via TCGA transcriptomes, spatial transcriptomics, and mouse tumor models confirms the correlation of these cell types across patients, specific ligand-receptor usage, and increased proportions of epithelial and stromal cells in aged mouse models. Among epithelial cell-intrinsic age-associated transcriptional changes, midkine (MDK) emerges as a rare but robust tumor-derived signal linked to stromal remodeling, immunosuppression, and invasive epithelial programs. These findings reveal conserved mechanisms of age-dependent cellular reorganization in the tumor microenvironment and identify MDK and associated stromal-remodeling pathways as potential intervention points for age-stratified cancer therapy.

papers.title: Long-PDE4D degradation attenuates left ventricular cardiomyocyte hypertrophic remodelling
papers.abstract: Spatial compartmentalisation enables cyclic AMP (cAMP) to regulate distinct cellular functions, yet selectively targeting disease-associated signalling remains challenging. Phosphodiesterases constrain local cAMP responses, but conventional inhibitors offer limited isoform selectivity. Here we investigate whether targeted degradation of long phosphodiesterase-4D (PDE4D) isoforms can suppress pathological growth while preserving contractile function.
